bivy.name: The US 2 pullout by the maintenance yard
bivy.notes: This is the roadhead and, realistically, the accommodation. The pullout sits roughly seven miles east of Stevens Pass at the east tunnel end. The route walks west along the highway shoulder for a few hundred yards, crosses the Nason Creek bridge and drops onto an old logging spur that parallels the creek to the railway grade; parties then follow the tracks a short way before scrambling up the bank at about 2,700 ft and climbing steep timber to snowline around 3,700 ft. A variation stays on the spur, crosses Henry Creek, takes the right fork and then the left to the bottom of a clearcut at about 4,200 ft, climbs the clearcut directly south and traverses east into the trees to gain the north ridge. TWO CAUTIONS THAT ARE NOT ABOUT CLIMBING. The highway shoulder walk is on a fast, busy road with poor sightlines and is more dangerous than anything above it, and the railway line is active — treat both as hazards to be got off quickly rather than as part of the walk. Winter parking here is genuinely tight and the shoulder is where the ploughs put the snow, so an early arrival is worth more than an early start.
bivy.water: Nason Creek runs alongside and under the highway bridge the route crosses, and it needs treating. There is no potable supply. THERE IS NO WATER ON THE MOUNTAIN ITSELF once you leave the creek and the lower spur — the north ridge and the clearcut above carry nothing, so in summer everything is carried from here, and in winter the answer is melting snow.
bivy.permit: None. This is not designated wilderness, there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no lottery anywhere on this peak. Highway shoulder parking needs no forest pass, which is worth knowing because the trailheads a few miles either side of it do. There is no fee and no registration. Note that the WSDOT rest area further along the highway is a rest area and not a campground, and overnight camping there is not what it is for.
bivy.capacity: Shoulder parking and a pullout by the road turnoff for the maintenance station, with room for about three vehicles and space to sleep in one. There is no campground, no fee site, no table and no toilet. In winter the plough berm decides how much of it exists on any given morning.

bivy.name: The clearcut benches on the north ridge, around 4,200 feet
bivy.notes: Included as a contingency and as an honest negative. There is no reason to sleep on Arrowhead: the whole outing is six miles and three thousand feet and a fit party is up and down in seven or eight hours, so the only situation where this ground matters is a winter party that has broken trail through deep new snow, run out of daylight low down, and would rather bivouac than descend a steep wooded slope in the dark. Under those conditions the flat around the top of the clearcut at roughly 4,200 ft is the obvious place, being out of the timber and out of the terrain trap of the creek drainages. What you get is a snow camp with no shelter and no water; what you avoid is a night descent. In summer this same ground is slash and regrowth and there is nothing to recommend it. THE ROUTE IS CHOSEN FOR ITS AVALANCHE CHARACTER and is described as steep but safe by that measure, which is exactly the sort of judgement that changes with the year's snowpack — assess it rather than inheriting it.
bivy.water: None whatsoever. Henry Creek on the lower spur is the last water on the way up and it is a long way below. In winter this is a snow camp and you melt; in summer you carry, and the amount you would have to carry is the argument against being here at all.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness national forest and old logging ground, no permit, no quota, no fee. Fires are a poor idea in a clearcut full of dry slash and are prohibited under the summer restrictions that run most years on this side of the pass. Some of the lower spur network crosses a mix of ownership, so read the signs at the junctions rather than assuming everything is public.
bivy.capacity: No established site of any kind. Under deep snow the clearcut and the flat bench above it give as much room as a party wants; in bare conditions there is very little usable flat ground and it is all slash, stumps and brush. Recorded to say plainly that nobody camps on this mountain, rather than to invent a site for it.

bivy.name: Tumwater Canyon campgrounds on US 2
bivy.notes: The nearest developed drive-in camping to Arrowhead that is not already recorded in a neighbouring zone file, deliberately chosen over the Lake Wenatchee corridor camps for that reason. It is a drive of half an hour or so west along the highway to the pullout, which suits a party that wants a proper night with water and a table before a dawn start. The catch is the season: these canyon campgrounds run roughly late spring to early autumn, which is precisely the half of the year when Arrowhead is at its worst. FOR THE WINTER ASCENT, WHICH IS THE ONE MOST PARTIES WANT, THESE ARE CLOSED and the answer is a night in the vehicle at the pullout or a very early drive from town. Note also that the December 2025 storms damaged forest roads across this district and a closure order covering them runs into 2027, and that a large fire closure sat over the Lake Wenatchee and Leavenworth country through the autumn of 2026; neither touches the highway itself, but both change what is open either side of it, so check before relying on a specific campground.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed sites during the operating season, plus the river alongside. This is the one place where water is not a problem, and it is the sensible place to fill everything before driving up to the pullout.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee at the developed campgrounds, with some sites reservable in advance and the rest first come, first served. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply through the summer in the canyon and are commonly total bans by late season — this is one of the driest and most fire-prone stretches of highway in the state.
bivy.capacity: Small developed forest campgrounds strung along the highway in the canyon between Leavenworth and the Chiwaukum front, taking modest vehicles and a moderate number of parties. Sites are a mix of first come and reservable, and they fill on summer weekends with Leavenworth traffic that has nothing to do with the mountains.

bivy.name: The lower spur and Henry Creek flat
bivy.notes: Recorded chiefly as the water point rather than as a camp, because knowing where Henry Creek is matters more on this mountain than knowing where you could pitch. The spur climbs east-southeast off the highway after the Nason Creek bridge, crosses the creek, and then forks twice — right at the first junction by an unnamed creek, left at the second — before reaching the bottom of the clearcut at about 4,200 ft. In winter the fork-finding is the navigational crux of the day and it is done under snow with the road cuts filled in, which is why parties who have been up before make much better time than parties who have not. As sleeping ground it is a poor substitute for the pullout, being no warmer, no flatter and a mile further from the car, and its one genuine use is for a party arriving in the small hours who would rather walk a mile and sleep than sit on the highway shoulder. Bring an axe for the steep timber above regardless of season; the slope from the railway grade to snowline is unrelenting.
bivy.water: Henry Creek at the crossing, and Nason Creek below — both need treating and both run all year. This is the last water on the route and the only water on it, and its position at the very bottom of the climb is the whole water story of this peak: everything above is dry, so this is where you fill.
bivy.permit: None. No wilderness, no permit, no quota. The spur network crosses mixed ownership in places, including railway and utility corridors, so read the signage at junctions and do not assume a road is open ground just because it is drivable-looking. No fee, no registration.
bivy.capacity: Rough ground on the old logging road network in the first mile, where the spur crosses Henry Creek. Room for a tent or two on the road grade itself. Nothing established, nothing signed, and no reason to be here except timing.

access.rules: Leave No Trace
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest
access.passRequired: None required — unofficial roadside scramble with no maintained trailhead

bivy.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the western door to Azurite and Ballard, and the drive alone puts it a long way from anywhere — roughly thirty-three miles east of Marblemount and sixteen west of Rainy Pass, with no services in either direction. Parties commonly sleep in the lot before starting, and the low elevation means it is warm and buggy in early summer when the peaks above are still white. The trail from here runs about six miles up Canyon Creek before the Mill Creek trail branches right at around two thousand eight hundred feet, a third of a mile past the trail's own crossing of Mill Creek. The whole point of understanding this trailhead is the arithmetic that follows: the pass is around six thousand seven hundred feet and the car is at nineteen hundred, so this is a genuine multi-day trip with more than four thousand seven hundred feet of gain before any climbing starts. Access depends entirely on the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts this stretch of highway from late November or early December until somewhere between mid April and early May, occasionally much later after a damaging winter.
bivy.water: No potable water at the trailhead. Canyon Creek is close by and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. This is national forest and there is no quota or reservation of any kind. A separate trail from this same lot runs north into the Pasayten Wilderness, which does carry a free self-issue permit from the kiosk, so read the board and take one only if your route actually crosses that boundary.
bivy.capacity: A large parking area just east of milepost 141, roughly a third of the way between Newhalem and Rainy Pass. Rarely busy, because almost nobody uses the trail these peaks need.

bivy.name: Mill Creek valley and the old Azurite Mine
bivy.notes: This is the honest middle of the western approach and the reason parties allow three days rather than two. The Mill Creek trail has had almost no use since the mine closed and it shows — long sections are faint, missing outright, or buried in slide alder, and the walking is slow, wet and scratchy in a way the mileage does not convey. The mine site itself is the natural first camp, open enough to dry gear and the last obvious flat ground before the climb. Beyond it the trail continues about three miles, and a party can either leave it near five thousand six hundred feet and climb the west slopes of Azurite directly, or carry on another mile and a half to Azurite Pass. Which of those you pick decides where the second night goes. Nobody should treat this valley as a trail walk; treat it as a bushwhack that occasionally has tread.
bivy.water: Mill Creek runs alongside for most of the way and is the reliable supply on this side. Fill before leaving it for the climb toward the pass.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land — no permit, no quota, no reservation. Fires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in force, but forest-wide bans are routine from mid summer and the valley is dry, so plan on a stove. The mine workings are old industrial ground: leave the structures, timbers and hardware alone and do not go into any opening.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved. There is flat ground in the timber along the creek and open ground at the abandoned mine workings about five miles up from the trail junction, roughly eleven miles from the car. Room for a party or two in several places; nothing is built and nothing is maintained.

bivy.name: Azurite Pass
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole zone and the only camp that serves both summits well. Azurite Peak rises directly north of the pass and Mount Ballard stands about two miles further north again along the same ridge, so a party camped here can take Azurite by its south ridge and south-west gully and then continue to Ballard, or split the two across a pair of days. Both approaches converge on this spot, which is why it is worth carrying water and a tent this high rather than trying either peak from the valley. Reckon on the pass being under snow into July in a normal year and later after a heavy winter; the north-facing ground above it holds much longer. Weather comes across from the west with no warning here and there is no shelter for hours in any direction, so this is a camp to be conservative about.
bivy.water: Seasonal snowmelt only, and not to be relied on late in the summer. The dependable sources are down in Mill Creek on the west side and in the Brush Creek drainage on the east. Fill low and carry it up; a party that arrives here dry in September has a problem.
bivy.permit: None. National forest, dispersed camping, no permit and no quota. Camp on gravel or scree rather than the meadow. No fires — there is nothing to burn and a ban is likely in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at and just below the pass, at around six thousand seven hundred feet — mapping and reports put it anywhere between about 6,680 and 6,750, so take the figure loosely. Room for a couple of small tents. Exposed, with no shelter and no windbreak worth the name.

bivy.name: River Bend and Ballard campgrounds, Lost River Road
bivy.notes: These are the staging camps for the eastern approach and the comfortable answer to the night before. From Winthrop the drive runs west on SR 20 and then up the Lost River Road through Mazama to the end of the pavement, continuing a mile and a half or so on the gravel of the Harts Pass road. The West Fork Methow trailhead sits close by at around two thousand seven hundred feet, at a wooden fence just off a short spur. Being low and in timber, they are usable well before and after the high country is in condition, and they are far enough down the road that none of the Harts Pass driving difficulties apply. They also make a sensible base for a party that wants a look at the trail before committing to it, which on this side is worth doing — the West Fork Methow tread is badly overgrown and in poor repair, and the brush on the banks of the upper creeks is dense enough that the trail effectively disappears.
bivy.water: The river is right there. Treat these as basic sites and assume you will filter rather than find a working spigot.
bivy.permit: No permit and no reservation, just a nightly fee paid on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a campsite, only to park at a trailhead. These are outside any wilderness, so none of the Pasayten self-issue paperwork applies.
bivy.capacity: Two small forested Forest Service campgrounds a short distance apart along the West Fork Methow, roughly eight to nine miles up the road from Mazama. Both are first come, first served only — there is no way to reserve and you must arrive in person to claim and pay for a site. Each is modest, so a summer weekend is a gamble.

bivy.name: Horse Heaven Camp, West Fork Methow
bivy.notes: This is the natural first night on the eastern approach to Azurite Pass and it breaks a walk that is otherwise too long to enjoy. From the trailhead near two thousand seven hundred feet the trail follows the West Fork Methow past Trout Creek and Brush Creek toward Jet Creek, and the camp sits partway along at about four thousand three hundred and fifty feet. Two warnings are worth taking seriously. The lower trail is overgrown and faint in places, though the tread improves as it climbs. And the brush on the banks of Jet Creek becomes extremely dense with no clear path through it at all, which is the section that costs parties hours and tempers. From here it is a sustained climb of well over two thousand feet to Azurite Pass and the peaks beyond, so leave early. Anyone weighing the two approaches should know they are about the same length and about equally neglected — pick by which side of the mountains you are driving from, not by hoping one has a better trail.
bivy.water: Creek water close at hand, reliable through the season. This is the last comfortable water before the long climb to the pass, so fill completely here.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed national forest camping — no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the West Fork Methow trailhead. Fires only in an existing ring and only outside a burn ban, which by August usually means not at all.
bivy.capacity: An unimproved valley camp partway up the eastern approach, past the Trout Creek and Brush Creek junctions. Space for a party or two on flat ground in the timber. Nothing is maintained.

access.fees: None — no climbing permit fee (this is National Forest, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: Pasayten Wilderness regulations apply: group size limits, no bikes or mechanized travel past the wilderness boundary, Leave No Trace camping.
access.permit: Self-issued wilderness permit required at the trailhead (route lies within the Pasayten Wilderness).
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required at the West Fork Methow/Rattlesnake Trailhead.

bivy.capacity: An unimproved valley camp partway up the eastern approach, past the Trout Creek and Brush Creek junctions. Space for a party or two on flat ground in the timber. Nothing is maintained.

access.fees: None — no climbing permit fee (this is National Forest, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no camping within ¼ mile of Cutthroat Lake; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: No wilderness permit currently required (route lies just outside the Pasayten Wilderness boundary).
access.closures: Harts Pass Road (FR-5400) closed to wheeled vehicles Dec 1 through spring snowmelt; check current Forest Service alerts, as storm damage (e.g. rockfall, washouts) has caused additional out-of-season closures in some years
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District. The peak sits just outside the formal Pasayten Wilderness boundary (like neighboring Azurite Peak), so wilderness-specific rules do not apply here.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass required for trailhead parking (Canyon Creek and West Fork Methow River/River Bend trailheads).

bivy.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
bivy.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Deer Lake
bivy.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
bivy.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

bivy.name: Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Cat Basin
bivy.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
bivy.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
bivy.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

bivy.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
bivy.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
bivy.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
bivy.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.

access.rules: Standard Leave No Trace / NPS wilderness rules apply beyond the trailhead: no dogs or bikes on trail, stay on the established boot path on the summit block to limit erosion, pack out all trash.

bivy.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground

bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Deer Lake
bivy.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. bivy.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

bivy.name: Heart Lake

Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.

bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Cat Basin

This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Deer Lake
bivy.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
bivy.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

bivy.name: Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Cat Basin
bivy.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
bivy.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
bivy.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

bivy.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
bivy.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
bivy.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

bivy.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
bivy.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
bivy.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

bivy.name: Appleton Pass
bivy.notes: The direct base for Mount Appleton, a class 3 scramble of just over 6,000 ft sitting northwest of the pass on a ridge with a couple of genuinely exposed moves. From the Sol Duc trailhead it is about seven and a bit miles: roughly five easy miles up the river before the trail breaks north and climbs hard, gaining around 2,000 ft in the last two and a bit. This used to be a short outing from the Elwha side, but that road is washed out and closed to cars at the park boundary, so unless you are willing to ride a bike in and add many miles, Sol Duc is the approach. The meadows above the pass are open and windy, so the sheltered sites go first. Snow lingers on the final climb to the pass well into early summer.
bivy.water: Oyster Lake just above the pass, and closer snowmelt earlier in the summer; late in a dry season the snowfields go and the lake is the only option
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and the high camps in this area are quota-controlled, reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Bear canisters mandatory. No campfires — the pass is well above the 3,500 ft line and the meadow vegetation here is exactly what that rule protects.
bivy.capacity: Several tent sites spread between the pass and Oyster Lake, some fully exposed on the crest and some tucked into trees; a small nightly cap

bivy.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
bivy.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains close to 1,000 ft in under a mile to Klahhane Ridge, then a short westward stretch and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
bivy.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

access.fees: $8 per adult (16+) per night wilderness camping fee plus a non-refundable $6 reservation fee per permit (youth 15 and under free); standard Olympic NP entrance fee of $30/vehicle (7-day) or an America the Beautiful pass.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Bear canisters are required for the Seven Lakes Basin/Bailey Range cross-country zone (free loan available at the WIC); groups of 7+ in the Sol Duc/Seven Lakes area must use designated group campsites; practice Leave No Trace off-trail travel and camp at established sites such as Eleven Bull Basin.
access.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for all overnight stays, reserved via Recreation.gov; summer-season (May 15-Oct 15) reservations open April 15. Because the Bailey Range/Ruth Peak approach is a cross-country zone, it can't be booked through the standard online system — call the Wilderness Information Center at (360) 565-3100 to arrange it.
access.closures: Sol Duc Road closes seasonally for winter, typically November-May depending on snowpack; check the NPS current road-conditions page before driving in.

bivy.name: Hogsback Camp
bivy.notes: The standard planned high camp, two to three hours up from the trailhead on the moraine beside the Coleman Glacier. It is above the trees, so there is nothing to hang food from and nothing to break the wind coming off the glacier; the rock-walled spots are there for a reason. Reach it early in the day if you can — the three creeks on the approach are fed by glacial melt and run noticeably higher and pushier through the afternoon.
bivy.water: Running meltwater at camp, but nothing above it — carry everything you need for the summit day from here, and treat it
bivy.capacity: Unimproved sites scattered along the moraine crest roughly between 5,800 and 6,200 ft; exactly where parties end up depends on where the water is running and who arrived first

bivy.name: Kulshan Cabin site
bivy.notes: A lower fallback just below treeline where the cabin used to stand. Nothing remains of the structure, but there are trees for shelter and for hanging food, which Hogsback does not have. Worth knowing about as a foul-weather retreat rather than as a first choice, since it leaves another thousand feet of climbing before the glacier.
bivy.water: Creeks along the trail nearby; treat all of it
bivy.capacity: A few sites at the old cabin clearing

bivy.name: Hogsback Camp, Heliotrope Ridge
bivy.notes: The default first night for parties on the Coleman-Deming and the usual staging point for the North Ridge, on the moraine bench above the trail's stream crossings about 2.5 to 3 miles in. Access is the current problem rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road, the only driving approach, was damaged in the December 2025 floods and has been under a repair closure short of the trailhead, which turns the approach into a long road walk or bike ride — confirm the road status with the ranger district before committing to a weight-carrying plan. Waste handling has varied year to year, with toilets present some seasons and pack-it-out blue bags the rule in others, so carry bags regardless. Snow usually covers the camp until well into June, which makes a flat platform easier to find and liquid water harder.
bivy.water: Melt streams run below the moraine and near the trail crossings through most of the climbing season, but they retreat with the snowpack and can be gone or badly silted by late August — carry a stove capable of melting snow late in the year
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit; camping is dispersed and unregulated apart from wilderness rules (12-person party limit, no campfires at this elevation). A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat gravel and snow platforms along the moraine crest; the busiest camp on the north side and it fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: Kulshan Cabin site and Harrison Camp
bivy.notes: The cabin itself is long gone, and the name now marks a cluster of sites around 4,800 to 5,000 ft with Harrison Camp on the moraine above the lower Coleman. These suit a party arriving late, anyone who wants trees around them in bad weather, or a group that would rather climb from lower down than share the Hogsback. The trade-off is an extra thousand feet on summit day. Backcountry toilets have been maintained here in some seasons but not others, so plan to pack waste out.
bivy.water: Reliable — the approach streams below the moraine still carry water here later in the season than they do higher up, though the crossings themselves can run high and pushy on warm afternoons
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge.
bivy.capacity: Several small forested and moraine-edge sites; more sheltered and lower-capacity than the Hogsback

bivy.name: Upper Coleman Glacier snow camps, below the Black Buttes
bivy.notes: Pushing camp onto the glacier below the Black Buttes cuts a real chunk out of summit day and puts you above most of the weather that sits on the moraine. It costs you a fully exposed camp on snow, so platforms need walls, and everything about the site depends on that year's crevasse pattern — what was a flat bench one August can be broken up the next. Parties are already roped and on glacier travel terrain to reach it, which rules it out for anyone wanting a simple carry. Wind is the usual reason people retreat from here to the Hogsback.
bivy.water: None you can rely on — this is a melt-snow camp, so budget fuel accordingly. Occasional surface runoff appears on the rock of the Black Buttes in hot spells but should not be planned around.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit for camping. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Whatever platforms your party digs; commonly used between roughly 7,000 and 7,200 ft, with room for a handful of tents but no established sites

bivy.name: Colfax-Grant saddle bivy
bivy.notes: The saddle between Colfax Peak and the main summit is occasionally used as a very high bivy by strong parties shortening summit day, and more often as an emergency stop by parties caught out by weather or a slow descent. It is fully exposed to wind and to whatever the mountain is doing, with no shelter of any kind, and the Roman Wall above it is not somewhere to be improvising in a storm. Treat it as a contingency rather than a plan unless the forecast is settled and your party is fast. It is also the last place on the route with any option other than continuing up or going down.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, or carry everything from lower on the route.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties at most; an exposed high point rather than a campsite

bivy.name: North Ridge glacier bivy, upper Coleman
bivy.notes: North Ridge parties generally carry from the Hogsback out onto the Coleman and bivy somewhere around 6,800 to 7,000 ft to shorten the approach to the base of the ridge, which itself rises around 4,000 ft to the summit. Where exactly that camp sits is decided by crevasse conditions on the day rather than by any fixed location, so it is worth arriving with daylight left to scout. The camp is on glacier, exposed, and above the point where you can retreat without roping up. The same Glacier Creek Road closure that affects the Coleman-Deming applies to this whole approach, so confirm road access first.
bivy.water: None reliable. Melt snow, and carry enough fuel for a party that will also be melting for the climb.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required to camp. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Dug snow platforms for one or two parties; no established site, and the usable spot moves year to year

bivy.name: Sandy Camp, top of the Railroad Grade
bivy.notes: The standard Easton Glacier high camp, reached by following the Railroad Grade moraine up from Schriebers Meadow and Morovitz Meadow. The basin gives real wind protection, which is why it is preferred over the more scenic but more exposed ground on the moraine crest itself. The gravel road in is snowbound into June in most years and is rough enough to be worth checking before a long drive. There have been seasons with no toilet facilities anywhere on the mountain, with blue bags issued free at the Sedro-Woolley ranger office, so carry a pack-out system.
bivy.water: Contested and season-dependent. Some parties find runoff at the north end of the camp and on the rocky ground above it; others arrive to find nothing exposed at all and must melt snow. Plan for melting and treat running water as a bonus.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — the approach runs through the Mt. Baker National Recreation Area and the upper moraine into Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit. A recreation pass is required to park at the Schriebers Meadow / Park Butte trailhead. Registering your climb at a ranger station is voluntary but sensible.
bivy.capacity: The main climbers' camp on the south side, in a sheltered sandy basin at the crest of the moraine; multiple tent sites, busy in July and August

bivy.name: Railroad Grade and Morovitz Meadow camps
bivy.notes: These lower sites suit parties arriving in the evening, anyone wanting shelter from wind, and low-snow years when the higher ground has no water at all. They are meadow and subalpine terrain, so camp on durable surfaces and off the vegetation, which is slow to recover here. Summit day from this elevation is long, and most parties treat these as a first night before moving camp up rather than as a base for the climb. In heavy snow years the alternative runs the other way and people camp as high as 6,800 ft because that is where flat snow is.
bivy.water: Generally reliable — meadow streams and melt channels run here later into the season than they do at the top of the moraine, which is much of the reason to camp low
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker National Recreation Area and Mount Baker Wilderness). No overnight permit; recreation pass required to park at Schriebers Meadow.
bivy.capacity: Scattered sites in the trees behind the eastern moraine and on the ridge east of the Railroad Grade, roughly 5,500 to 5,800 ft; smaller and quieter than Sandy Camp

bivy.name: Hogsback
bivy.notes: Shared with the Coleman-Deming route and reached by branching off Trail 677 at the old Kulshan Cabin site and climbing the moraine crest. There are no trees at this elevation, so food has to go in a bear canister or Ursack — the nearest suitable trees for hanging are lower, at Harrison Camp. Human waste goes out in blue bags; burial is not permitted on snow, rock or alpine ground. From here the North Ridge parts company with Coleman-Deming: rope up, cross the Coleman climbers' right below the Colfax icefall, and gain the ridge on the glacier's true right.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams run at camp — this is the last running water, and there is none once you are on the Coleman. Treat it; nothing here is potable as found. Flow swings hard with the sun, so a channel that is a step across at dawn can be a torrent by mid-afternoon.
bivy.permit: No quota or overnight permit; a valid Recreation Pass must be displayed at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead (a Washington Sno-Park permit for winter parking on Glacier Creek Road). Mount Baker Wilderness rules apply: parties of 12 or fewer, no campfires of any kind, self-contained stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Sites are scattered along roughly 200 ft of moraine crest between 6,000 and 6,200 ft, so exactly where you end up depends on water and on who got there first. It is a busy camp — several parties most summer weekends.

bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker National Recreation Area and Mount Baker Wilderness). No overnight permit; recreation pass required to park at Schriebers Meadow.
bivy.capacity: Scattered sites in the trees behind the eastern moraine and on the ridge east of the Railroad Grade, roughly 5,500 to 5,800 ft; smaller and quieter than Sandy Camp

bivy.name: Bearpaw Lake
bivy.notes: The base for Bearpaw Mountain and the only camping anywhere near its own line. Canyon Creek Road leaves the Mount Baker Highway about two miles east of Glacier and runs north for a long, slow fourteen miles or so of alternating tarmac and serious potholes before a signed spur climbs right to the lake trailhead; the last couple of miles are single lane with brush closing in that will mark a car. From the trailhead it is roughly a mile to the lake, short but steep. The peak's easiest line is a class three scramble from the southwest, following the timbered ridge east of the lake, with a direct variation onto the steeper part of the ridge that gives a narrow and locally exposed scramble. ROAD ACCESS IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK AND NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: Canyon Creek Road has been closed at around mile four by a landslide carrying large timber and debris, with more downed trees below the block, which cuts off the lake spur and the road end entirely. When that closure is in force there is no alternative approach to this peak, only a very long road walk. Snow lies on this ground into July in most years.
bivy.water: The lake, at camp. Treat it. This is the only water on the peak's own approach and there is nothing on the ridge above.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, OUTSIDE any designated wilderness — this ground sits west of the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary, so there is no self-issue permit and no wilderness party limit here, and the twelve-person rule and blanket fire ban that govern the Heather Meadows half of this zone do not automatically apply. What does apply is a recreation pass at the trailhead, and whatever county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry summer is usually a total one. Pack out everything including human waste; there is no toilet.
bivy.capacity: A few rough informal sites at a small lake in the trees; low use, no facilities, no toilet and nothing built

bivy.name: Excelsior ridge camps and the high spring, Canyon Creek Road end
bivy.notes: This is the established high camping on the Canyon Creek road system, at the far end of the same road that serves Bearpaw, and it is listed with the caveat that IT IS NOT ON BEARPAW'S OWN ROUTE. Bearpaw is the prominent summit standing to the west, seen across the drainage from the pass and the ridge, and reaching it from here means dropping and re-climbing rather than walking a connecting line. Its value is as the answer to what a party does when the day goes wrong or when they want two objectives out of one long, slow drive: legal, watered, established camping at the road end of a road most people will only want to drive once. The trail leaves the road end, meets a junction in less than a mile with the Canyon Ridge trail going left, reaches the small lakes just beyond and then climbs through forest and into open meadow towards the pass. The same landslide closure that gates the Bearpaw spur gates this trailhead as well; the alternative is to walk up from the highway instead, which is a far bigger day. Meadows here are at their best in July and August and again for autumn colour in September and October.
bivy.water: A spring about half a mile short of Excelsior Pass is the best and most dependable water in this high country and is the reason the camps are where they are. The lakes lower down at the trailhead end are shallow and warm late in the season. Treat everything, and fill at the spring rather than counting on anything on the crest.
bivy.permit: The ridge camps sit inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, which the High Divide trail enters at the pass — so from there on it is party size twelve, no campfires of any kind, carry-in stoves only, camp on durable ground and pack out all waste including human waste. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead and there is a self-issue register. The ground below the pass around the lakes is outside the wilderness and less strictly governed, but the burn bans still apply.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites on the ridge running south from Excelsior Peak and along the High Divide, plus a cluster near the spring; a handful of small parties, spread out, with no built sites and no toilet

access.fees: None — no climbing fee (National Forest, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.rules: Standard Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF regulations apply. The Church Lake/Bearpaw Mountain route follows an unmaintained boot path (not an official FS trail); it's a short (~3.7 mi RT) outing from the FS 3160 road end, not a remote multi-day approach.
access.permit: None required — a self-issue climbing register may exist at some trailheads but is optional and free.
access.closures: Recent Forest Service road-status reports note FS 31 (Canyon Creek Road) closed at mile 4 by landslide debris, which also blocks the FS 3160 spur used for this route. Verify current status with the Glacier Public Service Center or MBS road-conditions page before the trip.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Ranger District

access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at most trailheads — $30/year or $5/day.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful Interagency Pass

bivy.name: Artist Point and the Heather Meadows road end
bivy.notes: The obvious place to sleep is, plainly, the one place you cannot. Table Mountain is a short, steep switchbacked climb from the Artist Point lot and is usually done in an hour or two; Mount Herman goes from the Bagley Lakes trailhead across from the ski area, past the lakes and up towards Herman Saddle, leaving the trail at the last switchback for the ridge between Mazama Dome and the summit; Mount Ann leaves the Lake Ann trail at the Austin Pass trailhead a little below Artist Point and is a much bigger day, around ten and a half miles with four thousand feet of gain, ending in a genuine scramble. All three are car-to-car objectives for a fit party. THE SEASONAL GATE IS THE PLANNING CONSTRAINT: the last stretch of highway above Heather Meadows to Artist Point is narrow, steeply banked and closed to vehicles every winter, typically shutting somewhere between mid-October and the start of November with the first real snow and not reopening until the plows get through, which in a heavy year is well into July. The highway is kept open to Heather Meadows through the winter for the ski area, so a closed gate costs you the top two and a half miles rather than the whole road. Parties arriving before the gate opens are walking or skinning that section with the peaks still under snow, which changes all three from scrambles into snow climbs.
bivy.water: None. There is no potable water anywhere along this stretch of road or on the trails above it, and every lake and stream on the Chain Lakes circuit has to be treated.
bivy.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at Artist Point and at the Bagley Lakes trailhead; the state parks pass is not valid at these Forest Service sites. There is a self-issue wilderness register near the trailhead. The camping rules here are the strict part and they are easy to fall foul of: camping is prohibited on Table Mountain from mid-May to mid-November, prohibited at the Bagley Lakes trailhead over the same window, and prohibited within a mile of the Chain Lakes trail junction on the Ptarmigan Ridge side. Camping outside that window, in deep winter, is legal on Table Mountain. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve, campfires are prohibited outright and only carry-in stoves are allowed, and dogs must be leashed through the developed area.
bivy.capacity: A large paved turnaround at Artist Point and a second big lot at Heather Meadows below it; parking for many vehicles, and NO legal camping at either. Treat this as a start line rather than a site.

access.rules: No camping within 2 miles of the Lake Ann trailhead between May 15 and November 14; standard Mount Baker Wilderness group-size and Leave No Trace rules apply.

access.closures: SR 542 (Mount Baker Highway) beyond the ski area is gated for winter and typically reopens mid-to-late June (WSDOT reopened it June 10 in 2026) and closes again with the first significant snowfall, usually mid-October — check the WSDOT mountain pass report before driving up.

bivy.name: Mazama Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
bivy.notes: The nearest legal backcountry camping to the Heather Meadows peaks and the only overnight option in the immediate basin, in the string of subalpine lakes that the Chain Lakes trail drops into on the far side of Herman Saddle. From Artist Point the circuit is around six miles with roughly seventeen hundred feet of gain and loss, and the lakes sit a bit under halfway round. For Mount Herman this is genuinely useful: the saddle is on the route, so a party that camps here is above the trailhead with a very short morning to the south ridge. For Table Mountain it is a detour rather than an approach, and the reason to know about it is the ban on camping on Table Mountain itself through the summer. Snow lingers in the basin into mid-August in a heavy year, which is worth knowing before committing to a site that may be under a drift. Trekking poles earn their weight on the snow traverses. This is a busy, family-friendly circuit and the sites go early on a summer weekend, so arrive with a plan for finding all four taken.
bivy.water: The lakes, and they are reliable all season. There is no potable water anywhere on the circuit, so treat everything.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit is required or issued. Recreation pass on the vehicle at whichever of the four trailheads you start from. CAMPING IS RESTRICTED TO THE MARKED SITES — the meadows here are heather over thin soil and the designation exists because they were being destroyed. No campfires at all, carry-in stoves only. Party size twelve. Food must go in a bear-resistant canister or be hung at least ten feet up and four feet out from the trunk and branches; there is no hardware provided.
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites marked by posts with a tent symbol, and a backcountry toilet. First come, first served, with no reservations and no permit to obtain — which means four parties get in and the fifth has nowhere legal to go.

bivy.name: Hayes Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
bivy.notes: The upper pair of the Chain Lakes camps, a short distance on from the lower lake and a little higher, closer to the climb back up to Herman Saddle. For a party that has come over from the Artist Point side and intends to finish the circuit in the morning this is the better position, and it catches the evening light on Baker; for a party using the basin as a base for Mount Herman it is marginally further from the saddle than the lower lake and marginally more exposed to weather coming across the ridge. Elevation is not stated because the usable ground spreads across the shore rather than sitting at one identifiable point. Everything the basin holds is heavily used — camp on the marked pads, keep well back from the shoreline, and do not add a ninth site because the eight are taken. The right answer when they are full is to walk out; the trailhead is not far and the road is paved.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Iceberg Lake nearby holds floating ice well into summer and is the colder and less pleasant draw of the two.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, same rules as the sister camp: no overnight permit, recreation pass at the trailhead, camping only at the marked sites, no fires of any kind, party limit twelve, food canistered or hung with no provided hardware. Nothing here is reservable, so the eight sites across both lakes are the entire legal capacity of the basin on any given night.
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites marked with posts, slightly more open and more exposed than the lower lake, with a pit toilet on the stretch between Iceberg Lake and here

access.fees: $5 per vehicle/day or $30/year for a Northwest Forest Pass; self-pay iron ranger at the trailhead, or buy in advance at the Glacier Public Service Center, 10091 Mt. Baker Hwy, Glacier, WA (open daily 8am-4:30pm, 360-599-2714).
access.rules: Pack out human waste (blue bags) — no burial or glacier deposition.
access.permit: Northwest Forest Pass (or America the Beautiful interagency pass) required to park at the Heather Meadows/Bagley Lakes day-use lot.
access.closures: SR 542 gates for winter each year at Heather Meadows (~milepost 54), closing the final 2.7 miles to Artist Point; reopening date depends on snowpack and has slipped into July in heavy years — check WSDOT's SR 542 page before driving up.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Ranger District; the route lies within the Mount Baker Wilderness above Heather Meadows.

bivy.capacity: Four designated sites marked by posts with a tent symbol, and a backcountry toilet. First come, first served, with no reservations and no permit to obtain — which means four parties get in and the fifth has nowhere legal to go.

bivy.name: Hayes Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
bivy.notes: The upper pair of the Chain Lakes camps, a short distance on from the lower lake and a little higher, closer to the climb back up to Herman Saddle. For a party that has come over from the Artist Point side and intends to finish the circuit in the morning this is the better position, and it catches the evening light on Baker; for a party using the basin as a base for Mount Herman it is marginally further from the saddle than the lower lake and marginally more exposed to weather coming across the ridge. Elevation is not stated because the usable ground spreads across the shore rather than sitting at one identifiable point. Everything the basin holds is heavily used — camp on the marked pads, keep well back from the shoreline, and do not add a ninth site because the eight are taken. The right answer when they are full is to walk out; the trailhead is not far and the road is paved.
bivy.water: The lake, treated. Iceberg Lake nearby holds floating ice well into summer and is the colder and less pleasant draw of the two.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, same rules as the sister camp: no overnight permit, recreation pass at the trailhead, camping only at the marked sites, no fires of any kind, party limit twelve, food canistered or hung with no provided hardware. Nothing here is reservable, so the eight sites across both lakes are the entire legal capacity of the basin on any given night.
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites marked with posts, slightly more open and more exposed than the lower lake, with a pit toilet on the stretch between Iceberg Lake and here

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/interagency pass required, displayed in the vehicle at the Artist Point Trailhead
access.rules: No pets permitted on the trail; not recommended for small children; avoid kicking or throwing rocks off the switchbacks since other hikers are frequently below on the trail
access.permit: No permit required for day hiking
access.closures: No camping on the trail May 15-Nov 14; SR 542 to Artist Point is gated and unplowed in winter, typically closed by the first significant snowfall (late Sept-early Nov) and reopening once cleared, typically in mid-to-late June (WSDOT reopened the road June 10, 2026; June 27, 2025; and June 21, 2024)
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mt. Baker Ranger District (Glacier Public Service Center, 10091 Mt. Baker Hwy, Glacier, WA 98244)
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker Ranger District) — Mount Baker Wilderness, with some upper routes crossing into North Cascades National Park
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at most trailheads — $30/year or $5/day.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / interagency pass

bivy.name: Lower Blum Lake
bivy.notes: This is the base camp for both peaks and effectively the only one. Getting here is the whole difficulty of the trip: leave trail 606 a short distance past the Baker River suspension bridge, before Blum Creek, and find the faint path that works away from the creek through old timber. The first section is genuine devil's club, fern and deadfall bushwhacking, and the path comes and goes; above that it settles into a steep, tiring forest ridge, then an ascending traverse along the south side of that ridge into the lake basin. Five hours from the car is a good day, and parties routinely take longer. For Mount Blum, the south ridge and southeast slopes go from here up through gullies and snow to the east ridge. For Hagan, climb southeast from the lower lake to about 5,600 ft on the east-west ridge, then traverse south toward the pass below the Hagan peaks. Best from mid-July into September; earlier and the traverse to the lakes is a snow slope with a long runout, later and the water thins. There is no shelter of any kind and no cell coverage.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small outlet stream. Treat everything. This is the first reliable water since the river, four thousand feet below
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, required year-round for any overnight stay. The Blum cross-country zone is not one of the reservable zones, so it is walk-up only through the wilderness information center near Marblemount. No campfires anywhere in the zone. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadow, and keep a hundred feet back from the water. Human waste goes in a cathole or, on snow and glacier, in a blue bag carried out. Bear canisters are the sensible answer where the heather gives you nothing to hang from, and can be borrowed in person at the permit office
bivy.capacity: Two or three small tents on heather shelves and gravel near the outlet; the basin is tight and the park caps this cross-country zone at six people and two parties at a time

bivy.name: Middle Blum Lake
bivy.notes: A few hundred yards and a hundred feet of gain above the lower lake, and the more common choice for parties who want to shorten summit day on Blum. The ground is heather and slab, so tent sites are where the rock is, not where the flat grass is. It holds snow later than the lower lake and it catches more wind, which is a fair trade for mosquitoes in July. From here the line to Blum's summit continues past the upper tarn and into the gullies below the east ridge, and the Hagan traverse also starts from this shelf. Nothing about the position changes the approach problem — you still spend a full day getting up from the river.
bivy.water: Lake water. Treat it
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades National Park backcountry permit and the same Blum zone rules as the lower lake — walk-up only, six people, no fires, durable surfaces, hundred-foot setback from water
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on the benches above the shore; smaller and more exposed than the lower lake

bivy.name: Upper Blum tarn, southeast of the main lakes
bivy.notes: The highest practical ground on the Blum side, on the way from the main lakes toward the gullies and snow slopes leading to Blum's east ridge. It buys perhaps an hour on summit day and costs an extra 700 ft of carrying at the end of an already brutal approach day, so most parties leave it to those going on to Hagan or continuing the traverse east. Exposed to weather from every direction. In a low-snow year the tarn is dry and this stops being an option at all.
bivy.water: The tarn, when it is out; it is snow-covered well into summer and may be a snowpatch rather than water in early season. Carry from the lakes below if in doubt
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, Blum cross-country zone, walk-up only. No fires. Because this sits above the meadow line, expect to be camping on snow or bare rock, which is what the zone rules ask for anyway
bivy.capacity: One or two tents at most, on rock and gravel; there is no established site here, only ground that happens to work

bivy.name: South Hagan bench
bivy.notes: Open benches on the south side of Hagan Mountain, reached from the Blum Lakes by climbing to the ridge crest near 5,600 ft and traversing south. This is where parties stage for Hagan's south slopes: from the bench, talus and a scree couloir lead to the southwest end of the Hagan crags, and slabs on the south side give the final scramble to the summit. It is also the natural stop for anyone continuing east toward Hidden Lake and Bacon. The bench is comfortable and the position is superb, but it is fully exposed and the water is seasonal, which is the reason most parties still base at the lakes and do Hagan in a long day.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small pools that shrink through the season; late summer parties should plan to carry water up from the Blum Lakes or from Hidden Lake below
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This ground sits on the boundary between the Blum and Bacon Peak cross-country zones, so confirm which zone your permit is written for when you pick it up. Six-person party limit either way, no fires, no camping in meadow
bivy.capacity: Two tents on heather and gravel benches; informal, with no fixed site

bivy.name: Hidden Lake, below the Blum-Hagan divide
bivy.notes: A small lake in the saddle country between Hagan and Bacon, reached from the Blum Lakes by crossing the ridge southeast of them and dropping to it. It matters here as the reliable water on Hagan's far side and as the standard second night for parties traversing east. It is a considerable drop below the Hagan bench, so it is a poor choice if Hagan is your only objective — you give back four hundred feet you will re-climb in the morning. Reaching it involves snow into midsummer and steep heather afterwards. Do not treat this as an approach camp for Bacon Peak from the Baker River side; the practical way to Bacon is from a different road entirely.
bivy.water: The lake. Treat it. Reliable all season, which is not true of the benches above
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. This lake sits toward the Bacon Peak side of the divide, so check which cross-country zone the ranger writes your permit for. No fires, six-person limit, camp a hundred feet back from the water
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents on the flats near the shore

bivy.name: Sulphide Camp, end of the Baker River trail
bivy.notes: This is the only designated, built camp anywhere near this trailhead: flat sites and a toilet at the end of trail 606, a couple of easy valley miles past the suspension bridge. IT IS NOT ON THE WAY TO BLUM OR HAGAN. The climbers' path for both peaks leaves the trail near Blum Creek, well before this, and heading up-valley to Sulphide takes you in the wrong direction. It is listed because it is the legal, comfortable option for a party that arrives late, wants a short first evening, or is waiting out weather at the bottom, and because low-elevation valley ground here is otherwise wet, brushy and off-limits. Elevation is valley-bottom, only a little above the trailhead.
bivy.water: Sulphide Creek and the Baker River, both close by. Treat the water; the river runs silty in high melt
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for a designated camp, which is a different reservation than a cross-country zone — book it or ask for it at the permit office rather than assuming a zone permit covers it. No fires
bivy.capacity: Two established sites and a backcountry toilet; a small party each

bivy.name: Blum Creek spur ridge, forest bivy
bivy.notes: THERE IS NO ESTABLISHED CAMP ON THIS APPROACH, said plainly rather than recommending a place that does not exist. The 4,000 ft of steep forest between the Baker River and the Blum Lakes has no benches worth the name, no water on the crest and no clearings; parties who run out of daylight here flatten a spot among the trees and move on at first light. The right plan is to start early and reach the lakes in one push. Keep it in mind only as what you will actually do if the bushwhacking at the bottom eats more of the day than you expected, which it often does in wet conditions, or if somebody in the party is struggling with the load.
bivy.water: None dependable. Blum Creek is below the path and hard to reach from the ridge; carry what you need from the river or push on to the lakes
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit if you sleep here — the park boundary sits close to the river crossing, so assume the whole climb is inside the park and ask at the permit office where the line actually falls before you plan on it. No fires
bivy.capacity: One tent, found rather than chosen; the ridge is steep, timbered and littered with deadfall, and genuinely flat ground is rare

access.fees: A Northwest Forest Pass or other interagency pass is required to park at Watson Lakes Trailhead. NPS backcountry permits (if camping in the park) carry a $6 non-refundable reservation fee plus a $10 per-person, per-night recreation fee.
access.rules: Pack out human waste (blue bags) — no burial or glacier deposition. Some approaches cross into North Cascades National Park land on the upper mountain, where a NPS backcountry permit is required only if camping overnight past the boundary.

Only high-use cross-country zones can be reserved in advance and the Blum zone is not one of them, so the permit is obtained as a walk-up in person at the North Cascades NP Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. No permit is needed for a single-push day climb.

bivy.name: Coleman Glacier bivy under the Black Buttes north faces
bivy.notes: Colfax's three north-side ice lines — the Cosley-Houston, the Polish Route and Kimchi Suicide Volcano — all start off the Coleman somewhere near 8,000 ft, and this is the staging ground for a party that does not want to cover the whole approach from the Hogsback on climb morning. The important thing about it is where you do not put the tent: ice and rock come off the Colfax seracs onto this part of the glacier with some regularity, so the usable camping is out on the flats well clear of the fall line, never tucked in against the toe of the face because it looks sheltered. Many parties skip this camp entirely and climb these routes in a long day from the trailhead or from the Hogsback, which is a reasonable answer to the same hazard. These are cold-season routes, roughly late October into May, and the ice changes character completely across that window.
