bivy.name: Cougar Divide meadow camps
bivy.notes: This is the north-side approach to Hadley Peak and it has nothing to do with the Black Buttes or the Coleman — a party here is on the far side of the mountain from the Heliotrope Ridge climbers. Cougar Divide is an unofficial, unmaintained path along the ridge crest, reached from Wells Creek Road, whose first several miles are badly potholed to the Nooksack bridge and then improve. From the meadows at the head of the divide the ground opens onto Chowder Ridge, and the connection east along the ridge leads to Hadley. The gate opening in July combined with mosquitoes that are genuinely bad here until midsummer pushes the sensible window to mid-August through early October, which is also when the talus is clear and the route is straightforward walking with the odd second-class step.
bivy.water: Better than anywhere else on this side. A creek fed by a lingering snowfield runs at the upper camp through most of the season, and there are ponds along the divide that are worth treating and not drinking untreated. Water gets scarce once the snowfield goes.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit and no climbing permit. The access road is gated seasonally, closed from the start of November until the second week of July for wildlife, which is the single biggest planning constraint on this side of the mountain. Party size 12, no campfires, pack out all waste.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites in the meadows near the head of the divide; pick rocky ground rather than heather, which recovers slowly here

bivy.name: Skyline Divide crest camps
bivy.notes: The other approach to Hadley Peak, from the west along the divide and over Chowder Ridge. The road in has been the problem for years rather than the trail: flood damage at around mile three has left the trailhead inaccessible to vehicles for extended periods with no firm repair date, and the trail has been listed as closed on that account, so this is the first thing to confirm and not an afterthought. When it goes, the crest is easy walking with big views and the last three quarters of a mile up to Chowder Ridge is talus with one steeper step before you top out west of the Hadley Glacier. Camping on the open crest means taking whatever weather arrives off the mountain, and the exposure is the reason parties often drop into the basin instead.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead and none along the trail after early summer, when the snow patches below the crest are gone. Carry everything or plan the trip around a lingering snowfield you have confirmed is still there.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead. No campfires anywhere, party size capped at 12, all waste packed out. There is no permit or quota for camping, but the meadows are heavily used and heavily damaged, so camp on bare ground.
bivy.capacity: Several exposed sites along the open crest of the divide once the trail tops out; popular and visible, with no screening from wind or weather

bivy.name: Deadhorse Creek basin, below Chowder Ridge
bivy.notes: The basin sits between Skyline Divide and Cougar Divide, just short of the climb onto Chowder Ridge, and it solves the problem both crest camps have: it has water and it has shelter. A party approaching Hadley from either road can drop into it, sleep out of the wind, and take the ridge in the morning with full bottles. Summit day from here is short by any standard on this mountain. It is subalpine meadow and creek terrain, so camp on durable ground well back from the water. Season is the same as everything else on the north side, mid-August into early October, held back at the front end by mosquitoes and by the road gate on the Cougar Divide side and at the back end by the first real snow.
bivy.water: The most reliable water on the Hadley approach — the creek runs from snowmelt above the basin and holds up later than anything on the ridge crests. Treat it. This is the reason to camp here rather than higher.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, no overnight permit required. Recreation pass at whichever trailhead you start from. Party size 12, campfires prohibited, human waste and everything else packed out — there are no toilets on either divide.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the basin between the two divides; sheltered, low use, no facilities of any kind

access.rules: Pack out human waste (blue bags) — no burial or glacier deposition. Some approaches cross into North Cascades National Park land on the upper mountain, where a free NPS backcountry permit is required only if camping overnight past the boundary.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit available at the trailhead
access.closures: Forest Service Road 33 (the sole vehicle access) is gated and closed November 1 - July 7 each year for wildlife protection.

bivy.name: Crag View, Squak Glacier
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Sherman Peak's Squak Glacier route and it is the site the Mount Baker file does not cover, since everything written there is on the Easton or the Coleman. It sits about 3.5 miles and 3,300 ft above Schriebers Meadow: the Park Butte trail past Sulphur Creek and the meadows, then a climbers' path leaving the trail around 4,600 ft and running up onto the moraine. From here the route makes a rising traverse of the Squak toward Sherman's south ridge, roughly 3,600 ft to the summit. The Squak is an early-season objective and the reason is specific — a bergschrund opens across the line as the season goes on and can shut the route down entirely by late summer, so a July plan is a different proposition from a May one. The lower part of the approach is outside the wilderness and carries snowmobile traffic into early July. Forest Road 13 off Road 12 is gravel and holds snow late; check it before a long drive.
bivy.water: No potable water at the trailhead or anywhere on the route. Melt channels run near the moraine edge in early summer and are gone or unreliable by August, so plan on melting snow and carry the fuel for it.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit, but camping below 6,000 ft on this route is prohibited, which is the practical reason Crag View exists where it does. A recreation pass is required to park at the Park Butte trailhead. Party size is capped at 12 once you enter the wilderness, campfires are prohibited, and there is no toilet anywhere on the route — carry blue bags, which are handed out free at the ranger offices in Sedro-Woolley and at Glacier. Nothing may be buried in snow or dropped into a crevasse or moat.
bivy.capacity: The established climbers' camp on the Squak, with room for several parties on gravel benches and snow platforms at the toe of the glacier; quieter than the Easton side even on a summer weekend

bivy.name: Upper Squak benches, Sulphur moraine and the rock prow
bivy.notes: Parties who want Sherman's summit day short move above Crag View and camp on the Sulphur moraine at the glacier's edge around 7,000 ft, or push on to the flatter ground below the rock prow closer to 7,600 ft. The gain is real, since it takes a good chunk out of the traverse to the south ridge and puts you at the base of the steep snow with the night's freeze still holding. The cost is a fully exposed camp on a volcano's south flank, where wind is the usual reason parties come back down to Crag View, and you are already on glacier and roped to get here. Camping this high also means committing to melt water, which drives fuel weight up. Where exactly the platforms are usable moves year to year with the crevasse pattern, so arrive with daylight to scout rather than in the dark.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow. Anything running here in early summer is a bonus and will not be there later in the year.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness rules as at Crag View — no permit to camp, recreation pass at the Park Butte trailhead, 12-person party limit, no campfires, all waste packed out in blue bags.
bivy.capacity: Dug snow platforms and moraine gravel for one or two parties along the right-hand edge of the glacier, with a second bench under a rock prow several hundred feet higher; no established sites and no shelter

access.fees: No climbing fee. A Recreation Pass (Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass, ~$5/day or annual) is required to park at the Park Butte Trailhead.
access.rules: Campfires prohibited; group size capped at 12 in designated wilderness; camp only at established sites (Railroad Grade camps ~2.25-2.75 mi in, high camps at 5,600 ft, or Sandy Camp at 5,900 ft); no backcountry toilets — pack out human waste with blue/WAG bags; remove any route wands you place; pets discouraged due to steep drop-offs and crevasses.
access.permit: No climbing permit or summit registration is required for Mt. Baker/Sherman Peak; a free self-issue wilderness register may be present at the trailhead.
access.closures: The lower Railroad Grade sees snowmobile traffic into late spring/early summer. FS Roads 12/13 can be gated or storm-damaged over winter and early spring — confirm current road status with the Mt. Baker Ranger District before driving.

bivy.name: North Fork Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT junction
bivy.notes: This sits right at the junction where the PCT leaves Bridge Creek for the North Fork, roughly ten miles in from the SR 20 trailhead, so it is the natural first-night stop for a party that started late. It is a long way below the climb, which means a very big second day to reach the glacier bivies. Its value is logistical rather than tactical — it shortens the drive-day push without needing a cross-country zone permit. Being a valley-bottom camp in forest, expect bugs through midsummer.
bivy.water: Reliable year round — Bridge Creek and the North Fork run beside the camp
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round; reserve the specific camp on Recreation.gov or take a walk-up from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee applies.
bivy.capacity: Small designated hiker camp with a handful of numbered sites; the site is reserved by name on the permit

bivy.name: Walker Park Camp
bivy.notes: Roughly two miles up the North Fork trail from the junction, this is the first camp that meaningfully shortens the walk to the Goode Glacier drainage. The tread to here is still ordinary maintained trail, so it is an easy target even arriving in the dark. Parties usually treat it as a place to shed weight rather than a base, since the climb is still hours of rough ground above. No elevation is recorded — the valley section stays well under 4,000 ft, but no confident figure was sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — sits on the North Fork of Bridge Creek
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit, booked by camp name; same NPS fee structure as any Bridge Creek camp, and it must be carried for the night you actually sleep there.
bivy.capacity: Small designated camp, a couple of parties at most

bivy.name: Grizzly Creek Camp
bivy.notes: About four miles up the North Fork trail, this is the last designated camp before the country turns unpleasant, and the practical decision point for the whole approach. Beyond it the tread gets brushy and faint — stinging nettles are a recurring complaint and long trousers are worth carrying regardless of the heat — and the North Fork has to be forded or crossed on a log, with difficulty that swings hard with snowmelt. A party arriving late, or facing high water, is usually better off sleeping here than committing to the bushwhack and the crossing in poor light.
bivy.water: Reliable — Grizzly Creek and the North Fork are both at hand
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit reserved by name through Recreation.gov or issued walk-up at Marblemount; per-person and reservation fees apply.
bivy.capacity: Larger than the other North Fork camps and open to stock parties, so you may be sharing it

bivy.name: Fireweed Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT
bivy.notes: A Bridge Creek corridor camp on the PCT well short of the North Fork junction, near the Twisp Pass trail area. It is only useful to a Goode party as an overflow choice when the North Fork camps are booked out, which happens in peak season because so few sites serve this valley. Camping here adds miles to an already long approach day. Treat it as a fallback rather than a plan.
bivy.water: Reliable — Bridge Creek
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit, same Recreation.gov / Marblemount walk-up system and the same per-person and reservation fees.
bivy.capacity: Designated camp with hiker and stock use

bivy.name: Goode Glacier approach bivy, timbered knoll
bivy.notes: Reached by leaving the North Fork trail after Grizzly Creek, fording the creek and grinding up timber and scree beside the drainage off the Goode Glacier, this is the classic first bivy under the buttress. Reports differ on whether it is the better choice: it sits noticeably west of the line of travel, so some parties consider the extra push to higher ground worth doing. Sparse timber gives a little shelter, which matters more here than the small elevation saving. Human waste goes in a cathole or is packed out above treeline, and there is no toilet.
bivy.water: Meltwater from the Goode Glacier drainage nearby, but flow is seasonal and can be a walk away or thin late in the year
bivy.permit: Inside the Goode CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE, not a designated camp — the permit is issued for the zone, party size is capped at six, no campfires, and camping is only allowed on durable ground such as snow, rock or bare earth.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground for one or two small tents on a timbered knoll

bivy.name: Upper bivy in the rock bands east of the buttress toe
bivy.notes: Sitting in the rock bands just east of where the Northeast Buttress meets the ground, this puts you at the base with a few hundred feet already banked for summit day, which is the argument for grinding past the lower knoll. The exact elevation is reported inconsistently — figures in the 5,400 to 5,600 ft range all refer to broadly the same shelf system, so navigate to the terrain rather than to a number. It is exposed and rocky, so a poor choice in unsettled weather compared with the timbered ground lower down. Confirm you have water before committing to it late in the summer.
bivy.water: Running meltwater has been found at or near these sites, but it is snow-fed and not dependable once the drainage dries out later in the season

bivy.name: North Fork Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT junction
bivy.notes: This sits right at the junction where the PCT leaves Bridge Creek for the North Fork, roughly ten miles in from the SR 20 trailhead, so it is the natural first-night stop for a party that started late. It is a long way below the climb, which means a very big second day to reach the glacier bivies. Its value is logistical rather than tactical — it shortens the drive-day push without needing a cross-country zone permit. Being a valley-bottom camp in forest, expect bugs through midsummer.
bivy.water: Reliable year round — Bridge Creek and the North Fork run beside the camp
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round; reserve the specific camp on Recreation.gov or take a walk-up from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee applies.
bivy.capacity: Small designated hiker camp with a handful of numbered sites; the site is reserved by name on the permit

bivy.name: Walker Park Camp
bivy.notes: Roughly two miles up the North Fork trail from the junction, this is the first camp that meaningfully shortens the walk to the Goode Glacier drainage. The tread to here is still ordinary maintained trail, so it is an easy target even arriving in the dark. Parties usually treat it as a place to shed weight rather than a base, since the climb is still hours of rough ground above. No elevation is recorded — the valley section stays well under 4,000 ft, but no confident figure was sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — sits on the North Fork of Bridge Creek
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit, booked by camp name; same NPS fee structure as any Bridge Creek camp, and it must be carried for the night you actually sleep there.
bivy.capacity: Small designated camp, a couple of parties at most

bivy.name: Grizzly Creek Camp
bivy.notes: About four miles up the North Fork trail, this is the last designated camp before the country turns unpleasant, and the practical decision point for the whole approach. Beyond it the tread gets brushy and faint — stinging nettles are a recurring complaint and long trousers are worth carrying regardless of the heat — and the North Fork has to be forded or crossed on a log, with difficulty that swings hard with snowmelt. A party arriving late, or facing high water, is usually better off sleeping here than committing to the bushwhack and the crossing in poor light.
bivy.water: Reliable — Grizzly Creek and the North Fork are both at hand
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit reserved by name through Recreation.gov or issued walk-up at Marblemount; per-person and reservation fees apply.
bivy.capacity: Larger than the other North Fork camps and open to stock parties, so you may be sharing it

bivy.name: Fireweed Camp, Bridge Creek / PCT
bivy.notes: A Bridge Creek corridor camp on the PCT well short of the North Fork junction, near the Twisp Pass trail area. It is only useful to a Goode party as an overflow choice when the North Fork camps are booked out, which happens in peak season because so few sites serve this valley. Camping here adds miles to an already long approach day. Treat it as a fallback rather than a plan.
bivy.water: Reliable — Bridge Creek
bivy.permit: Designated-camp permit, same Recreation.gov / Marblemount walk-up system and the same per-person and reservation fees.
bivy.capacity: Designated camp with hiker and stock use

bivy.name: Goode Glacier approach bivy, timbered knoll
bivy.notes: Reached by leaving the North Fork trail after Grizzly Creek, fording the creek and grinding up timber and scree beside the drainage off the Goode Glacier, this is the classic first bivy under the buttress. Reports differ on whether it is the better choice: it sits noticeably west of the line of travel, so some parties consider the extra push to higher ground worth doing. Sparse timber gives a little shelter, which matters more here than the small elevation saving. Human waste goes in a cathole or is packed out above treeline, and there is no toilet.
bivy.water: Meltwater from the Goode Glacier drainage nearby, but flow is seasonal and can be a walk away or thin late in the year
bivy.permit: Inside the Goode CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE, not a designated camp — the permit is issued for the zone, party size is capped at six, no campfires, and camping is only allowed on durable ground such as snow, rock or bare earth.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground for one or two small tents on a timbered knoll

bivy.notes: Sitting in the rock bands just east of where the Northeast Buttress meets the ground, this puts you at the base with a few hundred feet already banked for summit day, which is the argument for grinding past the lower knoll. bivy.name: 5,500 ft bivy below the slabs
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the most commonly used one on this side of the peak. Reached after the slide-alder section and a crossing of the creek, tucked just below the low-angle slabs with rock walls around it and running water on hand. Nothing above it is comfortable, and the slabs above lead straight onto the glacier in the morning.
bivy.water: the creek right at camp
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: about four people

bivy.name: 5,200 ft camp to the west
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the fallback if you run out of daylight in the brush below. Perfectly serviceable, but reports consistently say the extra three hundred feet up to the higher bivy is worth carrying, because summit day from here is long enough already.
bivy.water: creek nearby
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips

bivy.name: Goode Glacier toe
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp on the moraine and rubble between roughly 6,400 and 6,800 ft. Flat ground is genuinely limited and the good spots are specific rather than general — expect to hunt for them, and expect glacier noise all night. It is the highest planned camp and the one that makes the couloir a reasonable day, but the water problem is real by late summer.
bivy.water: scarce near camp late season; fill at the last reliable stream below
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: limited — a small number of usable flat spots, not a big-party site

bivy.name: West Tower ledge, upper mountain
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY ledge, not a camp. A narrow shelf on the north side of the crest between the West Tower and the main summit, where a solo climber spent a night wedged between rocks and still lost sleep to constant south wind. No water, no flat ground worth the name, and a serious place to be caught. It exists, and that is the only reason to know about it.
bivy.water: none
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips

bivy.name: Valley bivy below the buttress
bivy.notes: The classic first night, and it is earned: parties commonly take about eight hours from the trailhead, down the PCT to the North Fork Bridge Creek trail, then up past Grizzly Creek into slabs, brush and talus. The usual log over Grizzly Creek has broken and a replacement has been found roughly 200 ft south of the trail; the trail beyond that crossing is badly overgrown. Reports place sites in sparse timber around 5,200 ft and on rock benches east of the buttress toe nearer 5,600 ft.
bivy.water: Running water in the drainage below the buttress; the approach itself crosses Grizzly Creek, which is the last easy fill before the brush.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit. A cross-country zone permit covers one party for one night in that zone; most zones cap a party at six people, camping is restricted to snow, rock or bare ground, fires are prohibited, and waste is buried or carried out in blue bags above treeline.
bivy.capacity: A small site — a party or two on sparse timber and rock benches near the toe of the buttress.

bivy.name: Goode Glacier moraine
bivy.notes: The higher option, on the lateral moraine looking across at the seracs of the Goode Glacier, variously reported between about 6,400 and 7,000 ft. It shortens the climbing day considerably over the valley bivy and puts you in wildflower meadow with a view, at the cost of carrying the load higher on approach day.
bivy.water: Meltwater — parties describe waterfalls running beside the moraine camp.
bivy.capacity: A couple of tents on the moraine crest and meadow benches.

bivy.name: Summit bivy
bivy.notes: Parties who start from the valley often finish the buttress too late to descend and sleep on the summit itself. There is also a grassy ledge reported around 8,500 ft on the upper route that one party found softer and more comfortable than the top. Both are dry, exposed perches, so they only work in settled weather.
bivy.water: None on top. The nearest is a large snow patch a few hundred feet down at the saddle northwest of the summit, which has to be fetched and melted.
bivy.capacity: Room for about three — a fourth party member or a second rope team has to drop off and find something else.

bivy.name: Chiwaukum Chain Lakes
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Bulls Tooth and the only place a party should plan to sleep for the standard scramble. From the upper lake the route works around the shore to the base of a northwest-facing couloir filled with big white talus, climbs that to the ridge, and finishes on the summit block; the top section is reversed as a short, exposed Class 3 downclimb with no rappel, so no rack is needed; a short rope is optional for confidence. The rappels some parties describe belong to the lower, fang-shaped tower nearby, not this summit. Reaching the basin from the Icicle side is about two and a half miles and two thousand feet of climbing off the Icicle Creek trail on the Chain Lakes trail, which itself is roughly five miles and nineteen hundred feet from the junction — a full day with an overnight load. That trail was destroyed by a landslide a couple of miles south of Lake Josephine and has never been rebuilt to its old standard: it is passable on foot, it is not recommended for stock, and it is slow and vague where the slide crossed. From the west the basin is reached over Frosty Pass instead. Snow lingers in these basins into July in a normal year and the couloir holds it longer, which suits a party carrying an axe and hurts one that is not.
bivy.water: Excellent and the reason this is the camp. All three lakes hold water through the season, the inlet streams run well into late summer, and the basin is the last dependable supply before the scramble. Everything above the lakes is dry once the snow has gone, so fill completely here for summit day. Treat it; the shoreline sees steady if light use.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register and covers both day and overnight use; there is no quota, no reservation and no lottery on this side of the wilderness, which is the opposite of the Enchantments permit zone a few miles south. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed at the Icicle Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this wilderness, which includes every lake in this basin — carry a stove. Party size is capped, camp on existing bare ground and keep well back from the lakeshores.
bivy.capacity: Numerous informal sites spread around the three lakes, on benches and in the timber edges. There is room for several parties and you will rarely be competing for ground — the walk in is long enough from either end that this basin stays quiet even in high summer.

bivy.name: Doelle Lakes
bivy.notes: About one and eight tenths miles from the Chain Lakes over a gap that takes some six hundred feet of climbing, this basin sits at nearly the same height as the upper Chain Lake and is the more scenic option and it looks straight across at Bulls Tooth, which is the highest thing in view from here. It is the natural camp for a party that is traversing rather than going in and out — the usual line runs Icicle Creek to the Chain Lakes, over to Doelle, out past Bulls Tooth to Frosty Pass and down Wildhorse Creek to Whitepine, and this basin is the middle of it. As a base for the scramble alone it is slightly further from the couloir than the Chain Lakes are, so parties climbing the peak and returning the same way usually stay lower. The meadows here are exposed and hold weather; there is very little shelter and nights are cold well into August at this height. The connecting ground between here and the Chain Lakes is open enough to be simple in clear weather and genuinely confusing in cloud.
bivy.water: Both lakes, reliable through the climbing season, plus snowmelt in the talus early. This is the other dependable supply in the group and the one to use if the Chain Lakes basin is occupied.
bivy.permit: Same free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the trailhead register, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass at the Icicle Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 5,000 feet, and at this elevation the ground is thin subalpine meadow that scars for years, so pitch on bare gravel or existing sites and use a stove.
bivy.capacity: Flat camping in alpine meadow threaded with talus, with room for several parties spread out. Genuinely lightly used — most people who reach the Chain Lakes stop there.

bivy.name: Frosty Pass and the Wildhorse Creek headwaters
bivy.notes: This is the pivot of the western approach to Bulls Tooth and the last camp before the peak from that side. The Frosty and Wildhorse Creek trail runs about eleven miles and thirty-five hundred feet from the Whitepine side to the pass, where it meets the Icicle Ridge trail; from the pass the high country opens out east and north toward Lake Grace, Snowgrass Mountain, the Doelle Lakes and Bulls Tooth itself. THE TRAIL IS NOT MAINTAINED BEYOND THE PASS, so the ground linking this camp to the peak is route-finding on open high country rather than trail walking, and it is the part of the trip most likely to go wrong in poor visibility. Lake Grace lies off to the side and is the better camp of the two if you want water you can count on and shelter from the wind, at the cost of some distance. Parties doing the full traverse come over this pass in either direction, and it works as well for a party who has climbed the peak from the Chain Lakes and is walking out west as it does for one coming in. Season is roughly mid-July through early October; the north-facing approach slopes hold snow late and the pass is a cold, exposed place to be caught out.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small streams in the headwater meadows below the pass on the Wildhorse side, dependable into midsummer and thinning badly by late season. The pass itself carries nothing you can rely on. This is the last water on the western approach before the high ground, and the Icicle Ridge trail east of here is notoriously dry, so fill in the meadows rather than at the crest.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the register at whichever trailhead you started from, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required at the White Pine trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet — this camp is above that line and there is very little to burn regardless. Camp on the existing bare sites; the meadow here is fragile and heavily walked.
bivy.capacity: Established ground at and just below the pass for a couple of parties, with more scattered spots in the meadows on the Wildhorse side. A crossroads rather than a destination, so expect the occasional through party in July and August and nobody at all in September.

bivy.name: Whitepine Creek valley camps and the Wildhorse junction ford
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk, and on an approach this long that matters more than it sounds. It is roughly three miles of easy valley trail from the road end to the Wildhorse Creek junction, and then six and a half miles of climbing to Frosty Pass — a poor single day with a loaded pack after the drive out from the west side. THE CRUX OF THE WHOLE APPROACH IS THE WHITEPINE CREEK FORD, a few hundred yards short of the Wildhorse junction near the ruins of the old bridge. Early in the season with snowmelt running it is a serious crossing and it is the thing that turns parties round; by late July or August it is usually a boots-on wade with a stick. Camping short of it and crossing in the morning, when the flow is at its lowest and you are fresh, is the standard tactic and the right one. Coming out, most parties walk straight through. The valley is forested and pleasant and the walking is fast, which is the argument for the Whitepine approach over the Icicle one whenever the Icicle road or the French Creek bridge is out.
bivy.water: Whitepine Creek runs alongside for the whole of this stretch and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is the generous part of the approach, and it is worth knowing because the climb to Frosty Pass and everything above it is a different story.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the White Pine trailhead register. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal below 5,000 feet in existing rings outside a burn ban, but this is dry east-side timber and the district runs restrictions through most of the summer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the first few miles of the Whitepine Creek trail, most taking one or two tents, each with its own bit of creek. Nothing developed and no toilets.

bivy.name: White Pine road end trailhead
bivy.notes: The staging point for the western approach and the shorter drive from anywhere on US 2. The road leaves the highway west of Leavenworth and runs about four miles of gravel to the trailhead at roughly 2,800 feet. Sleeping here rather than pushing into the valley in the dark is worth doing, because the ford above wants daylight and a party that arrives at it tired in the evening will camp short of it anyway. THE ROAD IS THE PART TO CHECK. The December 2025 storms damaged forest roads across this whole district and a closure order covering the damaged ones runs into 2027; the Icicle road on the other side of the range carries multiple landslides limiting vehicles to the end of the road, and a large fire closure sat over the Lake Wenatchee and Leavenworth country through the autumn of 2026, shutting more than sixty trails in these two districts. Confirm the White Pine road and the Whitepine and Wildhorse trails are open before committing to the drive, and have the Icicle side as a fallback rather than an assumption, because in some seasons it has been the worse of the two.
bivy.water: Whitepine Creek is at hand and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap. Fill everything here before starting, since the good water lasts only as far as the valley and the high country above Frosty Pass has almost none.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park. The free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit is taken from the register here rather than arranged in advance — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book. Fire restrictions on this dry east slope are close to permanent through the summer and commonly ban all open flame including in rings.
bivy.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the end of the road with room for a modest number of vehicles and space to sleep in one. There is no campground here, no facilities and no fee site — this is a roadhead, recorded because a party arriving late from the west side needs somewhere to be.

access.fees: None — no climbing fee (National Forest wilderness, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.notes: Climbable roughly June–October; heavy winter snowfall and frequent avalanche control closures on I-90 affect access the rest of the year.
access.rules: Alpine Lakes Wilderness regulations: campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft and within 1/2 mile of numerous named lakes on the Wenatchee River Ranger District; Chain and Doelle Lakes both sit above 5,000 ft, so plan on a stove regardless. Maximum group size is 12 people and stock combined.
access.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead, required for day and overnight use mid-May through October 31 (no fee, no quota).
access.landManager: Trailhead is on Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Skykomish Ranger District); Chain/Doelle Lakes and Bulls Tooth itself sit across the Cascade crest in the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest's Alpine Lakes Wilderness (Wenatchee River Ranger District, Icicle Creek drainage).
access.land_manager: Trailhead is on Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Skykomish Ranger District); Chain/Doelle Lakes and Bulls Tooth itself sit across the Cascade crest in the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest's Alpine Lakes Wilderness (Wenatchee River Ranger District, Icicle Creek drainage).

access.passRequired: A Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency/America the Beautiful pass, or other valid Forest Service recreation pass is required to park at the Stevens Pass PCT-South trailhead lot.

bivy.name: Cache Col and the Cache Glacier shoulder
bivy.notes: The col is the gateway to everything here. From the Cascade Pass trail a boot path climbs south along the arm and onto the mellow Cache Glacier, which is corniced at the col early in the season and can need a careful step through. Parties who leave the car in the afternoon and lose the light on the climb sometimes stop here rather than commit to the awkward descending traverse beyond it, and parties coming back north at the end of a trip do the same. It is a fair-weather choice only: it is a high, open saddle with no shelter and no water, and in cloud the ground on both sides is easy to lose. Treat the elevation as approximate, since published figures for the col vary by a couple of hundred feet.
bivy.water: None at the col itself. Early in the season there are melt runnels on the shoulder below it; by August there is usually nothing, and parties either carry up from the Cascade Pass side or melt snow. This is the single most common reason people push on down to the tarn below instead of stopping here.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE LAST GROUND ON THE PARK SIDE, and the distinction decides which permit you need. A night at or above the col is inside North Cascades National Park and requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, with part of the inventory reservable in advance and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage applies. One step south of the col you are in Glacier Peak Wilderness and a free self-issue register slip is all that is needed. Do not assume the wilderness self-issue covers a night at the col.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

bivy.name: Le Conte Pass
bivy.notes: The pass sits on the shoulder above the lakes in the basin below Le Conte Mountain, and it is the direct base for Le Conte itself, which is climbed by working up its east slope on talus and blocky rock by the line of least resistance rather than by any single defined route. It is also where parties running late stop instead of dropping into and re-climbing out of the steep basin below, which is the trade that decides most itineraries on this stretch: better position and worse water, against reliable water and a thousand feet of extra work. From the pass the next day crosses the Le Conte Glacier, which is the most broken ice on this part of the crest and has turned parties around outright, so this is a camp to leave early and roped. Published elevations for the pass vary, so treat the figure as approximate.
bivy.water: Small tarns at the pass hold water through midsummer and are the practical source, but they are snowmelt pools with tiny catchments and they can be gone or foul by September. Late in the season this is a dry camp and the lakes below are the honest answer.

No permit is required once you cross Cache Col into Glacier Peak Wilderness, though signing trail registers is requested.

Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest) on the west/south approach and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest to the east; the northern approach via Cascade Pass and Cache Col lies within North Cascades National Park.

access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass (Downey Creek TH, south approach) and/or NPS wilderness permit (Cascade Pass corridor, north approach).

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: PLANNED first camp on the traverse, roughly three hours past Cascade Pass and the usual night one for a Formidable trip. Good sheltered ground and easy water. Mountain goats work the camp for salt — stow sweaty gear and pee well away from the sites. It is still a long day from here to the peak, so parties chasing a single summit day usually push higher.
bivy.water: lake at camp
bivy.capacity: several small parties; established sites around the tarn

bivy.name: Spider-Formidable Col
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the closest ground to the north side of the peak — the col is the only non-technical crossing of the Spider-Formidable wall and it puts you directly above the Middle Cascade Glacier. Fully exposed on a notch, so expect wind and no shelter at all in weather. The slab trickle is unreliable; confirm it before counting on it, and be prepared to melt. The col itself holds steep snow into the season and parties have needed hand lines to descend the far side.
bivy.water: a trickle down nearby slabs when running; otherwise melt snow
bivy.capacity: one to two tents on small levelled spots on the col

bivy.name: Ridge benches above Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: PLANNED launching camp specifically noted by parties climbing Formidable, sitting on the ridge above the lakes with a much shorter summit day than camping at the lakes themselves. The trade is water: there is none up here except what you melt or carry from below. Gaining this ridgeline out of the lakes is the most consequential bit of travel in this section of the traverse.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: small; scattered flat spots on the ridge

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp on the south side of the col, the standard traverse night and the fallback when the col is windbound. Sheltered, easy water, and a comfortable place to sit out weather — but it is well below the peak and adds a steep, loose climb back to the ridge in the morning.
bivy.water: lakes at camp
bivy.capacity: several parties; established sites

access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.

access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: North Cascades Backcountry Permit
access.closures: Campfires banned in all portions of the North Cascades NPS Complex since 29 June 2026; Washington statewide burn ban from 2 August 2026

bivy.name: Drop Creek high camp
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE OTHER WAY TO FORMIDABLE AND IT IS NOT THE TRAVERSE. access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.

access.closures: Cascade River Road has a seasonal winter closure and may have additional washout-related closures; check the NPS road-conditions page before driving.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex (National Park Service)
access.land_manager: National Park Service
access.parking_pass: None required — there are no trailhead or parking fees for trails that begin on National Park Service land.

bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and a few rock benches on the shoulder below and at the col, room for one or two parties. Nothing built, no toilet, no windbreaks worth the name.

bivy.name: Sentinel Pass and Lizard Col

bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice only. Pack out human waste, which matters here because the meltwater below feeds the lakes people are drinking from.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms and small rock benches at each of the two saddles, one party at a time at either. Nothing built, no toilet, nothing sheltered.

bivy.name: Crest bivouacs above the South Cascade and Chickamin glaciers

It gets a handful of ascents in a decade and there is no established camp for it, so parties climbing it either work out from the lake basin below or level a spot on the divide and accept a dry, exposed night. bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or ice, never on the heather benches. Pack out human waste. No fires; there is nothing to burn and nothing that would recover.
bivy.capacity: Whatever the party can level. Rock rings, gravel benches and snow platforms for one party at a time, scattered along the divide. No toilet and no established sites of any kind.

access.fees: A Northwest Forest Pass (or America the Beautiful pass) is required to park at Forest Service trailheads such as Downey Creek; no fee is charged at the Cascade River Road trailhead inside the national park boundary.
access.rules: Standard Leave No Trace wilderness rules apply: pack out all trash, use existing campsites, and use a bear canister or proper food storage. Campfires are prohibited above roughly 5,000 ft in the Stephen Mather Wilderness portion of the park complex. Group size limits apply (parties are capped, generally 12 in the Glacier Peak Wilderness and smaller near popular North Cascades NP camps). Dogs are prohibited within North Cascades National Park Complex but permitted in the Forest Service portion of Glacier Peak Wilderness.
access.permit: A free North Cascades NP backcountry permit is required for any overnight camping within the park-complex boundary near Cascade Pass/Pelton Basin (2026 lottery ran March 2-13; remaining permits opened to walk-up/online booking April 29). Get permits from the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount, (360) 854-7245, or email noca_wilderness@nps.gov; self-issue permits are available outside the station when it's closed. Once you're camped beyond the park boundary in the Glacier Peak Wilderness (Forest Service land), no quota permit is required, but a self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead is expected.
access.closures: Cascade River Road closed at MP 8 (fire-related, status can change) and Suiattle River Road closed at MP 4 through at least January 2028 (flood damage) as of mid-2026 — both add substantial extra approach mileage.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, split between Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District, west/south side) and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (east side); the standard north approach passes through the North Cascades National Park Complex / Stephen Mather Wilderness via Cascade Pass before entering the Forest Service wilderness.
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: None at the Cascade River Road trailhead inside the national park boundary — there are no trailhead or parking fees for trails that begin on National Park Service land.

bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Keep camps back from the tarns, camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather, and pack out human waste. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Heather and gravel benches around the pass and its tarns, enough for two or three parties spread out. Unimproved, no toilet.

access.fees: No park entrance fee; overnight backcountry permit costs $10/person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee
access.permit: Backcountry permit required year-round for any overnight stay (day climbs need no permit); reservable via recreation.gov, picked up at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount
access.closures: Cascade River Road is gated/closed for winter and reopens seasonally (typically late June); Cascade Pass is a high-demand quota zone and cannot be reserved for trips starting before ~July 1 due to snow.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

bivy.name: Boston Basin high camp
bivy.notes: The upper camp, roughly 6,400 ft, with a composting toilet. It is the practical base for Boston: from here you gain the Quien Sabe and traverse under Sharkfin toward the peak's east side. The rock on this route is notoriously rotten, so most parties climb it unroped to keep out from under each other, and having camp close by is what keeps the exposure time short.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams below the Quien Sabe Glacier; reliable early, patchier late in a dry summer
bivy.permit: Overnights need a North Cascades backcountry permit, collected at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, and camping is restricted to the two designated sites; the basin is popular enough that summer weekends often have nothing left
bivy.capacity: One of only two legal camping areas in the basin, shared with parties bound for Forbidden, Sharkfin, Sahale and Buckner

bivy.name: Boston Basin low camp
bivy.notes: About 5,300 ft on a morainal rib with a little tree cover. Slower parties and early-season trips use it because it melts out sooner and is more sheltered; the trade is a longer summit day.
bivy.water: Basin creeks run beside the site
bivy.permit: Same park permit and designated-sites-only restriction as the high camp
bivy.capacity: The basin's second designated area, also with a composting toilet

access.fees: No park entrance fee. A backcountry/wilderness permit is required for all overnight stays; NPS charges a summer-season (mid-May–early Oct) backcountry fee of $10 per person plus a $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (no charge for youth 15 and under, and no fee mid-Oct–mid-May).
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Camping in Boston Basin is limited to two designated sites — low camp (~5,300 ft) and high camp (~6,400 ft), each with a composting toilet. IGBC-approved bear canisters are required for all food storage below the vegetation line in Boston Basin from June 1 to November 15 (free loaners available at the Marblemount WIC). Blue-bag human waste removal is required above the designated sites.
access.permit: Reserve online via Recreation.gov (60% of permits released in advance, 40% held for walk-ins), then activate the permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center the day before or by 11 a.m. the day of your trip.
access.closures: Access depends on Cascade River Road's seasonal/weather status; check current NPS road-status postings before driving. Camping in Boston Basin is restricted to the two designated hardened sites.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: None for day-use at NPS trailheads along Cascade River Road.

bivy.name: Pelton Basin
bivy.notes: Pelton Basin lies roughly half a mile down the east side of Cascade Pass and is the fallback when Sahale Glacier Camp is full, since camping at the pass itself is not allowed. From here Mixup Peak, Magic Mountain and the Middle Cascade Glacier approach to The Triad are all straightforward day objectives. It is lower and more sheltered than Sahale, which makes it the better choice in poor weather even though it costs extra vertical on summit day.
bivy.water: A creek runs through the basin just below the camp and is reliable across the normal summer season, which makes this the most dependable water of the Cascade Pass camps.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit for the specific site, obtained in person at Marblemount; a mix of Recreation.gov reservations and a walk-up allocation.
bivy.capacity: A few designated sites including one that suits a larger party, plus smaller tucked-away spots; booked as individual sites.

bivy.name: Johannesburg Camp
bivy.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
bivy.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

access.fees: North Cascades National Park charges no entrance fee. Overnight backcountry permits cost $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee (free for climbers 15 and under).
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Practice Leave No Trace; blue-bag human waste removal where required.
access.permit: Required for any overnight stay or bivy in the backcountry. Cascade Pass is a high-demand, walk-up-only zone — permits must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center (360-854-7245) rather than reserved online in advance; go midweek or arrive early, since Cascade Pass permits can fill by mid-morning in summer. High-country zones like this one generally can't be reserved for trips starting before July 1 due to snow.
access.closures: As of early summer 2026, Cascade River Road is closed to vehicle traffic at Eldorado (milepost 20) due to flood and landslide damage, which is roughly 4 miles (about an hour of walking or a short bike ride) short of the Cascade Pass trailhead; foot and bicycle travel is permitted past the gate. The road has a history of storm washouts (e.g., the Boston Creek washout of August 2013), so check current NPS road-conditions updates before driving up.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.
bivy.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.

bivy.name: Johannesburg Camp
bivy.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: North Cascades National Park backcountry regulations apply (this descent is entirely within the park).
access.permit: North Cascades NP wilderness/backcountry camping permit (required for any overnight stay; day climbs need none)
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.

access.rules: Group size limit is 12 in trail corridors and camps and in the Mount Shuksan, Eldorado Peak and Forbidden Peak cross-country zones, which this route is in; 6 in the remaining cross-country zones. access.permit: Overnight camping requires a wilderness permit; ~60% of Boston Basin sites reservable in advance on Recreation.gov, remainder walk-up at the Marblemount WIC.

bivy.name: Buttress bivy at the heather-to-rock transition
bivy.notes: This is a planned bivy, not an emergency ledge, and it is what makes the route a two-day climb for most parties — it typically takes eight to twelve hours of climbing from the base of the buttress to reach it, with two to three hours of glacier and summit snow above. It sits where the steep heather and rock give way to the snow and glacier, so it is the last flat, watered ground before the upper mountain. It is also the point of no easy return: the ground below is 4,000 ft of steep brush, heather and rock above the valley, and retreating down it in the dark is far worse than sitting out the night. Wind is the main comfort variable; some nights are dead calm and warm, some are not.

bivy.name: Boston Basin lower camp
bivy.notes: The first hardened camp on the climbers' trail up from the Cascade River Road pullout near mile 21.7, with a composting toilet. It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.
bivy.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.

bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

bivy.name: Boston Basin high camp
bivy.notes: A comfortable planned camp, roughly 6,300 to 6,400 ft, on a small sandy flat at the foot of a permanent snowfield with a privy and a food storage bin nearby. This is the standard staging camp for the traverse: about two to two and a half hours from here to the base of Torment. It is the most crowded alpine camp in this part of the range, biting flies are notorious in midsummer, and the park rules that apply everywhere apply here — camp on snow, rock or bare ground, never in the meadows, and stay 100 ft back from water.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks and the permanent snowfield at the back of the basin; reliable all season, though the surface streams shrink late
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required, and Boston Basin is one of the few zones that accepts advance reservations rather than walk-up only. Composting toilets serve both the upper and lower camp areas.
bivy.capacity: Hardened sites in a zone capped at six parties per night, twelve people per party

bivy.name: Torment Basin camp below the southeast face
bivy.notes: A planned alternative camp for parties who want to start the traverse from the base of the climbing instead of from Boston Basin. It sits under the southeast side of Torment near the foot of the east couloir. Early in the season the ground is still part snow and gets excavated with an axe; late in the season the rocky patches are bare. It puts you above the basin traverse, which is the section that is genuinely easy to lose in a whiteout.
bivy.water: Snowmelt from the surrounding snowfields and the Taboo Glacier; early in the season you may be chopping a platform out of snow rather than looking for water
bivy.permit: Separate cross-country zone from Boston Basin, so a party crossing the Torment saddle to sleep here needs Torment Basin on the permit itinerary
bivy.capacity: Room for a small party; the zone allows six parties per night, twelve per party

bivy.name: Mid-traverse ridge bivy
bivy.notes: This is the emergency-and-committed option rather than a planned camp: a flat spot at a notch on the ridge roughly midway along the traverse, reached after the snow and ice section on the north side. Parties who get benighted mid-ridge use it, and parties intentionally splitting the traverse into two short days sleep there for the position — views out to Eldorado on one side and the Ptarmigan Traverse peaks on the other. Assume you may have to melt snow, and assume wind: there is no shelter on the crest.
bivy.water: A snowfield beside the notch, with running water audible under the boulders in some years; unreliable, and dry by late July or August in a low-snow year
bivy.capacity: Two, on a flat notch — this is a ledge, not a campsite

It is the usual base for Forbidden Peak's West Ridge and North Ridge, Sharkfin Tower and the Torment-Forbidden traverse, and it stays snow-covered well into early summer. accounts differ on the exact elevation of the two Boston Basin camps — figures between roughly 5,300 and 5,700 ft are quoted for this one — so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. Bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.water: Meltwater creeks braid through the basin below the Quien Sabe and Boston glaciers and are normally reliable through the climbing season, though flow drops noticeably by late August and September in a light snow year.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, and for all Cascade River Road trailheads it must be collected IN PERSON at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Roughly 60% of capacity is reservable in advance through Recreation.gov, about 40% held for walk-ups the day of or day before. These permits are NO LONGER FREE — older write-ups still say they are, which is out of date; confirm current pricing when you book.
bivy.capacity: Zone quota is 6 parties per night for the whole Boston Basin cross-country zone, shared with the upper camp; maximum party size 12. Weekend permits go early.

bivy.name: Boston Basin upper (high) camp
bivy.notes: Several hundred vertical feet above the lower camp and also served by a composting toilet, this shortens the morning to the Forbidden West Ridge couloir and to Sharkfin Tower considerably. There is a real tension in the published guidance worth knowing before you go: park zone rules describe camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while much of the practical guidance for Boston Basin says to use only the two established camps. In practice rangers direct climbers to the hardened sites, so plan on them and ask at Marblemount if you intend otherwise.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and glacier outflow are usually running nearby, but this is the less certain of the two camps late in the season — parties arriving in September should be ready to melt snow or carry it up from below.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the lower camp, collected in person at Marblemount; reservable portion on Recreation.gov, remainder held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: Shares the same 6-party, 12-person Boston Basin zone quota as the lower camp; a handful of hardened tent platforms.

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.notes: Reached by the maintained trail to Cascade Pass and then up Sahale Arm, this is the natural high camp for Sahale Peak and for the Quien Sabe Glacier side of Boston Peak. It is fully exposed to weather and wind, which is what the stacked rock walls around each site are for, and there is a composting toilet. Camping is confined to the marked sites — the arm below is closed to camping.
bivy.water: Glacier melt runs beside the camp through summer and is generally dependable, but it is fed entirely by the shrinking Sahale Glacier, so flow is weakest late in a dry season and can require walking uphill toward the ice.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit for a specific designated SITE, not a zone; Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at Marblemount. Most sites are reservable through Recreation.gov with roughly 40% held for walk-ups.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated tent platforms ringed by rock windbreaks, booked individually rather than as a zone; one of the most sought-after camps in the park and it fills fast.

bivy.name: Pelton Basin
bivy.notes: Pelton Basin lies roughly half a mile down the east side of Cascade Pass and is the fallback when Sahale Glacier Camp is full, since camping at the pass itself is not allowed. From here Mixup Peak, Magic Mountain and the Middle Cascade Glacier approach to The Triad are all straightforward day objectives. It is lower and more sheltered than Sahale, which makes it the better choice in poor weather even though it costs extra vertical on summit day.
bivy.water: A creek runs through the basin just below the camp and is reliable across the normal summer season, which makes this the most dependable water of the Cascade Pass camps.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit for the specific site, obtained in person at Marblemount; a mix of Recreation.gov reservations and a walk-up allocation.
bivy.capacity: A few designated sites including one that suits a larger party, plus smaller tucked-away spots; booked as individual sites.

bivy.name: Johannesburg Camp
bivy.notes: A walk-in camp a short, steep and often slick few minutes above the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the road — not a drive-up campground, you carry everything in. It is the practical staging point for the Cascade-Johannesburg Couloir, Cascade Peak, and any pre-dawn start where you want to be at the road end the night before. If it is full, Marble Creek and Mineral Park down the Cascade River Road are the car campgrounds, at the cost of driving the rough section twice.
bivy.water: A creek runs beside the sites and normally holds water through the season, being fed by drainage off the north side of Johannesburg Mountain rather than by a single small snowfield.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required even though the camp is minutes from the car; Cascade River Road permits are issued in person at Marblemount, part reservable on Recreation.gov and part held for walk-ups. Approved bear-resistant food storage is required.
bivy.capacity: Three small primitive sites, so it is easily filled by one or two parties.

bivy.name: Informal snow and rock bivouacs above the basins
bivy.notes: Parties attempting the Torment-Forbidden traverse, a long day on Boston Peak, or a late finish on the Forbidden North Ridge sometimes end up bivouacking on snow or rock above the established camps, in the Sharkfin Col area, or in a notch on route. Treat these as unplanned or emergency shelter rather than as an itinerary: they are exposed, they have no water once the snow goes, and the surrounding terrain is glaciated. Human waste must be packed out, and food still needs bear-resistant storage.
bivy.water: Entirely snowmelt and therefore seasonal. Early in the summer there is running water almost everywhere; by late season the high ground can be bare rock with nothing running, so plan to carry water up or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Still requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, from Marblemount. Whether an unestablished high bivouac is acceptable in Boston Basin is genuinely CONTESTED — the general zone regulation allows camping on durable surfaces such as snow, rock or bare ground, while the site-specific guidance for Boston Basin says to use the two designated camps. Ask when you collect the permit rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Party-sized ledges and snow platforms only; no facilities, no toilet, and no reliable flat ground once the snow has melted out.

access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size limit is 12 in trail corridors and camps and in the eleven named cross-country zones — Boston Basin, Eldorado, Forbidden, Hidden Lake, Icy, Inspiration, Nooksack, Price, Sulphide Glacier, Torment Basin and Triad — one of which this route is in; 6 in the remaining cross-country zones. Limits include people and stock. Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.

access.rules: Camping in the Eldorado zone is restricted to designated open-camping areas (e.g., the Roush Creek rib around 5,400 ft and the Inspiration/Eldorado Glacier apron around 7,500 ft), with limits on both the number of parties and people per party; no camping is allowed at the trailhead.

Reserve in advance on Recreation.gov (watch the mandatory orientation video and email noca_wilderness@nps.gov within 3 days of the trip), or try for one of the roughly 40% of sites held back for in-person, walk-up issuance at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.closures: Cascade River Road is prone to seasonal, flood, and landslide closures -- it has been gated at Eldorado Creek (milepost 20) in past and recent seasons, with foot/bike travel still allowed beyond a vehicle closure. Check the NPS road-conditions page and Skagit County road-closures page before driving.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (NPS) for the upper approach and peak; the lowest trail miles from the Hidden Lake Trailhead are in Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest.
