bivy.name: Hannegan Camp, below Hannegan Pass
bivy.notes: The obvious staging camp for a party that drives up Ruth Creek late and wants the pass behind them early. Because it sits on the forest side of the divide, the paperwork is entirely different from everything down the far side — parking pass only, no Marblemount errand. Road conditions on FS 32 have been unreliable in recent seasons and access has at times stopped short of the trailhead, so confirm before committing to a long drive. The 2026 Chilliwack Complex closures were written to include trails and camps entering the park from this trailhead, which can leave the camp reachable while the country beyond the pass is not.
bivy.water: Side streams and snowmelt near camp, but they are seasonal and can dry or go silty by late summer — treat everything and carry a reserve on a hot September approach
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness) — NO North Cascades National Park permit needed here, since the park boundary is still ahead at the pass. What you need is a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Hannegan trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid at this Forest Service fee site.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated tent spots with a shared cooking area and a backcountry toilet; a second toilet sits at the pass itself

bivy.name: Boundary Camp
bivy.notes: Boundary sits just over Hannegan Pass at the line where Forest Service ground becomes national park, which is exactly why it trips people up: you park under a Northwest Forest Pass and then sleep under an NPS permit. With only three sites it books out on summer weekends, and a party arriving without a reservation has no legal fallback nearby. It is the natural first night for anything heading down the Chilliwack or up onto Copper Ridge. Fire closures in 2026 affected camps and trails on this side of the pass, so check the park's current closure page rather than assuming a reservation implies open ground.
bivy.water: A nearby subalpine stream normally runs through the climbing season, though it is a snowmelt source and thins out late
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, obtained through the park's reservation system and picked up in person at Marblemount. Campfires are not allowed here.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, each rated for up to four people, with a pit toilet

bivy.name: Copper Lake Camp, Copper Ridge
bivy.notes: Of the three camps strung along Copper Ridge, this is the one that solves water: the others are drier, and one is normally described as having no water source at all, which forces a long carry from lower down. That makes it the sensible high camp for anyone using the ridge as a high traverse toward the Chilliwack drainage rather than dropping straight into the valley. The ridge is exposed and the sites are small, so a party of more than four has to split across permits. Copper Ridge and the wider Copper Loop were inside the 2026 fire closure footprint, and burned ground stays hazardous for years afterward.
bivy.water: The lake is immediately at hand and reliable all season — a real advantage on this ridge
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, picked up at Marblemount. Food, rubbish and scented items must go in the provided lockers or an approved canister.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites for parties of up to four, with a composting toilet and food-storage lockers

bivy.name: US Cabin Camp, Chilliwack River
bivy.notes: A deep-forest valley camp rather than a climbing bivy, and its value is positional — it is roughly where a party bound for Bear Mountain or the peaks further up the drainage stops before leaving the trail. The lack of a food locker is worth planning around, because the neighbouring camps have them and it is easy to assume continuity. Old-growth valley bottom means it stays cool and damp, so expect wet gear in the morning. The Chilliwack River Trail was among the 2026 closures and its status should be confirmed before a trip is built around it.
bivy.water: The Chilliwack River is a few steps away and runs year round, though it carries glacial silt and needs filtering rather than just treating
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit from Marblemount. Unlike the ridge camps this one has NO food-storage hardware, so bring a canister or be prepared to hang.
bivy.capacity: Four sites, split between a pair near the trail and a pair down by the river, with a pit toilet

access.fees: $10 per person camping fee plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee (2026 NPS rate); day use is free.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Hard-sided bear canister strongly recommended in this drainage given limited hanging trees and reported aggressive bear activity; parkwide summer fire restrictions (no campfires) are typically in effect by late June; pets and bikes are prohibited beyond the national forest boundary; permit and written itinerary must be carried.
access.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required for the overnight stay this peak realistically requires. Reserve via Recreation.gov, watch the mandatory orientation video, then email noca_wilderness@nps.gov up to 3 days before your trip for ranger review and permit issuance, or get a walk-up permit at the Wilderness Information Center (7280 Ranger Station Rd, Marblemount). A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park at the Hannegan Trailhead.
access.closures: Brush Creek Trail (the final approach corridor toward Whatcom Pass/Indian Mountain) reopened Sept. 2025 after a 3-year closure from the 2022 Brush Creek Fire; Graybeal, Graybeal Stock, and Whatcom Camps remain closed, and the trail is not fully stock-accessible. The Chilliwack River Trail section between the Brush Creek junction and Indian Creek Camp has major fire-related blowdown requiring slow travel. Bear Creek Camp is closed from 2021 fire damage. A bypass has been built around a prior washout at the end of FR 32 to keep the Hannegan Trailhead reachable — check Mt. Baker Ranger District alerts before driving.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness) for the peak and most of the approach; the first several miles from the Hannegan Trailhead to Hannegan Pass cross Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker Wilderness).
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: Forest Service Recreation Pass for trailhead parking (not the Discover Pass)

bivy.name: Lake Constance — the standard base for the South Chute
bivy.notes: The base camp for essentially every ascent by the standard South Chute, reached by a savage climbers' path that gains roughly 3,300 to 3,400 ft in under two miles of hand-over-hand scrambling above the Dosewallips road. Published elevations for the lake vary between about 4,650 and 4,800 ft, a fair reflection of how imprecise everything about this approach is. From camp the route runs north into Avalanche Canyon and then up the chute toward the south ridge notch, so a summit day from here is short by Olympic standards. The 20-person ceiling is the real planning constraint — it is a basin, not a campground, and it is full most fine weekends.
bivy.water: Reliable at the lake itself. Constance Creek, which the climbers' trail follows, runs well early in the season and can be dry by late summer — carry water up rather than assuming you will find it on the climb.
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and Lake Constance is a NAMED QUOTA AREA. Reserve on Recreation.gov; the 20-person cap makes this one of the scarcest permits in the Olympics. Bear canisters required. Older write-ups describing a free self-issued permit at the trailhead are OUT OF DATE.
bivy.capacity: HARD overnight quota of 20 people for the whole basin; roughly five individual sites plus one group site are commonly reported, and parties of seven or more must take the group site

bivy.name: Dosewallips road-end camps, staging for the washed-out road
bivy.notes: THE ROAD HAS BEEN CLOSED BY A WASHOUT SINCE THE EARLY 2000s, so what used to be a drive-in trailhead is now several miles of road walking — estimates range from about 6.5 extra miles on the round trip to over five miles each way to the Lake Constance turn-off, so plan on the longer number. Parties who cannot face the road walk and the 3,400 ft climbers' trail in one day use the old campground area as a staging night, then hit the path fresh in the morning. It is the single biggest variable on this side of the range and it rules out a casual car-to-car attempt for most people. Bikes are allowed on the closed road and cut the approach time significantly.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Dosewallips River
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required for any night inside the park boundary, booked on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters required. Sites on the Forest Service side of the boundary below the park have their own rules, so check which side of the line you intend to sleep on.
bivy.capacity: Several riverside sites in and around the old drive-in campground at the end of the closed road, plus sites near Dose Forks; rarely full

bivy.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — NOT the standard Constance camp
bivy.notes: Home Lake sits just below Constance Pass and is a genuine high camp, but it MUST NOT BE CONFUSED WITH LAKE CONSTANCE — it does not serve the South Chute and cannot substitute for the quota at the lake. Parties camp here for the Inner Constance country, the northern approaches and traverses, or as a through-hike stop, and reaching it from the Dosewallips means the full road walk plus a long valley trail rather than the short brutal climbers' path. If your objective is the standard route, this is the wrong basin. Its practical value to a Constance trip is as a bail-out when the 20-person quota at the lake is gone.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, and it is the last dependable water before the pass
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters required, and no fires are permitted at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A few small individual sites in an exposed subalpine basin

bivy.name: Lake Constance
bivy.notes: The only practical camp for the route and a brutal one to reach: an unmaintained climbers' path gaining roughly 3,200 ft in about 1.8 mi from the Dosewallips, steep enough that you are pulling on roots and logs, and that is after walking or biking several miles of the road washed out since 2002. Parties climb Constance from here and come back to the same camp the same day rather than moving a camp higher — there is no established upper camp on this side, and the ground above through Avalanche Canyon and the traverses is not somewhere you want to be carrying overnight loads.
bivy.water: The lake itself — clear, cold and holding trout. It is the only water at camp, and there is none on the climb above.
bivy.permit: An Olympic National Park wilderness camping permit is required and Lake Constance is a designated quota area, so a reservation through Recreation.gov effectively has to be secured the morning the window opens — one party booked at 7 a.m. on the March release date for an August weekend. Fees are charged per person per night plus a reservation fee. Bear canisters are required. Campfires are prohibited (the lake is above the 3,500 ft fire closure elevation). There is a composting toilet at the lake; elsewhere solid waste is buried well away from camp and water and toilet paper is packed out.
bivy.capacity: A quota area with a small number of sites; parties describe pitching at the north end of the lake. Demand far exceeds supply.

access.fees: $6 non-refundable reservation fee plus $8 per person per night (age 16+; camping is free for 15 and under). An annual Olympic Wilderness Camping Pass ($45/person) covers nightly camping fees but not the $6 reservation fee.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Overnight quota of 20 people at Lake Constance — reserve ahead, especially for summer weekends. Camp only at established sites near the lake outlet to protect fragile subalpine ground, and store food to avoid marmot/bear conflicts.
access.permit: NPS wilderness permit required for any overnight stay at Lake Constance; reserve in advance at recreation.gov (Olympic NP Wilderness Permit) or through the Wilderness Information Center, (360) 565-3100. No permit is needed for a single-push day climb.
access.closures: Dosewallips Road remains closed to vehicles at ~600 ft — budget extra time and mileage. Confirm current trail/washout status with Hood Canal Ranger District (360-765-2200) or the WIC before driving out.
access.landManager: Approach lands: Olympic National Forest / Buckhorn Wilderness (Hood Canal Ranger District, Quilcene). Lake Constance basin and upper mountain: Olympic National Park wilderness. The summit itself straddles the NP/Buckhorn Wilderness boundary.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — Olympic National Park (Olympic Wilderness)
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: No day-use pass is needed to climb; a wilderness permit (above) is required only for overnight camping.

bivy.name: Graves Creek Campground — drive-in staging for the East Fork Quinault
bivy.notes: This is the only realistic drive-in base on the Quinault side and the natural place to sleep the night before starting up the East Fork toward Anderson Pass and Anderson's Thumb. Vault toilets, fire grates, tables and bear lockers, and nothing else. Reach it from the North Shore Road only — the South Shore Road has a washout roughly eight miles up from the highway, and a phone will still try to route you that way and add several miles of driving for nothing. The last six miles are narrow gravel and RVs and trailers are banned regardless of what the road is doing on the day. Treat the road status as a live question rather than a settled one: this stretch has been closed to vehicles by erosion before, and when it is, both the campground and the trailhead become a two-mile walk or ride. Sleeping here costs you nothing in approach distance, which matters when the first day out is thirteen miles to Enchanted Valley.
bivy.water: None piped — there is no potable water at all, so arrive with everything you need or filter from the Quinault beside the campground
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit is needed for a night here, and no reservation is possible. The moment you walk past the trailhead you need an Olympic wilderness permit booked on the federal recreation site: eight dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen or over, plus a six dollar non-refundable booking fee, or a forty-five dollar annual wilderness pass that covers the nightly charge. A bear canister is required in every wilderness camp area in this park, and they are loaned free to permit holders at the wilderness information centres.
bivy.capacity: About 30 first-come, first-served sites, open year round and rarely full outside high summer weekends; no reservations are taken

bivy.name: Enchanted Valley and Anderson Pass — the approach to Anderson's Thumb
bivy.notes: The East Fork Quinault runs about thirteen miles from Graves Creek to the Enchanted Valley chalet, with staged camps at Pony Bridge around three miles, O'Neil Creek around six and a half and Pyrites Creek around nine, all of which are useful for breaking the walk in. This is the approach to ANDERSON'S THUMB, the pinnacle on the Anderson massif, reached by continuing from the valley up to Anderson Pass at 4,480 ft and then onto the glacier remnant and the rock above. Camping at the pass rather than in the valley saves you several miles and roughly two thousand feet on climbing day and puts you in quiet country; camping in the valley gets you a flatter, warmer night and a spectacular setting at the cost of a very long summit day and a great deal of company. Bears are habituated and confident here, so the canister rule is enforced rather than advisory, and food left out is food lost. The same pass is reached from the Dosewallips on the east side, which is the shorter approach to the Anderson massif if that road is open — worth checking before committing to the Quinault side.
bivy.water: Reliable everywhere — the East Fork Quinault runs the length of the valley and small streams cross the trail up toward the pass
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, and the EAST FORK QUINAULT RIVER IS A QUOTA AREA — reserve on the federal recreation site rather than turning up hopeful. Summer season runs mid-May to mid-October and reservations for it release on 15 April at seven in the morning Pacific time. Eight dollars per person per night for adults, six dollar booking fee. BEAR CANISTERS ARE SPECIFICALLY AND STRICTLY REQUIRED HERE: this valley was closed to camping over bear problems and reopened on that condition. Canisters are loaned free at the Quinault and Port Angeles wilderness information centres.
bivy.capacity: A large valley camping area at the chalet meadow that can hold well over a hundred people on a summer weekend, plus a much smaller and quieter camp up near Anderson Pass

access.fees: $8/person/night (16+; free for 15 and under) + $6 non-refundable reservation fee per permit. An optional annual Wilderness Pass ($45/person) covers per-night fees for 12 months but not the $6 reservation fee.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; bear canisters where required; group size limits in wilderness

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and CROSS-COUNTRY ZONES CANNOT BE BOOKED ONLINE — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Dodger Point Camp — the southern gateway to the Bailey Range
bivy.notes: Dodger Point is 13.5 miles from the old Whiskey Bend trailhead by way of the Long Ridge trail, which leaves the Elwha at Michael's Cabin and crosses the river on a suspension bridge. With the road walk added it is about nineteen miles and well over ten thousand feet of gain to the lookout, so this is a serious approach in its own right. It is the way in to MOUNT DANA and MOUNT WILDER, the southern end of the Bailey Range, and the connecting ridge toward Ludden Peak and on to Ferry Basin, MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER. That connection is not a trail: it involves a faint path off the ridge, a steep gully of loose rock and a section where you climb a tangle of roots and branches to regain the crest. Cream Lake below Ferry Basin is infamous for mosquitoes and for steep alder-choked gullies that swallow time, so budget generously and go in a dry spell if you can. The lookout is the best viewpoint in the valley and the camp is worth a night on its own merits.
bivy.water: THE WEAK POINT. There is no water between the Elwha crossing near Michael's Cabin and the tarns just below Dodger Point — a long climb. Fill everything at the river, and expect the tarns to be low or gone by late season.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. The camp itself books normally, but any night spent off-trail on the Bailey ridge beyond it is a cross-country zone and must be arranged by telephone with the wilderness information centre. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites near the old lookout, on an exposed ridge crest; small, and seldom busy

access.fees: Olympic Wilderness camping: $6 reservation fee plus $8/person/night for ages 16+ (15 and under free), in addition to the standard Olympic NP entrance fee/pass for vehicle access.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Bear-resistant food canisters are required for all overnight stays anywhere in the Olympic Wilderness, including cross-country zones. Rangers will not deny a permit based on a party's stated skill or gear, so honest self-assessment of the off-trail difficulty is essential.
access.permit: Wilderness camping permit required year-round for all overnight stays, reserved through Recreation.gov — but the Elwha Basin/Bailey Range cross-country camping zones are call-in only and must be booked by phone with the Wilderness Information Center, (360) 565-3100, rather than the standard online quota system.
access.closures: The Olympic Hot Springs Road (drive to Whiskey Bend Trailhead) has been washed out and closed to vehicles about 1 mile south of the park boundary since September 2024 — confirm current status before a trip. The Bailey Range Traverse beyond Cat Basin (which includes the approach to Barnes) was closed during the August 2023 Olympic lightning fires and can be re-closed in future high fire-danger periods; check current fire/trail conditions with the WIC.

access.fees: Wilderness camping fee is $8 per person (age 16+) per night plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee per permit (youth 15 and under free); an annual Olympic Wilderness Pass ($45/person) covers the nightly fee. A standard Olympic NP entrance fee also applies to drive in ($30/vehicle for 7 days, $55 for an annual Olympic NP pass, or a valid America the Beautiful pass).
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Bear canisters are required park-wide for all overnight wilderness stays (bear wires and hangs are not accepted); free loaner canisters are available at Wilderness Information Centers. Practice Leave No Trace and confirm current campfire restrictions at the WIC before the trip.
access.permit: A Wilderness (backcountry) camping permit is required for every night spent in Olympic NP backcountry, including Low Divide/Martins Park -- reserve online via recreation.gov before your trip. There is no separate climbing permit or mandatory summit registration, but checking in with a ranger or Wilderness Information Center is strongly advised given the route's remoteness.
access.closures: The North Fork/North Shore Quinault Road has a history of multi-month closures -- e.g., closed at Milepost 10.2 for culvert replacement roughly July-September 2025, cutting off all vehicle access to the North Fork and Graves Creek trailheads -- and is washout-prone after storms. Check the park's Road & Weather line (360-565-3131) or the NPS current road conditions page before driving out.
access.landManager: Olympic National Park wilderness, administered from the park's South District/Quinault Ranger District; the trailhead and most of the route lie in Jefferson County.

It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and CROSS-COUNTRY ZONES CANNOT BE BOOKED ONLINE — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

bivy.name: Low Divide — the pass camp for Mount Seattle and Mount Christie
bivy.notes: Low Divide is the saddle between MOUNT SEATTLE and MOUNT CHRISTIE and the obvious base for both, and by all accounts it is the most comfortable camp in the interior — flat, watered, with a toilet and a bear hang. Mount Seattle has three established scramble lines from here, by Noyes Basin, by Seattle Creek Basin and by the south slopes, and the upper meadows above camp are open walking. Mount Christie is usually taken by dropping to Martins Park, a boulder garden about three miles below the Christie Glacier, and climbing the north couloir from there. The honest planning point is which side you walk in from: this is 28.4 miles from Whiskey Bend up the Elwha, and 16 miles from the North Fork Quinault trailhead, so unless you are traversing the range you should be coming from the Quinault. Wasps have been a real problem on the lower forest sections in late summer, and stings there have put people out of action for days.
bivy.water: Reliable — a stream runs through the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not itself a quota area, but it is a long way from any road and may not appear in an online search, so telephone the wilderness information centre if the site will not show. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: Around five sites, with a bear hang, a toilet and flat ground; small enough that a large party will fill it

bivy.name: Dodger Point Camp — the southern gateway to the Bailey Range
bivy.notes: Dodger Point is 13.5 miles from the old Whiskey Bend trailhead by way of the Long Ridge trail, which leaves the Elwha at Michael's Cabin and crosses the river on a suspension bridge. With the road walk added it is about nineteen miles and well over ten thousand feet of gain to the lookout, so this is a serious approach in its own right. It is the way in to MOUNT DANA and MOUNT WILDER, the southern end of the Bailey Range, and the connecting ridge toward Ludden Peak and on to Ferry Basin, MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER. That connection is not a trail: it involves a faint path off the ridge, a steep gully of loose rock and a section where you climb a tangle of roots and branches to regain the crest. Cream Lake below Ferry Basin is infamous for mosquitoes and for steep alder-choked gullies that swallow time, so budget generously and go in a dry spell if you can. The lookout is the best viewpoint in the valley and the camp is worth a night on its own merits.
bivy.water: THE WEAK POINT. There is no water between the Elwha crossing near Michael's Cabin and the tarns just below Dodger Point — a long climb. Fill everything at the river, and expect the tarns to be low or gone by late season.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. The camp itself books normally, but any night spent off-trail on the Bailey ridge beyond it is a cross-country zone and must be arranged by telephone with the wilderness information centre. Bear canister mandatory. No fires at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites near the old lookout, on an exposed ridge crest; small, and seldom busy

access.fees: Park entrance fee $30/vehicle (or $15/person on foot or bike), valid 7 days; a $55 Olympic National Park annual pass or an America the Beautiful pass is also accepted. The park is cashless (credit/debit only).
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Food storage requirements vary by campsite — consult the current Olympic Wilderness Trip Planner map; some Elwha camps have bear wires, others require a hard-sided canister (free loaner canisters available at the Port Angeles Wilderness Information Center). The Elwha River and its tributaries are closed to fishing.
access.permit: Wilderness camping permit required for any overnight stay (essentially mandatory given the trail mileage involved); reserve via Recreation.gov. Cost is $8 per adult per night plus a non-refundable $6 reservation fee, or cover nightly fees with a $45 annual Olympic Wilderness Pass (reservation fee still applies). Summer-season (May 15-Oct 15) permit reservations release around mid-April.
access.closures: Olympic Hot Springs Road washout beyond Madison Falls currently closes vehicle access to the Whiskey Bend trailhead, adding roughly 7 miles of road approach each way — check NPS alerts before you go.
access.landManager: National Park Service — Olympic National Park, Daniel J. Evans Wilderness
access.land_manager: National Park Service — Olympic National Park (Olympic Wilderness)
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: Olympic National Park entrance pass/fee at the park boundary

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
bivy.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
bivy.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake
bivy.notes: The base camp for the route, about 4-4.5 mi and 2,200 ft from the Stuart Lake trailhead. Parties heading for the couloir generally camp toward the far, south end of the lake so they are already at the moraine in the morning; a large flat boulder there is a well-used pitch. In cold conditions, camping back in the trees off the shore is warmer and far more sheltered than the open lakeside. Typical starts from camp run between about 3 and 5 a.m., which puts you at the base of the couloir in the couple of hours before the sun reaches it.
bivy.water: The lake, which is often still part-frozen in the season this route is in condition.
bivy.permit: An Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit is required from 15 May to 31 October and must be obtained in advance through Recreation.gov, with the advance lottery running mid-February to 1 March. Group size is capped at eight, campfires are prohibited, dogs are not allowed anywhere in the permit area, and there is no dispersed camping between FR 7601 and Icicle Creek. Day use needs only a free self-issued wilderness permit. Because the quota season starts on 15 May, an early-spring ascent — when this couloir is normally in its best condition — falls outside the overnight permit requirement.
bivy.capacity: Numerous sites strung along the shoreline and more clustered at the north end. Under the overnight quota the Colchuck zone issues a small number of permits a day, group permits included, so the camp is never as crowded as the day-hiker traffic suggests.

bivy.name: Perfection Lake and Inspiration Lake basin camps
bivy.notes: The natural base for Prusik Peak's West Ridge and South Face, putting the approach at well under an hour of walking and scrambling to Prusik Pass. Most parties reach it over Aasgard Pass from Colchuck Lake, which is a steep loose grind with a heavy pack rather than a trail in any real sense. Camp on rock, sand or gravel and stay off the heather — the meadows here recover very slowly. No fires at any elevation in the basin.
bivy.water: Reliable — the chain of lakes and the connecting streams hold water all season
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. This is the hardest overnight permit in the area to draw; the advance lottery through recreation.gov is the main route in, with a small number of Core spots also released in the geofenced daily lottery at Leavenworth. A Core permit is the flexible one — it is valid for camping in any of the five zones (Core, Colchuck, Snow, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline).
bivy.capacity: Numerous hardened sites on granite benches and sand between the two lakes; the whole Core zone is held to roughly two dozen people a night, so it is never crowded once you are in

bivy.name: Gnome Tarn
bivy.notes: The tarn sits almost directly under Prusik's south side and gives the shortest approach of anywhere to the South Face routes and the West Ridge. Getting there means leaving the main basin route and scrambling up from around Perfection Lake toward Prusik Pass on a faint, easily lost path over granite. It is exposed and high, so a night here can be considerably colder and windier than the lakes below. The camping is on rock, which is both the right surface to use and the reason a level spot takes some hunting.
bivy.water: The tarn itself, though it is small and can drop low or silty late in a dry season; the lakes below are the fallback
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone, same permit and same lottery reality as the Perfection Lake camps. There is no separate allocation for climbers and no exemption for a single night below a route.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on slab and sand; realistically one or two parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass
bivy.notes: Crossing Prusik Pass and dropping north puts a party on the shaded side of the ridge with far fewer people around, while still leaving Prusik's West Ridge within a short reverse approach in the morning. The trade is that everything is on the wrong side of a pass, so the walk out over Aasgard at the end of the trip is longer. Tree cover here gives real shelter that the open basin camps do not, which matters if weather is forecast. Ground is soft in places, so pick an existing site rather than making a new one.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, with inflow streams running into late summer in most years
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment zone. It lies on the far side of Prusik Pass in the Lost World Plateau, but that ground is still Core, so the same lottery permit applies. Do not assume a quieter, less-visited corner sits outside the quota — it does not.
bivy.capacity: Several sheltered sites in the trees and on benches near the lake; quiet enough that a party usually has its choice

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

access.fees: $5/vehicle day-use fee (or $30 annual Recreation Pass) at the Snow Lakes Trailhead, paid via Recreation.gov Scan & Pay; $6 non-refundable fee to enter the overnight permit lottery.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

bivy.name: Shield Lake, north of Prusik Pass

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road

bivy.name: Tarn below Isolation Lake
bivy.notes: A climbers' base camp rather than a scenic one: an unnamed tarn a tier below Isolation Lake, the first large lake reached coming over Aasgard Pass. Chosen for easy water, comparatively few insects and shelter below the open upper benches, at the cost of about two miles with a little climbing to reach the peak. Fires are prohibited here, as everywhere in the basin.
bivy.water: The tarn, with a snowfield just above it feeding meltwater.
bivy.permit: Core Enchantment Zone overnight permit — see the note on the Inspiration Lake entry; the same rules apply everywhere in the basin.

bivy.name: Inspiration and Perfection Lakes
bivy.notes: The most used camping ground in the basin, on the benches and the bluff between the two lakes, and the closest general camp to the peak — the signed path toward Prusik Pass leaves the western shore of Perfection Lake. Open granite and heather, thoroughly worn in, and shared with mountain goats that come in for salt. The exposed benches right at Isolation and Tranquil Lakes are above treeline and windy by comparison.
bivy.water: The lakes.
bivy.permit: An Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit is required from 15 May to 31 October, and Prusik's camps lie in the Core Enchantment Zone, which is allocated by lottery. Maximum group size is eight. Camp only on ground already worn bare — do not clear vegetation, move rocks or build walls. Fires are prohibited anywhere above 5,000 ft or within half a mile of a lake, which rules them out at every camp in this basin; solid-fuel and wood-burning stoves are also prohibited above 5,000 ft, but liquid and canister gas stoves are allowed. Dogs are not permitted anywhere in the Enchantment Permit Area, and no stock is allowed in the Core Zone. Maximum stay is fourteen consecutive days. Two traps worth knowing: a Snow Zone permit lets you climb here for the day but you must camp at or below Upper Snow Lake, and a Colchuck Zone permit does not allow camping above the 6,500 ft contour below Aasgard Pass. A Core Zone permit, by contrast, allows camping in any of the five zones on the way in or out.
bivy.capacity: No published tent count for any site in the basin. The permit is the real constraint: the Core Zone quota counts people entering per day rather than groups, and the whole of a permitted group must camp together at one site.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
