bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the standard high camp for the route, on an open ridge crest of snow and pumice reached by a climbers' path leaving the PCT. Pumice takes stakes poorly — bring something to anchor to snow or rock. Fully open to weather in every direction, with a straight view up at the mountain. Everything above this is snow and glacier, so this is the last comfortable ground.
bivy.water: snowmelt; last running water is the creek crossings on the approach below
bivy.capacity: several parties spread along the ridge crest

bivy.name: Vista-Kennedy saddle
bivy.notes: PLANNED intermediate camp on the saddle where the route rounds Kennedy Peak and steps onto the Kennedy Glacier. Bivy sites exist here and it is used to shorten summit day, but it puts you above the last easy ground with nothing to hide behind.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: a couple of bivy-scale sites

bivy.name: 8,800 ft saddle at the foot of Frostbite Ridge
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the last dependable bivy before the crater. Rocky ridge ground at the top of the Kennedy Glacier's loose moraine, and it is exposed enough to cost you the night — one party was battered by wind here until dawn and concluded afterwards that a platform cut into the lee snow would have been the right call. Site low and downwind of the crest, not on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only; a documented trick is bagging snow on sun-warmed rock
bivy.capacity: a small tent or two on rock, better platforms cut into lee snow

bivy.name: Ledge near 9,900 ft below the ridge crux
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY only. A spot has been reported at about this height below the steep sections, and the party who found it said plainly they would not count on it being there. No shelter, extreme exposure, and immediately below the loose rock of the Rabbit Ears where warm dry conditions turn the ground overhead into a rockfall hazard. Use it if you must, never plan on it.
bivy.water: snowmelt only

access.notes: Northwest Forest Pass required for parking at North Fork Sauk Trailhead (no climbing permit required). White Chuck Trail (alternate approach) currently washed out; North Fork Sauk Trail #649 is primary access. Recommended to check current trail conditions with USDA Forest Service before departure.

bivy.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
bivy.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
bivy.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

bivy.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
bivy.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
bivy.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
bivy.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
bivy.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

bivy.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
bivy.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
bivy.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

bivy.name: Boulder Basin
bivy.notes: The standard planned high camp, in an open meadow basin at the treeline with the glacier toe above. It is a pleasant place — flowers, waterfalls, and correspondingly aggressive marmots and bugs — but earning it means a long approach and then a steep, unmaintained climbers' path straight up a forested ridge with a full pack. It is about ten miles from the road end, and the road itself has a long history of washouts, so confirm where the trailhead actually is before you plan the day.
bivy.water: Waterfalls and snowmelt streams run through the basin; dependable into late summer but shrinking as the season goes on. Filter it
bivy.permit: No backcountry permit is required for overnight use in this wilderness
bivy.capacity: Several established sites on heather and rock benches at treeline, spread through the basin between roughly 5,500 and 6,000 ft

bivy.name: Sitkum Creek / PCT junction camp
bivy.notes: A lower fallback for parties who run out of daylight on the long walk in, sitting where the climbers' path leaves the maintained trail. Below treeline, so it is sheltered and out of the weather, but it leaves the entire steep climbers' path plus 1,500 ft of gain before you are even at the standard camp.
bivy.water: Sitkum Creek
bivy.capacity: A small forested site or two just north of the trail junction

bivy.name: Kennedy Guard Station area
bivy.notes: The lowest planned stop, about 5.5 miles in and still widely used. Do not plan on soaking: the historic hot pool, lodge and guard station here were buried by the 2003 flood and debris flow and were never rebuilt. Useful as a first night for parties splitting the approach, or as a retreat in bad weather, but it is a long way and a lot of gain below the glacier.
bivy.water: The river and its tributaries
bivy.capacity: Popular established riverside sites

bivy.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
bivy.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
bivy.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
bivy.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

bivy.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
bivy.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
bivy.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

bivy.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
bivy.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
bivy.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

bivy.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
bivy.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30 annual day-use fee at White River Trailhead; Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency Pass, or Recreation.gov Digital Day Pass accepted
access.permit: Free self-issuing wilderness permit, available at the White River Trailhead — no quota or reservation required
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, which is this route's access. As of mid-2026, White River Road (FR 6400) itself was not on the Wenatchee River Ranger District's storm-damage closure list, but numerous other district roads remain closed through Dec 31, 2027 following the December 2025 storm event, and Stage 1 fire restrictions are common in late summer — check current Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest alerts before driving

bivy.name: Napeequa Valley floor near Louis Creek
bivy.notes: This is the way into the Napeequa for Luahna Peak, Chalangin Peak, the Napeequa side of Clark, and Tenpeak's east end. From the Little Giant trailhead the very first obstacle is fording the Chiwawa itself — the old bridge is gone and its remains are in the brush by the water, so the crossing is a wade and its depth decides the trip. The trail then climbs, drops a couple of hundred feet through the Little Giant Creek drainage and switchbacks up open meadow to Little Giant Pass at about 6,400 feet, roughly four and a half miles in, with Clark Mountain filling the view on the far side. Dropping into the Napeequa costs about two thousand feet, and from the valley floor the standard progression is two miles up-valley to Louis Creek and then a crossing of the Napeequa before climbing out toward Butterfly Butte. This valley camp is what a party uses on the way in when the day runs out at the bottom of the descent, or on the way out with the pass still to reclimb. Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
bivy.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

bivy.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
bivy.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
bivy.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

bivy.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
bivy.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

bivy.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
bivy.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
bivy.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
bivy.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

bivy.name: Mackinaw Shelter camp, North Fork Sauk
bivy.notes: This is the first night for a Glacier Peak climb by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, which is the route most parties use now that the western approaches have gone. It sits about five flat miles up the North Fork Sauk trail through genuinely large old-growth, and the walk in is easy enough that a party arriving late in the day can still reach it. The shelter the camp is named for collapsed years ago and there is no roof here — treat the name as a map label rather than a promise. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the next three miles gain three thousand feet in relentless switchbacks with no reliable water on them, so this is the place to drink, fill everything you carry, and start that climb cool. Coming out, most parties pass straight through. Access is the problem rather than the camp: the December 2025 storms damaged roads and trails across this side of the wilderness and reaching the North Fork Sauk trailhead at all should be confirmed before the drive, not assumed.
bivy.water: Excellent and year-round — the North Fork Sauk runs right past the camp, and this is the last dependable water before White Pass
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in and deposited at the trailhead box. Party size is capped at twelve, counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass covers parking at the road end. Fires are not banned outright at this elevation but summer forest-wide restrictions routinely prohibit all open flame from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites in the trees on a river bench, comfortably two or three parties, and the only organised camping in the valley bottom

bivy.name: White Pass and the Foam Creek benches under White Mountain
bivy.notes: White Pass at about 5,900 feet is the second night for a Glacier Peak climb, or the first if a strong party pushes the whole eight and a half miles and three thousand feet from the road in one go. It is the point where the North Fork Sauk trail meets the long-distance crest trail and where the climbing approach turns east. From here a boot path runs east-northeast under the southeast side of White Mountain for a bit over a mile toward a high shoulder, then the Foam Creek path traverses on toward an eastern col at around 6,600 feet for the first view of the mountain. Parties who want to break the approach differently camp somewhere along that traverse rather than at the pass itself, which trades a sheltered established site for wind and a shorter summit day. It is exposed ground once you leave the pass, with nothing to hide behind in a thunderstorm, and the traverse is genuinely confusing in fog.
bivy.water: A small spring and snowmelt at the pass, dependable early but often down to a trickle by late season; the benches toward Foam Creek hold snowmelt into midsummer and then dry out
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person party limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Camp on the existing bare sites — this is fragile subalpine meadow that recovers slowly and is heavily used. Carry a stove; open flame is inappropriate here and is usually prohibited outright under summer restrictions.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites just south of the pass, plus scattered ground on the benches east of it; a popular crossroads with a long-distance trail running through it, so expect other parties in July and August

bivy.name: Kennedy Ridge and the Glacier Creek camps, Suiattle side
bivy.notes: This is the base for Glacier Peak's Kennedy Glacier and for the Frostbite Ridge line above it, and since the White Chuck approach died it is the only practical way at the mountain's north and west sides. The walk in is long even when the road is open — the Suiattle River trail runs about seven miles to the river bridge and the crest trail then carries you south toward Kennedy Ridge, so this is a full day before the climbing camp is even in sight. Kennedy Creek has no bridge and will not get one; the standard tactic is to camp short of it and cross in the morning when the flow is at its lowest, using whatever logs are currently in place rather than wading the main channel. Above the forest the route climbs the ridge and the glacier toward the saddle between the Kennedy and Vista glaciers at around 8,000 feet, where bivouac sites exist for parties willing to sleep on snow and rock with no shelter and no clean water. With the road washed out the trailhead is still reachable on foot or by bike from the closure point, which adds roughly nine miles each way to an approach that was already the longest on the mountain.
bivy.water: Glacier Creek and Kennedy Creek are both right there and both silty with glacial flour — let it settle or filter accordingly. Higher on the ridge water disappears entirely by late season and has to be carried or melted.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Suiattle road end. Stove only above the forest. Check the road order before driving: the Suiattle River road washed out about four and a half miles in during the December 2025 storms, temporary bridge work was scheduled across the middle of the 2026 season, and the campgrounds and trailheads up that road were shut for the season while it stood.
bivy.capacity: Forested sites in ones and twos scattered along the crest trail near the creek crossings, plus rougher bivouac ground higher on the ridge; nothing organised, and no single site takes a large party

bivy.name: Boulder Basin above Sitkum Creek — and the White Chuck situation
bivy.notes: Boulder Basin sits somewhere around 5,500 to 6,000 feet on a rib south of Sitkum Creek and is the historic high camp for the Sitkum Glacier, once the shortest and most popular route up Glacier Peak. The approach that made it popular no longer exists, and the story is worth getting right rather than repeating old published mileage. In October 2003 a storm put a record flood down the White Chuck, a debris flow off the mountain buried Kennedy Hot Springs under about five feet of material, and the river rebuilt its own valley floor. The hot springs are gone — not damaged, gone, and not being rebuilt. By 2006 less than a third of the White Chuck River trail survived and there are no plans to repair it. The road reopened partway in 2011 to a point near the old trailhead area, which for a while allowed a long road walk and a rough approach up what remained, but it is closed again from under four miles in and the surviving trail is a treacherous bushwhack rather than a route. Anything you read describing five and a half easy miles to the hot springs and a steep climbers' path to the basin is describing an approach that has not been available for twenty years. Parties wanting the north and west sides of the mountain now go in from the Suiattle instead.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams through the basin, dependable through the climbing season and thinning late
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit and a twelve-person limit still apply in theory. In practice the binding constraint is the road: the White Chuck road is closed from a little under four miles in all the way to its far end, and the trail beyond it is not maintained and not going to be. Treat any plan that relies on this basin as needing a specific check with the district first.
bivy.capacity: Open basin ground with room for several tents; historically the busiest camp on the mountain, and now one of the emptiest

access.fees: No fee or permit charge to climb or camp — a free self-issue wilderness permit is completed at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass is required to park at the trailhead.
access.rules: Standard Glacier Peak Wilderness rules: campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft elevation (effectively all of this route), camp at least 200 ft from water and trails where possible, and pack out all trash.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register; no quota or reservation required.
access.closures: As of the 2026 season, FS Road 23 (White Chuck River Road) is closed by Forest Order #06-05-25-02 from milepost 3.7 to its end at the FS Road 27 (Rat Trap Pass) junction, due to flood damage — this adds roughly 7 miles (14 round trip) of road-walking to the approach. Note: this closure order took effect March 19, 2025 (originally through Dec 31, 2025, and still active per spring 2026 NF alerts), so it predates and is unrelated to the separate, much larger December 2025 Pacific Northwest atmospheric-river floods — the road damage behind this order is from an earlier storm. Separately, White Chuck River Trail #643 and Kennedy Hot Springs have never been fully rebuilt since the October 2003 flood destroyed the springs and buried sections of trail, so the route between the old trailhead and Sitkum Creek remains rough, brushy, and involves unbridged crossings. Check current Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alerts before heading out, as access has changed repeatedly over the past two decades.

access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads — $5/day or $30/year.

bivy.name: Glacier Gap
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for Glacier Peak by the Cool Glacier and Gerdine Ridge, and the single most-used climbing camp on the mountain. It sits at about 7,300 feet at the head of the basin, reached by crossing what is left of the White Chuck Glacier northeast from the White Pass area — and what is left is the point, because that glacier has retreated faster than almost anything else in the range and the crossing is now largely bare rock, pumice and meltwater ponds rather than ice. From camp the route works up the ridge to about 8,400 feet, traverses onto the upper Suiattle Glacier, gains the upper Cool Glacier around 9,200 feet and climbs it westward to regain the ridge for the summit. Summit day from here runs long by any measure and thirteen hours camp to camp is normal rather than slow. Being a gap it funnels wind, so build or use the rock walls. Most parties take three days from the North Fork Sauk road and a fourth is worth having for weather.
bivy.water: Meltwater streams off the surrounding snowfields, running through most of the climbing season but silty; late in a hot summer it can be reduced to a drip from the base of a snow patch, so scout it on arrival rather than at dinner time
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit. No fires — this is bare rock, pumice and alpine ground above treeline with no wood and nothing that recovers. Twelve-person party limit. Human waste needs carrying out or burying properly well away from the meltwater, which everybody camped here is drinking.
bivy.capacity: A large basin with many bivouac sites and rock-walled platforms — it takes a lot of parties without feeling crowded, and there is always room to build another windbreak

Crossing the Napeequa is a real decision rather than a formality: it is glacier-fed, it runs high through early summer and it peaks in the afternoon, so cross in the morning and be willing to walk the bank looking for something better.
bivy.water: The Napeequa runs the length of the valley and is heavy with glacial silt off Clark and Luahna, so it needs settling as well as filtering; Louis Creek and the side streams run clearer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Little Giant trailhead, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove rather than fire in the meadow. Both closures that matter land on this approach: the Chiwawa River road is shut above Atkinson Flat under a multi-year storm order, and the 2026 fire closure named the Little Giant trail itself along with the Napeequa trails and the roads either side, running from mid-August to the end of October.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground on the valley flats and in the timber edge — no developed sites, room for a couple of parties, and rarely anybody else there

bivy.name: Butterfly Butte and the Pilz Glacier basin camps
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Luahna Peak and Chalangin Peak and the Napeequa-side base for Clark Mountain, roughly eleven hundred feet above the Napeequa floor after the river crossing near Louis Creek. The benches around Butterfly Butte at about 5,850 feet are the comfortable choice and look straight across at Clark; a broad basin below the Pilz Glacier headwall around 6,200 feet is the higher option and shortens summit day meaningfully. Parties pushing for a very early start use bivouac ground higher again on the northeast ridge, at roughly 6,800 and 7,200 feet, where there is no water and no shelter. Luahna is reached over the Pilz Glacier, so an ice axe, crampons and glacier gear belong on any list here. Chalangin sits half a mile northwest of Luahna and is more often taken by its own north side, bypassing the glacier, than by traversing the connecting ridge from Luahna — the traverse is long and the direct approach is the better plan. These are lightly visited summits and the register entries are years apart, so assume no boot track, no other party and no help.
bivy.water: A stream serves the benches around 5,850 to 6,200 feet and is the practical water for this camp; there is a pond at about 6,500 feet below the glacier, and above that it is snowmelt or nothing
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the Little Giant trailhead. No fires this high — carry a stove. Camp on bare ground and rock rather than the heather benches. Subject to the same Chiwawa road closure and 2026 fire closure as the valley below it.
bivy.capacity: Small flat clearings on the benches around the butte for one or two parties, and higher up a broad basin under the glacier headwall with room for several; everything above is genuine bivouac ground rather than campsites

bivy.name: Boulder Pass and Thunder Basin, White River
bivy.notes: This is the standard base for Clark Mountain and the reason Clark is a White River peak rather than a Little Giant one. From the trailhead at about 2,300 feet the White River trail runs flat for four miles, then the Boulder Creek trail turns east and climbs for another seven, crossing Boulder Creek at around 4,000 feet — a wade or a log, and high water there turns parties round early in the season. Good camps exist in a large open basin at about 4,900 feet and again just below the pass around 6,000 feet, with the pass itself at about 6,200 feet holding dry ground even when there is snow about. From the pass the Walrus Glacier route traverses the basin east of the ridge point, crosses the northeast ridge around 6,700 feet and gains the glacier for the east side of the mountain; the whole thing runs to about twenty-five miles round trip and six and a half thousand feet of gain. Tenpeak Mountain is served from the same trailhead by a different drainage — six miles up the White River, then an old unmaintained sheep path toward Thunder Creek and Thunder Basin, with dense slide alder between roughly 4,200 and 5,000 feet that is the hardest part of the day. Tenpeak is a technical summit with a north couloir and a milder-looking southeast face, it sees very few ascents, and most parties want a third day to climb it properly from a basin camp rather than pushing it in one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and streams through the basin below the pass and at the pass itself well into the season; Thunder Basin runs on creeks that are dependable in summer. The lower Boulder Creek crossing is the water hazard rather than the water supply.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Stove only up here. The White River road was inside the 2026 fire closure that ran from mid-August to the end of October along with the Chiwawa side, so this approach and the Little Giant one were shut at the same time by the same order — do not assume that losing one leaves the other.
bivy.capacity: Open ground at the pass with plenty of dry spots for several tents, a good basin camp about a mile below it, and separate rough ground over in Thunder Basin for one or two parties

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass (or America the Beautiful interagency pass) required to park at either the White River or North Fork Sauk trailhead.
access.rules: Standard Glacier Peak Wilderness rules: maximum group size 12 people/stock combined, camp at least 200 ft from water and trails where possible, no wheeled or mechanized equipment, pack out all trash and waste.
access.permit: Free, self-issued wilderness permit required at the trailhead register for all Glacier Peak Wilderness travel (day and overnight).
access.closures: CLOSED RIGHT NOW: Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead, which is this route's access. White River Road (FR 6400) has a history of flash-flood and winter-storm washout closures (e.g., a 2023 flash flood closed it, and winter-storm damage has repeatedly required repairs); check the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest current-conditions page before driving in. The sheep-trail approach beyond the White River Trail is not an official, maintained trail and is frequently choked with brush and blowdown after heavy-snow winters.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (White River side, Chelan County); Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District (North Fork Sauk/Suiattle side, Snohomish County) — the summit sits on the shared boundary within the Glacier Peak Wilderness.
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass

bivy.name: Last stream crossing, top of the forest
bivy.notes: Listed for the water rather than for the camping, and the water is the point. The trail climbs steeply from the trailhead through about a dozen switchbacks in the first mile and stays in deep forest for two and a half, crossing several small creeks on the way; the highest of them sits right where the trees thin into heather and huckleberry. Above this line the mountain gives you nothing. Parties heading to the benches or the crest should stop here, top up, and accept carrying the weight for the last stretch. Late in a dry summer even these crossings run thin, so do not assume the lower ones are still flowing on the way down. Elevation is not stated because the exact crossing shifts with the season and the snowpack; navigate to it by the transition out of the timber, not by an altimeter reading.
bivy.water: THIS IS THE LAST RELIABLE WATER ON THE MOUNTAIN, at roughly mile 2.7 where the final creeks cross the tread. Treat it. Everything on the ridge above is dry, so fill every container here whether or not you intend to camp
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary the trail crosses around mile 2. No overnight permit is required and none is issued. Twelve-person party limit. Campfires are not permitted on this trail, so carry a stove. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required at the trailhead; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid here. Black bears work this slope in huckleberry season and food must be secured overnight
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on rough ground beside the trail where the timber gives out; there is no established site and the slope is steep, so flat spots are few

bivy.name: Open benches on the broad ridge
bivy.notes: The best camping on the mountain if you are willing to haul water, and the natural base for the south ridge scramble. A series of level shelves on a broad, open ridge above treeline, past a viewpoint knob near 5,200 ft, with Baker, Shuksan and Sefrit filling the skyline and the Border Peaks and the Pickets beyond. From here the maintained trail continues to its end on the shoulder and the scramble to the summits goes on from there, so a camp at the benches leaves a short and pleasant summit morning. The slope faces south and melts early, so this is usually accessible from late June, sometimes earlier; the trade is that it bakes and stays dry all summer. It is fully exposed to wind and to weather rolling in from the west with nothing to duck behind. Excellent huckleberries in early autumn, and bears know it.
bivy.water: NONE. Everything must be carried up from the last crossing in the forest. Snow patches linger into July in shaded pockets and can be melted early in the season, but by August the whole crest is dry
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass at the trailhead. No campfires. Camp on bare ground, gravel or an existing flat rather than in the heather, and store food securely against bears
bivy.capacity: Two or three small tents spread across the benches, kept apart so the heather is not trampled into one bare patch

bivy.name: Ridge crest at the end of the maintained trail
bivy.notes: The highest ground with anything like a flat pitch, where the maintained trail ends on Goat Mountain's shoulder and the route becomes a steep boot path up grass and heather to the false summit and the west peak. The crest carries on upward from here toward 5,600 ft and above, and the east peak, which is the higher of the two, is a further meadow scramble along the ridge with no trail. Camping here shortens summit day to almost nothing, which is the only argument for it: it is stony, cramped and completely exposed, and it is the driest spot on a dry mountain. Snow can lie across the upper slope into July and the grass traverse above is genuinely slippery when wet, so this is a fair-weather choice. Sunrise and sunset from the crest are the reason people put up with all of it.
bivy.water: NONE, and the nearest is the forest crossings far below. In early season there are snow patches on the north side of the crest to melt; from midsummer there is nothing at all
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the trailhead, no campfires. This is national forest rather than national park — the park boundary lies well east beyond Hannegan Pass — so no park backcountry permit applies
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on the shoulder where the tread runs out; small, stony and windy

bivy.name: Basin below the east peak
bivy.notes: The one camp on Goat Mountain that solves the water problem, in the basin lying east and below the higher east peak, seen from the overlook near the top of the maintained trail. It has ample flat terrain and running water, which nothing on the ridge does. The cost is that reaching it means leaving the trail entirely and dropping off the crest on trackless ground, which is more commitment than most parties want for a scramble that can be done in a day from the benches — so it is chosen mainly by people camping two nights, going for the east summit as well as the west, or arriving too late in the season for the crest to hold snow. Approach it from the end of the maintained trail rather than trying to contour in low. No elevation is given because the usable ground spreads across the basin floor rather than sitting at one identifiable spot.
bivy.water: Present, which makes this basin unique here — snowmelt streams and pools that last well into the season, unlike anything on the crest. Treat it, and check that it is still running before relying on it in a dry late summer
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass at the trailhead, no campfires. Camp on durable ground away from the water and secure food overnight
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents with room to spread out; the most generous ground on the mountain

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the trailhead — $5 for a day pass or $30 annual; the Washington Discover Pass is not honored.
access.rules: Pack out human waste (blue bags) — no burial or glacier deposition. Some approaches cross into North Cascades National Park land on the upper mountain, where a free NPS backcountry permit is required only if camping overnight past the boundary.
access.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead register once the trail enters Mount Baker Wilderness (~2 miles in); maximum party size 12.
access.closures: Forest Road 32 is gated/closed to vehicles in winter (it's groomed/used for backcountry ski and snowshoe touring up to about 6 miles) and reopens as snowpack allows, typically by late spring — check the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie NF current conditions page before early-season or late-fall trips.
access.landManager: Mount Baker Ranger District, Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mount Baker Wilderness)
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker Ranger District) — Mount Baker Wilderness, with some upper routes crossing into North Cascades National Park
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at most trailheads — $30/year or $5/day.

bivy.name: Conrad Meadows and Surprise Lake, South Fork Tieton
bivy.notes: This is the correct side of the range for Gilbert Peak's Conrad Glacier and Meade Glacier routes, and there is no sensible way to reach either from the Snowgrass trailheads — the two approaches are separated by the whole crest. From the road end the trail runs level through meadows for around four miles before the loop divides, and the northern fork leads toward Surprise Lake and eventually the benches, waterfall and Barren Lake below the Conrad Glacier. Most parties camp once in the basin and climb from there, since the glacier and the traverse across the Meade to Gilbert's south ridge make for a long day on their own. The meadows at the road end are a legitimate first night if you arrive late, but they are low, buggy in early summer and a long way from anything. This side is far quieter than Snowgrass, and the corresponding cost is a much longer approach and much less traffic if something goes wrong.
bivy.water: The South Fork Tieton and its tributaries throughout, and the lake itself higher up; abundant by the standards of the range's east side but still to be treated
bivy.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead board once you cross into the wilderness. Camping is prohibited within 100 feet of lakes. Note this trailhead sits on the drier eastern forest rather than the Gifford Pinchot side, so confirm which parking pass the board is asking for before leaving the car. Heavy stock use means the meadows are shared with horse parties.
bivy.capacity: Primitive dispersed and stock camping in the broad meadows at the road end, and established backcountry sites at Surprise Lake several miles up the loop; no reservations and no numbered sites

access.fees: Some Goat Rocks trailheads require a day-use fee or valid recreation pass.
access.permit: Free, self-issued wilderness permit required at the trailhead.
access.closures: No campfires; no camping within 100 ft of the PCT or lakes; Shoe Lake basin and Snowgrass Flats closed to camping.
access.landManager: Goat Rocks Wilderness (Gifford Pinchot / Okanogan-Wenatchee NF boundary); borders the Yakama Indian Reservation, closed to public access except along the PCT
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful pass at some trailheads.

bivy.capacity: Primitive dispersed and stock camping in the broad meadows at the road end, and established backcountry sites at Surprise Lake several miles up the loop; no reservations and no numbered sites

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or equivalent Interagency Pass may be required at trailhead parking
access.notes: Straddles Gifford Pinchot NF (west) and Okanogan-Wenatchee NF (east, White Pass side); the standard approach (Snowgrass Flat, Berry Patch trailheads) is on the Gifford Pinchot side.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) per 36 CFR 261.58(f).
access.permit: Free, self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit required at the trailhead
access.closures: No camping within 100 ft of the Pacific Crest Trail or lakes; group size and campfire restrictions apply within the Wilderness.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Naches Ranger District) for the Conrad Meadows approach; the summit itself sits within Goat Rocks Wilderness (jointly administered with Gifford Pinchot National Forest)
access.land_manager: Gifford Pinchot National Forest (Cowlitz Valley Ranger District) — Goat Rocks Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Not required at Snowgrass Flat; required at Berry Patch trailhead — $5/day or $30/year Northwest Forest Pass.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful Interagency Pass

bivy.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

bivy.name: Goat Lake basin
bivy.notes: The other basin camp on this side, reached by the loop that swings north from the Snowgrass trail, and a reasonable alternative when the Snowgrass sites are taken. It sits under Old Snowy's western flank and is slightly further from the crest than Snowgrass, which costs you distance on a summit morning but buys a quieter night. The basin is a cirque and holds snow late, so early-season parties frequently find the lake iced and the campsites buried — the trade for a genuinely alpine setting. Vegetation here is fragile and slow-growing, which is why the existing sites are the only acceptable ones.
bivy.water: The lake, plus outlet streams; the lake can stay partly frozen into midsummer, in which case take water from the outlet
bivy.permit: Same free self-issued wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass as the rest of this trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED within a quarter mile of the lake shore, so bring a stove and do not plan on a fire. The 100-foot setback from lakes applies here and is actively enforced by the condition of the ground.
bivy.capacity: A modest number of established sites scattered back from the shore; the closest ground to the water is off limits, which cuts the usable count sharply

bivy.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
bivy.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.
bivy.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. CAMPFIRES ARE SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITED at this location by wilderness regulation, and the 100-foot setback from the Pacific Crest Trail applies — the trail passes right through, so a legal pitch here takes some walking.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small tents on the crest at best; there is no shelter left to sleep in and the ground is broken rock

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
bivy.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

access.fees: Valid Recreation Pass / Northwest Forest Pass required at the trailhead
access.notes: Straddles Gifford Pinchot NF (west) and Okanogan-Wenatchee NF (east, White Pass side); the standard approach (Snowgrass Flat, Berry Patch trailheads) is on the Gifford Pinchot side.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) per 36 CFR 261.58(f).
access.permit: Free, self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit required at the trailhead
access.closures: No camping or campfires at Snowgrass Flats itself (camp at designated sites such as Lower Snowgrass or Bypass Camp instead); no camping within 100 ft of the PCT or lakes.
access.landManager: Gifford Pinchot National Forest (Cowlitz Valley Ranger District)
access.land_manager: Gifford Pinchot National Forest (Cowlitz Valley Ranger District) — Goat Rocks Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Not required at Snowgrass Flat; required at Berry Patch trailhead — $5/day or $30/year Northwest Forest Pass.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful Interagency Pass

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass ($5/day or $30/yr) or America the Beautiful interagency annual pass ($80) required to park at the Snowgrass Flat/Berry Patch trailhead; wilderness entry itself is free.
access.rules: Group size (people + stock combined) is capped at 12. Camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself and within 100 ft of the PCT or any lake shoreline (Dana Yelverton Shelter excepted). Campfires are banned in Shoe Lake Basin, at Dana Yelverton Shelter, and within 1/4 mile of Goat Lake.
access.permit: Free, self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk (Snowgrass Flat/Berry Patch) — required for all Goat Rocks Wilderness entries, no quota.
access.closures: Forest Road 2150 (the spur to Chambers Lake/Berry Patch/Snowgrass Flat trailheads) is gated and closed to wheeled vehicles each winter for snow-recreation use, typically into early June depending on snowpack — check Gifford Pinchot NF road alerts before an early-season trip.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful Interagency Pass

bivy.name: Climbers Bivouac
bivy.notes: The summer roadhead for Monitor Ridge, and effectively the only place to sleep close to that route, since the mountain above 4,800 feet is closed to camping. bivy.name: Marble Mountain Sno-Park
bivy.notes: The winter and shoulder-season staging point, and the start of the Worm Flows route when the road to Climbers Bivouac is under snow. Avalanche conditions on the Worm Flows gullies, not the permit, are the season's real gate.
bivy.water: None liquid in winter — melt snow, and carry water in the shoulder seasons. Two vault toilets are provided, and a warming hut is open through the winter months
bivy.permit: A Washington Sno-Park permit is required from December 1 to March 31, and this is a non-motorised area. The Mount St. Helens climbing permit is still required for anyone above 4,800 feet, but through the winter window it is free, self-issued at the trailhead and unlimited — the single easiest time of year to climb this mountain from a paperwork point of view. The 4,800-foot camping prohibition applies in winter exactly as it does in summer.
bivy.capacity: Two large plowed lots plus adjacent forest; winter parties routinely pitch tents in and beside the lots, so capacity is generous and informal rather than defined

access.fees: A Washington Sno-Park permit (or Forest Service equivalent) is required to park at Marble Mountain Sno-Park during the winter Sno-Park season.
access.notes: Daily quota: 350 climbers/day (Apr 1–May 14), 110 climbers/day (May 15–Oct 31). This is a distinct fee/permit system from both Mount Rainier’s $82 Climbing Cost Recovery Fee and Mount Adams’ $20 Climbing Pass — do not conflate them.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12. Stay at least 30 ft back from the crater rim — cornices are unstable and have caused fatalities; entry into the crater is strictly prohibited. Blue bags required for human waste above treeline.
access.permit: November 1-March 31: climbing permits are free and self-issued at the Marble Mountain Sno-Park kiosk. April 1-October 31: permits are limited and must be purchased in advance on Recreation.gov (released one month at a time), since the quota season applies mountain-wide regardless of which trailhead is used.
access.closures: Crater entry is prohibited year-round; stay back from the cornice-prone rim edge.
