bivy.name: Snowgrass Flat area backcountry camps
bivy.notes: The standard base for Old Snowy and Ives Peak, and for the West Route on Gilbert. The name misleads: the flat proper is a closed meadow and the legal camping is in the timber and on the benches a little below it, around 6,000 to 6,300 feet, roughly three to four miles from the road. From here Old Snowy is a walk-up on a spur off the crest, Ives is a scree-and-ridge scramble off the col between the two, and Gilbert is a long committing day traversing goat ledges across Cispus Basin at 7,400 to 7,600 feet before the southwest slope. This is the most heavily used corner of the wilderness and the parking fills on weekdays, so arriving Friday evening for a Saturday climb is a poor plan. The meadows hold snow into July in a normal year, which is pleasant for the scrambles and awkward for finding a dry pitch.
bivy.water: Goat Creek and its tributaries run through the basin and are reliable well into the season; treat everything
bivy.permit: Goat Rocks Wilderness permit, free and self-issued from the box at the trailhead — no reservation and no fee. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at Berry Patch or the Snowgrass trailhead. CAMPING WITHIN SNOWGRASS FLAT ITSELF IS PROHIBITED, along with camping within 100 feet of the Pacific Crest Trail and within 100 feet of any lake. Camp only in pre-existing sites.
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites in the timber and benches below and around the meadow; no quota and no numbered pads, so capacity is whatever the pre-existing sites hold, and on summer weekends that is fully subscribed

bivy.name: Goat Lake basin
bivy.notes: The other basin camp on this side, reached by the loop that swings north from the Snowgrass trail, and a reasonable alternative when the Snowgrass sites are taken. It sits under Old Snowy's western flank and is slightly further from the crest than Snowgrass, which costs you distance on a summit morning but buys a quieter night. The basin is a cirque and holds snow late, so early-season parties frequently find the lake iced and the campsites buried — the trade for a genuinely alpine setting. Vegetation here is fragile and slow-growing, which is why the existing sites are the only acceptable ones.
bivy.water: The lake, plus outlet streams; the lake can stay partly frozen into midsummer, in which case take water from the outlet
bivy.permit: Same free self-issued wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass as the rest of this trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED within a quarter mile of the lake shore, so bring a stove and do not plan on a fire. The 100-foot setback from lakes applies here and is actively enforced by the condition of the ground.
bivy.capacity: A modest number of established sites scattered back from the shore; the closest ground to the water is off limits, which cuts the usable count sharply

bivy.name: Dana Yelverton Shelter site
bivy.notes: A named point on the crest just below Old Snowy, where a stone shelter once stood and where a hiker died in a summer blizzard in the early 1960s. The shelter is now a scatter of rubble and offers no protection whatsoever, so treat the name as a map label rather than a resource. Its value is position: it is the highest place on this side you can legally sleep, which shortens a summit morning on Old Snowy to almost nothing and puts Ives within an easy pre-dawn traverse. The cost is that it is fully exposed at the high point of the Pacific Crest Trail in Washington, with no water, no wind shelter and no retreat that is not a long descent. The history is the warning: weather arrives here fast and out of season.
bivy.water: None. Snow patches persist nearby into midsummer and can be melted, but from late summer this is a dry camp and water must be carried up from the basin
bivy.permit: Free self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit. CAMPFIRES ARE SPECIFICALLY PROHIBITED at this location by wilderness regulation, and the 100-foot setback from the Pacific Crest Trail applies — the trail passes right through, so a legal pitch here takes some walking.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small tents on the crest at best; there is no shelter left to sleep in and the ground is broken rock

bivy.name: Chambers Lake Campground
bivy.notes: The obvious drive-in base for the Goat Rocks crest, under a mile from both the Berry Patch and Snowgrass trailheads, so you can sleep at the car and be walking at first light without the four-mile carry to Snowgrass. That makes it the right choice for a car-to-car attempt on Old Snowy, and a sensible staging night before shouldering a pack for Ives or Gilbert. It is heavily timbered and low, so there is no view and no acclimatisation value, and the approach roads are long gravel with washboard — allow more driving time than the mileage suggests. Snow closes the access road well into spring, which is the practical limit on early-season attempts from this side.
bivy.water: No potable water on site — bring your own or filter from the lake. Vault toilets are provided
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed for the campground itself, since it sits outside the boundary. A modest per-night fee has been charged in some seasons and waived in others, so carry cash and check the board on arrival. A Northwest Forest Pass is still required at Berry Patch and the Snowgrass trailhead a short distance up the road.
bivy.capacity: A small forested campground with basic single and double sites; first come, first served

access.fees: $5 per vehicle per day, or a $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass, required at the Snowgrass Flats (Trail #96) trailhead; payable by cash/check envelope, Recreation.gov Scan & Pay, or a valid Recreation Pass.
access.notes: Straddles Gifford Pinchot NF (west) and Okanogan-Wenatchee NF (east, White Pass side); the standard approach (Snowgrass Flat, Berry Patch trailheads) is on the Gifford Pinchot side.
access.rules: Group size (people plus stock) capped at 12. No camping at Snowgrass Flat itself or in Shoe Lake Basin, and no camping within 100 ft of any lakeshore. Campfires are banned in Shoe Lake Basin, at the Dana Yelverton Shelter, and within a quarter-mile of Goat Lake's shoreline. Leave No Trace / pack out all waste.
access.permit: Free, self-issued Goat Rocks Wilderness permit at the Snowgrass Flats trailhead kiosk — no quota, reservation, or fee for the wilderness permit itself.
access.closures: Forest Road 21, the access road to Snowgrass Flats, was washed out near milepost 3 from US-12 in the December 2025 atmospheric-river floods (with a second washout reported further south); the Forest Service was still assessing repairs. Confirm current road status with the Cowlitz Valley Ranger District, (360) 497-1103, before driving in. FR-2150 is separately closed to wheeled vehicles roughly Dec 1–Apr 1 for winter recreation.
access.landManager: Gifford Pinchot National Forest — Cowlitz Valley Ranger District, 10024 US-12, Randle, WA 98377, (360) 497-1100
access.land_manager: Gifford Pinchot National Forest (Cowlitz Valley Ranger District) — Goat Rocks Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Not required at Snowgrass Flat; required at Berry Patch trailhead — $5/day or $30/year Northwest Forest Pass.

bivy.name: Lower Gothic Basin — the slab benches and tarns short of Foggy Lake
bivy.notes: The basin lip, where the climbers' trail finally stops climbing and opens out among tarns and slabs, sits about a mile below Foggy Lake and is the quieter alternative to it. For GOTHIC PEAK this costs almost nothing — Gothic's ordinary line goes up from the basin side and the extra mile to the lake buys no advantage — while for DEL CAMPO it does cost you, because Del Campo's southeast ridge is entered from the north side of Foggy Lake and camping short of it adds a mile and several hundred feet to summit day. Choose accordingly: this is the Gothic camp and the bad-weather camp, not the Del Campo one. Getting here means the Weden Creek trail, which is a mining-era path rather than a graded one — steep, direct, rocky, with slabby sections that are genuinely unpleasant when wet and a few spots where hands come out. It gains close to three thousand feet in under five miles after the flat mile of road walking. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to dig in, so waste comes out with you. Snow lies here well into July in an ordinary year and the timing moves by weeks between a heavy and a light winter. Old adits and workings are scattered through the basin and some are open holes in bad light; keep to the used ground.
bivy.water: Melt streams and the tarns run through the basin most of the season and thin out late in a hot August. TREAT THE PROVENANCE OF THIS WATER SERIOUSLY: the whole drainage is old mining ground and metals leached from tailings, arsenic in particular, are documented through this valley system. Filters, tablets and boiling deal with organisms and do nothing whatever about dissolved metals. Draw from snowmelt and small feeder runnels well above any workings rather than from anything draining a spoil heap, and if in doubt carry it in.
bivy.permit: National forest land OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no camping permit, no quota and no party-size limit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass to leave a vehicle. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED throughout the basin regardless of season, and there is nothing to burn anyway — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small parties spread wide. The ground is polished slab, boulder and thin heather with pockets of flat gravel rather than any built-up site, so it takes two or three tents comfortably and rewards walking another five minutes to find your own rather than crowding the first flat spot.

bivy.name: Weden Creek trail junction, one mile up the Monte Cristo road
bivy.notes: This is for the party that runs long rather than the party that plans well. The walk out from Gothic Basin is a steep descent on greasy slab in fading light and it is where people get hurt on this approach, so a known flat spot at the bottom of the climbing — before the last mile of road back to Barlow Pass — is worth recording. It is also a legitimate soft start: a party arriving late can walk the flat mile up the old road, sleep beside the creek, and be climbing at first light with the whole basin ahead of them rather than the drive still in their legs. The first three quarters of a mile of the Weden Creek trail runs almost level along the creek before it turns uphill in earnest, and that stretch is where the usable ground is. Do not confuse this with the Monte Cristo townsite four miles further up the same road, which is a different place serving different peaks. The road from Barlow Pass is gated to vehicles and stays that way, so everything here is on foot. Being valley bottom, it is buggy in early summer and stays cold and damp long into the morning.
bivy.water: Weden Creek runs right there and is the easiest water on the whole approach, but it drains the same mineralised ground as the basin above and carries the same metals question. Treat it as washing and cooking-fire water at best, and carry drinking water in.
bivy.permit: National forest, outside wilderness, so dispersed camping is allowed and needs no permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Fires are a poor idea in a wooded valley bottom under summer restrictions and are usually banned outright from midsummer; assume a stove.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents at most, on flat forest ground near where the trail leaves the road and follows the creek. This is dispersed camping on undeveloped ground, not a site — no table, no ring, no toilet, nothing signed.

bivy.name: Red Bridge Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Sunrise Mine road, about ten miles below it on the paved section of the loop, and therefore the sensible base for SPERRY when you want a real night rather than a car bivy at a crowded road end. It is markedly closer to the Sunrise Mine spur than the larger campgrounds down at Verlot and much quieter, at the cost of fewer sites and no drinking water. Being on the paved lower loop it stays reachable all year and is entirely unaffected by whether the gravel section beyond Barlow Pass has opened for the season, which matters more here than it looks: that gravel stretch between Barlow Pass and the Bedal gate shuts each winter and typically does not open until somewhere in the second half of May. Barlow Pass itself is reached from this paved western side and normally opens earlier, but a slide anywhere below it closes everything above at a stroke and has done so recently, in which case basing low here and driving in each morning is the way to keep the trip. Sixteen sites go quickly on a fine Friday and none of them are reservable, so arrive early or have a fallback. Two group-only campgrounds sit within a couple of miles further up the same stretch, both reservation-only, and both are worth knowing about for a club climb that needs one site for a large party rather than several small ones. No cell coverage.
bivy.water: No potable supply on site. The South Fork Stillaguamish runs alongside and filters fine here — this is a different drainage from the mineralised Sauk-side ground above Barlow Pass, so the metals problem that dogs Gothic Basin does not apply.
bivy.permit: A developed fee campground on national forest land — the per-night fee is all that is needed and no pass or permit applies to the site itself. Nothing here is inside wilderness. Fires are allowed in the rings when seasonal restrictions permit, and those restrictions routinely shut them from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Around sixteen developed sites on the river bar, taking tents and small vehicles, with tables, fire rings and vault toilets. Fee campground, first come first served, open roughly late spring through early autumn.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required at the trailhead ($30 annual / $5 day-use), or a valid Interagency/National Park pass.
access.rules: The trail and basin lie within the Morning Star Natural Resources Conservation Area — campfires are prohibited throughout, and visitors should stay on trail, snow, or bare rock to avoid damaging fragile heather and meadow vegetation.
access.permit: None required — free self-issue wilderness permits available at trailheads/ranger stations for day/overnight travel where the peak is inside designated wilderness.
access.closures: Mountain Loop Highway is typically gated for the winter beyond this area (exact dates vary by snow year — check with the ranger district); the Weden Creek Trail crosses snow gullies with avalanche/runout hazard that can persist into July.
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District (Verlot Public Service Center, (360) 691-7791)
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / America the Beautiful pass

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass required: $5/day or $30 annual (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF / USFS Region 6 pricing). This pass system does not offer a separate multi-day pass in Washington.
access.rules: Campfires prohibited throughout Gothic Basin; camp only on established, durable sites and stay off fragile subalpine meadows; pack out all waste; bear canister required for overnight stays.
access.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required at the Weden Creek trailhead; a National Park pass is also honored. No separate climbing permit needed.
access.closures: Mountain Loop Highway's unpaved section from Barlow Pass to Bedal Campground (and the Deer Creek–Bedal Campground stretch) is gated and closed to vehicles every winter; it only reopens once Snohomish County/USFS clear spring washouts, sometimes not until late spring or early summer — call Darrington Ranger District (360) 436-1155 or Verlot Public Service Center (360) 691-7791 for current status. Monte Cristo Road beyond Barlow Pass is permanently closed to motor vehicles (foot/bike only) due to washouts.
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District; upper trail and basin cross into WA DNR's Morningstar Natural Resources Conservation Area
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads — $5/day or $30/year.

bivy.name: Sunrise Mine road end — the Sperry and Vesper Creek staging point
bivy.notes: This is the working start for SPERRY PEAK, and Sperry is honestly a day objective with no camp of its own — parties leave from here in the dark, ford the South Fork Stillaguamish, grind up through the talus of Wirtz Basin under Morning Star, take the switchbacked chute to Headlee Pass and traverse under Sperry's south side before scrambling the summit blocks. The only established camp on that line lies beyond the pass in the upper Vesper Creek basin, which the earlier upper-loop file already carries, so the realistic choice here is a long day from the car or a night in that basin. Sleeping at the road end is what most parties do and it works: the spur is short, and a pre-dawn start gets you through the chute before the day's rockfall gets going. Three things decide whether the trip happens at all. The FORD half a mile in is the real gate and it is not a formality — it runs hard in snowmelt and log crossings that worked one season are gone the next. The CHUTE below Headlee Pass is loose, narrow and known for rock coming down it, so parties should not stack up in it and helmets belong on well before the base. And SNOW holds in that chute and on the pass long after the valley is bare, which regularly turns a June or early-July attempt around. The spur itself is rough with potholes and encroaching brush; a low car can usually manage it slowly but scrapes are common. There is no cell coverage from the moment you leave the main loop road.
bivy.water: None at the road end. The creek crossings begin half a mile in and the first of them is the difficult one, so load every litre down in the valley rather than planning to draw here.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass to leave a vehicle, and nothing else. This is national forest but NOT designated wilderness, so there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no party-size cap. Overnight parking is allowed. Fires at the road end are governed by whatever seasonal forest-wide restrictions are running, which from midsummer usually means no open flame at all.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only. A small gravel turnaround at the end of the spur with room for perhaps a dozen vehicles and no sites, tables or pads. It overflows onto the road shoulder on summer weekends and the last cars in walk a fair way back to the trail start.

bivy.name: Red Bridge Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The nearest developed campground to the Sunrise Mine road, about ten miles below it on the paved section of the loop, and therefore the sensible base for SPERRY when you want a real night rather than a car bivy at a crowded road end. It is markedly closer to the Sunrise Mine spur than the larger campgrounds down at Verlot and much quieter, at the cost of fewer sites and no drinking water. Being on the paved lower loop it stays reachable all year and is entirely unaffected by whether the gravel section beyond Barlow Pass has opened for the season, which matters more here than it looks: that gravel stretch between Barlow Pass and the Bedal gate shuts each winter and typically does not open until somewhere in the second half of May. Barlow Pass itself is reached from this paved western side and normally opens earlier, but a slide anywhere below it closes everything above at a stroke and has done so recently, in which case basing low here and driving in each morning is the way to keep the trip. Sixteen sites go quickly on a fine Friday and none of them are reservable, so arrive early or have a fallback. Two group-only campgrounds sit within a couple of miles further up the same stretch, both reservation-only, and both are worth knowing about for a club climb that needs one site for a large party rather than several small ones. No cell coverage.
bivy.water: No potable supply on site. The South Fork Stillaguamish runs alongside and filters fine here — this is a different drainage from the mineralised Sauk-side ground above Barlow Pass, so the metals problem that dogs Gothic Basin does not apply.
bivy.permit: A developed fee campground on national forest land — the per-night fee is all that is needed and no pass or permit applies to the site itself. Nothing here is inside wilderness. Fires are allowed in the rings when seasonal restrictions permit, and those restrictions routinely shut them from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Around sixteen developed sites on the river bar, taking tents and small vehicles, with tables, fire rings and vault toilets. Fee campground, first come first served, open roughly late spring through early autumn.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or other Interagency Recreation Pass required at Sunrise Mine Trailhead: $5/day or $30/year, payable by Scan & Pay on-site or a displayed valid pass. Washington's Discover Pass is NOT accepted at this federal fee site.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) inside Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft in wilderness.
access.permit: No separate climbing/wilderness permit required; the Forest Pass covers day use at the trailhead.
access.closures: No seasonal gate reported on FS Road 4065 or at the trailhead (open 24 hrs/day), but the trail typically holds snow into midsummer, and the Mountain Loop Highway/FS roads in this forest are subject to periodic washout closures — check current Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before driving out.

access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads — $5/day or $30/year.

bivy.name: Lena Lake designated sites
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
bivy.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.
bivy.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit or fee — this is inside The Brothers Wilderness on Forest Service land, not in the national park. Wilderness regulations bind: STOVES ONLY, no campfires at all, party limit of twelve, and gathering wood above 3,500 ft is prohibited outright. Practise strict Leave No Trace, the camp has no toilet
bivy.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered

bivy.name: Upper Lena Lake
bivy.notes: The high camp for the northern approach to Mount Stone. Seven-odd miles and around 3,900 ft from the Lena Lake trailhead, of which the last three miles above the lower lake are steep and rooty and feel far longer than the distance suggests. From here the traverse runs southwest past Scout Lake to St. Peter's Gate, the notch under Mount Stone, and parties often continue over the gate and out via Lake of the Angels and the Putvin trail, which needs a car shuttle between two Hamma Hamma trailheads. Getting the permit is the whole planning problem: eight sites against considerable demand means the reservation window matters more than the weather. If it is gone, camp at Lena Lake below and accept a much longer summit day, or come at Mount Stone from the Putvin side instead. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake, plus meltwater in the basin early in the season. This is the last certain water before the high traverse toward Scout Lake and St. Peter's Gate
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED, AND THIS IS A NAMED QUOTA AREA — the boundary is crossed on the climb up from Lena Lake, so the rules change midway. Reserve through Recreation.gov, choosing Staircase as the entry area and Upper Lena Lake as the camp; the reservation season runs roughly July into mid-October and permits for the summer are released in a single April window that clears quickly. Per-person nightly fees apply on top of a booking fee. An animal-resistant food container is required throughout the park wilderness. No campfires — well above the 3,500 ft fire limit. A Northwest Forest Pass is still needed at the trailhead, because the parking is on Forest Service ground
bivy.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
bivy.water: The lake, but READ THIS ONE CAREFULLY. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. NO CAMPFIRES — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

bivy.name: Staircase Campground, North Fork Skokomish
bivy.notes: The park-side alternative at the head of Lake Cushman, a few miles beyond Big Creek. For the climbing in this zone it is a SECOND-CHOICE CONTINGENCY rather than a plan: it is further from the Ellinor and Washington trailheads than Big Creek, it costs more because of the park entrance fee, and the road in is less dependable. It earns its place for two reasons. It is the entry area named on the permit for Upper Lena Lake, so a party collecting or sorting out a park wilderness permit may already be dealing with this side of the boundary. And it is the fallback with real amenities when the Forest Service campgrounds below Ellinor are full on a summer weekend, which they routinely are. Worth knowing that the developed area has had extended seasonal closures in recent years, so confirm it is open before committing to the drive.
bivy.water: Potable water in season; the North Fork Skokomish runs through the campground
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park entrance fee applies, plus a per-night campground fee. Reservations through Recreation.gov are used for the peak midsummer window and the campground reverts to first come, first served either side of it; it runs primitive with reduced services through the winter. NO WILDERNESS PERMIT IS NEEDED FOR THE CAMPGROUND ITSELF — that is only for backcountry nights. Standard park food storage rules apply. Access is by the unpaved FR 24 beyond Lake Cushman, which closes in bad weather and is frequently shut through the winter and spring
bivy.capacity: Around 49 sites along the river, some reservable in high summer and the rest first come, first served

access.fees: $5/vehicle day-use fee or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the upper trailhead — pay via the on-site Scan & Pay/fee machine or display a valid Interagency/Digital Pass (cash not accepted on site). The lower trailhead is fee-free.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: This is a car-to-car day scramble with no camping — no NPS wilderness-permit or bear-canister rules apply here. Standard Olympic National Forest day-use etiquette (Leave No Trace, stay on the boot path) applies.
access.permit: Northwest Forest Pass (or equivalent Interagency/America the Beautiful pass) required only for upper-trailhead parking; no wilderness permit needed for day hiking.
access.closures: FS Road 2419/2419-014 is gated and snow-covered in winter and early spring; USFS lists the upper trailhead as open 'early summer through fall.' Check the Olympic National Forest alerts page for current road washouts or closures before driving up.
access.landManager: Olympic National Forest, Hood Canal Ranger District (Mount Skokomish Wilderness); district office relocated to Quilcene (295142 US-101 S, Quilcene, WA 98376), (360) 765-2200, after the former Hoodsport office closed in 2005.

bivy.name: Jefferson Creek roadside pull-outs, FR 2401
bivy.notes: This is the staging spot for MOUNT PERSHING and effectively nothing else, which is why it earns a line despite being a patch of gravel. The route starts where FR 2401 crosses Jefferson Creek at around 2,400 ft, reached by leaving FR 25 for FR 2480 and then FR 2401, and there is no trailhead, no sign and no established camp — a faint flagged path on the north side of the creek is the whole infrastructure. Sleeping at the crossing turns a long drive on rough gravel plus a steep bushwhack and class 3 ridge into a manageable day. Treat the road itself as the main uncertainty: the Jefferson Creek spurs are lightly maintained, subject to washouts and blowdown, and a low-clearance car may not reach the crossing at all, in which case the walk gets considerably longer. There is no water and no shelter once you leave here.
bivy.water: Jefferson Creek at the crossing, filtered. Nothing above it on the climb, so fill here
bivy.permit: Dispersed camping on Olympic National Forest roads needs no permit and no fee, but it is bound by the usual rules: stay within about 150 ft of the road centreline on a road open to it, camp well back from water, pack everything out, and observe the fourteen-day stay limit. Check the district motor vehicle use map before relying on a particular spur, since some roads are seasonally gated or closed to camping. Fire restrictions are common in late summer and are worth confirming
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of turnouts and flat spots along the spur near where the road crosses Jefferson Creek. No facilities of any kind, no toilet, no table

access.fees: No day-use fee is charged at the Jefferson Creek / Jefferson Lake trailhead; some other nearby Olympic NF trailheads still request a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass.
access.notes: No day-use fee is charged at this Olympic National Forest trailhead; no NP permit applies. Self-issue wilderness registration only.
access.rules: Mount Skokomish Wilderness regulations and Leave No Trace apply once past the wilderness boundary; a self-issue wilderness permit box is typically at the trailhead.
access.permit: No permit required for day scrambles; self-issued wilderness registration applies once inside Mount Skokomish Wilderness.

bivy.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. bivy.name: Lena Lake designated sites
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. bivy.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline

bivy.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.

bivy.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered

bivy.name: Upper Lena Lake

Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for MOUNT ELLINOR AND MOUNT WASHINGTON, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

bivy.name: Staircase Campground, North Fork Skokomish
bivy.notes: The park-side alternative at the head of Lake Cushman, a few miles beyond Big Creek. For the climbing in this zone it is a SECOND-CHOICE CONTINGENCY rather than a plan: it is further from the Ellinor and Washington trailheads than Big Creek, it costs more because of the park entrance fee, and the road in is less dependable. It earns its place for two reasons. It is the entry area named on the permit for Upper Lena Lake, so a party collecting or sorting out a park wilderness permit may already be dealing with this side of the boundary. And it is the fallback with real amenities when the Forest Service campgrounds below Ellinor are full on a summer weekend, which they routinely are. Worth knowing that the developed area has had extended seasonal closures in recent years, so confirm it is open before committing to the drive.
bivy.water: Potable water in season; the North Fork Skokomish runs through the campground
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park entrance fee applies, plus a per-night campground fee. Reservations through Recreation.gov are used for the peak midsummer window and the campground reverts to first come, first served either side of it; it runs primitive with reduced services through the winter. NO WILDERNESS PERMIT IS NEEDED FOR THE CAMPGROUND ITSELF — that is only for backcountry nights. Standard park food storage rules apply. Access is by the unpaved FR 24 beyond Lake Cushman, which closes in bad weather and is frequently shut through the winter and spring

Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is EXPLICITLY A CONTINGENCY RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a NORTHWEST FOREST PASS IS REQUIRED AT THE MOUNT ELLINOR UPPER TRAILHEAD BUT NOT AT THE LOWER ONE, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

bivy.name: Staircase Campground, North Fork Skokomish
bivy.notes: The park-side alternative at the head of Lake Cushman, a few miles beyond Big Creek. For the climbing in this zone it is a SECOND-CHOICE CONTINGENCY rather than a plan: it is further from the Ellinor and Washington trailheads than Big Creek, it costs more because of the park entrance fee, and the road in is less dependable. It earns its place for two reasons. It is the entry area named on the permit for Upper Lena Lake, so a party collecting or sorting out a park wilderness permit may already be dealing with this side of the boundary. And it is the fallback with real amenities when the Forest Service campgrounds below Ellinor are full on a summer weekend, which they routinely are. Worth knowing that the developed area has had extended seasonal closures in recent years, so confirm it is open before committing to the drive.
bivy.water: Potable water in season; the North Fork Skokomish runs through the campground
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park entrance fee applies, plus a per-night campground fee. Reservations through Recreation.gov are used for the peak midsummer window and the campground reverts to first come, first served either side of it; it runs primitive with reduced services through the winter. NO WILDERNESS PERMIT IS NEEDED FOR THE CAMPGROUND ITSELF — that is only for backcountry nights. Standard park food storage rules apply. Access is by the unpaved FR 24 beyond Lake Cushman, which closes in bad weather and is frequently shut through the winter and spring
bivy.capacity: Around 49 sites along the river, some reservable in high summer and the rest first come, first served

bivy.name: Lower Lena Lake
bivy.notes: Three miles in, and worth knowing about mainly so you do not mistake it for the climb's camp — it is a further three miles and about a thousand feet below the ground climbers actually use. It suits a party arriving late in the day or a first night split, not a summit bid.
bivy.water: The lake. There is no potable water at the trailhead, so this is the first fill.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Forest. No overnight fee and no permit, but a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at the Lena Lake trailhead. Camp in the designated sites only; fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Designated sites on both sides of the lake, first come and no reservation.

bivy.name: Brothers base camp at Lena Forks
bivy.notes: The base camp for the route, at the confluence of the forks of the East Fork of Lena Creek, roughly five to six miles in and about three miles beyond the north end of Lena Lake. Deep forest with little sun, and the ground is a lumpy mess of long-decayed fallen trees rather than flat duff. The trail beyond Lena Lake is unmaintained — blowdown, washouts and flagging tape — and parties routinely lose it, especially walking in at night. The reliable cue that you have gone past the forks is sound: the creek suddenly drops away and goes quiet. Snow lies at camp into spring. There is a fire ring, but one party found it burned over a foot down into the root mat, so think before lighting it.
bivy.water: The East Fork of Lena Creek runs beside the flat spots, so filtering is easy and reliable. Do not be alarmed on the way in: lower down the valley the creek sinks into the boulders and runs underground, and the bed can be dry on the surface in late summer. That is normal and says nothing about the water at camp.
bivy.permit: Olympic National Forest, The Brothers Wilderness — and note this is national forest, not the national park, so there is no wilderness permit, reservation or quota, whatever some route pages say. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Party size is capped at twelve, and caching gear for more than twenty-four hours is prohibited. Camp sits just below the wilderness fire line, which makes it the one place on this route where an open fire is legal.
bivy.capacity: Four or five separate sites scattered through the trees. It does fill — parties have arrived to find every one taken and had to walk on to the next.

bivy.name: Upper camp above the forks
bivy.notes: A second camp area further up the basin, reached by following the cairned way trail toward the left fork until a small meadow opens. One trip record names it the East Lena Creek Basin and treats it as a separate place from the forks camp, and it is the only source for the elevation, so treat that figure as unconfirmed. It buys a little height at the cost of losing the legal fire and the known water.
bivy.water: Not published for the camp itself. The last water on the route is at or near treeline, around 4,000 ft; above that everything is carried, and parties fill two or more litres there for the summit and the return.
bivy.permit: This camp is above the 3,500 ft wilderness fire line: stoves only, and gathering wood here is prohibited outright.

access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead register; The Brothers Wilderness itself is not quota-limited (unlike Upper Lena Lake camping, which requires a reserved permit May 1-Sep 30)
access.closures: FS Road 25 and the trailhead are generally open year-round, but can wash out or be snow-covered in winter/early spring — check current Hood Canal Ranger District road status before off-season trips

bivy.name: Lena Lake designated sites
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the whole Hamma Hamma side and the single most useful site in this zone. Three easy miles and about 1,300 ft of gain on a wide graded trail from the road, so a party can leave the car after work and be in camp before dark, which is exactly how most Brothers and Mount Stone trips are staged. From here two entirely separate objectives open up: north into the Valley of the Silent Men for The Brothers, and west and up for Upper Lena Lake and the traverse toward Mount Stone. Being outside Olympic National Park is the point — no quota, no reservation, no fee, so it is the fallback when the park permits above it are gone. The cost is crowding and noise; this is a family backpacking destination as much as a climbers' camp, and the shoreline shows it. Snow-free and usable most of the year, which makes it a genuine early-season and late-season base when everything higher is buried.
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake itself, and the inlet creeks at the north end. Filter or treat everything — this is a heavily used shoreline
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass required to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit, no reservation and no fee for the sites themselves — it is Forest Service ground, first come first served. Camping is restricted to the numbered sites. Wilderness rules apply once you leave the lake basin: stoves only, no campfires, and a party limit of twelve. Plan on cooking on a stove at the lake as well
bivy.capacity: Large by Olympic standards — roughly 28 to 29 numbered sites strung along the west and north shores, with a couple more on the east side; two pit toilets. It is the biggest backcountry camp in this zone and it still fills on summer weekends

bivy.name: The Brothers climbers camp, Valley of the Silent Men
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for The Brothers and the reason the traverse between the north and south peaks is a two-day trip rather than a brutal one. Reached by continuing past the north end of Lena Lake, crossing the inlet and following the East Fork up the Valley of the Silent Men through mossy old growth — call it three miles and 1,200 ft beyond the lake, so about six miles and 2,300 ft total from the car. From camp the south couloir rises directly above, and the summit day is short enough to allow an early start and a return to the tents before the couloir softens. It is a forest camp, not an alpine one: no views, damp, and the mosquitoes are memorable in early summer. The couloir is the season-limiting factor rather than the camp — good neve through late spring and early summer, loose and unpleasant once it melts out, so most parties come between April and early July and bring an axe and crampons.
bivy.water: Reliable while the creek runs. The East Fork of Lena Creek is right beside the pitches, and this is the last dependable water — carry everything you need for the climb from here, because the couloir and the upper mountain hold none
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Pass to park at the Lena Lake / Brothers trailhead. No camping permit or fee — this is inside The Brothers Wilderness on Forest Service land, not in the national park. Wilderness regulations bind: STOVES ONLY, no campfires at all, party limit of twelve, and gathering wood above 3,500 ft is prohibited outright. Practise strict Leave No Trace, the camp has no toilet
bivy.capacity: A scatter of flat, obvious tent spots in old-growth forest beside the creek, generally reported at around half a dozen usable pitches, informal rather than numbered

bivy.name: Upper Lena Lake
bivy.notes: The high camp for the northern approach to Mount Stone. Seven-odd miles and around 3,900 ft from the Lena Lake trailhead, of which the last three miles above the lower lake are steep and rooty and feel far longer than the distance suggests. From here the traverse runs southwest past Scout Lake to St. Peter's Gate, the notch under Mount Stone, and parties often continue over the gate and out via Lake of the Angels and the Putvin trail, which needs a car shuttle between two Hamma Hamma trailheads. Getting the permit is the whole planning problem: eight sites against considerable demand means the reservation window matters more than the weather. If it is gone, camp at Lena Lake below and accept a much longer summit day, or come at Mount Stone from the Putvin side instead. Snow lingers in the basin into July in a heavy year, and the meadow is the reason the sites are designated — stay on them.
bivy.water: Reliable. The lake, plus meltwater in the basin early in the season. This is the last certain water before the high traverse toward Scout Lake and St. Peter's Gate
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK WILDERNESS PERMIT REQUIRED, AND THIS IS A NAMED QUOTA AREA — the boundary is crossed on the climb up from Lena Lake, so the rules change midway. Reserve through Recreation.gov, choosing Staircase as the entry area and Upper Lena Lake as the camp; the reservation season runs roughly July into mid-October and permits for the summer are released in a single April window that clears quickly. Per-person nightly fees apply on top of a booking fee. An animal-resistant food container is required throughout the park wilderness. No campfires — well above the 3,500 ft fire limit. A Northwest Forest Pass is still needed at the trailhead, because the parking is on Forest Service ground
bivy.capacity: Eight designated wilderness sites in the meadow basin, and that is the hard ceiling — the basin is small, fragile and closely managed

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a CONTINGENCY AND STAGING SITE RATHER THAN THE NORMAL PLAN for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: NO POTABLE WATER AT EITHER CAMPGROUND — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

access.fees: $5 per vehicle day-use fee at the Lena Lake/Brothers Trailhead.
access.permit: No permit for day climbs; overnight camping within the Olympic National Park boundary requires a park wilderness permit.
access.landManager: Olympic National Forest (Hood Canal Ranger District) / The Brothers Wilderness; upper mountain near the Olympic National Park boundary.

bivy.name: Basin Creek Camp
bivy.notes: The closest designated camp to the Horseshoe Basin trail junction, which sits at about 3,600 ft on the valley trail, so it is the practical base for anything up in the cirque. It has a separate cooking area, a bear box and its own privy. Capacity is tiny — three sites — so a party of four fills most of it and a weekend permit is not something to count on. From here the basin trail climbs roughly 1,300 ft in about 1.5 miles to the Black Warrior Mine and the waterfall headwall below Ripsaw Ridge and Buckner's north side.
bivy.water: Reliable — Basin Creek runs beside the camp all season
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required (North Cascades NP / Lake Chelan NRA); designated camp reserved by site on Recreation.gov, with roughly 40% of inventory held for walk-up the day before at Marblemount or Golden West in Stehekin. Per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
bivy.capacity: 3 sites, 12 people total

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp
bivy.notes: The eastern gateway to the basin, at the end of what used to be the upper Stehekin Valley road. It has a privy, fire rings, picnic table and bear boxes, though the boxes are set well back from the cooking area. ACCESS IS THE THING TO PLAN AROUND: the road washed out for the last time in 2003 and the Stehekin shuttle now turns around at High Bridge, so reaching Cottonwood from the boat means an extra day of walking the old roadbed rather than the bus ride older descriptions assume. Check the current shuttle schedule before committing — upper-valley service has varied year to year.
bivy.water: Reliable — creek water a short walk below the camp
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp, same Recreation.gov reservation and walk-up system as the rest of the complex.
bivy.capacity: Several sites, including one that takes a larger group and a few small secluded ones

bivy.name: Pelton Basin Camp
bivy.notes: Pelton Basin sits about half a mile east of and below Cascade Pass, on the Stehekin side, which makes it the obvious first night for a party coming in over the pass rather than up from the lake. It puts Horseshoe Basin within a long day, though the basin itself is still several miles and a substantial descent-then-climb away. Snow lingers here well into summer and the trail across the basin can be hard to follow when it does, so early-season parties should expect to navigate rather than follow tread.
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creek through the basin, though flow drops late in a dry summer
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camp on the Recreation.gov system, and among the harder Cascade Pass sites to draw in midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp — the number of sites is not published, and it is few enough that it goes early on summer weekends. Assume it may be full and carry a plan that does not depend on it.

bivy.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
bivy.notes: A set of hand-built rock-walled tent platforms at the toe of the glacier, at the top of Sahale Arm. It is high, exposed and above the last dependable water, so late-season parties should plan to melt snow or carry up from lower on the arm. For the Horseshoe Basin peaks it is a high camp rather than a basin camp — it serves approaches that cross Sahale Arm and drop toward Doubtful Lake and the head of the basin, and it puts you on the right side of the divide for Buckner's north aspect. Reported elevation varies slightly between sources.
bivy.water: Unreliable — snowmelt and glacier runoff only, and the seasonal trickles commonly dry up by late summer
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; one of the most contested designated camps in the park. Realistically needs the early-access lottery or the general on-sale window in late April.
bivy.capacity: 4 sites, 4 people per site

bivy.name: Doubtful Lake Camp
bivy.notes: Doubtful Lake lies in a cirque below Sahale Arm, reached by a spur that drops off the arm trail. It is the natural middle camp on the Sahale Arm variation of the approach, breaking up a long crossing between Cascade Pass and the head of Horseshoe Basin. Water is the one thing never in question here, which matters if the alternative is Sahale Glacier Camp late in the season. The spur loses meaningful elevation off the arm, so factor the reclimb into the next day.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus its inlet and outlet streams
bivy.permit: NPS backcountry permit required; designated camping at the lake, reserved or walked up like the other Cascade Pass-area sites.
bivy.capacity: A small designated camp at the lake, site count not published. Treat it as a handful of spots rather than a place a large party can count on.

bivy.name: Buckner cross-country zone bivy
bivy.notes: The option for climbers who want to sleep on the route rather than at a valley camp — high bivies on moraine, slab or snow under Buckner's north side and the Ripsaw Ridge peaks. Zone rules are strict and worth reading before you go: camp at least a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight, and only on snow, rock or bare ground. No meadow camping, nothing within 100 ft of water, no fires. Because the permit is walk-up only, a trip built around a zone bivy is one you cannot lock in ahead of time — carry a fallback.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent — snowmelt and seasonal streams in the upper basin, dependable early, thin or gone by late season
bivy.permit: NPS cross-country zone permit required, WALK-UP ONLY. Buckner is not among the zones that take advance reservations, so it cannot be booked on Recreation.gov and must be picked up in person, generally no more than a day ahead.
bivy.capacity: 6 people per party, 6 parties per night in the zone

access.fees: $10/person + $6 reservation fee for overnight backcountry camping (2025 rate); day use/climbing with no overnight stay does not require a fee.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Camp only at designated/permitted sites (e.g., Sahale Glacier Camp, Pelton Basin) — this is a high-demand zone with an early-access lottery for peak season. Standard Leave No Trace / pack-out-waste rules apply; no campfires above treeline.
access.permit: Overnight backcountry permit required year-round; as of 2025 the fee is $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee (youth 15 and under free). Cascade River Road trailheads (Cascade Pass, Boston Basin, Eldorado) require in-person permit pickup at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount — advance Recreation.gov reservations must still be finalized there, or picked up walk-up (about 40% of sites are held for walk-ups).
access.closures: Cascade River Road is currently closed to vehicles at Eldorado (milepost 20) due to flooding/landslide damage; foot and bicycle travel is permitted beyond the gate, adding roughly 3 miles of road travel each way to reach the Cascade Pass trailhead. Check the NPS road-conditions page and Skagit County road-closures page before heading out.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex (Stephen Mather Wilderness) — Marblemount Wilderness Information Center issues permits

bivy.name: Hozomeen Campground, north end of Ross Lake
bivy.notes: This is the roadhead for every route on the mountain and the only developed camping anywhere near it. It sits in deep forest on flat ground by the lake, with vault toilets, boat ramps and no trash service, so everything you bring comes out with you. There is no cell coverage and the nearest supplies are hours away in either country. The season runs roughly late May into October, bounded at the front by snow on the gravel road and at the back by the road being left unmaintained. The other way in is by water: a boat from the resort at the south end will run parties the length of the lake, taking up to six people with packs on a chartered trip that is booked and paid in advance. That is expensive and inflexible but it does not involve a border at all, which through several recent seasons has made it the only way anybody got here. In summer 2026 a lightning fire on the border grew to many thousands of acres immediately east of the mountain, crossed into Canada, and closed the entire Hozomeen area including the docks, the campground and the lake north of Silver Creek. Treat access to this peak as something to verify from scratch each season rather than as a fixed thing.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is provided while the campground is staffed. Outside that window, and any time the system is off, the lake and the creeks are the supply and need treating.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No fee and no reservation for the campground itself, and no backcountry permit to sleep here — but one is required the moment you walk in to the lake camps or up onto the mountain. THE BORDER IS THE COMPLICATION. The only road access is a long gravel road running south from the Trans-Canada Highway near Hope, British Columbia, and it crosses into the United States at a point with no staffed port of entry. The gate on the American side has been closed to vehicle traffic from Canada for several years, and at times foot traffic across the line has been prohibited as well. A party driving down from Canada is entering the United States, so it needs the documents for that regardless of whether anyone is there to check; the practical position has been that you cannot legally drive through, and that a normal port of entry plus the boat is the way in. Confirm the current gate status with the park and with the border agency before committing to the road, because the answer has changed more than once.
bivy.capacity: Around 75 sites across two loops, all first-come and first-served with no reservations taken. The Upper Loop has been closed for hazard trees, which removes a good share of that number and also happens to be where the lake trail starts, so check what is actually open before counting on a spot.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Lake camp
bivy.notes: Something under four miles in from the campground's upper loop on an established trail, this is the obvious first night for anyone who wants to start the climb from higher than the road. It is a genuinely pleasant forested lake sitting directly beneath the mountain, and it is the better of the two lake camps by some distance. The climbing route leaves from here: parties work around the eastern shore and then angle up into the basin between the peaks, and that is where the day stops being a hike. Expect heavy deadfall and thick brush from the moment you leave the trail. The loon closure and the fire closures between them have shut this camp for large parts of recent seasons, so confirm it is open before building an itinerary on it.
bivy.water: The lake is right there and is the supply. It is standing water in a shallow forested basin, so filter or treat rather than drinking it as found.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, obtained at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing system. A SEASONAL CLOSURE APPLIES: the lake is closed to entry and to camping from the first of April through the end of May to protect nesting loons, which rules out the early-season window entirely. Fires and food storage are governed by the permit; a canister is the sensible choice here whatever the minimum requirement says.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, a few sites with a privy and food storage. Sites are assigned by night on the permit, so a walk-up can be turned away if the nights you want are taken.

bivy.name: Willow Lake camp
bivy.notes: Roughly two trail miles south of the junction for Hozomeen Lake, on the long north-south trail that runs the entire east shore of Ross Lake. It matters to this peak mainly as an overflow and as the link to the alternative approach: a party that cannot get to the north end at all can walk in from the Highway 20 end of that trail instead, which is a multi-day proposition but does not depend on a border gate or a chartered boat. The lake itself is marshy and buggy through midsummer and is a worse camp than Hozomeen Lake, so take it only if the better one is full. Both camps sit low in dense forest with no view of the climbing.
bivy.water: The lake, which is a long shallow marshy basin rather than clear open water. Treat it, and expect to walk a little to find a spot worth drawing from.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same system as the rest of the east shore. No advance reservation for most nights here; plan on the walk-up allocation and carry a fallback night in mind.
bivy.capacity: Small designated camp reached by a short spur off the main trail to the west end of the lake. A handful of sites, assigned by night.

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs in the western basin between the peaks
bivy.notes: The mountain is two rock summits above a basin, and the approach to that basin from the lake is the crux of the whole trip for most parties: a slow grind through blowdown and heavy brush with no path, on which fifteen miles and seven thousand feet of gain and loss is a fair reckoning for the round trip. Strong parties do go car to car, and parties often describe regretting that decision around hour twelve. Sleeping up here shortens the summit day considerably, at the cost of hauling water up a slope with almost none on it and sleeping on ground that is not flat. There is a second line from the road along the cleared border swath running east from near the ranger station, which is shorter and is described by people who have used it as more unpleasant than the lake approach rather than less. Both are late-summer propositions: snow lingers in the basin, and the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: This is the hard part and worth planning around. The one stream in the basin runs in a channel that deepens into a slot as you climb, and parties have found it reachable at a single awkward spot at around four thousand feet and nowhere above that. Fill everything you are carrying when you can get to water, because you may not get another chance before the ground goes flat enough to sleep on.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Hozomeen cross-country zone, which allows a maximum party of six and a maximum of three parties on any night. It is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one, so the permit is collected in person, in practice at Marblemount. Cross-country camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight of both, and only on snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadow and never within a hundred feet of water. NO FIRES in the zone. Waste goes in a cathole, or is carried out where the ground will not take one.
bivy.capacity: No established site and no site count. Parties have reported scratching out a few rough platforms among scattered boulders on a steep forested slope, enough for one small party sleeping poorly. THERE IS NO CAMP HERE — this is where people stop because they have run out of daylight, not somewhere anyone chose.

access.fees: No park entrance fee. Hozomeen Campground is free and first-come, first-served, late May through October. Backcountry permits $10 per person plus $6 reservation fee; 15 and under free.
access.permit: No permit needed for a day climb, which is how this route is usually done. Any overnight bivouac on the ridge requires an NPS wilderness permit for the relevant cross-country zone, reserved through Recreation.gov and issued by email after the safety video, or picked up in person at Marblemount.
access.closures: NPS border gate at Hozomeen closed until further notice to vehicle and foot traffic. Silver-Skagit Road closed at km 6 as of 24 July 2026 for the Border 2 Fire. Both must be verified before the trip.
access.landManager: National Park Service - Ross Lake National Recreation Area, North Cascades National Park Complex. Approach drive crosses B.C. Parks' Skagit Valley Provincial Park.
access.passRequired: No US trailhead pass. Passport or NEXUS required because the drive is through Canada, with entry and re-entry at a staffed port of entry - Hozomeen is not one.
