bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No fee and no reservation for the campground itself, and no backcountry permit to sleep here — but one is required the moment you walk in to the lake camps or up onto the mountain. THE BORDER IS THE COMPLICATION. The only road access is a long gravel road running south from the Trans-Canada Highway near Hope, British Columbia, and it crosses into the United States at a point with no staffed port of entry. The gate on the American side has been closed to vehicle traffic from Canada for several years, and at times foot traffic across the line has been prohibited as well. A party driving down from Canada is entering the United States, so it needs the documents for that regardless of whether anyone is there to check; the practical position has been that you cannot legally drive through, and that a normal port of entry plus the boat is the way in. Confirm the current gate status with the park and with the border agency before committing to the road, because the answer has changed more than once.
bivy.capacity: Around 75 sites across two loops, all first-come and first-served with no reservations taken. The Upper Loop has been closed for hazard trees, which removes a good share of that number and also happens to be where the lake trail starts, so check what is actually open before counting on a spot.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Lake camp
bivy.notes: Something under four miles in from the campground's upper loop on an established trail, this is the obvious first night for anyone who wants to start the climb from higher than the road. It is a genuinely pleasant forested lake sitting directly beneath the mountain, and it is the better of the two lake camps by some distance. The climbing route leaves from here: parties work around the eastern shore and then angle up into the basin between the peaks, and that is where the day stops being a hike. Expect heavy deadfall and thick brush from the moment you leave the trail. The loon closure and the fire closures between them have shut this camp for large parts of recent seasons, so confirm it is open before building an itinerary on it.
bivy.water: The lake is right there and is the supply. It is standing water in a shallow forested basin, so filter or treat rather than drinking it as found.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, obtained at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing system. A SEASONAL CLOSURE APPLIES: the lake is closed to entry and to camping from the first of April through the end of May to protect nesting loons, which rules out the early-season window entirely. Fires and food storage are governed by the permit; a canister is the sensible choice here whatever the minimum requirement says.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, a few sites with a privy and food storage. Sites are assigned by night on the permit, so a walk-up can be turned away if the nights you want are taken.

bivy.name: Willow Lake camp
bivy.notes: Roughly two trail miles south of the junction for Hozomeen Lake, on the long north-south trail that runs the entire east shore of Ross Lake. It matters to this peak mainly as an overflow and as the link to the alternative approach: a party that cannot get to the north end at all can walk in from the Highway 20 end of that trail instead, which is a multi-day proposition but does not depend on a border gate or a chartered boat. The lake itself is marshy and buggy through midsummer and is a worse camp than Hozomeen Lake, so take it only if the better one is full. Both camps sit low in dense forest with no view of the climbing.
bivy.water: The lake, which is a long shallow marshy basin rather than clear open water. Treat it, and expect to walk a little to find a spot worth drawing from.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same system as the rest of the east shore. No advance reservation for most nights here; plan on the walk-up allocation and carry a fallback night in mind.
bivy.capacity: Small designated camp reached by a short spur off the main trail to the west end of the lake. A handful of sites, assigned by night.

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs in the western basin between the peaks
bivy.notes: The mountain is two rock summits above a basin, and the approach to that basin from the lake is the crux of the whole trip for most parties: a slow grind through blowdown and heavy brush with no path, on which fifteen miles and seven thousand feet of gain and loss is a fair reckoning for the round trip. Strong parties do go car to car, and parties often describe regretting that decision around hour twelve. Sleeping up here shortens the summit day considerably, at the cost of hauling water up a slope with almost none on it and sleeping on ground that is not flat. There is a second line from the road along the cleared border swath running east from near the ranger station, which is shorter and is described by people who have used it as more unpleasant than the lake approach rather than less. Both are late-summer propositions: snow lingers in the basin, and the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: This is the hard part and worth planning around. The one stream in the basin runs in a channel that deepens into a slot as you climb, and parties have found it reachable at a single awkward spot at around four thousand feet and nowhere above that. Fill everything you are carrying when you can get to water, because you may not get another chance before the ground goes flat enough to sleep on.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Hozomeen cross-country zone, which allows a maximum party of six and a maximum of three parties on any night. It is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one, so the permit is collected in person, in practice at Marblemount. Cross-country camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight of both, and only on snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadow and never within a hundred feet of water. NO FIRES in the zone. Waste goes in a cathole, or is carried out where the ground will not take one.
bivy.capacity: No established site and no site count. Parties have reported scratching out a few rough platforms among scattered boulders on a steep forested slope, enough for one small party sleeping poorly. THERE IS NO CAMP HERE — this is where people stop because they have run out of daylight, not somewhere anyone chose.

access.fees: $10 per person, per night backcountry camping fee, charged mid-May through early October (no charge the rest of the year); $6 non-refundable Recreation.gov reservation/lottery fee per permit application.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: No cell service at Ross Lake/Hozomeen; pack out all trash (no services at Hozomeen Campground); Ross Lake water taxi requires advance reservation.
access.permit: Overnight backcountry permit required year-round for any camping en route (e.g., Lightning Creek, Hozomeen Campground, or high camps). Obtain at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount or reserve in advance via Recreation.gov (about 60% of backcountry sites are reservable; the rest are walk-up, first-come, first-served and can be competitive at Ross Lake in summer). Reserved permits must be picked up by 11:00 AM PT on the trip start date or the reservation may be cancelled.
access.closures: The US/Canada border crossing at Hozomeen (used for the historic Silver Skagit Road approach from Hope, BC) has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic since the COVID-19 pandemic and remains closed as of 2026.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex / Ross Lake National Recreation Area (NPS)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.
bivy.capacity: Informal; a handful of vehicles at each pullout, with the hairpin lot the largest and busiest on summer weekends

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
bivy.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
bivy.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

bivy.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
bivy.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
bivy.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
bivy.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. The pass's elevation is uncertain, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

bivy.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
bivy.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
bivy.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
bivy.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and many parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. bivy.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo

bivy.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
bivy.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
bivy.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.

bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

bivy.name: Kangaroo Pass and the upper Early Winters Creek meadows
bivy.notes: The approach from the hairpin is short enough that camping up here is widely DISCOURAGED rather than encouraged, and several parties say so plainly: the meadows and the pass take damage quickly and most parties simply do Kangaroo Temple in a day. Some do carry up and sleep near the tarn to get an early start on a longer link-up, so the practice exists even though it is not recommended. If you go, use bare ground well away from the meadow and expect the tarn to be a dry hollow after midsummer. Elevation figures for the pass are not consistently reported, so plan on a cold, exposed camp rather than a specific number.
bivy.water: A small tarn below the pass is the only source and it commonly dries out by late summer and autumn. Treat it as unreliable and carry water from the road.
bivy.permit: None required — Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, outside any quota area. Leave-no-trace practice is the only constraint, and it is a real one here.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties at most, on the flats south of the pass; the ground is fragile

bivy.name: Upper Cedar Creek basin, east of Big Kangaroo
bivy.notes: Anything on the east side of Kangaroo Ridge is far enough from the road that a bivy makes sense, and the barren upper basin east of Big Kangaroo is the accepted place for it. The usual way in is to follow the Half Moon north-ridge approach from the hairpin and cross the ridge at a low saddle between Half Moon and Big Kangaroo. The ground is stony and almost lunar, which makes it durable but also means no shelter and no vegetation to screen a camp. Reported elevations vary, so plan for a high, cold, waterless site rather than a number.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small seasonal pools early; expect nothing dependable once the snow has gone. Carry capacity for a dry camp.
bivy.permit: None required. Still Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest on this side of the divide — no quota permit and no reservation, in contrast to the national park backcountry zones a short distance west.
bivy.capacity: Open, rocky basin with room for a few parties on durable ground

bivy.name: SR 20 climbers' pullouts — the hairpin and the Silver Star Creek pullout
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE HONEST ANSWER FOR MOST OBJECTIVES HERE: they are day climbs from the car, and the usual overnight plan is to arrive late and sleep at the pullout. The hairpin lot serves Kangaroo Temple, Half Moon, Big Kangaroo, Poster Peak and the crags immediately above the highway, while the broad pullout further east sits at roughly 4,300 ft and serves the M&M Wall, the Wine Spires and Vasiliki Ridge. Elevations across these pullouts run from about 4,300 ft up to near the 5,477 ft pass, so nights are cool even in midsummer. Nothing is developed — no toilet, no table, no water — and highway noise carries.
bivy.water: None at either pullout. Carry everything, or filter from Early Winters Creek where the Wine Spires climbers' trail crosses it.
bivy.permit: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — no quota permit and no reservation of any kind. A Northwest Forest Pass covers day-use parking at the fee trailheads; sleeping in a vehicle at a pullout needs no separate permit, and the general 14-day stay limit applies.

bivy.name: Bench Camp — larch bench above the Wine Spires pullout
bivy.notes: The one genuinely used high camp on the Kangaroo Ridge side, reached by a steep switchbacking climbers' trail that gains roughly 2,000 ft from the highway. It is the sensible base for Vasiliki Ridge and Vasiliki Tower, for the WEST side of Juno Tower, and for linking two or three routes over a weekend rather than re-walking the approach each morning. Juno's east-side routes are a different problem — a 2.5 to 3.5 hour approach with a valley camp in Silver Star Creek — and this camp does not serve them. Bugs can be bad in July; water availability is what actually varies.
bivy.water: Present early in the season from snowmelt and the creek drainage, but limited to non-existent by late summer and early autumn. Higher up, a tarn around 7,100 ft and year-round snow at Burgundy Col are the late-season backups.
bivy.permit: None — no reservation, no quota, no backcountry permit. Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle at the pullout below.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent spots among the larches; the standard base for the north end of the ridge

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside parking
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the Liberty Bell group frequently sleep here, and it works as a fallback for the Kangaroo Ridge and roadside objectives when the hairpin lot is full, since it is only a few minutes' drive west. Be clear on the distinction: sleeping in the lot is tolerated, but walking up and pitching a tent at the lake is not. There is no water source you can rely on at the parking area.
bivy.water: No potable supply at the trailhead. Blue Lake itself is a mile up the trail and is off limits for camping.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park. No overnight backcountry permit and no reservation — this is national forest, not a North Cascades park camping zone. Overnight camping is prohibited within a quarter mile of Blue Lake.
bivy.capacity: A moderate paved lot that fills early on weekends; overnight use is vehicle-based only

bivy.name: Lone Fir, Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds
bivy.notes: The nearest developed options and the standard choice for a party wanting a table, a toilet and a guaranteed spot rather than a night in a gravel pullout. They descend eastward down the Early Winters Creek valley — Lone Fir around 3,600 ft, Early Winters near 2,200 ft — so they are warmer and considerably lower than the climbing, and Lone Fir is about seven miles from the Blue Lake area. Klipchuck sits back off the highway and is the quietest of the three. All are seasonal and closed when the road is.
bivy.water: Developed campgrounds with seasonal water systems; all three also sit on or near creeks. Water is shut off outside the operating season.
bivy.permit: Fee per night, first-come first-served at all three — no reservations, no climbing or backcountry permit. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to occupy a site. Fourteen-day stay limit.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 27 sites at Lone Fir, 46 at Klipchuck and about a dozen tent-only sites at Early Winters

access.fees: None at the roadside pullout. If car-camping the night before, Early Winters Campground (first-come, first-served, open roughly April-November) charges a nightly fee.

access.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit is required; the Forest Service's regional climbing/caving page lists no permit requirement for the Silver Star/Wine Spires/Vasiliki Ridge area.
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) is gated and closed to all traffic every winter, typically reopening mid-to-late April, but reopening can slip well into June after a heavy snow year or storm damage — in 2026, washouts and a slope failure near Diablo Lake delayed full reopening until June 14. The approach trail itself is a further limiting factor: it often isn't snow-free until several weeks after the highway opens.

bivy.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
bivy.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

bivy.name: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
bivy.notes: THE BASE CAMP FOR SNOWKING MOUNTAIN AND MUTCHLER PEAK, and the standard end of the Kindy Ridge approach. From the lakes the route follows the Kindy and Found ridge crest south-southwest above Cyclone Lake, keeping south of a cornice that overhangs the ridge, then turns west up moderately steep snow to the summit block; the alternative from the east side of the lake is heather and easy slabs up Snowking's east ridge, finishing on the south. Mutchler is the high point of the long curving ridge running southeast off Snowking and is reached along that crest, and the cirque between the two once held a substantial mid-elevation glacier of which only the highest north-facing ice remains. Getting here from the car is around thirty kilometres and two and a half thousand metres of cumulative gain by the time the undulating ridge is done, which is why nobody does this peak in a day. Snow lingers in the basin well into summer, which is when the camping is flattest and the water is easiest.
bivy.water: The lakes, reliable through the normal climbing season. This is the last certain water before the glacier and the ridge crest, and there is nothing running once you are up on the ice.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp back from the shoreline, use a stove rather than a fire at this elevation, and pack out what you bring in. No agency permit is reserved or quota'd anywhere in this zone, which is the practical difference from the park country up the road.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved sites around the small lakes north of Cyclone Lake, room for two or three parties. No toilet, nothing built.

bivy.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
bivy.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.
bivy.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
bivy.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.

bivy.name: Slide Lake
bivy.notes: The western gateway, and by a long way the easiest walking: about 2.5 miles round trip and 300 feet of gain to a lake formed when a landslide dammed the creek. For a climber it is a staging camp rather than an objective, since Snowking's west side and the lakes beyond are hours further on. Getting to the trailhead is the part to plan: from Darrington it is 16 miles north on the highway and then 20.5 miles up Illabot Creek Road, a long remote road with blind curves through the middle section and a small rock slide around mile 13.8 that can stop a low-clearance vehicle. Illabot Creek Road and the Cascade River Road have both been closed by washouts in the past and both are subject to seasonal closure, so confirm the road before committing to a trip that depends on it. The trail itself carries significant blowdown and boulder fields.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet. Reliable, though the exposed lakebed in late summer is slick and muddy and the shallow edges are not pleasant to draw from.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the register, which is passed at about 0.9 miles where the boundary is marked. THIS IS THE ONLY OFFICIAL TRAILHEAD IN THE ZONE and so realistically the only place a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed on the vehicle. Camp back from the shore, stove rather than fire.
bivy.capacity: Several rough sites, with the last good ones at about 1.25 miles where the well-beaten path ends. Parking at the trailhead takes roughly eight vehicles, which is a fair measure of how busy it gets.

bivy.name: Enjar Lake and Hamar Lake
bivy.notes: The working camps on the western side of Snowking Mountain, reached by continuing past Slide Lake for roughly four hours of increasingly rough going. Either lake serves; parties pick whichever the light allows. From here Snowking is climbed on its west and northwest ground rather than by the east ridge and glacier line used from Cyclone Lake, which is the practical reason the two approaches are worth keeping apart. No elevations are recorded because no confident figures were found for either lake. This side is quieter than the Kindy Ridge side and correspondingly less travelled, so route-finding is on you and the boot path is intermittent to absent. Best from July into September, and expect wet brush on the way through regardless.
bivy.water: Both lakes, dependable through the season. These are the last reliable water on the western approach before the ice.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit taken at the Slide Lake register. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Slide Lake trailhead. Camp back from the water, stoves only, pack out human waste.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved lakeside spots for a party or two at either lake. No toilet, nothing established.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass (or $8 day-use fee) recommended for parking at the Cascade River Road/FR-1570 trailhead.
access.notes: No reservation, lottery, or quota system applies to this Glacier Peak Wilderness approach; access is via the free self-issued trailhead permit noted under "permit."
access.rules: Standard Wilderness Act group-size limit (12) applies; no bear-canister requirement or NPS-style off-trail cross-country zone cap is documented for this Forest Service approach.
access.permit: No climbing permit required, but a free self-issued wilderness travel permit must be filled out at the trailhead register when entering the Glacier Peak Wilderness. Overnight camping along the route (Cyclone Lake basin, ridge bivies) is dispersed/undesignated.
access.closures: FR-1570 has a long-standing washout near the Cascade River crossing that keeps vehicles from reaching the historical trailhead; verify current road status with the Mt. Baker Ranger District before driving in.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.

bivy.name: Head of Kindy Creek and the Kindy-Buck Creek pass
bivy.notes: THE GROUND THAT PUTS MOUNT BUCKINDY IN RANGE. Buckindy's standard route is a class 4 scramble on the north slopes, with glaciers on the north and east flanks, and the parties who climb it are camping either in the basins at the head of Kindy Creek or at the pass between the Kindy and Buck Creek drainages. Coming in from road 1570 this is a second or third night out, well beyond the Cyclone Lake ground. There is a second way in from the south, over Green Mountain and the Horse Lake saddle from the Suiattle side, with camps on the divide and in the basins on the way, but that country has its own long road problems and is not the approach this zone is built around. Nothing here is a site in any developed sense: it is remote, lightly visited ground where the answer to where you sleep is wherever the light runs out, and a party should carry the fuel to melt snow and the tolerance for a dry, windy night.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small basin streams, generally running through midsummer and thinning badly after that. There is ice on Buckindy's north and east flanks, so late in the season the water that is left is glacier outflow rather than clean snowmelt.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on durable ground, pack out human waste, no fires. There is no quota and no reservation anywhere in this zone, so the constraint on a trip here is the approach rather than the paperwork.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on snow, moraine or heather at the passes and in the basins beneath them. Nothing built, no toilet.

bivy.name: Jug Lake
bivy.notes: THE BASE FOR MOUNT CHAVAL, which sits immediately southwest of Snowking and has three standard approaches and one longer non-standard one, none of them simple and all of them brushy. This is the most used of them. Park at the prominent switchback where Arrow Creek meets Illabot Creek Road at about 2,220 feet, roughly 16 miles up the road, and follow an old overgrown fishermen's path up the right bank of Arrow Creek to the lake; it is reasonably defined and flagged at the doubtful places. From the camps on the north shore the route climbs north-northeast to gain the ridge around 5,200 feet, traverses to the pass between the two points just over 6,350 feet, and then commits to a genuine cross-country bushwhack through cliffy ground into the Arrow Creek amphitheatre before steep hillsides and talus lead to the mountain. Reckon on about ten miles and 4,600 feet for the round trip from the road, and on the vegetation being the crux. No elevation is recorded for the lake because no confident figure was found.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable. Nothing dependable above it once you are on the ridge and in the Arrow Creek amphitheatre.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Parking is at the Arrow Creek switchback on Illabot Creek Road rather than at a developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass may not apply there in the way it does at Slide Lake; check with the district rather than assume either way. No fires at the lake, and pack out human waste.
bivy.capacity: Several good camps on the north side of the lake, roomy by the standards of this zone. Unimproved, no toilet.

access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness (Forest Service) generally requires only a free self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead register for day or overnight use — no quota/reservation system like the Enchantments. Illabot Creek Road ends at an informal pullout rather than a developed trailhead, so verify current signage/registration locally before you go.

No agency permit is reserved or quota'd anywhere in this zone, which is the practical difference from the park country up the road.

access.rules: No maintained trail exists to Mutchler Peak — travel is off-trail/cross-country; practice Leave No Trace on the fragile heather and cross into NPS land only with the required permit if camping

access.closures: The Cascade River Road / FR 1570 spur has a long-standing washout near the river crossing about 14.2 miles from Marblemount; the drivable endpoint shifts year to year, so check current Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF road status before driving

bivy.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
bivy.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.
bivy.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
bivy.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.

bivy.name: Slide Lake
bivy.notes: The western gateway, and by a long way the easiest walking: about 2.5 miles round trip and 300 feet of gain to a lake formed when a landslide dammed the creek. For a climber it is a staging camp rather than an objective, since Snowking's west side and the lakes beyond are hours further on. Getting to the trailhead is the part to plan: from Darrington it is 16 miles north on the highway and then 20.5 miles up Illabot Creek Road, a long remote road with blind curves through the middle section and a small rock slide around mile 13.8 that can stop a low-clearance vehicle. Illabot Creek Road and the Cascade River Road have both been closed by washouts in the past and both are subject to seasonal closure, so confirm the road before committing to a trip that depends on it. The trail itself carries significant blowdown and boulder fields.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet. Reliable, though the exposed lakebed in late summer is slick and muddy and the shallow edges are not pleasant to draw from.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the register, which is passed at about 0.9 miles where the boundary is marked. THIS IS THE ONLY OFFICIAL TRAILHEAD IN THE ZONE and so realistically the only place a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed on the vehicle. Camp back from the shore, stove rather than fire.
bivy.capacity: Several rough sites, with the last good ones at about 1.25 miles where the well-beaten path ends. Parking at the trailhead takes roughly eight vehicles, which is a fair measure of how busy it gets.

bivy.name: Enjar Lake and Hamar Lake
bivy.notes: The working camps on the western side of Snowking Mountain, reached by continuing past Slide Lake for roughly four hours of increasingly rough going. Either lake serves; parties pick whichever the light allows. From here Snowking is climbed on its west and northwest ground rather than by the east ridge and glacier line used from Cyclone Lake, which is the practical reason the two approaches are worth keeping apart. No elevations are recorded because no confident figures were found for either lake. This side is quieter than the Kindy Ridge side and correspondingly less travelled, so route-finding is on you and the boot path is intermittent to absent. Best from July into September, and expect wet brush on the way through regardless.
bivy.water: Both lakes, dependable through the season. These are the last reliable water on the western approach before the ice.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit taken at the Slide Lake register. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Slide Lake trailhead. Camp back from the water, stoves only, pack out human waste.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved lakeside spots for a party or two at either lake. No toilet, nothing established.

access.fees: FR-1570 ends at a washout with no developed trailhead, so a recreation pass is not normally required to park there. Where this district does require one at a developed trailhead it is a Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass — check the sign at the trailhead you actually use.
access.notes: No reservation, lottery, or quota system applies to this Glacier Peak Wilderness approach; access is via the free self-issued trailhead permit noted under "permit."
access.rules: Standard Wilderness Act group-size limit (12) applies; no bear-canister requirement or NPS-style off-trail cross-country zone cap is documented for this Forest Service approach.
access.permit: No climbing permit required, but a free self-issued wilderness travel permit must be filled out at the trailhead register when entering the Glacier Peak Wilderness. Camping at Cyclone Lake or on the glacier approach is dispersed/undesignated.
access.closures: FR-1570 has a long-standing washout near the Cascade River crossing; verify current road status with the Mt. Baker Ranger District before driving in.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mt. Baker Ranger District (Sedro-Woolley office, 810 State Route 20, Sedro-Woolley, WA 98284)
access.land_manager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — Glacier Peak Wilderness (Mt. Baker Ranger District)

bivy.name: Wallace Creek basin ridge camp
bivy.notes: This is the established high camp for Lincoln and the one nearly every ascent uses. It sits on the ridge overlooking the Wallace Creek basin, right at the last stand of trees, with the Black Buttes and the summit block in view above. Reaching it means walking the road to about the seventh switchback, picking up the old track that leads toward Rankin Creek, scrambling into the basin, passing east Rankin Lake, then climbing mellow snow north to the saddle near 5,480 ft and east up the basin below Seward to the ridge. From here the X Couloir on the southwest face and the north ridge are both single-push summit days, and both are long, steep, exposed snow and ice, which is why the camp is high. The peak is in condition in spring, when fresh snow has mostly stopped falling but nights are still cold enough to hold the snow, ice and rock together; by high summer the face becomes loose and dangerous. Expect the trees to be buried and the ground to be snow. Nothing here is sheltered from weather coming off Baker.
bivy.water: Running water is unreliable at this height. In spring, when the peak is in condition, you melt snow, which is what nearly every party does. Later in the year expect to carry from the tarns at the saddle below
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, whose boundary you cross on the way up into the basin. No overnight wilderness permit is required and none is issued for this area. Party size is capped at twelve. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass covers parking at the road end. This is national forest, not national park, so no park backcountry permit applies and none can be obtained for it. Stoves rather than fires, and pack out everything including waste on snow
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents on the last flat ground beside the highest trees; more parties than that and people are pitching on open snow

bivy.name: East Rankin Lake
bivy.notes: The lower of the two natural stopping places on the approach, in the Rankin Creek basin below the saddle. It is the sensible camp for a party that started late, that is walking extra road miles because of the washout, or that wants an easier carry on day one and a longer summit day on day two. From here the route continues north on easy-angled snow to the small saddle and then east into the upper basin, so nothing is wasted. The cost is close to a thousand feet of climbing left over for summit morning on a route where the difficulties start high. In spring the lake is a flat white plain and easy to camp on; later in the season the basin brushes up and the ground around the water is soggy.
bivy.water: The lake, once it has melted out. In the spring climbing season it is frozen and buried, so plan on melting snow
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required, twelve-person party limit, recreation pass for the vehicle at the road end. No campfires above treeline; use a stove. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and keep off the heather when it is out
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents around the lake basin on snow or, late in the year, on gravel and heather away from the shore

bivy.name: Saddle tarns above Rankin Creek
bivy.notes: The small saddle north of the Rankin basin, with a pair of tarns beside it, sitting between east Rankin Lake and the climb east into the upper basin below Seward. It is a stopgap rather than a destination: only a few hundred feet above the lake and still well short of the ridge camp, so it is chosen mostly by parties caught by weather or darkness on the way up. It is a windy notch, which is worth knowing before you commit to it in a storm. The one thing it does well is mark the point where the approach turns from valley travel to open alpine snow, so it is a useful place to re-assess conditions before carrying a heavy load higher.
bivy.water: Two small tarns sit right at the saddle. They are usually still under snow through the spring climbing season, so treat them as a summer source and otherwise melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit, twelve-person limit, recreation pass at the road end. Stove only
bivy.capacity: One or two tents on the flats beside the small lakes; informal ground with no established site

bivy.name: Middle Fork Nooksack road switchbacks
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the vehicle the night before is the normal way to start this climb, because the approach is long and parties want to be walking in the dark. The switchbacks above the road's lower section give rough pullouts around 2,650 to 3,420 ft depending on how far the surface lets you drive; past the first switchback the brush closes in and the potholes get serious, and a small car will not make it far. With the road currently barriered at milepost 7 the practical bivouac is wherever the closure puts you, and the Rankin Creek switchbacks are then a long walk or bike ride away — a bicycle to the closure point is worth considering. No elevation is given here because the usable spot depends entirely on how far up the road is open in a given season, which changes.
bivy.water: Creeks cross and run down the road in spring, and Rankin Creek is nearby. Treat anything you take
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, outside the wilderness boundary at this elevation. Dispersed roadside camping, no permit, no reservation. Check the current fire restrictions before lighting anything and expect fires to be banned outright in dry spells; a stove is the safe assumption. Pack out all rubbish
bivy.capacity: Roadside pullouts at the lower switchbacks take a couple of vehicles each; there are no built sites, no tables and no toilets

access.permit: No wilderness permit required, and none is issued for this wilderness — trailhead registration is voluntary. The self-issue wilderness permit some parties expect is an Alpine Lakes requirement and does not apply here.
access.closures: Access roads in this district are subject to washout closures.

bivy.name: Summerland Camp
bivy.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet

bivy.name: Meany Crest
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for Little Tahoma, and the one that makes the climb reasonable. It is a large flat area within the cliff band directly above Summerland, gained by the climbers' path and scrambling out of the basin, and it also serves Whitman Crest and the spires on that shoulder. From here the Fryingpan Glacier lies immediately ahead and the summit is a manageable morning rather than an epic. It is exposed — the shelf catches wind off the mountain and there is nothing to hide behind — so build walls if the forecast is doubtful and site the tent where a rockfall from the band above cannot reach it. Getting a permit for the zone is generally far easier than getting one of Summerland's few designated sites, which is a second, practical reason to camp high.
bivy.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
bivy.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities

bivy.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
bivy.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
bivy.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
bivy.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

bivy.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
bivy.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. bivy.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed

bivy.name: Silver Springs Campground

This covers the campground only, and has nothing to do with either the wilderness permit or the climbing fee, both of which you still need.

access.notes: Northwest Forest Pass required ($5/day or $30/annual). No specific climbing permit.
access.rules: Blue bags required for human waste above high camp — pack out and deposit only in barrels marked "Human Waste" at Camp Muir or the trailhead; do not cache on-route. Check-out is required after every climb.

The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.

access.fees: Park entrance fee; wilderness camping permit for overnight stays; separate climbing pass for travel above 10,000 ft/on glaciers
access.notes: This is NPS land, not USFS -- a Northwest Forest Pass does not apply. A $82/person climbing registration is required for travel above 10,000 ft or on any glacier, and a separate wilderness permit is required for overnight camping.
access.permit: Overnight wilderness permit and climbing permit required
access.closures: Paradise Road subject to winter storm closures/chain requirements
access.landManager: National Park Service, Mount Rainier National Park
access.passRequired: America the Beautiful pass or park entrance fee

bivy.name: Summerland Camp
bivy.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet

bivy.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
bivy.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
bivy.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
bivy.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

bivy.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
bivy.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself.
