access.fees: $82/person climbing registration, required year-round for any travel above 10,000 ft or onto a glacier, plus a $12/person/night wilderness permit for overnight camping (charged May 1-Sep 15 only); park entrance is $30/vehicle for 7 days.
access.notes: How to get it: pay online in advance (pay.gov / recreation.gov), then register in person. Winter (Sept 16–May 21): self-issue at the Paradise Old Station kiosk after paying online. Summer (May 22–Sept 30): no self-issue — register at a Wilderness Information Center (Longmire, Paradise, or White River); roughly half of summer registration slots are held for walk-up, up to 24 hrs ahead. No timed-entry vehicle reservation is in effect for the 2026 season, so park entry itself is first-come, first-served.
access.rules: Camp only at designated Summerland-area wilderness sites; stay on the maintained trail through the fragile Summerland meadow; pack out human waste above the toilets (required for high camps and glacier travel).
access.permit: Climbing registration required for all travel above 10,000 ft or on any glacier (self-issued for free after paying the $82 climbing fee); a separate wilderness permit is required for overnight camping at Summerland or the high camp — reserve ahead or get a walk-up permit at a wilderness information center within 24 hrs of your trip during the May 22-Sep 30 walk-up season.
access.closures: The Sunrise/White River Road is snow-gated and typically doesn't open until late June-early July; it closes for the season by mid-October, with nightly gate closures at the White River Campground junction beginning in late September. Check the NPS road-status page before driving up.
access.land_manager: National Park Service
access.parking_pass: Not a Northwest Forest Pass (that's a USFS pass and doesn't apply inside the park). Standard NPS entrance fee applies: $30/vehicle (7 consecutive days), $55 Mount Rainier annual pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: America the Beautiful / interagency annual pass covers only the $30 vehicle entrance fee — it does NOT cover the separate $82 climbing registration fee.

bivy.name: Massie Lake basin
bivy.notes: This is the climbing camp for Massie Peak and effectively the only one, because everything above it is dry and everything below it is a long way down. From the Trinity trailhead the Buck Creek trail runs a mile and a half to the junction, the Chiwawa River trail carries on up the valley and crosses the river on a bridge, and about three miles along it the Massie Lake trail turns off and climbs roughly two miles and fifteen hundred feet to the lake. THAT LAST STRETCH IS THE DIFFICULTY AND IT IS NOT A TRAIL IN ANY USEFUL SENSE. It is an unsigned and unmaintained old sheep driveway, steep, brushy and lost altogether in places, and the standard complaint about this lake is the amount of bushwhacking involved in reaching it. Expect to lose the line more than once and to be pushing through vegetation on the steepest part of the day. From camp the west route on Massie Peak goes on open slopes above the basin and is a scramble rather than a climb. The reward for the thrash is genuine solitude and good fishing; the register-level traffic here is a fraction of what the Buck Creek Pass side sees. Season is roughly mid-July into early October, later than a lake this height would suggest because the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable all season. This is the last certain water on the climb and the reason to camp here rather than higher: the slopes and benches above the basin run on snowmelt only and are dry by August in an ordinary year. Fill completely before going up. Treat it, though the shoreline sees very little use.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the Trinity trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book in advance. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock together. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at Trinity. Camp back from the shoreline and on existing bare ground; this is a small basin and it marks easily. Carry a stove — summer fire restrictions on this dry east side are routine and often total.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake for one or two parties. There is nothing developed, nothing signed and no toilet, and the basin is small — but it is also so little visited that competition for space is not a realistic worry.

bivy.name: The Chiwawa River trail camps above the bridge
bivy.notes: These are the first-night camps for a party that has driven a long way, or the last-night camps for one walking out, and on this approach both cases are common. The river bridge where the Buck Creek trail crosses is the usual spot and is the obvious place to stop, being flat, sheltered and on good water. Camping here rather than pushing on matters because the Massie Lake turn is unsigned and the driveway above it is steep and vague — that is ground you want to meet in the morning with fresh legs and a full day, not at dusk. The valley walking below is gentle and fast, so a party that gets away from the road in the afternoon can be here comfortably. THE ROAD CLOSURE CHANGES THE ARITHMETIC ENTIRELY. With the Chiwawa River road shut above Atkinson Flat, Trinity is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns the walk to these camps into a long day on its own or a bike shuttle, and turns the trip as a whole from two nights into three or four.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is alongside for this whole stretch and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is where the approach is generous with water, and it is worth knowing because the climb to Massie Lake is the steep, hot, brushy part and there is nothing dependable on it.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit from the Trinity trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal below the high country in existing rings outside a burn ban, but the Chiwawa valley is dry and bans are the norm from midsummer, so plan on a stove.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites in the timber along the valley floor, including good ground where the trail crosses the river on the bridge. One or two parties each, nothing developed, and rarely anyone else there.

bivy.name: Trinity trailhead roadhead
bivy.notes: The staging point, and it is recorded because the drive is the part of this trip that most often goes wrong. In a normal year the Chiwawa River road runs about twenty-two miles from the Lake Wenatchee end, with the last stretch rough gravel genuinely unsuited to low clearance, and arriving at the end of it late and tired is how parties end up starting the walk in badly. From the roadhead a short section of closed road leads onto the Buck Creek trail, and the junction where the Chiwawa River trail branches right for Massie is a mile and a half in. THE ROAD IS SHUT ABOVE ATKINSON FLAT under a storm-damage order running into 2027, with the 2026 fire closure sitting over the same corridor on top of it, and while that stands there is no legal way to drive to this roadhead at all. When the road is open again, expect it to remain the fragile part of any plan here: it has been damaged repeatedly, it carries no through traffic to justify quick repair, and the trailhead is far enough up it that a single washout removes the whole approach.
bivy.water: The Chiwawa River is close by and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap anywhere at this end of the road. Fill everything here, since the valley trail above is good for water and the climb to the lake is not.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is taken from the register here — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit including stock. Fire restrictions bite hard on this side from midsummer and commonly ban all open flame including in existing rings.
bivy.capacity: A gravel parking area at the end of the public road with room to sleep in a vehicle. It is a roadhead, not a campground — no fee site, no tables, no toilet you should count on. The developed campgrounds strung along the Chiwawa River road below it are the proper drive-in option and are recorded in the Entiat and Holden file rather than repeated here.

bivy.name: The benches above Massie Lake — no established camp
bivy.notes: Recorded honestly: Massie Peak is a day objective from the lake and there is no practical reason to sleep higher. The scramble from the basin is short enough that the only argument for going up is to be on the crest at first light, and the cost is carrying water two thousand feet and sleeping exposed with nothing to shelter behind. The one situation where these benches genuinely earn their place is the traverse northwest on the old sheepherder's line toward Pass No Pass and the Buck Creek Pass country, which runs two and a half to three miles on faint stock and game tracks that come and go, and which a party will not finish in the same day they climb the peak. If you are doing that, sleeping high on the way out makes sense. If you are climbing Massie and walking back down the driveway, it does not. Either way, do not plan on finding water and do not plan on finding a flat, cleared spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. By August there is usually nothing at all above the lake, and a party sleeping up here is carrying every drop from the basin below. This is the single most common way to get the trip wrong.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at Trinity. No fires this high — carry a stove. The ground is thin subalpine turf that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the meadow alone.
bivy.capacity: None established. There is open ground on the benches and in the meadows above the lake where a small party could put down a tent, but nothing has been built, nothing is marked, and nobody camps here as a matter of course. That is worth saying plainly rather than inventing a site.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/interagency pass required to park at the Chiwawa-corridor trailheads (Trinity/Phelps Creek); $5/vehicle/day or $30 annual if you don't already hold a pass.
access.rules: Glacier Peak Wilderness caps group size at 12 people and stock combined; larger parties must split into separate groups with at least 1 mile of separation.
access.permit: Free self-issued wilderness permit required at the trailhead.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District)

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is currently cut by a washout at about road mile seventeen that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.
bivy.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
bivy.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
bivy.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.

bivy.name: Green Ridge Lake
bivy.notes: The staging point for two of this zone's objectives and the one genuinely useful high camp on the north side of the valley. Treen Peak's Green Ridge approach starts here, and so does the East Peak ridge on the Garfield massif, which is the one part of that mountain with a walking line rather than a climb. Access is a faint unmaintained miners' and fishermen's path leaving the upper road at about 1,350 ft, roughly a mile below the Dingford Creek trailhead, climbing steeply northeast through timber; it is easy to lose in the first thousand feet and the brush is heavy when wet. Above the ridge crest at about 4,700 ft the ground opens into heather and scattered tarns and travel becomes pleasant. For most parties this is a contingency rather than the plan, since Treen goes in a long day when the road is open, but the road washout and the sheer gain from 1,350 ft make an overnight the sensible choice at present, and the ridge camp splits a brutal day into two reasonable ones. Season is July into October; the approach is snow-free early but the brush stays soaking until the summer settles.
bivy.water: The lake is reliable through the summer, and the tarns above hold water into late season most years. Nothing between the road and the lake once the low creeks are behind you, so fill before the steep section.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit where the boundary is crossed, group size capped at twelve. The start is an unsigned roadside pull-out rather than a developed trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle. The lake sits just below the 4,000 ft campfire line and the ridge camps above it are stoves-only regardless; treat the whole area as no-fire in practice.
bivy.capacity: Small informal camp on the benches by the lake, room for a couple of tents. Nothing designated or maintained. Tarns on the ridge above take another tent or two.

bivy.name: Garfield Mountain improvised bivouac
bivy.notes: The honest answer for Garfield is that there is no camp, and inventing one would do a party more harm than saying so. It is a low mountain carrying enormous relief straight out of the valley floor, and every documented line begins with steep unmaintained bushwhacking and long rock gullies before any climbing starts. There are no trails, no signs and no established approach; you leave the road at a pull-out and go up. Ascents here are commonly described as needing either a bivouac or the very longest days of the year to finish in daylight, and the bivouacs that actually happen are improvised where a party runs out of light rather than chosen in advance. Plan for that rather than around it: carry a bivy kit on any attempt, expect to sleep on rock or in brush, and treat the multi-summit outing in particular as an opportunistic link-up rather than a route with a known camp on it. Substantial rappels separate some of the summits, so retreat is not always the quick option once committed. The one exception is the East Peak, whose ridge is gained from Green Ridge; a party going that way should use the Green Ridge Lake camp above instead of anything on this face. Season here is governed by dry rock and daylight rather than snow: the valley is open most of the year, but the brush stays wet late and June through September is when this goes.
bivy.water: Nothing reliable and nothing to plan around. The gullies run in spring and after rain and are dry by late summer, and there is no snow to melt on this mountain in season. Carry water for the whole push and know where the last certain source below you was.
bivy.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the mountain beyond the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit if your line crosses the boundary, plus a Northwest Forest Pass at whichever pull-out you start from. Note that sleeping at the car is not an option here: the pull-outs at the base of Garfield fall inside the lower-valley dispersed camping closure.
bivy.capacity: Nothing established, and no honest capacity figure to give. Parties sleep where the terrain offers a flat dry patch, a bench in a gully, a ledge system or a heather shoulder, usually one or two people at a time.

access.fees: $5/day or $30/year Northwest Forest Pass

bivy.name: Mount Teneriffe and the Mount Si conservation area, no overnight
bivy.notes: Recorded because it is the honest answer rather than a place to sleep. Mount Teneriffe is state conservation land at the very front of the range, reached from its own trailhead at the end of the Mount Si road and not from any of the Middle Fork trailheads that serve the other peaks here, so it has a different land manager, a different pass and different rules. Both the standard trail and the Kamikaze scramble up the southwest ridge are done car-to-car in a day by everyone who climbs them, and there is no camp on the mountain and nothing legal near the trailhead. A party that wants to start from a tent has to drop back to the valley, where the Middle Fork Campground is the nearest developed option, about twenty minutes' drive up the road system. The compensation is season: the lower mountain is snow-free most of the year and this is a genuine winter and shoulder-season objective, though the steep upper section of the Kamikaze line becomes icy and unpleasant once the freeze sets in and the standard trail is the safer choice then.
bivy.water: The falls and the creeks crossed low on the trail run most of the year and are the last certain water. There is nothing on the upper mountain and nothing on the Kamikaze line at all. Carry what you need for the day.
bivy.permit: A Washington Discover Pass is required in every vehicle at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass is not valid here, which is the commonest mistake parties make arriving from the national forest roads further up the valley, and the fines are real. Camping and campfires are both prohibited, group size is capped at twelve, and the trails are hiking-only.
bivy.capacity: None. Camping is prohibited across the entire conservation area, at any elevation, so there is no legal overnight option anywhere on this mountain.

bivy.name: Rainy Lake
bivy.notes: Sits directly beneath the exposed south face of Preacher Mountain and is the natural base camp for the Standard Scramble. From the Middle Fork trailhead cross the bridge and follow the Pratt connector west to the junction with the unofficial Rainy Creek path, which the Forest Service abandoned years ago; volunteers keep the brush down in places and much of it is flagged, but it is not maintained tread and route-finding is required, particularly in the lower half. Preacher is around eleven miles and five thousand feet of gain from the road when it goes well, so most parties do it car-to-car. Treat this as the contingency for a slow day, wet brush or a late descent, and as the sensible plan for a winter attempt, when Preacher becomes a real snowshoe objective and the daylight will not stretch. The valley floor here is low enough to be open most of the year, but the lake and the ridge above hold snow into June.
bivy.water: The lake and Rainy Creek are both reliable through the season. Treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit, group limit twelve. Northwest Forest Pass at the Middle Fork trailhead where the approach begins. The lake is just under the 4,000 ft campfire line, but the sites are small and the ground is thin, so use a stove and expect seasonal bans in late summer.
bivy.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the lake shore. Quiet and rarely busy, since the access path keeps the numbers down.

bivy.name: Green Ridge Lake
bivy.notes: The staging point for two of this zone's objectives and the one genuinely useful high camp on the north side of the valley. Treen Peak's Green Ridge approach starts here, and so does the East Peak ridge on the Garfield massif, which is the one part of that mountain with a walking line rather than a climb. Access is a faint unmaintained miners' and fishermen's path leaving the upper road at about 1,350 ft, roughly a mile below the Dingford Creek trailhead, climbing steeply northeast through timber; it is easy to lose in the first thousand feet and the brush is heavy when wet. Above the ridge crest at about 4,700 ft the ground opens into heather and scattered tarns and travel becomes pleasant. For most parties this is a contingency rather than the plan, since Treen goes in a long day when the road is open, but the road washout and the sheer gain from 1,350 ft make an overnight the sensible choice at present, and the ridge camp splits a brutal day into two reasonable ones. Season is July into October; the approach is snow-free early but the brush stays soaking until the summer settles.
bivy.water: The lake is reliable through the summer, and the tarns above hold water into late season most years. Nothing between the road and the lake once the low creeks are behind you, so fill before the steep section.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit where the boundary is crossed, group size capped at twelve. The start is an unsigned roadside pull-out rather than a developed trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass for the vehicle. The lake sits just below the 4,000 ft campfire line and the ridge camps above it are stoves-only regardless; treat the whole area as no-fire in practice.
bivy.capacity: Small informal camp on the benches by the lake, room for a couple of tents. Nothing designated or maintained. Tarns on the ridge above take another tent or two.

bivy.name: Glacier Basin — Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill
bivy.notes: This is the working high camp for the northern half of the group. Cadet forms the basin's north arc and Monte Cristo Peak the southeast arc, so both go as reasonable summit days from here rather than the brutal round trips they are from the road. Foggy Peak rises straight out of the ground immediately northeast of the townsite and is climbed off this same trail, and the Wilmans Peaks and the Spires are reached by leaving the Glacier Basin trail low and working up towards the '76 Glacier side. Getting here means the four-mile road walk to the townsite, then the trail past the cabins and over 76 Creek, half a mile of old road grade along Glacier Creek, then a long steep stretch beside Glacier Falls that is more slick rock scramble than trail and is genuinely unpleasant wet or iced. Snow holds in the basin into July most years and the falls section is the part that turns parties around early season. The whole basin is old mining ground, so stay on the established pads and off the thin heather.
bivy.water: CARRY IT IN. Surface water through this basin and the drainage below has been measured with arsenic and other heavy metals above drinking water standards, and filtering, boiling and chemical treatment remove none of that. Snowmelt high in the basin, well away from old workings and tailings, is the least bad option if you run dry, and it is not a plan to rely on.
bivy.permit: Inside the HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue wilderness permit from the trailhead box, no quota or reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in Glacier Basin and within a quarter mile of the trail; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the timbered knoll in the middle of the basin and on the rise beyond it, enough for several parties spread out, but they are the only durable ground and they fill on a fine weekend

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite campground, four miles up the closed road
bivy.notes: Because the road is gated at Barlow Pass, staging here is the normal plan for this group rather than a luxury: it turns a four-mile approach walk into an evening stroll and puts Glacier Basin, Poodle Dog Pass and every summit above them within a sane day. The walk in follows the old road and railway grade with almost no gain, and it is flat enough that many parties ride bikes and stash them at the townsite. About a mile up, the old road bridge over the South Fork Sauk is long gone; the crossing is on logs or a ford, and it is the one piece of the approach that varies year to year and can be genuinely serious in snowmelt or after heavy rain. Beyond it the timber road bridges over the creek gullies are intact. The ground here was remediated after the tailings and mine debris were found to be badly contaminated, and that cleanup is why the area is open at all, but old workings, adits and metal remain scattered off the paths. Access is seasonal at the margins: Barlow Pass is at the end of the pavement and stays reachable from Granite Falls when the gravel stretch of the loop towards Bedal is gated shut for winter.
bivy.water: DO NOT DRINK THE LOCAL WATER. The South Fork Sauk and the creeks around the townsite carry arsenic and heavy metals from a century of mining and milling, at levels above drinking water standards, and a backcountry filter or a rolling boil deals with the biology and leaves the metals exactly where they were. Bring every litre you intend to drink, for the stay and for the walk out.
bivy.permit: The campground and townsite flat sit OUTSIDE designated wilderness, so no wilderness permit is needed to sleep here and fires are allowed in the provided rings; the boundary is crossed a short way up either the Glacier Basin or the Poodle Dog trail, where the free self-issue permit applies. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass at Barlow Pass. MUCH OF THE TOWNSITE IS PRIVATE LAND — roughly half the original lots are still in private hands with inherited mining rights, cabins are posted no trespassing, and some are occupied. Camp only in the marked sites and treat everything else as somebody's property.
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly six developed walk-in sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet on the flat by the old townsite, plus a scatter of informal spots along the road grade coming in

bivy.name: Twin Lakes basin, under the west face of Columbia
bivy.notes: The high camp for the southern half of the group. Columbia Peak's west spur rises straight off this basin and is the reason most parties come, and the Columbia Glacier route on Kyes is staged from here too, working up the glacier pinched between Columbia and Kyes to the weakness high on it. Reaching the lakes is the hard part of the trip and is routinely underestimated: four miles of road to the townsite, then a mile and a half up to Poodle Dog Pass at 4,350 ft, then a braided, intermittent boot path east that gains a viewpoint around 5,400 ft before dropping five hundred feet down to the lakes on ground steep enough to count as a scramble in places. Nobody makes good time on that last mile. Summit days are long from here, and the climb back out of the basin at the end is what people remember.
bivy.water: The lakes and their outlet, high above the mined ground and the usual source for parties camped here; treat for biology as normal. Snow and ice cover the basin well into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt.
bivy.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lakes and within a quarter mile of them; the basin is high, heavily used and has almost no wood to spare.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of sites on the rocky lakeshore with two backcountry toilets, and better, more sheltered pitches on the knoll at the lakes' outlet half a mile further on

bivy.name: Silver Lake, below Poodle Dog Pass
bivy.notes: A short side trail from Poodle Dog Pass drops to the lake, which makes it the softer option on this side of the group: it is a good thousand feet lower than Twin Lakes and it avoids the steep, loose drop into and back out of that basin at the end of a summit day. Parties heading for Columbia often sleep here instead and accept the longer approach in the morning, and it is a sensible bail if the boot path east of the pass is still snowed and the Twin Lakes descent looks like a bad idea. It is also the practical camp for anything on the Silvertip side of the pass. Snow lingers around the lake into early summer and the pass itself holds it longest. Fires are out, so carry a stove.
bivy.water: The lake, above the old workings and reliable through the season; treat for biology.
bivy.permit: HENRY M. JACKSON WILDERNESS — free self-issue permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake.
bivy.capacity: Small — established sites in the trees and on the benches around the lake, with a box toilet; comfortably fewer parties than Twin Lakes

bivy.name: Barlow Pass roadhead
bivy.notes: Sleeping at the car is what most parties actually do the night before a long single push into this group, because the four-mile road walk to the townsite is flat and fast enough to be swallowed by a pre-dawn start. It is the last point vehicles reach: the gate closes the Monte Cristo road here, and it is also where the Weden Creek trail towards Gothic Basin and Del Campo branches off a mile up the road, so the same parking serves objectives that have nothing else in common. Break-ins at a busy roadhead are a known problem, so leave nothing visible. Nothing here has any shelter and there is no reason to linger; treat it as a staging point rather than a night out, and if you want a real camp, walk the four miles in.
bivy.water: None. Nothing potable here and nothing potable anywhere up the road, so this is where you load every litre for the trip.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to leave a vehicle. No wilderness permit needed at the pass itself, but pick up the free self-issue permit here for anything crossing into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness above the townsite.
bivy.capacity: Car bivy only — a gravel parking area at the gate, no sites, no tables, no pads. It fills on summer weekends and it is not a campground.

Fires, except self-contained carry-in devices such as stoves, are prohibited within a quarter mile of the Glacier Basin Trail - this route's own approach - and of Goat Lake, Silver Lake, Upper and Lower Twin Lakes, Lake Sally Ann, Lake Minotaur, Lake Theseus, Heather Lake, Glasses Lake and Lake Valhalla.

bivy.name: Airplane Lake
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Mount Saul and effectively the only one, and camping here is what turns a brutal outing into a reasonable two days. Done in a single push from the road the standard route runs about sixteen miles round trip with five thousand three hundred feet of gain, which is a long day by any measure and a very long one on ground this rough. The lake sits roughly two thousand two hundred feet above Indian Creek, in a large depression under the upper east slopes, with the summit still some two thousand feet above it — so a party sleeping here has the worst of the climbing behind them and a clean morning on the east slope and east face. THE APPROACH PATH IS THE HARD PART. It leaves the Indian Creek trail at about four and a half miles, immediately before a valley campsite, marked only by a sign stating that marking of routes is prohibited; there is no other signage and the track is faint. It climbs steeply through the 2016 burn, which means loose footing, no shade, blowdown that changes with every windstorm and standing dead timber overhead. Recent volunteer work has had the trail in good condition in places, but that is a season-by-season matter rather than a promise. Season is roughly mid-July into early October; the east side melts out reasonably early but the upper slopes hold snow and an axe is worth carrying in the first half of the summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the climbing season along with snowmelt into the inlet early on. This is the last certain water on the mountain: the two thousand feet of slope between the lake and the summit carry nothing once the snow has gone. Fill everything here for the climb and for the night, and treat it.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the White River trailhead register — no quota, no reservation, nothing to book. Party size is capped at twelve counting people and stock. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass covers parking at the trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline on existing bare ground; the basin is small. Carry a stove — the district runs summer fire restrictions on this dry east side as a matter of course and they are often total bans.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground on benches around the lake for one or two parties. Nothing developed, nothing signed, no toilet — and almost certainly nobody else there. This is a genuinely lightly visited basin and solitude is the main thing it offers.

bivy.name: The Indian Creek valley camps and the Airplane Lake junction site
bivy.notes: The junction camp is the useful one and it is the landmark as much as the site: the climbers' path for Airplane Lake turns off immediately before it, so a party that reaches an obvious valley campsite and has seen no turning has just walked past the only one there is. Sleeping here rather than at the lake trades a shorter, easier first day for a much harder second one, and most parties would rather push to the lake. Where it earns its place is on the way out, and for a party that has been slowed by the road or the burn and does not want to start the two-thousand-foot climbers' path in the evening. The valley trail itself runs about ten and a half miles in total to the Pacific Crest Trail at Indian Pass, crossing the White River on a bridge right at the trailhead and then climbing very gently; it is brushy and boggy in places, which is a nuisance rather than an obstacle. Expect burn for long stretches, and treat the dead timber overhead as a real reason not to pitch under it in wind.
bivy.water: Indian Creek runs beside the trail for the whole of this stretch and water is abundant; parts of the valley trail are boggy in early season for the same reason. Every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. This is the generous half of the approach and it ends the moment you start climbing.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the White River trailhead register, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Fires are legal in existing rings at this elevation outside a burn ban, but bans are usual here from midsummer and much of the surrounding forest is fire-killed, so use a stove.
bivy.capacity: Scattered informal sites along the Indian Creek trail, one or two tents each, including the established spot immediately past the unsigned turn for Airplane Lake. Nothing developed and no facilities.

bivy.name: White River road end trailhead
bivy.notes: The staging point for the whole trip, and worth its own entry because the drive is where this approach most often fails. The White River road leaves the Lake Wenatchee end and turns to gravel several miles before the trailhead, ending at about 2,300 feet where the White River trail, the Indian Creek trail, the Mount David trail and the Boulder Creek trail all begin. Getting the right one matters: only Indian Creek leads to Mount Saul. There are small developed forest campgrounds spaced along the road below the trailhead which are a better place to spend a night than the parking area itself if they are open, but they are primitive, first come and first served, and carry no potable supply. THE ROAD IS THE FRAGILE PART, AND IT IS CLOSED RIGHT NOW. Okanogan-Wenatchee closure order 06-17-07-2026-40 (Little Giant Fire), effective 3 September 2026 through 31 October 2026 unless rescinded sooner, closes FSR 6400 to the end of the road and lists the White River Trailhead. It is not named in the Wenatchee River District storm-damage road order (06-17-07-2026-11, 20 May 2026 through 31 December 2027), which closes seventeen other roads. When the road is shut low, the trailhead is a substantial road walk or bike ride further on and the trip changes character completely.
bivy.water: The White River is at the trailhead and needs treating. There is no potable supply and no tap. Fill here, and fill again from Indian Creek on the way up, because everything above the valley is dry.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. The free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit comes from the register here rather than being arranged in advance — no quota, no reservation. Twelve-person party limit. Fire restrictions on this side are near-permanent through summer and commonly ban open flame entirely.
bivy.capacity: A gravel parking area at the road end with room to sleep in a vehicle, and no campground facilities. This is a roadhead recorded because a party arriving from the west side in the evening needs somewhere to be before starting an approach this long.

bivy.name: The east slope above Airplane Lake — no established camp
bivy.notes: The honest answer for this peak is that Airplane Lake is the camp and there is nothing above it worth having. The lake already puts the summit within a straightforward morning on the east slope and east face, so climbing higher with a pack buys almost nothing and costs the water, the shelter and the flat ground all at once. The northwest face is sheer and is not the way anyone goes; the east side is open scrambling terrain and the difficulty of this mountain lies in the approach rather than in the climbing. Where a high bivouac has any argument at all is for a party linking Saul with the ridge country toward Indian Head and the crest, which is a different and much longer trip, and even then the sensible pattern is to sleep at water and move over the tops in the day. Treat anything above the lake as emergency ground.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and only early in the season. From roughly August onward there is nothing at all above the lake, and anyone sleeping here carries every drop up two thousand feet. This is the mistake to avoid rather than a plan to make.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, twelve-person limit, Northwest Forest Pass at the White River trailhead. No fires at this elevation and nothing to burn. The ground is thin alpine turf and scree that scars for years — camp on rock or gravel if you camp at all.
bivy.capacity: None established. There is broken ground and the occasional flat spot on the slope between the lake and the summit rocks where a small party could put a tent down, but nothing has been built and nobody camps here as a matter of course. Recorded so the absence is stated rather than filled in with an invented site.

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

bivy.name: Bedal Campground, Mountain Loop Highway
bivy.notes: The closest road camp to the Sloan Peak and Bedal Creek trailheads, and the standard place to sleep the night before a Sloan attempt since the useful start time is well before dawn. It sits on the UNPAVED stretch of the loop, so access depends entirely on whether the seasonal gate between Barlow Pass and the Bedal area is open — the road normally closes around early November and reopens in the second half of May, with the exact date set by snow and washout repairs. Coming from Granite Falls when that gate is shut means the long drive around through Darrington. Check the Darrington district's road status, because the gate has opened as late as Memorial Day in heavy years.
bivy.water: No treated drinking water at the sites — bring your own or filter from the adjacent river

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. bivy.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
bivy.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. EVERYTHING ABOVE THE TRAILHEAD DEPENDS ON THE NORTH FORK SAUK FORD, which is the genuine crux of the trip: it has no bridge, runs fast and thigh-deep or worse in snowmelt, and log jams that worked one season are gone the next. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.
bivy.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow

bivy.capacity: Small, scattered pockets — a few tents on heather and gravel benches; no single site holds a large party

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but OUTSIDE any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

bivy.name: Sloan Peak high camp — heather benches above Cougar Creek
bivy.notes: Camps here sit on open heather with the Sloan Glacier and the start of the corkscrew ledge system directly above, which makes for a short summit morning. Lower bivy pockets exist around 3,500 ft where the trail eases off, and some parties stop there when the river ford has eaten the day. Camp on bare ground or snow rather than the meadow turf, which is thin and slow to recover.
bivy.water: Cougar Creek below the benches and snowmelt runnels near camp are reliable into midsummer; by late August the higher pockets can dry and parties may need to descend or melt snow

bivy.name: Foggy Lake, Gothic Basin
bivy.notes: From here both Del Campo and Gothic go as short snow-and-scramble outings, which is why parties carry in rather than push either from the road. The approach leaves Barlow Pass on the old road grade before turning up a steep, rocky climbers' trail with slabby sections that are unpleasant when wet. The basin is bare rock and thin alpine soil with almost nothing to bury waste in, so pack it out. Whether the basin is a July trip or an August one moves year to year with the snowpack.
bivy.water: The lake is the water source and is dependable, but it is frequently frozen or snow-covered into July, so early-season parties should expect to melt or find running melt below the outlet
bivy.permit: National forest land, NOT wilderness — no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass at Barlow Pass. Campfires are prohibited in the basin.
bivy.capacity: Moderate — established pockets on the south shore and on the bench toward the base of Gothic; the basin absorbs a fair number of parties but fills on good weekends

bivy.name: Monte Cristo townsite, walk-in from Barlow Pass
bivy.notes: Reaching it is a flat four-mile walk on the old road and rail grade from the Barlow Pass gate, which makes it an easy place to stage a long approach without a real backpacking day. Climbers use it mainly as a jumping-off point deeper into the Monte Cristo group rather than for Vesper or Sloan. Barlow Pass itself is the usual car-bivy for early starts on Gothic Basin, though it is a parking area rather than a campground — no water, no facilities, and it fills. The site is historic mining ground with old debris and open workings, so wander off the beaten paths carefully.
bivy.water: Creek and river water is plentiful and must NOT be treated as ordinary backcountry water. This drainage carries arsenic and other heavy metals from the mining era at levels above drinking-water standards, and filtering, boiling and tablets do none of them any good — those methods address organisms, not dissolved metals. Carry what you need for the road walk, or draw from tributaries well above the old workings rather than from the valley bottom.
bivy.permit: Outside designated wilderness at the townsite itself; no camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Barlow Pass. The peaks above, including the Columbia Glacier group, sit in the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness where the free self-issue permit applies.
bivy.capacity: Small — roughly half a dozen developed sites with tables, fire rings and a toilet, plus scattered backcountry spots along the way in

bivy.name: Bedal Creek roadhead
bivy.notes: Worth recording because it is the overnight most Sloan parties actually use. The Corkscrew from Bedal Creek is a reasonable single day of thirteen or fourteen hours for a fit party, and successful ascents in under twelve hours are common, so the usual pattern is to sleep at the trailhead and start around four in the morning rather than carry a camp to the ridge.
bivy.water: Carry it, or take it from Bedal Creek on the way in.
bivy.permit: A Northwest Forest Pass is usually reported as the required parking permit, though not universally; carry one.
bivy.capacity: Roadside parking, not a designated site.

bivy.name: Bedal-Sloan saddle
bivy.notes: The first camp on the ridge, reached by traversing open and partly brushy slopes past a small lake. Usable, but the ridge above is the better camp and most parties who carry a camp go the extra distance. Elevation is given as either 5,330 or 5,380 ft depending on the account.
bivy.water: A tarn at the saddle, and it is the weak point — it is stagnant, and parties have found frog and mosquito larvae in it. Better water is a short way above, around 5,500 ft, where small streams cascade down; fill there rather than at the pond.
bivy.capacity: Four to six tents, so leave room for another party.

bivy.name: Ridge above the Sloan Glacier
bivy.notes: The preferred high camp, on the crest overlooking the glacier with a long view. From here it is about half a mile of traverse east-southeast to the saddle near 5,900 ft and then up to gain the glacier around 6,800 ft, which makes for a short summit morning. Expect to camp on snow through June; the route's window is squeezed at both ends, with routefinding through the heather benches hard when they are still buried and the glacier growing impassable late in the season.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams below camp; the last running water is around 6,000 ft, and above that you are melting snow.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant spots, with one dry site big enough for about four tents — more if you are willing to pitch on snow.

bivy.name: Big Four north-side staging and base bivouac
bivy.notes: Big Four is a car-to-car objective by design: the trailhead sits at low elevation barely a mile from the base of a face that rises about 4,000 feet, so the climbing starts almost immediately and there is no approach worth camping to shorten. Parties on the north-side lines, including the long winter couloir routes, typically leave overnight gear at the base and go up and down in a push rather than carrying a bivouac onto the face, which is a considered choice on a wall this active — rockfall and avalanche off it are constant and audible through the night. That same activity is why this is a contingency and not a recommendation: sleeping under this face means sleeping under a debris cone that is there because things fall on it. Position any bivouac well out of the runout, not at the toe of the snow. THE ICE CAVES AT THE BASE ARE LETHAL and collapse every year — do not camp near them, on them, or in them, and stay off them entirely. The nearest legal drive-in beds are the developed campgrounds down the paved loop toward Verlot.
bivy.water: Creeks draining the face run all season near the base, and the debris field itself is meltwater. Treat everything. There is no developed water at the picnic area.
bivy.permit: Not inside any wilderness — this side of the highway is ordinary national forest with no camping permit requirement. A federal recreation pass is required to park at the picnic area. Fire restrictions are common from midsummer and are frequently forest-wide.
bivy.capacity: No established camp of any kind. The picnic area at the trailhead is DAY USE ONLY and camping there is not permitted; parties climbing the north side bivouac informally at the base of the face on the avalanche debris and boulder ground beyond the maintained path.

bivy.name: Bathtub Lakes basin, east of Mount Pilchuck
bivy.notes: This is the only real camp on Pilchuck and it serves the east side rather than the standard route. It is reached from below, from the Bear Lake and Pinnacle Lake trailhead on a spur road off the loop east of Verlot, then up past the lower lake and into the gulch above — a loose, brushy, steep piece of ground with vegetation-pulling and poor rock that is the genuine difficulty of the East Ridge, not the ridge itself. Camping in the basin splits that so the gulch is climbed fresh. It has no bearing on the standard summit trail, which leaves the end of the Mount Pilchuck road on the other side of the mountain and is a straightforward day hike to the restored summit lookout with no camping along it and none needed. Treat this as a plan for the east side and as a contingency for anyone who commits to the gulch late and would rather not descend it in the dark.
bivy.water: The lakes and their outlets, dependable through the season and needing treatment. This is a wet basin, which is the whole reason it works as a camp.
bivy.permit: The summit and upper mountain are a STATE CONSERVATION AREA rather than national forest, but this basin and the approach to it are forest land and no camping permit applies. The parking requirement at the trailheads on this mountain is the FEDERAL pass — a state Discover Pass is not valid at them, which catches people out because of the state park name. No fires on the state land above, and fire bans are routine below in late summer.
bivy.capacity: Informal sites among the small lakes and benches of the basin; a few parties, nothing developed

bivy.name: Three Fingers Lookout, south summit
bivy.notes: This is the reason to come here overnight and it is genuinely one of the few summit cabins in the state a climbing party can sleep in. It sits on the southernmost of the three summits, on ground that was blasted flat to seat it, and the final approach to the door is a set of steep wooden ladders bolted against the cliff — vertical, exposed, and not somewhere to be carrying a loose pack or moving in the dark. Getting to them means crossing the glacier on the peak's north side above the gap, which is a real crossing rather than a snowfield walk: axe and crampons all year, a rope and the ability to use it, and late in the season a moat between ice and rock that some parties follow instead, when they can find its entrance. It has been rebuilt and repaired repeatedly by volunteers over the decades, most recently in the structure itself, so it is sound but spartan — bare boards, shutters, no stove worth relying on, no facilities. Coming as a climbing party rather than a hiking one, the sensible plan is to camp lower and go up light, because a full lookout at nine at night with the ladders behind you is a bad position.
bivy.water: None at the lookout. The last dependable water is the tarns and runnels around Goat Flats and the snowmelt near the gap below; above that you are melting snow off the glacier or carrying it. Plan on hauling several litres per person up the final stretch and expect to melt if you arrive late in a dry summer.
bivy.permit: No permit and no reservation, and none is available — it cannot be booked. Inside the Boulder River Wilderness, which requires no self-issue permit to camp. A federal recreation pass is the parking requirement at forest trailheads on this side. Campfires are prohibited the whole way from the lake below up to the peak, and there is nothing to burn at the top anyway. The cabin is volunteer-maintained: leave it swept, close the shutters and the door properly against weather and rodents, pack out every scrap including food waste, and do not take or move anything belonging to it. If it has been closed for repair, stay out.
bivy.capacity: First come, first served, and small. A single sleeping platform takes two comfortably; the floor absorbs another two or three on pads, and parties have squeezed six to eight in at the cost of everyone's night. Treat four as the realistic number and anything above six as an emergency. THERE IS NOWHERE TO PITCH A TENT OUTSIDE — the cabin occupies the whole blasted summit block, so a full lookout means descending.

bivy.name: Tin Can Gap high camp
bivy.notes: The last flat ground before the glacier, roughly a mile short of the lookout, and the correct camp for a party that wants the summit block early and cold rather than soft. The maintained trail effectively ends here, so everything above is a bootpath, snow and the ladders. Its value is that it puts the glacier crossing and the ladders in the first hour of the day, when the snow is still firm — a real advantage over starting from the meadows two miles back. The cost is exposure: it is a gap, it catches weather, and there is nothing sheltering about it. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin vegetation, and take a hard look at whether the crossing above is in condition before committing to a camp that only makes sense if you go up.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only for most of the season, and nothing at all once the snow around the gap has gone. Assume you are melting or carrying from Goat Flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit required. Federal recreation pass to park. Campfires prohibited on this whole stretch of trail; there is no fuel here regardless.
bivy.capacity: A few small pitches on rock and snow at and just below the gap; one or two parties, not a group site

bivy.name: Goat Flats
bivy.notes: Open subalpine meadow about two miles beyond the lake, and the default base for anything on Three Fingers — the lookout, the middle summit, or a look at the south face. From here the gap and the glacier are within a straightforward morning. It is also the honest fallback for a party that walked up hoping for a bunk in the lookout and found it occupied: about two miles back down from the ladders, which is a long but manageable retreat with headlamps. The meadow soil is thin and heavily used, so pitch on the bare established spots and not on fresh turf. Snow lies here well into summer and the meadows are boggy for weeks after it goes.
bivy.water: Reliable through most of the season from the tarns and small streams in the meadows, though the standing water is shallow and warms up late in summer. Treat everything. Later in a dry year the tarns shrink and the better water is the running melt above the flats.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. Federal recreation pass at the trailhead. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED in the Goat Flats area and along this trail generally. Bears work this basin, so hard-sided or hung food storage is expected rather than optional.
bivy.capacity: The main camping area on this approach — several established pockets spread through the meadows and around the tarns. It absorbs a fair number of parties but is genuinely crowded on summer and autumn weekends, and it is the overflow when the lookout is full.

bivy.name: Saddle Lake
bivy.notes: About two and a half miles in from the road end, in dense timber, and low enough that it is a contingency rather than a plan for anyone climbing. It matters for two reasons. First, the road: the Tupso Pass road has a long washout history and has at times been cut miles short of the trailhead, leaving parties to walk or bike the road grade — when that is the situation the lake is as far as many get on day one. Second, it is where a party that started late, or turned around at the gap in bad conditions, can stop without pushing all the way out. Do not plan a Three Fingers climb from here; it is too low and too far. Bugs are heavy in early summer.
bivy.water: The lake, which is dependable all season and needs treating. This is the last easy water before the meadows above.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no camping permit. CAMPING IS PROHIBITED within 200 feet of the shoreline, so the lakeside spots that look obvious are not all legal. Campfires are prohibited within 200 feet of the lake and along the trail above it.
bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of spots in the timber and meadow near the lake, plus an old volunteer-built shelter at the meadow edge that should be treated as rough emergency cover rather than accommodation

bivy.capacity: Small — a handful of spots in the timber and meadow near the lake, plus an old volunteer-built shelter at the meadow edge that should be treated as rough emergency cover rather than accommodation

access.fees: None — no climbing fee (National Forest, not Mount Rainier NP)

bivy.name: Saddle Lake
bivy.notes: Two and a half miles in from Tupso Pass on a rough, root-bound forest trail — the first water and the first flat ground, but low and far from the mountain. Volunteers built a shelter at the meadow edge here in the early 1970s; no current source confirms it still stands or is usable, so do not plan on sleeping in it.
bivy.water: The lake — there is no running water here, and in a warm year it has been reported shrinking and buggy by mid-summer.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Boulder River Wilderness. Camping is prohibited within 200 ft slope distance of the shoreline of Saddle Lake and of Bandana Lake, and campfires are prohibited within the same 200 ft of both. No trailhead permit or quota is published for this trail, and the wilderness is closed throughout to pack and saddle stock.
bivy.capacity: Not published. It is a small four-acre lake and the setback rule below pushes camps back off the water.

bivy.name: Goat Flats
bivy.notes: The main camp for the peak, an open subalpine meadow on a ridge crest a little over two miles beyond Saddle Lake and roughly two and a half miles short of the lookout, with a view west to Puget Sound. Bears work the area, so bring a canister or another way to secure food.
bivy.water: Tarns only — there is no running water at the flats, and the tarn water has been described as stale by autumn. The last dependable running water is a stream well below, around the 4,200 ft mark; above the flats the next water is glacier and snow melt beyond Tin Can Gap. Late in a dry season, plan to carry from low down.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Boulder River Wilderness. Campfires are prohibited in the Goat Flats area outright, and also anywhere within a quarter mile of Trail 641 above Saddle Lake. No overnight permit or quota is published. There is a backcountry toilet at the flats; note that it must not be used for packed-out waste bags.
bivy.capacity: A number of established sites spread across the meadow, and it is regularly crowded on summer and autumn weekends. Camp only on ground that is already bare — the meadow is fragile and the Forest Service asks for existing sites only.

bivy.name: Tin Can Gap
bivy.notes: The last ground before the climbing starts: the Forest Service names it Tin Pan Gap, most climbers say Tin Can Gap, and it is where the route stops being a walk and starts needing equipment and judgement. accounts disagree on the distance in, from roughly six to eight miles, so do not plan a turnaround time off one figure. Useful mainly to parties who want a short summit morning on the glacier.
bivy.water: Glacier and snow melt only.
bivy.permit: The campfire closure along Trail 641 above Saddle Lake extends here.
bivy.capacity: A few spots at the gap and at the foot of the snow slope below it — small, and second choice to Goat Flats.

bivy.name: Three Fingers Lookout
bivy.notes: A 1930s fire lookout on the South Peak that climbers sleep in, reached by ladders with serious exposure — decide for yourself whether the final block is safe on the day. The door is never locked, but in winter and spring it can be frozen, swollen or buried, and the summit block itself is hard to climb then; summer is the season for it. Bring a tent as a fallback: it fills on good weekends and visitation is heavy even midweek. accounts disagree on whether there is usable ground to camp outside — some say pitch below the lookout, others say there is nowhere safe on the summit at all — so do not count on it.
bivy.water: None at the site — there is no potable water at the lookout and nothing to melt but snow.
bivy.permit: No fee, no reservation and no permit — it is open to whoever reaches it first. There is no toilet: carry a waste bag and pack everything out, and do not put it in the Goat Flats toilet or leave it below the lookout. The volunteers who maintain the building ask that you take crampons off before going in, keep the shutters closed in bad weather and when you leave, leave nothing behind, and not force shutters that are locked.
bivy.capacity: Maximum occupancy of eight, first come first served. Accounts of the actual floor put it nearer three or four people plus two more on the sleeping platform, so eight is a squeeze rather than a plan. Arrive early or expect to be turned away by whoever got there first.

access.fees: $5 day-use Northwest Forest Pass (or annual pass) at the trailhead
access.notes: None required for day use; Northwest Forest Pass recommended for parking. Digital Recreation Day Pass available via Recreation.gov for Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest day-use sites. Overnight use requires separate permits; verify current conditions with Verlot Public Service Center (360) 691-7791. Tupso Pass Road (FS 41) washed out 4.8 miles in (past Canyon Creek bridge at mile 8); permanently closed to vehicles. Hiking and biking allowed. Approximately 9 additional miles to actual trailhead required - bicycle recommended for approach.

bivy.name: Moose Creek bridge roadhead
bivy.notes: The bridge on the Mine Road was closed and barricaded in 2008 and the ground beside it is where parties sleep in their vehicles. The route's own description recommends it, and the reason is the length of the day: twelve to fourteen hours car to summit means a start well before dawn, and this is the only way to get one without carrying a camp uphill.
bivy.water: Moose Creek at the bridge.
bivy.capacity: A roadside pull-in, not a designated site.

bivy.name: Whitehorse Ridge platform above Lone Tree Pass
bivy.notes: The one large flat area on the entire route, about fifteen minutes of traversing beyond Lone Tree Pass, and by common consent where everyone camps; there is no ambiguity about where a party has pitched. Ground is usually snow, so expect to dig a platform. It is an exposed crest with a view from Baker to Dome Peak and nothing to hide behind. Watch the slope below the pass — parties have reported fresh rockfall and snow-roller debris appearing overnight. Published elevations for Lone Tree Pass itself differ, from about 4,800 to 5,000 ft.
bivy.water: None running. There is a snow patch below Lone Tree Pass and nothing else until well past High Pass, so this camp is melt-only — fine in the April-to-June snow season the route is normally climbed, and dry once the patch has gone.
bivy.capacity: Room for a dozen or more tents on the broad crest — you will not be short of ground.

bivy.name: Below High Pass at the first running water
bivy.notes: The mid-summer alternative, once the snow patch below Lone Tree Pass has melted and the ridge camp has no water at all. It costs another long traverse but puts you at the head of the basin, below the large talus field that is High Pass, with a short summit morning onto the Whitehorse Glacier. Note that High Pass is a feature of this route and not a separate approach.
bivy.water: The first running water on the route — the reason to come this far.

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.rules: Standard wilderness regulations apply: no bikes, carts, or other wheeled/mechanized equipment; keep groups small; minimize impact camping near the trail and pass.
access.permit: No self-issue or quota wilderness permit required for Boulder River Wilderness.
access.closures: The Moose Creek bridge on the Mine Road spur was removed and barricaded in 2008; park at the barricade and cross the creek on foot/boulders to reach the trailhead, adding a short distance to the approach. Check current Mount Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts for washouts on the gravel spur before driving.
access.landManager: USDA Forest Service — Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District (Boulder River Wilderness)

bivy.name: Whitehorse high camp, benches near Lone Tree Pass
bivy.notes: This is the high camp for the Northwest Shoulder, and most parties who do not intend a twelve-to-sixteen hour car-to-car day use it. The route is around 6,000 to 7,000 feet of gain from a low trailhead and the lower trail is notoriously steep and brushy, so splitting it at the pass converts a punishing single day into two reasonable ones and puts the glacier and the exposed summit scrambling in the morning. The sheltered meadow just beyond the pass is the pick — trees break the wind and it looks straight at the summit. Everything about this approach depends on the Mine Road out of the highway west of Darrington: it is rough, narrow, overgrown enough to scratch a vehicle, and has had bridge and washout closures that push the start well down the hill and add road walking. Confirm how far you can drive before you plan the day. Early season with snow cover over the brush is much the better time; by late summer the glacier above develops crevasses and a large bergschrund and the brush below is at its worst.
bivy.water: Snowmelt in season and the small tarn below the pass on the traverse east; both are seasonal. By late summer this side dries out and there may be nothing, so carry up or plan to melt. There is no water on the trail below.
bivy.permit: Boulder River Wilderness — no permit to camp, no quota, no self-issue box. No fee at the trailhead, which is unusual for this area and reflects how minimal the parking is. Fires are a bad idea on this ground and are commonly banned outright in late summer.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a flat sheltered meadow just past the pass takes a couple of tents, with smaller pockets on benches nearby and more ground on the traverse east toward the small lake below the pass. One or two parties.

bivy.name: Whitehorse Community Park campground, Darrington
bivy.notes: The nearest developed drive-in base to the Mine Road, sitting just outside Darrington with the mountain itself directly in view, which makes it a useful place to look at conditions on the northwest side the evening before. Its real role is staging: the Niederprum trailhead has room for only a handful of vehicles and nothing else, so sleeping in town and driving up in the small hours is the usual pattern rather than camping at the road end. Because it is county-run its season and fees are set separately from the forest campgrounds and change independently of them. The winter closure is the catch — the best window for the Northwest Shoulder is spring, and the campground may not be open yet.
bivy.water: Developed park water in season; confirm before relying on it outside summer
bivy.permit: COUNTY park, not national forest — a nightly fee applies and no federal or state pass does anything here. Seasonal: closed and winterized through the winter months, roughly mid-autumn to mid-spring, which rules it out for the spring snow season when Whitehorse is actually in condition.
bivy.capacity: A developed county campground with tent and equestrian sites on a large park property; nightly fee

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.rules: Standard wilderness regulations apply: no bikes or mechanized/wheeled equipment; keep groups small; minimize impact.
access.permit: No self-issue or quota wilderness permit required for Boulder River Wilderness.
access.closures: Moose Creek bridge removed/barricaded since 2008; park at the barricade and cross on foot. Check MBS NF alerts for gravel-road washouts before driving.
