bivy.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
bivy.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward

bivy.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
bivy.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirely exposed, with no shelter of any kind and nothing to anchor to but snow, so it needs a settled forecast and the discipline to walk back down to the ridge if the weather turns. The cornice line along the summit ridge is real and changes through the season, so pitch back from the edge and look at where the ground drops away before dark rather than after. Snow cover is what makes the site work; late in a thin year the top is rock and heather and much less pleasant.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. Food needs an approved canister or a proper hang; the food lockers in this zone are at designated valley camps, not up here.
bivy.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites

bivy.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
bivy.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. Icy Peak is much the more serious of the two summits, with loose exposed rock and a narrow final ridge, so arriving there rested matters. The bivy is small, on snow, and fully committed — retreat from it means reversing the traverse over Ruth. Conditions on this ridge change quickly through the summer and the connecting terrain is more broken later in the season, which is why most parties go in June or July.
bivy.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites

access.fees: No permit fee; a Northwest Forest Pass (or America the Beautiful pass) is needed for trailhead parking
access.permit: Backcountry/wilderness camping permit required for overnight use within North Cascades National Park, available at the Glacier Public Service Center
access.closures: FR 32 (Hannegan Pass Road) is generally inaccessible in winter/early spring due to snow
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker Ranger District); Icy Peak's summit area within North Cascades National Park
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass (parking) / NPS backcountry permit (overnight camping in the Park)

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass (or Interagency/America the Beautiful pass) required for day-use parking at Hannegan Trailhead; NPS backcountry permit fee is $10/person plus a $6 nonrefundable reservation fee during the mid-May-early-October summer season (no charge the rest of the year).
access.notes: Northwest Forest Pass required ($5/day or $30/annual). No specific climbing permit.
access.rules: Pack out human waste (blue bags) — no burial or glacier deposition. Some approaches cross into North Cascades National Park land on the upper mountain, where a NPS backcountry permit is required only if camping overnight past the boundary.
access.permit: Overnight camping once the route crosses into North Cascades National Park (e.g., the Ruth Mountain notch camp or Ruth-Icy col) requires an NPS backcountry permit, reservable on Recreation.gov or issued in person/first-come at the Glacier Public Service Center; the Ruth-Icy area is managed as one of the park's cross-country (off-trail) zones.
access.closures: Ruth Creek/Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32) is not gated, but after normal-to-heavy winters its upper stretch and the Hannegan Pass Trail can hold snow into June; check Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before an early-season trip.

access.rules: No pets allowed within the North Cascades National Park boundary; no campfires, hunting, or mushroom collecting within the Park; secure food and scented items — black bears are common in the valley.
access.permit: No permit needed for a day climb. Overnight camping within the North Cascades National Park portion of the approach requires a paid backcountry permit — $10/person plus a non-refundable $6 fee during the mid-May-to-early-October fee season (no charge the rest of the year). Reserve in advance via Recreation.gov (email-issued permits for the Mount Baker Highway/Nooksack area), or pick one up in person at the Glacier Public Service Center, which now issues NCNP backcountry permits only on Thursdays and Fridays (seasonally) — the Forest Service itself stopped issuing NCNP permits there in September 2023.
access.closures: Ruth Creek has no bridge at the trailhead; wade or cross on a log if one is present — logs can be submerged and the ford can become too high to safely wade in early summer. Nooksack Cirque Road #34 and Trail #750 are primitive with limited maintenance (brush, blowdown).
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Ranger District; the uppermost approach passes near/into the North Cascades National Park boundary (roughly a mile past the wilderness boundary).

bivy.name: Shoulder camp above Price Lake, between the Price and East Nooksack glaciers
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Nooksack Tower and the only established position on the mountain, used by both the classic line on the north side and the much harder south face. It sits on the shoulder dividing the Price Glacier from the Nooksack Cirque, reached by leaving Price Lake, following the boot path onto the moraine as it rounds the north side of the lake and lower glacier, then peeling up left through a small defile onto the ridge where a goat path runs nearly to the slabs. Do not confuse it with the bivy on Shuksan's north face rib, which is a different place approached from the opposite side of the range entirely. From here the north side route drops to the bergschrund and the south face is reached by downclimbing and a rappel to a pocket glacier and a couloir onto the East Nooksack. Nooksack Tower is one of the harder summits in the range, with loose rock throughout and a descent of ten or more rappels, so the camp is a working platform rather than a comfort. Everything about it depends on the approach below being passable, which is the real problem.
bivy.water: Snowmelt cascades down the cliffs around 5,000 ft on the way up, which is the last dependable water and the place to fill. At camp it is melt or nothing.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone at the head of the Nooksack. Reserved online or issued as a walk-up within 24 hours, collected in person, with per-person and transaction fees. Cross-country rules apply: durable surfaces only, no camping in meadows or within a hundred feet of water, food in an approved canister, and no fires. The lower part of the walk in crosses Mount Baker Wilderness on the forest side, so the parking pass at the road end and the park permit are two separate things you need at once.
bivy.capacity: Flat rock slabs with room for two or three bivy sacks, snow-covered into midsummer; a small party only, and no facilities

bivy.name: Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower
bivy.notes: SAY THIS PLAINLY: there is no real camping in the Nooksack Cirque, and any party heading for Nooksack Tower should expect to improvise a night on gravel or in the trees rather than arrive at a site. The way in is a genuine bushwhack. The spur road dead-ends at Ruth Creek with no bridge, so the trip begins by wading or crossing on whatever log is currently down, and a log that is crossable at dawn can be underwater by afternoon once the day's melt arrives. In early summer Ruth Creek alone can be too high to cross at all, and the North Fork above it is worse. Beyond the creek the route follows two miles of abandoned roadbed, then second growth to the wilderness boundary, then old growth to the river, after which progress depends entirely on whether the gravel bars are exposed or whether you are fighting through riverside brush. Cool weather and low water are what make it work, which is why this valley is best in the autumn — the exact opposite of the season that suits the climbing above. The first ascent party camped near this height on the river before starting up, and little about the ground has become easier since. Treat the water crossings as the crux of the trip, not the climb.
bivy.water: The river and its tributaries are everywhere and never fail, but the North Fork is heavily glacier-fed and runs opaque with rock flour. Filter from a clear side stream rather than the main channel where you can.
bivy.permit: Split. The lower miles are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and then Mount Baker Wilderness, needing only the parking pass and a self-issue wilderness registration. Past the boundary further up the valley it is North Cascades National Park, and a night on that side needs a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, arranged in advance or as a walk-up and collected in person before you start. There is no ranger presence out here to sort it out for you, so know which side of the line you intend to sleep on before you leave the road. No fires.
bivy.capacity: Nothing established. Parties make do on gravel bars when the river is low, or on flat ground in the old growth near the point where the route meets the North Fork. One party at a time in practice, and the ground moves year to year.

access.fees: No pass currently required for parking at the Nooksack Cirque (Ruth Creek) trailhead itself; the main access obstacle is the unbridged Ruth Creek ford, which can rise too high to cross safely in early summer
access.rules: Leave No Trace; blue bags on glaciers
access.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required for overnight stays. Reserve via Recreation.gov, then obtain the permit by email (noca_wilderness@nps.gov) up to 3 days out; walk-up permits can be requested by email the morning before. In-person pickup is available Thursdays and Fridays, June 25-September 25, at the Glacier Public Service Center. Fee is $10/person plus a $6 reservation fee.
access.closures: Ruth Creek has no bridge and may be too high to ford safely in early summer; best crossed in the morning or later in the season

bivy.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
bivy.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward

bivy.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
bivy.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirely exposed, with no shelter of any kind and nothing to anchor to but snow, so it needs a settled forecast and the discipline to walk back down to the ridge if the weather turns. The cornice line along the summit ridge is real and changes through the season, so pitch back from the edge and look at where the ground drops away before dark rather than after. Snow cover is what makes the site work; late in a thin year the top is rock and heather and much less pleasant.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. Food needs an approved canister or a proper hang; the food lockers in this zone are at designated valley camps, not up here.
bivy.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites

bivy.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
bivy.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. Icy Peak is much the more serious of the two summits, with loose exposed rock and a narrow final ridge, so arriving there rested matters. The bivy is small, on snow, and fully committed — retreat from it means reversing the traverse over Ruth. Conditions on this ridge change quickly through the summer and the connecting terrain is more broken later in the season, which is why most parties go in June or July.
bivy.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites

access.fees: $5 per vehicle per day or $30 annually (Northwest Forest Pass or any Interagency Recreation Pass) required at Hannegan Trailhead; WA State Discover Pass is not accepted.
access.rules: Maximum party size of 12 within Mt. Baker Wilderness; no campfires; store food/garbage/toiletries properly at Hannegan Camp (no good trees for hangs). Beyond the NCNP boundary: no pets, camping restricted to designated sites.
access.permit: No permit is required to climb Ruth Mountain or to camp on Ruth Arm within Mt. Baker Wilderness. A backcountry permit (via the Glacier Public Service Center / NCNP Wilderness Information Center) is required to camp above the wilderness boundary inside North Cascades National Park, e.g. near the summit.
access.closures: Hannegan Pass Trail #674 is open year-round to hikers; stock allowed Aug 1-Oct 31. Check Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts for current flood-damage road restrictions before driving in.

access.permit: No permit is required to climb Ruth Mountain or to camp on Ruth Arm within Mt. Baker Wilderness. A backcountry permit (via the Glacier Public Service Center / NCNP Wilderness Information Center) is required to camp above the wilderness boundary inside North Cascades National Park, e.g. near the summit.
access.closures: Hannegan Pass Trail #674 is open year-round to hikers; stock allowed Aug 1-Oct 31. Check Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts for current flood-damage road restrictions before driving in.
access.landManager: Mt. Baker Ranger District, Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, manages the approach and Mt. Baker Wilderness; North Cascades National Park manages the upper mountain above the wilderness boundary.
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker Ranger District) — Mount Baker Wilderness, with some upper routes crossing into North Cascades National Park
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at most trailheads — $30/year or $5/day.

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Beaver Pass Camp
bivy.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
bivy.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
bivy.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
bivy.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
bivy.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
bivy.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

bivy.name: Challenger Arm camp
bivy.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
bivy.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
bivy.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

bivy.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
bivy.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

bivy.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
bivy.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
bivy.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
bivy.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

bivy.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
bivy.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
bivy.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
bivy.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
bivy.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

access.fees: NPS backcountry permit: $10/person plus $6 reservation fee
access.permit: NPS backcountry permit required for overnight camping in the park/NRA
access.closures: Approach road/trail often snow-blocked early season
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (NPS)/Ross Lake NRA; upper approach on Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest
access.passRequired: USFS Recreation Pass required at the Hannegan Trailhead

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, flat dry ground near Whatcom Pass at the end of the maintained trail and the last comfortable night of the trip — reports describe it as vastly more pleasant than anything above. This is where the route leaves trail for the Whatcom Glacier traverse, about four and a half hours and 1,750 ft of gain below Perfect Pass. Sheltered valley-head position. A knoll above the pass around 6,500 ft is also camped, with water a rock-hop away at the creek.
bivy.water: running water beside camp
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: a party of several

bivy.name: Perfect Pass
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, and widely rated one of the finest bivy sites in the range — granite slabs, reliable running water, and the Challenger Glacier starting at the doorstep. It is the standard last camp before roping up. Open and high, so weather arrives without warning; parties have had to navigate back down to it in fog off the glacier, which is an argument for marking it before you leave in the morning.
bivy.water: running water at the pass
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: a few tents on slabs and heather

bivy.name: Crooked Thumb Glacier lateral moraine
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the base for the climb itself, on the narrow lateral moraine at the southern edge of the glacier after crossing the high bench near 8,100 ft and dropping through the West Challenger notch. Fully exposed alpine ground with no shelter and long views out to the volcanoes. The moraine is loose and the glacier below it is heavily crevassed with big moats late in the season — rope up leaving camp, not after.
bivy.water: glacier meltwater
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: tight — a narrow strip, enough for a small party

bivy.name: Ledge at 7,800 ft on the peak's ridge
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY ledge, not a camp — a small stair-stepped shelf on the descent ridge overlooking the precipitous east face, where a party spent an unplanned full night out. No water, no shelter, cold, and highly exposed. On a peak this far in, a benightment is a realistic outcome rather than a remote one, so it is worth knowing this ledge is there and worth carrying enough to survive it.
bivy.water: none
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit required for all overnight trips
bivy.capacity: three at a squeeze

access.fees: NPS backcountry permit fee: $10 per person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; cross-country zone camping rules apply above Perfect Pass.
access.permit: Wilderness/backcountry camping permit from North Cascades National Park Complex; obtain in advance via recreation.gov reservation or first-come walk-up at the Wilderness Information Center (WIC) in Marblemount, WA (on SR-20). Whatcom Pass has a designated NPS camp; the upper approach (Perfect Pass, Crooked Thumb Glacier) is in a cross-country zone.
access.closures: Seasonal snow access; Ruth Creek Road/Hannegan Trailhead access and SR-20 (for the Ross Lake option) are both subject to seasonal and washout-driven closures.

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.
bivy.water: None. These are snow-and-rock bivouacs — carry water up or melt snow, and assume there is nothing to find.
bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
bivy.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
bivy.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

bivy.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
bivy.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
bivy.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
bivy.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
bivy.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

bivy.name: Luna Cirque floor
bivy.notes: The floor of the great bowl beneath Luna Peak, walled on three sides, and the low point of the traverse that enters by Access Creek and Luna Pass and leaves over Challenger Gap onto Wiley Ridge. It sits directly under the eastern side of the crest that carries Spectre Peak, and parties coming off Challenger sometimes drop southeast into it rather than reversing the glacier. As a bed it is a long way below Luna Col, which remains the right camp for climbing Luna Peak itself; the value of the cirque is that it links the Access Creek and Wiley Ridge sides without going back over the top. Getting in and out is trackless in both directions and the brush low in Access Creek, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Meltwater running off the cirque walls, and a shallow seasonal lake on the floor that becomes warm sand as the summer dries it out. Early season is wet and late season is a search.
bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. CLOSED under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.name: Beaver Pass Camp
bivy.notes: A broad forested saddle about thirteen miles up from Ross Lake, and the jumping-off point for Wiley Ridge, which is the walking line onto the Challenger Glacier from the east. It is the largest camp on this side, with group and stock capacity, so it absorbs parties too big for the four-person camps below. A 1938 log shelter listed on the National Register stands at the pass; treat it as a historic structure rather than as shelter you can rely on. Because the camp sits on a divide rather than in a creek bottom, tank up lower down if the season has been dry.
bivy.water: Seasonal source near the saddle; the least dependable water on the Big Beaver trail and it can run thin in a dry late summer
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
bivy.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt streams and tarns; dependable while snow lingers, marginal to absent late season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Challenger Arm camp
bivy.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
bivy.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
bivy.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

bivy.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
bivy.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

bivy.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The upper half of Wiley Ridge, on the south-facing side, and the last bivouac ground before the glacier. A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

bivy.name: Luna Camp (Big Beaver Trail)
bivy.notes: The signed camp about 8 miles up the Big Beaver Trail from the boat landing, in old-growth cedar and only modestly above lake level. It is a trail camp, not a mountain one, and it earns its place because the water-taxi timetable often puts you on the trail late. From here it is another 1.5 miles north to the easy-to-miss boot path that leaves the trail just above the Access Creek confluence, so sleeping here sets you up to start the bushwhack fresh rather than at dusk.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek, right there and reliable
bivy.permit: A National Park Service backcountry permit is required for every overnight in the park complex, picked up from the Wilderness Information Center at Marblemount; Luna Camp is a designated site, not cross-country ground
bivy.capacity: A designated backcountry camp with a fixed number of sites; your permit itinerary names the camp and the night

bivy.name: Access Creek headwaters basin
bivy.notes: The open basin at the top of the Access Creek approach, roughly 1,700 ft above Luna Camp and the standard base for the peak. Getting here is the hard part: valley-bottom devil's club, a crossing to the north bank, then a swap back to the south side near 3,700-3,800 ft where cairns and a faint path use talus benches to duck the worst slide alder. Reports put the bushwhack alone at around three hours on the way out. From camp the climb goes up talus gullies southwest to a gap in the ridge, south of Point 6,730 on heather benches, then across the basin at about 6,600 ft to Luna Col at 7,200 ft — some 4,000 ft of gain, all of it above the last dependable water, so tank up before leaving.
bivy.water: Access Creek at the head of the drainage; reliable, but it is the last water until lingering snowmelt higher up
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. Cross-country camping is only allowed on durable surfaces — snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadows, and never within 100 ft of water
bivy.capacity: Open basin ground; parties describe it as pleasant camping for a small group rather than a set of established sites

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee for advance backcountry reservations (walk-up permits carry no fee). No park entrance fee. The Ross Lake Resort water taxi is a separate optional paid service (~$35 round trip per person, seasonal).

access.rules: A bear canister or approved food storage is required where a proper hang isn't possible; free loaner canisters are available at the Wilderness Information Center. Practice Leave No Trace; off-trail cross-country travel is legal in this zone but stay on rock/snow/durable surfaces where possible to protect fragile heather meadows.
access.permit: A backcountry permit is required for any overnight stay, year-round. Reserve in advance on Recreation.gov (the general on-sale window opens around 7 a.m. Pacific in late April) or apply for a walk-up permit; permits must be picked up in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. The Access Creek/Luna Camp zones carry limited nightly quotas and fill for summer weekends.

bivy.name: Perfect Pass
bivy.notes: The planned high camp for this route and the one everything else is scheduled around. Ground is limited: early in the season much of the pass is still snow-covered and parties either camp on the snow or scout the sandy patches slightly higher on the ridge. It is a pass, so it is windy and weather-exposed with no shelter. Getting from camp onto the glacier is itself part of the climb — depending on melt-out it can mean around 200 ft of wet class 4 downclimbing and sometimes a short rappel across a moat, so leaving camp in the dark or returning to it late is a real commitment, not a stroll.
bivy.water: Snowmelt at the pass; running water in the gully below it early in the season, drying back as the season goes on, so late-season parties should expect to melt snow
bivy.permit: The Perfect Pass cross-country zone allows exactly one party of up to six per night on a National Park Service backcountry permit, and it is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one. If it is taken, there is no second site here.
bivy.capacity: One party per night, maximum six people — the tightest camp quota in the park's cross-country system

bivy.name: Whatcom Pass camp
bivy.notes: The last established camp before the committing ground, used by parties coming in on the Chilliwack River approach. From here you still have to get around Whatcom Peak to reach Perfect Pass — the direct north ridge is loose and very exposed and is not the way most parties go, while the standard workaround crosses the Whatcom Glacier on the peak's east side, which has been reported down to bare ice with open crevasses in low-snow years. Treat this as the last comfortable night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and creeks at the pass
bivy.permit: A designated National Park Service backcountry camp; you may only camp in the camp area named on your permit itinerary for the date on it
bivy.capacity: A designated backcountry camp with a fixed number of sites assigned on the permit

bivy.name: Copper Creek camp
bivy.notes: About 7.5 miles in on the valley approach, with reliable water and a pit toilet. It is a trail camp, not a mountain one, and it exists on this list because the approach to Challenger is long enough that most parties sleep low at least once in each direction. It is also the sensible retreat target if the Chilliwack ford turns you around — the log crossings there are unreliable and have caught parties out.
bivy.water: Copper Creek, reliable
bivy.permit: Designated National Park Service backcountry camp; permit itinerary must name it
bivy.capacity: A designated backcountry camp on the Chilliwack River Trail

bivy.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
bivy.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. bivy.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger

bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. bivy.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

bivy.permit: Luna cross-country zone, walk-up only — it cannot be reserved, and a party that has already driven, boated and walked in can still be turned away if the night's slots are taken. Carry a fallback itinerary. Camp on sand, rock or snow, 100 ft from water, no fires.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on sand, gravel and slab; party limit 6

access.fees: No park entrance fee; backcountry wilderness permits cost $10/person plus a $6 reservation fee during the summer permit season (mid-May to early October).
access.permit: Wilderness permit required for overnight camping; obtain via Recreation.gov reservation or first-come, first-served at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex / Stephen Mather Wilderness (NPS)

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail

bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camp, reservable or walk-up. Closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure.
bivy.capacity: Mixed 4- and 12-person sites; party limit 12; group and stock sites

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.

A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
bivy.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
bivy.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
bivy.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
bivy.water: Seasonal tarns scattered along the crest. Some hold water and some are dry in the same summer, which makes this the least predictable water on the route. Fill at the Chilliwack River before starting up.
bivy.permit: Park wilderness permit required. This side is served by the wilderness information centres on both the Mount Baker Highway and at Marblemount, and the ranger will decide whether your night goes onto a designated camp or a cross-country zone — ask rather than assume, because the answer changes what the rest of the itinerary can say. Walk-up. Fires prohibited. Approved food storage required, and above treeline there is nothing to hang from, so a canister is the practical answer.
bivy.capacity: Small — one or two parties on the ridge crest; party limit 6

bivy.name: Tapto Lakes cross-country zone
bivy.notes: A basin of one large lake and several small ones in heather meadow, reached by an unmaintained boot route that climbs about 800 ft north out of Whatcom Pass over a ridge and then drops through boulders to the water. It looks straight across at Mount Challenger and the walls of Whatcom Peak. It is a scenic base more than a climbing camp — Perfect Pass is far closer to the glacier — but it matters for two reasons. It is bookable, so a party unwilling to gamble a four-day walk-in on a permit counter can guarantee at least one night. And with the trail camps under Whatcom Pass closed for hazard trees, it is one of the few legal beds left near the pass on that side.
bivy.water: The lakes themselves — the most reliable high water here. Camp 100 ft back from the shore.
bivy.permit: The ONE exception to walk-up permitting in this whole area: Tapto Lakes is one of only six cross-country zones the park lets you reserve in advance, alongside Boston Basin, Eldorado, Sulphide, Price and Triumph. Everything else in the Pickets is claimed at the counter on the day. Camp on bare ground, rock or snow rather than in the heather meadow, no fires, waste in a cathole.
bivy.capacity: Camp anywhere among the lakes once permitted; standard 6-person party limit

bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.name: Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
bivy.notes: The classic high camp for Mount Challenger and for Whatcom Peak, on benches at the western edge of the Challenger Glacier. It is reached either over Whatcom Pass from the Brush Creek side or along Easy Ridge, the latter demanding a substantial descent and reclimb to get around the gap short of the pass. Reported elevations vary between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft depending on the account, and there are no facilities of any kind.

bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the Perfect Pass cross-country zone. WALK-UP ONLY and capped at a single party per night. It cannot be booked ahead, so the permit is won or lost at the counter — this quota is usually the binding constraint on a Challenger trip, not the terrain.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6, and only ONE party per night in the whole zone — the tightest quota in this part of the park

bivy.name: Whatcom Camp, Brush Creek below Whatcom Pass
bivy.notes: The last trail camp beneath Whatcom Pass and the one that serves the Hannegan Pass and Chilliwack River approach to Whatcom Peak and Mount Challenger. Parties coming that way typically chain Boundary, Copper Creek or US Cabin, then Graybeal on Brush Creek, then here — three or four days of walking before any climbing begins. With both Whatcom Camp and Graybeal closed there is currently no legal trail camp close under the pass on that side, which pushes parties either back down the valley or straight up into the Tapto Lakes or Perfect Pass zones.
bivy.water: Brush Creek drainage — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; food hang or approved canister required. Listed as CLOSED for hazard trees on the park's August 2026 closure list, as is Graybeal Camp below it on Brush Creek. Campfires are prohibited here regardless of restrictions elsewhere.
bivy.capacity: Three 4-person sites; party limit 4; composting toilet; no campfires

bivy.name: Twin Rocks and Stillwell Camps, Little Beaver
bivy.notes: These two sit at the hinge between the Little Beaver and Big Beaver trails and are what make the water-taxi loop practical: get dropped at the Little Beaver landing, walk up to Whatcom Pass for Whatcom Peak and Challenger, and exit over Beaver Pass and down Big Beaver, or run it the other way. For the Northern Pickets they are through-camps on a long walk rather than climbing bases. The Ross Lake water taxi is chartered by the boat rather than per head, takes about six people, needs a reservation, and only runs during the resort's summer season — outside it, plan on walking in from Ross Dam and adding a day at each end.
bivy.water: Little Beaver Creek at both — reliable
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from Marblemount; trail-corridor camps, reservable or walk-up. Both closed under the 2026 Luna Fire closure, which covers Little Beaver from Ross Lake to Whatcom Pass.
bivy.capacity: Twin Rocks: two 6-person sites, party limit 6. Stillwell: four 4-person sites, party limit 4

bivy.name: Challenger Arm camp
bivy.notes: A rock cleaver at the eastern edge of the Challenger Glacier, reached at around 6,700 ft up a steep rock field, and the working high camp for anyone who has come in over Wiley Ridge rather than over Whatcom Pass. It is the closest bed to Poltergeist Pinnacle, which is the south subsummit of Challenger itself and needs several pitches of real rock climbing off the glacier, and it shortens the glacier crossing to Spectre Peak on the crest to the south. Unlike Perfect Pass on the far side, the ground here is broken and there are genuinely several usable platforms, so it does not carry the same one-party bottleneck. Crevasse conditions on the arm change through the season and the bergschrund below the summit block is the usual sticking point late in the year.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the Challenger Glacier immediately above, plus small tarns on the arm itself. Dependable while the glacier is running, and increasingly a matter of melting snow once the tarns dry in a hot late summer.
bivy.permit: Challenger cross-country zone, on a park wilderness permit. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be booked ahead, so it is claimed in person at a wilderness information centre the day before or the morning of. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than heather, keep 100 ft back from water, no fires at all, and carry waste out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier.
bivy.capacity: A few established tent platforms on the rock cleaver, with room to build more; the zone caps a party at 6 people

bivy.name: Eiley Lake benches, lower Wiley Ridge
bivy.notes: The first real camp on the eastern walking approach to Mount Challenger, roughly six hours along the ridge from Beaver Pass. Parties climbing Challenger from this side commonly use it for two nights, going to the summit and back on the middle day rather than moving camp, because the ridge is slow going in both directions. The terrain opens out of the timber into heather at about 5,200 ft and the walking improves from there. Below treeline expect insects and plan on a tent or a properly sealed bivy bag rather than sleeping out. IMPORTANT: the whole Big Beaver approach that feeds this ridge sits inside the 2026 fire closure, so confirm the trail and Beaver Pass are open before planning around it.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and snowmelt in the hollows around it. This is the last dependable water for a long stretch of ridge, so tank up here rather than counting on anything higher.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required, and this is cross-country ground rather than a designated camp — ask at the counter which zone the night is being written into, because the ridge straddles more than one. Walk-up only. No fires. Bury waste in a cathole below the snowline and carry it out above.
bivy.capacity: Two or three small parties spread along the benches; party limit 6

bivy.name: East Wiley Basin and the Wiley Lake benches, upper Wiley Ridge

A party that gets this far on the second day has a genuinely short summit day left: the ridge rolls over a gentle knoll near 7,100 ft past Wiley Lake and then reaches Challenger Gap at the edge of the Challenger Glacier. Camping here rather than at Eiley Lake is the difference between a long summit day and a reasonable one, and it is the sensible base for Poltergeist Pinnacle, which needs the early start that a technical face demands. The ridge is deceptively slow — five miles as the crow flies feels like double that with the constant rise and fall — so parties routinely need a night lower down as well as this one.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns. Wiley Lake is rimmed by ice and holds water well into the season, but the basin's tarns are seasonal and a late-summer party should expect to hunt or melt.
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit for the appropriate cross-country zone, walk-up only. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground and stay out of the heather meadows — this is the surface rule the park actually enforces up here. Fires prohibited, waste out in a blue bag once on snow.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties on gravel and heather benches; party limit 6

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs on the Challenger Glacier and the crest south of Challenger
bivy.notes: Spectre Peak sits well down the crest south of Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle is a multi-pitch rock climb off the glacier, so parties working the far end of the chain sometimes take a night out on the ice rather than commit to a very long day from Perfect Pass or Challenger Arm. These are made rather than found — a platform stamped into snow, or a gravel patch on a rib — and quality is entirely a matter of what the party can dig. There is no shelter and no water, crevasse hazard is present wherever you put the tent, and it only makes sense with a settled forecast. Anyone unwilling to melt snow for every drop should sleep at Challenger Arm or Perfect Pass instead and accept the longer day.

bivy.permit: Still inside the Challenger cross-country zone and still needs a wilderness permit with that night assigned to it. On the glacier the surface rule takes care of itself, but human waste MUST be carried out in a blue bag; there is no burying it here. No fires. Party limit 6.
bivy.capacity: One party, often on a levelled snow platform or a single gravel ledge

bivy.name: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
bivy.notes: This is the Hannegan Pass approach rather than a Ross Lake one, and it is how Spectre Peak is actually reached — in past ascents parties bivouacked near the summit of Easy Peak, dropped to the Imperfect Impasse and climbed through to the western slope of the range. From the trailhead you go over Hannegan Pass and down past Boundary and Copper Creek camps, then ford the Chilliwack River just above where Easy Creek comes in, and climb about five miles of ridge to open ground above 6,000 ft, with Easy Peak at 6,615 ft carrying the anchors of an old lookout. The sting is what comes after: reaching Perfect Pass from here means descending roughly 1,000 ft to get around the Imperfect Impasse gap and climbing back up, which is why parties who intend to camp at Perfect Pass often prefer the Whatcom Pass side instead. Two days in before any climbing starts.
