bivy.name: Horseshoe Basin — Sunny Pass, Louden Lake and the Smith Lake meadows
bivy.notes: This is the camp for WINDY PEAK and the reason the trip is worth doing at all — the basin is one of very few places in the lower states carrying genuine alpine tundra, open rolling meadow at seven thousand feet with bighorn sheep on it. From the Iron Gate trailhead the trail is nearly flat for a mile and then climbs steadily to Sunny Pass at about 7,200 ft at roughly four and a half to five miles, drops slightly to Horseshoe Pass at around 7,000 and opens into the basin; Louden Lake is a little beyond, and the usual round trip to the basin and back is around twelve miles. Windy Peak itself is taken off the basin trails on open ground and is a walk-up rather than a climb, which makes this a rare Pasayten summit a party can reach without route-finding. EXPECT BURN. Every approach into Horseshoe Basin passes through fire-killed forest, standing dead timber comes down in wind, and blowdown volume changes year to year. The last six miles of the Toats Coulee road to Iron Gate are rough enough to want high clearance. Late July through September; the tundra is exposed and there is nothing to shelter behind when weather comes over the border.
bivy.water: The limiting factor and it gets worse through the season. The climb from the trailhead is essentially dry after a tributary about a mile and a half up, and the basin itself is high rolling tundra rather than wet ground — Louden Lake and the small meadow ponds are the dependable supply and everything else is a gamble by August. Fill low and carry it up rather than counting on finding something at the pass.
bivy.permit: Pasayten Wilderness, national forest ground, and the permit expectation is the opposite of the Olympic files: a FREE self-issued permit filled out at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is needed to park at Iron Gate. Camp at least a hundred feet back from any lake shoreline. Stock parties need certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight. Campfires are legal in existing rings outside a burn ban, but bans run most of the summer here and firewood in the basin is scarce enough that most parties do without.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is room for several parties spread widely through the basin, with the usual spots at Louden Lake and around the Smith Lake meadows; horse parties use this country heavily and the good ground near water goes first.

bivy.name: Four Point Lake — the Chewuch-side base for Remmel Mountain
bivy.notes: The base for REMMEL MOUNTAIN, an 8,685 ft pile of granite carrying an old lookout site and one of the great viewpoints of the wilderness. The line in is the Chewuch trail from the Thirtymile trailhead out of Winthrop — a long, gentle valley walk of easy miles past Chewuch Falls with dispersed camping most of the way, to a signed junction at about thirteen miles for the Four Point Lake and Coleman Ridge trail. That trail FORDS THE CHEWUCH RIVER almost immediately and it is the crux of the approach: early in the season with snowmelt running it is genuinely difficult and there is not always a log. Past the ford the grade steepens sharply and about two miles of climbing reaches the lake at 6,850 ft, with a spur into the basin. From camp the summit goes on open ground by way of the Coleman Ridge side, and it is a scramble rather than a climb. Reckon on thirty-five miles and six thousand feet round trip over three or four days. THE LOWER VALLEY IS BURN, repeatedly, from fires in the early 2000s and since, so expect hot open walking, no shade and standing dead timber. This approach is chosen over the Remmel Lake side when the Andrews Creek road is shut, which in recent seasons has been often.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. This is the last certain water on the approach — the ridge above it carries nothing once the snow has gone, so fill here for the summit day rather than hoping.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Thirtymile trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight; this is heavily used horse country and the volunteers who keep the trail open are mostly equestrians. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are usual by late summer in this drainage.
bivy.capacity: Several good sites around the lake with open views to the ridge and the peak, room for two or three parties without stacking up. Lightly used, because almost everyone approaching Remmel comes the other way.

bivy.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. IT IS ALSO THE PIECE OF THIS ZONE MOST LIKELY TO BE OPEN. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Dot Lake and the Butte Pass basins — the far end of the traverse for Lost Peak
bivy.notes: LOST PEAK at 8,464 ft sits at the eastern end of this group between Monument Creek and the Lost River, and it is the awkward one — it does not fall out of a Carru and Lago camp the way those two fall out of each other. From the Shellrock country the usual line descends to Dot Lake, crosses a burned basin to Butte Pass and then works along a ridge with several false summits before the true top, which is a long day and one that parties routinely finish late. Camping at the lake rather than pushing back over Lago is what makes it sane, and it is the specific advice most trip accounts give: do not retrace the ridge, drop and camp. The alternative approach from the Monument Creek trailhead up the Lost River is a different trip entirely and its camps are covered in the Harts Pass file. Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.
bivy.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass, Robinson Creek or Monument Creek depending on which end you started. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.

access.fees: No wilderness entry fee; a Northwest Forest Pass is not required at the primitive Robinson Creek / Slate Pass / Monument Creek trailheads used to approach this peak (only posted developed day-use sites require it).
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 people / 18 head of stock.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the trailhead register (no quota, no reservation, no cost).
access.closures: Harts Pass Road (Lost River Rd / FR 9140 -> FR 5400) has been closed to vehicles from the Monument Creek Trailhead through Harts Pass since storm/flood damage in December 2025, cutting off the Robinson Creek, Slate Pass, and Slate Peak trailheads used for the standard approaches. As of a June 17, 2026 report the road remained closed with the Forest Service targeting a mid-July 2026 reopening at the earliest; the road stays open to foot/bike traffic even when vehicle-closed. Verify current status with the Methow Valley Ranger District or PCTA's closures page before planning a trip.

Reckon on thirty-five miles and six thousand feet round trip over three or four days. THE LOWER VALLEY IS BURN, repeatedly, from fires in the early 2000s and since, so expect hot open walking, no shade and standing dead timber. This approach is chosen over the Remmel Lake side when the Andrews Creek road is shut, which in recent seasons has been often.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. This is the last certain water on the approach — the ridge above it carries nothing once the snow has gone, so fill here for the summit day rather than hoping.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Thirtymile trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight; this is heavily used horse country and the volunteers who keep the trail open are mostly equestrians. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, and bans are usual by late summer in this drainage.
bivy.capacity: Several good sites around the lake with open views to the ridge and the peak, room for two or three parties without stacking up. Lightly used, because almost everyone approaching Remmel comes the other way.

bivy.name: The lower Chewuch River camps out of Thirtymile
bivy.notes: These exist to break the walk rather than to serve a summit, and on an approach this long that is worth more than it sounds. The Chewuch trail is gentle enough that a party can cover a lot of it quickly, but thirteen miles to the Four Point junction with a full pack is a poor first day after the drive from the west side, and the river ford above is better met in the morning with fresh legs and lower water. Stopping around the falls at six or seven miles makes the second day short and puts you at Four Point Lake by early afternoon with the summit still available. IT IS ALSO THE PIECE OF THIS ZONE MOST LIKELY TO BE OPEN. When the fires shut Iron Gate, Andrews Creek and the Harts Pass road, this corridor stayed passable and volunteers kept clearing it, which is why it is written up separately rather than folded into the Four Point entry. Expect burned forest for long stretches, little shade, and a trail whose blowdown situation changes with every windstorm. Ask the ranger district before building a schedule on it.
bivy.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness. The Chewuch runs beside the trail for the whole of the lower valley and every one of these sites has water at it into the autumn. Water only becomes a problem once you leave the river for the climb to Four Point Lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park at Thirtymile. Weed-free feed for stock; animals may not be tied to trees overnight or highlined close to them. Fires in existing rings outside a burn ban, and this is dry east-side country where bans are the norm from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites scattered along the first several miles of the valley, including good ground near Chewuch Falls. Most take one or two tents and they are seldom occupied — this is a corridor rather than a destination.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Dot Lake and the Butte Pass basins — the far end of the traverse for Lost Peak
bivy.notes: LOST PEAK at 8,464 ft sits at the eastern end of this group between Monument Creek and the Lost River, and it is the awkward one — it does not fall out of a Carru and Lago camp the way those two fall out of each other. From the Shellrock country the usual line descends to Dot Lake, crosses a burned basin to Butte Pass and then works along a ridge with several false summits before the true top, which is a long day and one that parties routinely finish late. Camping at the lake rather than pushing back over Lago is what makes it sane, and it is the specific advice most trip accounts give: do not retrace the ridge, drop and camp. The alternative approach from the Monument Creek trailhead up the Lost River is a different trip entirely and its camps are covered in the Harts Pass file. Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.
bivy.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass, Robinson Creek or Monument Creek depending on which end you started. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.

bivy.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The Thunder Creek trail leaves directly from the south loop, so most parties sleep here the night before rather than driving in from the west at dawn. It is a low forested car camp on Diablo Lake and carries none of the wilderness rules that apply the moment you walk past the trailhead. Book it separately from your climbing permit; the two systems do not talk to each other. Outside the open season you can still park and start walking, but you cannot camp in the loop.
bivy.water: Potable water on site during the operating season; Thunder Creek and Diablo Lake alongside
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed. A Recreation.gov reservation and the standard nightly campground fee apply, and the loop is only open roughly mid-May to early September. This does NOT cover any night spent in the backcountry.
bivy.capacity: 93 sites in the south loop, 19 of them tent-only; standard car-camping capacity per site

bivy.name: McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
bivy.notes: The last camp with any infrastructure — a pit toilet, a cook area and a food-hang setup — sitting at about mile 6.7 on an almost flat forest trail, so it is an easy first night rather than a real approach. Most parties treat it as the staging point, then start the steep work early the next morning. Because it is a designated site rather than open country, you are tied to the exact night and site your permit names. FILLING WATER HERE MATTERS: from the creek crossing upward there is nothing dependable until you are near 6,000 ft.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek is immediately at hand and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Designated backcountry camp inside North Cascades National Park, so an NPS wilderness permit is required for every night. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through Recreation.gov and about 40% held for walk-ups issued up to 24 hours ahead at Marblemount. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of numbered tent sites, plus a separate stock camp nearby; party size limits are set per site on the permit

bivy.name: Tricouni Camp, Thunder Creek trail
bivy.notes: Despite sharing the peak's name this camp is about a mile and a half further up the valley than the point where climbers leave the trail, so it is a fallback rather than a first choice. It is worth knowing about when McAllister is booked out on the night you need, since a short extra walk each way costs less than losing the trip. The forest here is more open than at McAllister. Nothing about it shortens the climb.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek and Thunder Creek nearby, reliable through the climbing season
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit system and fees as McAllister — designated site, part reservable and part held for walk-up at Marblemount.
bivy.capacity: Small designated hiker camp, a few sites

bivy.name: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
bivy.notes: The working base camp for both summits, on slabs and rubble near where the lower glacier has withdrawn into a lake. Ground is sloping and loose in places, so finding two flat platforms takes some hunting; camp on rock, snow or bare ground and stay well back from the water. Zone rules mean no fires, and human waste goes out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier. Allow the whole day to get here from the valley — parties routinely underestimate it. The steep climbers' trail above McAllister gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles.
bivy.water: Meltwater and the lake itself, dependable in summer; earlier in the year you may be melting snow
bivy.permit: CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE camping, not a designated site, and the rules differ sharply. The zone covering this basin does not accept advance reservations, so in practice it is WALK-UP ONLY from Marblemount, up to 24 hours before you start. Quotas are tiny — a small number of parties per night, with a low maximum party size — so a weekend plan can simply fail at the counter. Confirm the zone name and its current quota with the WIC rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Rock shelves and slabs above the lake; realistically two or three tents on good ground, and the party limit for the cross-country zone is small

bivy.name: Lucky Pass bivy, Primus-Tricouni col
bivy.notes: The col between the two peaks is high, exposed and windy, and it exists as an option rather than a plan — a spot to sit out weather or finish a day that ran long. Both summits are short from here, which tempts people, but hauling camp another 1,200 ft is rarely worth it against a comfortable night lower down. Whether it is usable at all depends on snow: early season gives flat platforms, late season leaves broken rock. Treat it as an emergency or opportunistic bivy and carry the means to melt water.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable late in the season once the col melts out
bivy.permit: Still inside the same cross-country zone as the Borealis camp, so the same walk-up-only permit, small party limit and blue-bag requirement apply. A permit issued for the zone covers a bivy here; it does not entitle you to camp wherever you like across zone boundaries.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties at most, on rock and snow; nothing prepared

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp, Eldorado ice-cap traverse approach
bivy.notes: This is the multi-day route in, from the Eldorado side across the ice, and it is NOT how most parties reach these two peaks — it is recorded so the option is visible, not recommended as a shortcut. It is a genuinely different undertaking: full glacier travel with crevasse rescue capability, several nights on snow, and a committing exit. Camps are on rock islands surrounded by ice, so they are windy and there is no shelter. Choose it because you want the traverse.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow across the ice cap; essentially always available in season but usually means melting
bivy.permit: A DIFFERENT approach means a different permit. Parties coming across the ice cap from Eldorado start in a zone that does accept advance reservations, but the zone boundaries out here are not obvious on the ground and a traverse can cross more than one. Sort the whole itinerary night by night with Marblemount, since a reservation for one zone is not a permit for the next.
bivy.capacity: Rock islands in the ice with room for a few tents; party size capped by the zone permit

access.fees: $10 per person recreation fee plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee, charged mid-May through early October; no camping fee October through mid-May (permit still required).
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: NPS wilderness climbing areas are under a moratorium on new fixed/bolted anchors — carry natural protection. No campfires above treeline; camp at durable/established sites.
access.permit: Backcountry/wilderness permit required for any overnight stay; obtained in person or via advance reservation at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount (810 State Route 20, Sedro-Woolley area; park HQ 360-854-7200).
access.closures: SR 20 access to Colonial Creek has been unusually volatile in 2025-2026: a Dec. 2025 atmospheric-river washout (MP 142-148) and a March 2026 rockslide right at Diablo Lake (MP 131, essentially at Colonial Creek) closed this stretch for months; WSDOT completed emergency repairs and fully reopened the highway June 14, 2026. Check current NPS/WSDOT conditions pages before driving.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (National Park Service)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: No day-use pass needed at Colonial Creek Campground/trailhead; the overnight backcountry permit is mandatory year-round for camping.

access.closures: Cascade River Road is closed to vehicles at Eldorado (mile 20) in winter and typically doesn't open to the Cascade Pass Trailhead until late June or early July depending on snowpack/storm damage; check current NPS road-conditions postings before your trip.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (National Park Service)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

bivy.name: Colonial Creek South Campground, Thunder Creek trailhead
bivy.notes: The Thunder Creek trail leaves directly from the south loop, so most parties sleep here the night before rather than driving in from the west at dawn. It is a low forested car camp on Diablo Lake and carries none of the wilderness rules that apply the moment you walk past the trailhead. Book it separately from your climbing permit; the two systems do not talk to each other. Outside the open season you can still park and start walking, but you cannot camp in the loop.
bivy.water: Potable water on site during the operating season; Thunder Creek and Diablo Lake alongside
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed. A Recreation.gov reservation and the standard nightly campground fee apply, and the loop is only open roughly mid-May to early September. This does NOT cover any night spent in the backcountry.
bivy.capacity: 93 sites in the south loop, 19 of them tent-only; standard car-camping capacity per site

bivy.name: McAllister Hiker Camp, Thunder Creek trail
bivy.notes: The last camp with any infrastructure — a pit toilet, a cook area and a food-hang setup — sitting at about mile 6.7 on an almost flat forest trail, so it is an easy first night rather than a real approach. Most parties treat it as the staging point, then start the steep work early the next morning. Because it is a designated site rather than open country, you are tied to the exact night and site your permit names. FILLING WATER HERE MATTERS: from the creek crossing upward there is nothing dependable until you are near 6,000 ft.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek is immediately at hand and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Designated backcountry camp inside North Cascades National Park, so an NPS wilderness permit is required for every night. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through Recreation.gov and about 40% held for walk-ups issued up to 24 hours ahead at Marblemount. NOT free — a per-person nightly fee plus a non-refundable reservation fee.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of numbered tent sites, plus a separate stock camp nearby; party size limits are set per site on the permit

bivy.name: Tricouni Camp, Thunder Creek trail
bivy.notes: Despite sharing the peak's name this camp is about a mile and a half further up the valley than the point where climbers leave the trail, so it is a fallback rather than a first choice. It is worth knowing about when McAllister is booked out on the night you need, since a short extra walk each way costs less than losing the trip. The forest here is more open than at McAllister. Nothing about it shortens the climb.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek and Thunder Creek nearby, reliable through the climbing season
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit system and fees as McAllister — designated site, part reservable and part held for walk-up at Marblemount.
bivy.capacity: Small designated hiker camp, a few sites

bivy.name: Borealis Glacier toe / Borealis Lake high camp
bivy.notes: The working base camp for both summits, on slabs and rubble near where the lower glacier has withdrawn into a lake. Ground is sloping and loose in places, so finding two flat platforms takes some hunting; camp on rock, snow or bare ground and stay well back from the water. Zone rules mean no fires, and human waste goes out in a blue bag once you are on snow or glacier. Allow the whole day to get here from the valley — parties routinely underestimate it. The steep climbers' trail above McAllister gains roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles.
bivy.water: Meltwater and the lake itself, dependable in summer; earlier in the year you may be melting snow
bivy.permit: CROSS-COUNTRY ZONE camping, not a designated site, and the rules differ sharply. The zone covering this basin does not accept advance reservations, so in practice it is WALK-UP ONLY from Marblemount, up to 24 hours before you start. Quotas are tiny — a small number of parties per night, with a low maximum party size — so a weekend plan can simply fail at the counter. Confirm the zone name and its current quota with the WIC rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Rock shelves and slabs above the lake; realistically two or three tents on good ground, and the party limit for the cross-country zone is small

bivy.name: Lucky Pass bivy, Primus-Tricouni col
bivy.notes: The col between the two peaks is high, exposed and windy, and it exists as an option rather than a plan — a spot to sit out weather or finish a day that ran long. Both summits are short from here, which tempts people, but hauling camp another 1,200 ft is rarely worth it against a comfortable night lower down. Whether it is usable at all depends on snow: early season gives flat platforms, late season leaves broken rock. Treat it as an emergency or opportunistic bivy and carry the means to melt water.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, and unreliable late in the season once the col melts out
bivy.permit: Still inside the same cross-country zone as the Borealis camp, so the same walk-up-only permit, small party limit and blue-bag requirement apply. A permit issued for the zone covers a bivy here; it does not entitle you to camp wherever you like across zone boundaries.
bivy.capacity: One or two parties at most, on rock and snow; nothing prepared

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp, Eldorado ice-cap traverse approach
bivy.notes: This is the multi-day route in, from the Eldorado side across the ice, and it is NOT how most parties reach these two peaks — it is recorded so the option is visible, not recommended as a shortcut. It is a genuinely different undertaking: full glacier travel with crevasse rescue capability, several nights on snow, and a committing exit. Camps are on rock islands surrounded by ice, so they are windy and there is no shelter. Choose it because you want the traverse.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow across the ice cap; essentially always available in season but usually means melting
bivy.permit: A DIFFERENT approach means a different permit. Parties coming across the ice cap from Eldorado start in a zone that does accept advance reservations, but the zone boundaries out here are not obvious on the ground and a traverse can cross more than one. Sort the whole itinerary night by night with Marblemount, since a reservation for one zone is not a permit for the next.
bivy.capacity: Rock islands in the ice with room for a few tents; party size capped by the zone permit

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee for advance permits (youth 15 and under free); no park entrance fee at North Cascades NP.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (12 in on-trail corridors). Boston Basin camping restricted to two designated sites (Low Camp ~5,300 ft, High Camp ~6,400 ft). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
access.permit: Overnight backcountry/wilderness permit required year-round for any camping on this route. About 60% of designated camps/zones are reservable in advance on Recreation.gov (requires watching a safety video and emailing the WIC within 3 days of your trip to confirm); the park holds roughly 40% of sites for walk-up permits issued in person at the WIC (Marblemount) or Glacier Public Service Center, day-of or day-before only.
access.closures: Colonial Creek Campground and the Thunder Creek Trailhead are reached via SR-20, which stays open essentially year-round this far west (well before the highway's seasonal closure gate near Ross Dam, MP 134); Cascade River Road to Eldorado Creek is not needed for this route unless linking into the Inspiration Traverse. The original Thunder Creek Trail bridge near mile 6.6 washed out in fall 2017 and has not been replaced — parties cross via a log felled downstream of the old bridge site.
access.seasonal: Cascade River Road (the access road for these trailheads) has a history of washouts/closures — check current NPS road-conditions page each season.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (NPS) — Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount, WA, (360) 854-7245, noca_wilderness@nps.gov
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: No entrance pass needed; wilderness camping permit is mandatory for overnight trips.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
bivy.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable all season. This is the last certain water for anyone heading up onto the ridge and glaciers, and the first on the way out.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Spire Col bivouac
bivy.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) in Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft.
access.permit: Backcountry overnight permit
access.seasonal: Mountain Loop Highway has a seasonal gate closure (Deer Creek–Bedal, ~14 mi), typically Nov–mid/late May. Suiattle River Road (FSR 26), the primary Glacier Peak access, has had storm-damage closures — check current conditions before a trip.
access.landManager: Glacier Peak Wilderness, jointly administered by Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads (e.g. Sunrise Mine TH for Vesper Peak) — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: America the Beautiful Annual ($80) or per-vehicle entrance fee

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest camp
bivy.notes: A timbered camp on the creek partway up the Bachelor Creek leg, used by parties who lose the day to the brush, blowdown and washed-out sections below. It is a bail-out night rather than a plan: car to Cub Lake is commonly reported at 9-11 hours, and the section above Bachelor Creek climbs steeply and crosses avalanche paths under Spire Point that need assessing in early-season snow.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek alongside
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness — no backcountry permit or quota; sign the trailhead register. A recreation pass such as the Northwest Forest Pass is honoured for the fee at the Downey Creek trailhead
bivy.capacity: Small forest sites; the Forest Service notes camping spots around mile 3 on the Downey Creek Trail and again at the Bachelor Creek end near mile 6.6

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: The lake camp at the top of the Bachelor Creek climb, reached after a drop of several hundred feet into the basin that most parties find unwelcome at the end of a long day. Water and flat ground are easy, which is why it gets used, but the meadows show it and the better-positioned option is the ridge another 900 ft above. If you sleep here, summit day starts with that climb.
bivy.water: The lake and the basin's streams; plentiful
bivy.permit: No permit or quota in Glacier Peak Wilderness; sign the trailhead register and carry a recreation pass for the trailhead. Standard Leave No Trace practice here means using existing hardened sites rather than making new ones in the meadow
bivy.capacity: A well-established camp with room for several parties, though the meadows around Cub and Itswoot Lakes have been heavily worn and camping there is discouraged in favour of the ridge above

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: The camp parties call the best on this approach, on the ridge crest roughly 900 ft above Cub Lake, with the lakes below and the Ptarmigan country opening out. Water is at hand and the ground is good. Expect mosquitoes. Moving up here from the lake costs about an hour but is the sensible split, since the published figure from the ridge to the summit is 6-9 hours and parties report 6-8. From camp the route crosses the south ridge toward Spire Point, drops about 200 ft, and traverses cairned but unmarked ground below cliff bands over polished slabs to the foot of the Dome Glacier.
bivy.water: A substantial creek near the ridge sites, fed by snow well above, plus running water at the ridge camp itself; snowmelt-dependent, so verify late season
bivy.permit: No backcountry permit needed in Glacier Peak Wilderness; sign the trailhead register
bivy.capacity: Good open camping along the crest for several parties

bivy.name: Dome-Dana col
bivy.notes: A high perch around 7,300 ft used by parties who want to shorten summit day or who are linking the Ptarmigan Traverse. It puts you above the traverse and its route-finding, with the upper Dome Glacier — which parties describe as mellow — immediately above. The trade is no running water and full exposure; the ridge camp lower down is the more common choice, and pushing this high is generally judged not to save enough time to be worth it.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only
bivy.permit: No permit or quota in Glacier Peak Wilderness
bivy.capacity: Small; two parties have camped there at once

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30/year Recreation Pass (Northwest Forest Pass) at Downey Creek Trailhead; pay via the Recreation.gov app or a physical pass. Washington's Discover Pass is not accepted at this US Forest Service fee site.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; Glacier Peak Wilderness group-size limit is 12 people/stock combined (larger groups must split and stay 1 mile apart); wood/charcoal campfires are prohibited in most alpine terrain and camp stoves are required.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk; no quota system.
access.closures: Suiattle River Road (FR 26) closed to vehicles beyond ~MP 4.5 under USFS order 06-05-26-03 (Apr 2, 2026 - Jan 1, 2028) after major flood/washout damage. Downey Creek Trail itself has downed old-growth timber in its first ~4 miles (easily stepped over on foot) and a tributary crossing below Downey/Pilot Lakes that can be difficult in early season/high water.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District / Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Downey Creek Trailhead — $5/day or $30/year.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.
bivy.water: The tarn itself plus snowmelt runnels feeding it. Reliable in July and through most of August, but it is a shallow pool with a small catchment and it can drop to a warm, silty puddle by September in a light snow year. Cache Col just above has no water at all, so parties camping high on the shoulder have to carry from here or melt snow.
bivy.permit: Once you cross Cache Col you are out of North Cascades National Park and into Glacier Peak Wilderness, so no park permit covers this camp. Sign the free self-issue wilderness register instead. If you spend a night on the park side, including at Cascade Pass or on the shoulder below the Cache Glacier, that night does need an NPS wilderness permit collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Campfires have no place at this elevation; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small heather and gravel platforms around a tiny tarn, comfortable for two or three parties and crowded beyond that. No facilities, no toilet, nothing built.

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: The second camp for most north-to-south parties, sitting in a shallow bowl below Le Conte Mountain after the drop off the Middle Cascade Glacier. It is the natural base for Old Guard Peak, whose summit is reached from the Le Conte Glacier above by a class 2 to 3 snow couloir and short scramble on the west side, or by two to three pitches of easy to moderate fifth class on the east ridge. Sentinel Peak is the other objective from here and the two are usually taken together. The descent into and climb out of this basin is steep on both sides, so parties running late often push instead to Le Conte Pass above and accept the thinner water. Snow lingers in the bowl well into July, which is when the camping is easiest and the heather is protected.
bivy.water: Two lakes, which makes this the most dependable water on the northern half of the traverse. Nothing above it is reliable: the ridge camps toward Formidable and the ground up at Le Conte Pass are snowmelt-only late in the season, though the pass usually holds tarns into midsummer.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the trailhead register. Camp at least 100 feet back from the lakeshores. No campfires; the ground here is thin alpine heather that does not recover.
bivy.capacity: Several unimproved sites in the heather between the two small lakes, enough for two or three parties. No toilet and no established platforms.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
bivy.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. It is the south-end hub: from the lake the trail climbs to Itswoot Ridge for Spire Point and Dome Peak, and everything on the Chickamin side including Sinister Peak and the Gunsight summits starts from the same ground. Because it is the established camp it also takes the impact, and there is a reasonable argument for camping on the ridge above instead where the ground is less worn, at the cost of carrying water. bivy.name: Bachelor Flats / Bachelor Meadows
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the standard first night after leaving maintained trail at the Bachelor Creek crossing. An informal but heavily used forest camp in a clearing — sheltered, buggy, and low. Most parties stop here because the unmaintained climbers' path above eats time and the day from the car is already long.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek
bivy.capacity: multiple tents in the clearing

bivy.name: Cub Lake meadows
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp in heather meadow past Cub Pass, and the busiest ground on the approach — a summer weekend has been described with a dozen or more parties spread through these meadows and several more on Itswoot Ridge above. Comfortable and well watered, but it leaves the glacier travel and the col for the following day.
bivy.water: Cub Lake and its outlet

bivy.name: Chikamin-Dome col
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one most parties use for Gunsight — an established site on the col reached by roping up at Itswoot Pass and crossing the Dome Glacier. Room is genuinely tight: one party spent half an hour of earthwork levelling ground for a four-person tent. It is a col, so it funnels wind, but it is reported as the sheltered option compared with the open glacier either side. Everything here is melted, so carry fuel accordingly.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: a small tent or several bivy sacks; a four-person tent needs building out

bivy.name: Chikamin Glacier bench below the west face
bivy.notes: PLANNED advanced camp, about ninety minutes of descending traverse below the col and directly under Gunsight's west face. Parties move here to shorten summit day rather than day-climbing from the col. It is a glacier bench: rope up moving to and from it, site the tent clear of the fall line off the face, and expect a cold, fully exposed pitch.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: small — a snow dome and rock outcrop, a tent or two

The only practical approach while this is in effect is the longer east-side route via the Lady of the Lake ferry to Stehekin and the PCT/Agnes Creek Trail to Bachelor Meadows/Cub Lake. bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: The first camp on the traverse coming from Cascade Pass, reached by climbing to Cache Col and dropping a short but awkward distance southwest to the tarn. It is where the permit regime changes, which is the practical reason to know it exists even if you are only passing through. Published elevations vary by a couple of hundred feet, with figures around 6,300 the most common and one outlier several hundred feet higher, so treat the number as approximate rather than a waypoint. From here the day ahead crosses the Red Ledge and the Middle Cascade Glacier toward Old Guard Peak and Sentinel, and there are further ridge bivouacs at around 6,300 ft just past the Red Ledge if the lake is full or the hour is late. Early season this is a snow camp with easy water everywhere; late season it is bare heather and rock and the tarn is the only source.

bivy.name: Cub Lake

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps

bivy.name: Spire Col bivouac
bivy.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.

bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.

bivy.name: Cub Lake
bivy.notes: Roughly 12 miles and about 3,900 ft of gain from the Downey Creek trailhead, reached by a steep switchbacking descent off the Bachelor Creek meadows and a walk around the north shore. bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Spire Col bivouac
bivy.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

Parties report anywhere from six hours to eleven getting here, which is a fair measure of how much the brush and the pack weight vary. Coming out, this is where the traverse ends and the brush begins.
