bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Downey Creek trailhead. Camp 100 feet back from the shore. Practically speaking no fires, and the site is heavily enough used that the surrounding wood is already gone.
bivy.capacity: A well established camp at the lake with room for a few parties, plus meadow sites nearby. It is the most used ground in the southern half of the zone and it shows.

bivy.name: Bachelor Creek forest and meadow camps
bivy.notes: This exists because of the brush, and the brush is the single most important thing to understand about the south end. From the Downey Creek trailhead at 1,440 ft the Downey Creek trail runs about six easy forested miles to Sixmile Camp; after that the abandoned Bachelor Creek trail deteriorates badly. The first two miles are tolerable, then it crosses to the south side and turns into slide alder and avalanche deadfall, with reports of sixty or more trees over the trail and long sections where following it is closer to bushwhacking than hiking. Parties routinely take nine to eleven hours from the car to Cub Lake and a slow group with heavy packs can lose the trail entirely. Splitting the approach with a night around the 4,500 ft meadows near the head of the creek is the honest answer for anyone who is not fast, and it is why some parties choose to enter from Cascade Pass and exit here rather than the other way round, so the brush is done downhill and with lighter packs. There is a north-side line through open forest paralleling the creek that some report as better than the trail itself. Everything about this approach is currently harder than the above suggests: the Suiattle River Road is closed to vehicles at about milepost 4 after flood damage, under an order running to the start of 2028 unless lifted sooner, which leaves roughly sixteen extra road miles each way to a trailhead at mile 20. The road also spent about a decade closed before reopening in 2014, so a long closure here is the normal state of affairs rather than a surprise. Confirm the road before committing to this end.
bivy.water: Bachelor Creek runs the whole way and is never the problem. The creek crossing itself can be, in high water or early season.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Spire Col bivouac
bivy.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass required to park at the Downey Creek trailhead.
access.rules: Standard Glacier Peak Wilderness group-size and camping regulations apply; no separate climbing registration is required outside the Park boundary.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Downey Creek trailhead kiosk; no NPS backcountry permit is required for this approach since it doesn't enter the Park.
access.closures: FR 26 (Suiattle River Road) closed to vehicles at milepost 4.5 due to December 2025 flood damage; closure order runs April 2, 2026 - January 1, 2028 unless rescinded. Trailhead remains reachable on foot or bike.
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Darrington Ranger District (Glacier Peak Wilderness); the approach and peak stay outside North Cascades National Park.
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads — $5/day or $30/year.

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: The third camp and the one most parties remember, reached from Yang Yang across the Le Conte Glacier and the Le Conte-Sentinel col, then down a long traverse under Sentinel and Old Guard. It looks straight across at Dome Peak and the Dana Glacier, which is the day that follows. Sinister Peak is not climbed from here directly, but this is the last camp with easy water before the ground gets serious: the Chickamin and Dome glaciers are the way to Sinister and to the Gunsight Range, and everything from here east is snow, ice and rock with no running water. It is a windy basin and the good sites are the sheltered ones near the outlet. Snow can cover the lakes into early July, which some parties prefer because it makes the camping flat and the water trivially available.
bivy.water: The lakes, fed by the snowfields and the Le Conte and Dana ice above them. Normally good all season, though the outlet stream can be reduced to a trickle late in a dry summer and the smaller pools go stagnant.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Keep camps 100 feet from the water. Stoves only.
bivy.capacity: Open benches near the outlet of the larger lake and scattered spots around the basin, wind-exposed but roomy enough for several parties. Unimproved, no toilet.

bivy.name: Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the southern peaks and the camp most parties coming in from Downey Creek actually use. Camps are quoted anywhere between roughly 5,900 and 6,400 ft depending on which bench you take, so the number here describes the lower, wetter end of the ridge rather than a single spot. From the benches it is moderate snow of about thirty degrees, or a scree-and-heather line on the left in late season, up to Spire Col at 7,760 ft, and from the col a short descending traverse onto the upper Dana Glacier puts you under the southeast and southwest faces of Spire Point. Dome Peak is the other objective, reached over the Dana Glacier and the Dome Glacier above. Reaching this ridge from the car is a full day with a heavy pack, so plan on arriving late and going nowhere else that evening.
bivy.water: Small running creeks below the lower benches, fed by snowfields on the north side of the ridge, and generally dependable through the normal climbing season. The higher benches toward the col dry out first, so drop back down for water rather than assuming it is there.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek trailhead register, plus a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle. No campfires up here.
bivy.capacity: A string of flat heather benches along the ridge rather than one site, so several parties can spread out without crowding each other. No toilet, no built platforms.

bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at Downey Creek. This is the one part of the zone low enough that a fire is not automatically out of the question, but the ground is wet forest and a stove is the sensible choice.
bivy.capacity: Rough forest sites and a meadow flat near the head of the creek, party-sized only. Nothing established, no toilet.

bivy.name: Spire Col bivouac
bivy.notes: The col at 7,760 ft between Itswoot Ridge and the upper Dana Glacier, and the highest useful bivouac for Spire Point. Taking it saves an hour or more off summit morning on the Southwest Face and puts you above the section of snow that softens in the afternoon. It is fully exposed, cold, and windy, which is the trade. Parties heading on to Dome Peak sometimes use it too, though the Dome Glacier camps further east are better placed for that. Treat this as a fair-weather option: there is no shelter, and retreating from here in bad weather means downclimbing snow you came up in daylight.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, or carry from the creeks below Itswoot Ridge. In late season the snow near the col can be gone entirely and then there is nothing at all.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground rather than on the heather. Pack out human waste; there is no toilet anywhere on this side of the zone.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on the col itself, with further spots scattered along the ridge below it. Rock and snow, nothing flat and nothing built.

bivy.name: Dome Glacier and Dome-Chickamin col high bivouacs
bivy.notes: These are the camps that put the eastern peaks in range, and they are the reason parties carry a full glacier kit past Itswoot Ridge. The col between the Dana and Dome glaciers holds a couple of rock rings around 7,470 ft, and further east the Dome-Chickamin col is a genuine high camp with figures around 8,000 ft and above quoted for it. From that eastern col the Chickamin Glacier is the highway to Sinister Peak, whose North Face and Southwest Route are both reached across it, and on to the three Gunsight Range summits beyond, which are granite spires ringed by the Chickamin and Blue glaciers and among the most remote objectives in the state. Parties on the Gunsight peaks routinely cross the Chickamin twice in a day from a camp on this ground. Season is short: the glaciers are best covered from July into August, later brings open crevasses and bare ice, and there is no water, no shelter and no quick way down from any of it.
bivy.water: None running. Every drop is melted snow, and on bare ice years even that takes hunting for. Carry what you can from Cub Lake or the Itswoot Ridge creeks and plan the fuel for melting.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness self-issue permit from the Downey Creek register. Camp on snow, rock or ice. Pack out human waste, which matters more here than anywhere else in the zone because the meltwater below runs straight into the glacier-fed creeks.
bivy.capacity: Rock rings and cleared platforms for one or two parties at a time. At the Dome-Chickamin col there is a flat, large, windy option on the west side and a smaller, harder, calmer one on the east. Nothing else, and no toilet.

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) in Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft.
access.permit: N/A
access.seasonal: Mountain Loop Highway has a seasonal gate closure (Deer Creek–Bedal, ~14 mi), typically Nov–mid/late May. Suiattle River Road (FSR 26), the primary Glacier Peak access, has had storm-damage closures — check current conditions before a trip.
access.landManager: N/A
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Darrington Ranger District) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Mountain Loop Highway trailheads (e.g. Sunrise Mine TH for Vesper Peak) — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: N/A

bivy.name: Camp Mystery — the last water below Marmot Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for Buckhorn Mountain, sitting at 4.6 miles and about 5,400 ft on the Upper Big Quilcene trail, roughly half a mile and 500 ft below Marmot Pass. From here the summit day is short: over the pass at 5,950 ft, then a rough open boot path climbing about a mile and 900 ft to the 6,996 ft southwest summit. Camping here rather than at the pass costs you the sunset and the view and buys you water, tree cover and shelter from wind, which on this crest is not a small trade. Below it, Shelter Rock Camp at 2.6 miles and about 3,600 ft is the wet-weather fallback if you start late. The season is roughly late June through October; snow lingers in the upper basin into early summer and the trail above camp is exposed once it leaves the trees.
bivy.water: The reason to stop here. A stream runs through camp and is the LAST RELIABLE WATER on the whole approach — everything above is dry ground. Fill for the summit day here, not at the pass.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. No advance permit and no fee to camp — sign the free self-issued register at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park. Group limit is twelve. OPEN FIRES ARE PROHIBITED above 3,500 ft, which includes this camp, so bring a stove and do not gather wood.
bivy.capacity: A scatter of established sites among the firs, perhaps eight to ten tents spread out along the trail; busy but rarely truly full

bivy.name: Marmot Pass — high dry bivy on the crest
bivy.notes: The obvious camp for anyone whose objective is Buckhorn Mountain and who is willing to haul water, because the summit path leaves directly from the pass and a party sleeping here is on top for sunrise with an hour of walking. It is also the hinge of this whole zone: the trail carries on over the pass and drops 1.7 miles down to Boulder Shelter, which is how a Quilcene-side party reaches the Warrior and Inner Constance country without driving around to the Dungeness. The cost of camping this high is real — the pass is a wind funnel with no tree cover, weather arrives with no warning off the Dungeness side, and the meadows here are fragile enough that you should use an existing pad rather than making a new one. Snow-free from roughly early July; a spring ascent on skis or snowshoes is common but then the pass is a genuine winter camp.
bivy.water: NONE. This is a dry camp and it is the single most common mistake made here — late-season accounts describe not a puddle or a patch of snow anywhere near the pass. Carry everything up from Camp Mystery, which is the last source half a mile below.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the trailhead, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires at this elevation. No quota and no reservation.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small hardened pads and windbreaks in the meadow and just over the far side; two or three parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Buckhorn Lake — the base for Mount Worthington
bivy.notes: Mount Worthington has no maintained trail to its summit and no route that anyone would call standard, so the camp does most of the work. Buckhorn Lake sits about half a mile off the Tubal Cain trail on a spur leaving at roughly five and a half to six miles, and from it the usual line crosses the outlet, works around the south end of the lake on a discontinuous path through moderate brush, climbs south into an open basin near 5,260 ft, and then heads up to the saddle between Worthington and Iron Mountain — the 6,938 ft summit is off-trail scrambling and routefinding from there. Camping lower at the old mine workings adds several hundred feet and a couple of miles to the morning; camping higher is not really an option, since above the lake there is neither water nor level ground until the ridge. Scope the descent line on the walk in, because it is much harder to identify from above. Best from July into October once the brush is dry and the basin has melted out.
bivy.water: Reliable at the lake all season. It is a shallow forested tarn rather than running water, so filter it, and there is nothing above once you start up toward the saddle.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park at the Tubal Cain trailhead. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft. No quota, no reservation, no bear canister requirement on this side of the divide — though the mine area sees enough traffic that hanging or canistering food is sensible anyway.
bivy.capacity: Modest, three or four small sites in dark timber at the lake; the Tubal Cain mine area lower down holds more parties if this is taken

bivy.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
bivy.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
bivy.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
bivy.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

bivy.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
bivy.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits

access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Buckhorn Wilderness limits groups to 12 people and/or 8 head of stock; no open fires or wood gathering above 3,500 ft elevation; Leave No Trace practices and standard federal wilderness regulations apply.
access.permit: Northwest Forest Pass (or another valid Forest Service interagency day/annual pass) is required to park at the Upper Big Quilcene Trailhead. No separate wilderness entry permit is required for day use.
access.closures: Check Olympic National Forest alerts (fs.usda.gov/alerts/olympic) for current washouts or damage on FR 27/FR 2750 before driving, especially in shoulder season; trail is generally snow-free and open roughly June–October, varying by year.

access.fees: Olympic NP wilderness camping $8 per person (16+) per night, free for 15 and under, plus a non-refundable $6 reservation fee per permit; an Annual Olympic National Park Wilderness Pass ($45/person) covers the nightly fee but not the reservation fee. Trailhead day use on the Forest Service side is $5/vehicle/day or $30/year.
access.permit: An Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required for any overnight and must be reserved in advance on Recreation.gov — there are no same-day walk-ups. Summer-season (May 15 - Oct 15) reservations are released around April 15 at 7 a.m. PT. Bear canisters are required in all ONP wilderness camp areas and can be borrowed on a first-come basis.
access.closures: Dogs are prohibited on the Olympic National Park portion of the trail. No campfires above 3,500 ft. Groups of seven or more must use designated group sites in quota areas. Check current conditions with the Port Angeles Wilderness Information Center at (360) 565-3100.

bivy.name: Camp Windy, below Mount Townsend
bivy.notes: The only real camp on Mount Townsend, sitting somewhere around 5,200 ft at roughly two and a half to three miles up the trail — published elevations for it vary by about a hundred feet, which is fair given it is a spread of sites rather than a point. Townsend is a walk-up by its standard trail and most parties do it as a day hike, so the case for camping is weather, an early start for the view east over Puget Sound, or linking it with the Silver Lakes basin. The switchbacks above camp reach the Silver Lakes junction near 5,500 ft at about three miles, and those lakes at roughly 5,400 ft are the quieter alternative if Camp Windy is full — but they sit in a side valley and add distance to the summit rather than saving any. Above camp the trail breaks out onto open, wind-scoured slopes to the 6,280 ft south summit; the name of the camp is not decorative, and a tent pitched carelessly here will not survive the night.
bivy.water: Windy Lake, a shallow tarn just off the trail below camp, is the water source and holds through the season, but it is a still pool rather than a stream — treat it. There is nothing above camp on the way to the summit.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the Mount Townsend trailhead. Accounts disagree about whether a parking pass is enforced at this particular trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass rather than find out. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, no quota and no advance booking.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites with plenty of flat ground; comfortably takes four or five parties, and it is popular with families

bivy.name: Marmot Pass — high dry bivy on the crest

bivy.capacity: A handful of small hardened pads and windbreaks in the meadow and just over the far side; two or three parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Buckhorn Lake — the base for Mount Worthington
bivy.notes: Mount Worthington has no maintained trail to its summit and no route that anyone would call standard, so the camp does most of the work. Buckhorn Lake sits about half a mile off the Tubal Cain trail on a spur leaving at roughly five and a half to six miles, and from it the usual line crosses the outlet, works around the south end of the lake on a discontinuous path through moderate brush, climbs south into an open basin near 5,260 ft, and then heads up to the saddle between Worthington and Iron Mountain — the 6,938 ft summit is off-trail scrambling and routefinding from there. Camping lower at the old mine workings adds several hundred feet and a couple of miles to the morning; camping higher is not really an option, since above the lake there is neither water nor level ground until the ridge. bivy.water: Reliable at the lake all season. It is a shallow forested tarn rather than running water, so filter it, and there is nothing above once you start up toward the saddle.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required to park at the Tubal Cain trailhead. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft. No quota, no reservation, no bear canister requirement on this side of the divide — though the mine area sees enough traffic that hanging or canistering food is sensible anyway.
bivy.capacity: Modest, three or four small sites in dark timber at the lake; the Tubal Cain mine area lower down holds more parties if this is taken

bivy.name: Camp Windy, below Mount Townsend
bivy.notes: The only real camp on Mount Townsend, sitting somewhere around 5,200 ft at roughly two and a half to three miles up the trail — published elevations for it vary by about a hundred feet, which is fair given it is a spread of sites rather than a point. Townsend is a walk-up by its standard trail and most parties do it as a day hike, so the case for camping is weather, an early start for the view east over Puget Sound, or linking it with the Silver Lakes basin. The switchbacks above camp reach the Silver Lakes junction near 5,500 ft at about three miles, and those lakes at roughly 5,400 ft are the quieter alternative if Camp Windy is full — but they sit in a side valley and add distance to the summit rather than saving any. Above camp the trail breaks out onto open, wind-scoured slopes to the 6,280 ft south summit; the name of the camp is not decorative, and a tent pitched carelessly here will not survive the night.
bivy.water: Windy Lake, a shallow tarn just off the trail below camp, is the water source and holds through the season, but it is a still pool rather than a stream — treat it. There is nothing above camp on the way to the summit.
bivy.permit: Buckhorn Wilderness, Olympic National Forest. Free self-registration at the Mount Townsend trailhead. Accounts disagree about whether a parking pass is enforced at this particular trailhead, so carry a Northwest Forest Pass rather than find out. Group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, no quota and no advance booking.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites with plenty of flat ground; comfortably takes four or five parties, and it is popular with families

access.fees: No day-use fee; no NW Forest Pass required at this trailhead.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Buckhorn Wilderness caps group size at 12 people / 8 head of stock; open fires (and gathering wood for them) are prohibited above 3,500 ft elevation; gear/food may not be cached or left unattended more than 24 hours.
access.permit: Free, self-issued wilderness permit at the Tubal Cain Trailhead register.
access.closures: FR-2870 can be gated or snow-blocked in winter and spring; check Olympic National Forest road alerts before heading out.
access.landManager: Olympic National Forest — Buckhorn Wilderness, Hood Canal (Quilcene) Ranger District
access.land_manager: Olympic National Forest — Buckhorn Wilderness, Hood Canal (Quilcene) Ranger District
access.parking_pass: None required.
access.passRequired: None

bivy.name: Camp Mystery — the last water below Marmot Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for Buckhorn Mountain, sitting at 4.6 miles and about 5,400 ft on the Upper Big Quilcene trail, roughly half a mile and 500 ft below Marmot Pass. From here the summit day is short: over the pass at 5,950 ft, then a rough open boot path climbing about a mile and 900 ft to the 6,996 ft southwest summit. bivy.capacity: A handful of small hardened pads and windbreaks in the meadow and just over the far side; two or three parties before it feels crowded

bivy.name: Boulder Shelter — the last camp outside the national park
bivy.notes: The working base for Warrior Peak, and the cheapest night in this zone by a wide margin because nothing has to be booked. It sits at about 4,950 ft and roughly 6.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness trailhead at 2,500 ft, past Camp Handy at 3,100 ft — an easy valley walk on maintained trail, which is why this and not the Dosewallips is how people actually get into this country. It is also 1.7 miles below Marmot Pass, so a Quilcene-side party can traverse in over the pass. For the Warrior Peak southeast summit the day runs south two-plus miles on the Dungeness trail, then up the prominent couloir north-northeast to a saddle near 7,000 ft; the couloir holds snow into late season and turns icy in cold weather, and the first twenty to fifty feet of rock above it is genuinely poor, low fifth class, and wants a rope. Camping higher in the cirque below the summit shortens that considerably and several parties recommend it, but it is a dry, unestablished bivy and you carry water for it. Best from July into September.
bivy.water: A stream runs by the site and is dependable. This is the last water you can rely on without a park permit, and it is worth topping off here whichever direction you are heading.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE JURISDICTION LINE AND IT IS THE MOST USEFUL FACT IN THIS ZONE. Boulder Shelter is in the Buckhorn Wilderness on national forest ground: free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, group limit twelve, no fires above 3,500 ft, NO reservation, NO quota and NO bear canister requirement. Walk a couple of miles further toward Home Lake and you cross into Olympic National Park, where every one of those rules changes. Dogs are legal up to the boundary and illegal past it.
bivy.capacity: Established sites around a three-sided wooden shelter plus the boulders it is named for; several parties fit, and it is quiet by Olympic standards

bivy.name: Home Lake, below Constance Pass — inside the park, and reached from the north
bivy.notes: The high camp for both Warrior Peak and the northwest side of Inner Constance, and the natural next step up from Boulder Shelter once you want to be closer to the peaks. Reach it from the UPPER DUNGENESS trailhead by way of Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter — the approach from the Dosewallips over Constance Pass is technically the same lake but adds the long closed-road walk on that side and is not how anyone sensibly gets here. Do not confuse this basin with Lake Constance: they sit on opposite flanks of the massif, the twenty-person quota that governs Lake Constance does not apply here, and neither camp substitutes for the other. From Home Lake the usual line for Inner Constance works up the northwest side toward the 7,670 ft summit on loose alpine rock; the northeast summit by way of Crystal Pass at the head of Avalanche Canyon is a different climb from a different camp altogether. Camping lower at Boulder Shelter saves you the permit and the canister at the cost of two miles and 400 ft each way on summit morning, which on a long alpine day is a real price. Snow-free from roughly July; the basin is exposed and holds weather off Constance Pass.
bivy.water: The lake, reliable through the season. It is the last dependable water before Constance Pass and before anything you climb from here, and the slopes above hold no running water once the snow has gone.
bivy.permit: OLYMPIC NATIONAL PARK, and everything changes at the boundary sign about a mile below the lake. An overnight wilderness permit is mandatory and is reserved in advance through the federal recreation booking site; the summer season runs roughly mid-May to mid-October with reservations opening in the spring. BEAR CANISTERS ARE REQUIRED — hangs and wires are not accepted, and free loaners can be collected from the park wilderness office. No fires at this elevation. Dogs are prohibited. None of this applies at Boulder Shelter two miles back down the trail, and confusing the two is the standard way to arrive here without a legal place to sleep.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites in an open subalpine basin; the park sets a maximum party size for the area, so check what your permit allows before assuming a big group fits

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass ($30/yr) or a $5/day recreation pass is required at the Upper Dungeness Trailhead. The site is cashless — pay via the Recreation.gov app or on-site QR scan.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Campfires are prohibited above 3,500 ft; bear canisters are mandatory for overnight camping in the park's subalpine zone (Home Lake/Constance Pass). The nearby Lake Constance drainage caps overnight use at 20 people, a useful indicator of how tightly the Park manages crowding in this area even though it's a separate permit zone from Home Lake.
access.permit: No permit required for day use or for USFS camping at Camp Handy or Boulder Shelter — just self-register at the trailhead kiosk. Camping at Home Lake or Constance Pass requires an Olympic National Park wilderness permit, reserved via recreation.gov or obtained from the Wilderness Information Center in Port Angeles, (360) 565-3100.
access.landManager: Olympic National Forest (Quilcene Ranger District) administers the lower Buckhorn Wilderness approach (Camp Handy, Boulder Shelter); Olympic National Park (Wilderness Information Center, Port Angeles) administers the upper cirque, Home Lake, Constance Pass, and the summit, which lie inside the park boundary.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — Olympic National Park (Olympic Wilderness)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency Pass or Scan & Pay at the Upper Dungeness Trailhead — $5 per vehicle per day or $30 annual. The trailhead is on Olympic National Forest land (Quilcene Ranger District), so no Olympic National Park entrance fee is charged to park there.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / Interagency Pass at the trailhead, plus an NPS wilderness camping permit for Home Lake/Constance Pass.

bivy.name: Camp Muir
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar routes, reached by the roughly 4,500 ft slog up the Muir Snowfield from Paradise. The Public Shelter is first-come and cannot be reserved, so treat it as a bonus rather than a plan and carry a tent regardless; it has been closed for maintenance in past seasons and its status is worth re-checking each year. Weather is the main hazard to the camp itself, and the snowfield below is notorious for whiteout navigation, so record your descent bearings before you need them. The Paradise road is plowed year-round, so unlike the north-side camps this one is not gated by a seasonal road closure.
bivy.water: No running water and no reliable melt stream. Every party must carry a stove and fuel and melt snow; snow is normally available on the Cowlitz year-round, but late in a dry season the cleanest snow can be a walk from the tent platforms
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for any overnight, obtained through Recreation.gov with roughly two-thirds reservable in advance and about one-third held for walk-ups within a day of departure. Separately, anyone travelling on glaciers, going above high camp or attempting the summit owes the climbing cost recovery fee, paid on Pay.gov before arriving; the amount is revised periodically, so confirm it at booking. Walking to Camp Muir and back as a day trip needs neither. In-person registration at a ranger station is still required on or before the climb date.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 25-35 tent parties on the Cowlitz Glacier snow platforms in a normal season, plus the 1921 stone Public Shelter which sleeps on the order of 15-20 on its bunks; permits are issued against a party quota rather than numbered pads, so the practical ceiling moves with snow cover

bivy.name: Ingraham Flats
bivy.notes: About a thousand feet above Camp Muir past Cathedral Gap, this bench shortens summit day meaningfully and is the usual overflow when the Muir quota is full. The trade is real: less acclimatisation, a colder and more exposed camp, and objective exposure to icefall off the Ingraham headwall above, which is why parties argue about whether the higher start is worth it. Whether it is sound in a given week is conditions-dependent and worth asking the climbing rangers about before committing. Sites are dug into snow, so bring a shovel and expect to build your own platform and walls.
bivy.water: Snow only, melted on a stove. There is no liquid water source at this elevation
bivy.permit: Same Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit as Camp Muir, issued for a specific camp — a permit written for Camp Muir does not authorise a night here. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to everyone camping here, since reaching it means crossing the Cowlitz Glacier and going above Camp Muir.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties, typically under ten tents; the usable flat ground shifts year to year as the Ingraham Glacier changes and crevasses open across the bench

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: The high camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, the standard north-side route, approached from the White River Campground through Glacier Basin and up the Inter Glacier. There is an NPS ranger hut with an emergency radio on its exterior and toilet facilities, but the hut is staff quarters and not a shelter climbers can sleep in, so a tent is mandatory. Access is gated by the White River Road, which typically does not open until late June, and by the Inter Glacier, which is small but crevassed enough that roping up is a judgement call that changes through the season. Late in a dry summer the Inter Glacier turns to bare ice and rubble.
bivy.water: Snow to melt in most conditions, and the camp generally has adequate clean snow through the season. Some parties find running meltwater near camp late in summer, but it is seasonal and should not be counted on when planning fuel
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required, same reservation and walk-up split as the rest of the park's climbing camps, with in-person registration before the climb. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to anyone continuing onto the Emmons or Winthrop glaciers or attempting the summit; walking to Camp Schurman as a day trip without going higher does not trigger it.
bivy.capacity: Considerably smaller than Camp Muir, on the order of a dozen tent sites on the snow and rock around Steamboat Prow; the quota fills quickly on good-weather weekends

bivy.name: White River Campground
bivy.notes: The roadhead camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, five miles up White River Road off Highway 410, and the Glacier Basin trail to Camp Schurman starts here. Being the highest of the park's drive-in campgrounds it is normally the last to open, around late June, and the first to close in September, so early-season parties often sleep outside the park. Its availability is not guaranteed year to year — it has been listed closed for fire activity — so confirm status before driving in. A reasonable place to sort gear and get a short night before an early start up the Inter Glacier.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground when it is open for the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed, but this is inside Mount Rainier National Park so park entrance applies, and the park has operated timed-entry reservations for corridor access in recent summers. Recent NPS listings show it as first-come rather than reservable, which contradicts several third-party campground sites still advertising reservations, so check the current NPS page before relying on either. A camping permit here does not cover the mountain: the wilderness permit and the climbing fee are separate.
bivy.capacity: 88 individual drive-in sites with flush toilets and fire grates; RV length is limited to about 27 ft

access.fees: $82 per person — Climbing Cost Recovery Fee (2026 rate). Annual: covers unlimited climbs that calendar year. Separate from the park entrance fee.
access.notes: How to get it: pay online in advance (pay.gov / recreation.gov), then register in person. Winter (Sept 16–May 21): self-issue at the Paradise Old Station kiosk after paying online. Summer (May 22–Sept 30): no self-issue — register at a Wilderness Information Center (Longmire, Paradise, or White River); roughly half of summer registration slots are held for walk-up, up to 24 hrs ahead. No timed-entry vehicle reservation is in effect for the 2026 season, so park entry itself is first-come, first-served.
access.rules: Blue bags required for human waste above high camp — pack out and deposit only in barrels marked "Human Waste" at Camp Muir or the trailhead; do not cache on-route. Check-out is required after every climb.
access.permit: Free climbing permit, self-register at Mowich Lake
access.closures: SR 165 Fairfax Bridge permanently closed (April 2025) — no vehicle access to the Mowich Lake trailhead until further notice
access.landManager: National Park Service - Mount Rainier National Park
access.parking_pass: Not a Northwest Forest Pass (that's a USFS pass and doesn't apply inside the park). Standard NPS entrance fee applies: $30/vehicle (7 consecutive days), $55 Mount Rainier annual pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: Annual Climbing Cost Recovery Fee

access.notes: $82 climbing registration per person (Pay.gov), $12-26 wilderness permit per person/night (May 1-Sept 15). Mount Rainier National Park requires backcountry permit. CRITICAL: Mowich Lake Road currently CLOSED (SR 165 bridge). When open: mid-July to mid-October. Helmet and rescue gear essential. Permit advance planning required via Recreation.gov.

access.permit: Free climbing permit, self-register at Mowich Lake ranger station/kiosk
access.closures: SR 165 Fairfax Bridge permanently closed (April 2025) — no vehicle access to the Mowich Lake trailhead until further notice

bivy.name: Glacier Basin camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED first camp for parties not pushing straight to Thumb Rock. Composting toilet, bear boxes. Last dependable running water on the route — from here it is snow and ice, and Thumb Rock has none.
bivy.water: creek/White River at camp, filter
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; designated site
bivy.capacity: five individual sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier access bivy
bivy.notes: PLANNED intermediate camp, and the usual way to split what is otherwise a 7-10 hour push from the car to Thumb Rock. Established sites sit in the ramp that gains the Carbon at about 7,300 ft, with more ground on the ridge crest above. Parties camp here specifically so they can cross the exposed ground under Willis Wall early and cold. Do not pitch out on the open Carbon under the wall to shorten the morning — that is the fall line for serac collapse off the summit icecap.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: a few small sites in the access gully and on the ridge

bivy.name: Thumb Rock
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the standard one — flat, partly wind-sheltered tent sites tucked behind the rock buttress, reached by moderate snow and loose rock bands. Reports place the platforms anywhere from about 10,400 to 10,700 ft depending on which bench and how much snow is in; the ground above the rock is more exposed and takes the full wind. There is no liquid water at any point. The approach ramps immediately below turn loose and unpleasant once they melt out, so late-season parties arrive slower than they plan.
bivy.water: none — melt snow or ice
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: a handful of existing snow platforms; can be crowded in season, and late parties dig their own

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: DESCENT camp. Liberty Ridge tops out near Liberty Cap and most parties come down the Emmons-Winthrop, so this is where a slow summit day ends rather than a forced night out high on the ice. Ranger hut and solar toilet, both potentially buried in snow — carry blue bags and pack them out. Reserve well ahead.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

access.fees: Climbing Cost Recovery Fee: $82/person for 2026; wilderness camping fee runs about $12/person/night for the Curtis Ridge and Thumb Rock camps; a separate $6 walk-up permit fee applies if you didn't reserve in advance.

access.rules: Carry-out of human waste (blue bags/WAG bags) is mandatory above the high camps; obtain bags at the ranger station before departing since Thumb Rock's disposal barrels don't stock extras.
access.permit: NPS Climbing Permit required in person for any travel above 10,000 ft or onto park glaciers; north-side climbs like Liberty Ridge are typically issued at the White River Wilderness Information Center, or can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov.
access.closures: The Carbon River Road approach is frequently washed out and has been closed to vehicles for extended periods; the White River Road/Campground approach used for Liberty Ridge typically opens around Memorial Day weekend and can be delayed by late snowpack.

access.land_manager: National Park Service

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: The high camp for the Emmons-Winthrop, the standard north-side route, approached from the White River Campground through Glacier Basin and up the Inter Glacier. There is an NPS ranger hut with an emergency radio on its exterior and toilet facilities, but the hut is staff quarters and not a shelter climbers can sleep in, so a tent is mandatory. Access is gated by the White River Road, which typically does not open until late June, and by the Inter Glacier, which is small but crevassed enough that roping up is a judgement call that changes through the season. Late in a dry summer the Inter Glacier turns to bare ice and rubble.
bivy.water: Snow to melt in most conditions, and the camp generally has adequate clean snow through the season. Some parties find running meltwater near camp late in summer, but it is seasonal and should not be counted on when planning fuel
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required, same reservation and walk-up split as the rest of the park's climbing camps, with in-person registration before the climb. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to anyone continuing onto the Emmons or Winthrop glaciers or attempting the summit; walking to Camp Schurman as a day trip without going higher does not trigger it.
bivy.capacity: Considerably smaller than Camp Muir, on the order of a dozen tent sites on the snow and rock around Steamboat Prow; the quota fills quickly on good-weather weekends

bivy.name: White River Campground

Being the highest of the park's drive-in campgrounds it is normally the last to open, around late June, and the first to close in September, so early-season parties often sleep outside the park. Its availability is not guaranteed year to year — it has been listed closed for fire activity — so confirm status before driving in. A reasonable place to sort gear and get a short night before an early start up the Inter Glacier.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground when it is open for the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed, but this is inside Mount Rainier National Park so park entrance applies, and the park has operated timed-entry reservations for corridor access in recent summers. Recent NPS listings show it as first-come rather than reservable, which contradicts several third-party campground sites still advertising reservations, so check the current NPS page before relying on either. A camping permit here does not cover the mountain: the wilderness permit and the climbing fee are separate.

bivy.name: Camp Muir
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar routes, reached by the roughly 4,500 ft slog up the Muir Snowfield from Paradise. The Public Shelter is first-come and cannot be reserved, so treat it as a bonus rather than a plan and carry a tent regardless; it has been closed for maintenance in past seasons and its status is worth re-checking each year. Weather is the main hazard to the camp itself, and the snowfield below is notorious for whiteout navigation, so record your descent bearings before you need them. The Paradise road is plowed year-round, so unlike the north-side camps this one is not gated by a seasonal road closure.
bivy.water: No running water and no reliable melt stream. Every party must carry a stove and fuel and melt snow; snow is normally available on the Cowlitz year-round, but late in a dry season the cleanest snow can be a walk from the tent platforms
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for any overnight, obtained through Recreation.gov with roughly two-thirds reservable in advance and about one-third held for walk-ups within a day of departure. Separately, anyone travelling on glaciers, going above high camp or attempting the summit owes the climbing cost recovery fee, paid on Pay.gov before arriving; the amount is revised periodically, so confirm it at booking. Walking to Camp Muir and back as a day trip needs neither. In-person registration at a ranger station is still required on or before the climb date.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 25-35 tent parties on the Cowlitz Glacier snow platforms in a normal season, plus the 1921 stone Public Shelter which sleeps on the order of 15-20 on its bunks; permits are issued against a party quota rather than numbered pads, so the practical ceiling moves with snow cover

bivy.name: Ingraham Flats
bivy.notes: About a thousand feet above Camp Muir past Cathedral Gap, this bench shortens summit day meaningfully and is the usual overflow when the Muir quota is full. The trade is real: less acclimatisation, a colder and more exposed camp, and objective exposure to icefall off the Ingraham headwall above, which is why parties argue about whether the higher start is worth it. Whether it is sound in a given week is conditions-dependent and worth asking the climbing rangers rather than deciding from a published description. Sites are dug into snow, so bring a shovel and expect to build your own platform and walls.
bivy.water: Snow only, melted on a stove. There is no liquid water source at this elevation
bivy.permit: Same Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit as Camp Muir, issued for a specific camp — a permit written for Camp Muir does not authorise a night here. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to everyone camping here, since reaching it means crossing the Cowlitz Glacier and going above Camp Muir.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties, typically under ten tents; the usable flat ground shifts year to year as the Ingraham Glacier changes and crevasses open across the bench

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: Between Longmire and Paradise on the southwest side, the practical roadhead camp for anything staging out of Paradise — Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar. Because the Nisqually entrance road is kept open through the year, it is the least season-gated approach on the mountain, though the campground itself runs roughly late May to late September. It sits low and forested at just over 3,000 ft, which makes for comfortable sleeping but no acclimatisation value whatsoever. Book early, since it is one of only two campgrounds in the park taking reservations and fills on summer weekends.
bivy.water: Potable water available at the campground during the operating season
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park entrance applies, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up on summit morning. Campsites are reservable through Recreation.gov and required during the peak midsummer window. This covers the campground only and is unrelated to the wilderness permit and climbing fee.
bivy.capacity: 179 individual sites across six loops, plus separate group sites

bivy.name: Glacier Basin
bivy.notes: The last forested camp on the route, in the valley below Mount Ruth and Burroughs Mountain, about 3.5 mi up the Glacier Basin Trail from White River Campground. There is a composting toilet a short walk from the sites and screw-top bear barrels for food. Parties who cannot get a Camp Schurman permit, or who want to break the climb into three days, sleep here and take the Inter Glacier the following morning.
bivy.water: Running creek water in the basin — the last easy water before the glaciers, and the reason most parties top off here rather than carrying from the trailhead.
bivy.permit: A National Park Service wilderness permit is required for any overnight stay in Mount Rainier's backcountry; roughly two thirds of summer sites are reservable on Recreation.gov and the remainder are issued first-come at a ranger station.
bivy.capacity: Five individual backcountry sites plus one group site.

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: Sits on the rock of Steamboat Prow where the Emmons and Winthrop glaciers part. There is a ranger hut with an emergency radio mounted on the outside that reaches dispatch when no ranger is in residence, and a single solar-dehydrating outhouse. That toilet is closed up from October through May, so off-season parties carry blue bags; early-season parties have also found the whole facility still buried in snow well into May. Nothing is hauled out for you — all rubbish goes back down in your pack.
bivy.water: None running. Everything is melted from snow, so budget fuel accordingly.
bivy.permit: Overnight stays require a wilderness permit, and a separate climbing permit covers travel above 10,000 ft or on glaciers.
bivy.capacity: Around 50 people a night — the second-busiest climbing camp on the mountain after Camp Muir.

bivy.name: Emmons Flats
bivy.notes: A bench a tenth or two of a mile up and over the hill from Camp Schurman, five minutes' walk in good conditions. Several large crevasses lie between the two camps, bridged in early season and not always later, so move between them roped as a team rather than walking over unroped with a water bottle.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, same as Schurman.
bivy.permit: Camping here is granted by the rangers rather than assumed — ask at Camp Schurman.
bivy.capacity: A handful of tents; used as overflow and by parties wanting a slightly shorter summit day.

bivy.name: Ingraham Flats

It also sits directly beneath the seracs of the icefall above; that slope is where an icefall killed eleven climbers in 1981, and parties keep their time in the fall line short.
bivy.water: Melted snow only
bivy.permit: Wilderness camping permit required and quota'd separately from the camp below, plus the climbing permit
bivy.capacity: 35 people overnight; tent camping only, no structures

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge
bivy.notes: The standard first night, on the broad snow shoulder near the gully used to drop onto the Carbon Glacier, reached over St. Elmo Pass and across the lower Winthrop. Flat ground and comparatively little rockfall exposure. It is not free of hazard: a party camped here watched a large avalanche off the Willis Wall push its debris cloud close to the bivy. Because Thumb Rock is cramped, leaving here early is the difference between a site and no site.
bivy.water: Melt snow; no running source.
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit for the night plus a climbing permit for the glacier travel above; walk-up registration is at the White River Wilderness Information Center.
bivy.capacity: Several flat spots — noticeably more room than Thumb Rock, which is why parties expecting company start here.

bivy.name: Thumb Rock
bivy.notes: The one real camp on the ridge itself, in the saddle just above the rock feature, reached by 45-55 degree snow and ice. Published elevations for it disagree — reports place it anywhere from about 10,400 to 10,800 ft. It is exposed to rock and ice coming off the Thumb and off the bands higher up, and that exposure has killed people here, so parties build up or repair the rock walls around the platforms. Strong teams in good conditions skip it entirely, camping at Curtis Ridge and climbing the ridge in a single push to cut the hours spent under the fall line.
bivy.water: Melt snow.
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for the overnight, plus the climbing cost recovery fee, which is unavoidable on this route. Registration is in person at a ranger station and climbing rangers will discuss current route conditions at that point, which on Liberty Ridge is worth treating as part of the planning rather than a formality.
bivy.capacity: Only a few tents. Sites are small and often staggered a few feet apart vertically down the slope rather than side by side.

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge bivy above Observation Rock
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the most sheltered ground on this side of the mountain: old stacked rock windbreaks sit here and parties describe it as the best bivy shelter in the area. The catch is position, not comfort — from here you still have to descend loose scree onto the North Mowich Glacier, and parties who camped here have called that descent the inefficient part of their trip. Cross-country zone; permit required.
bivy.water: none reliable — melt snow
bivy.capacity: a couple of tents on hand-built platforms

bivy.name: Edmunds/North Mowich glacier divide camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED alternative used by parties who cross the North Mowich above Needle Rock rather than staying high on Ptarmigan Ridge. Puts you on the correct side of the glacier for the face, at the cost of more elevation to regain in the morning.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: one to two tents

bivy.name: High camp below the North Mowich headwall
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp closest to the base of the face, and the most exposed of the three. Parties who have used it wore helmets in camp because of rockfall and icefall shedding off the deteriorating headwall above; there is no fully sheltered ground up here. Worth it only when conditions are cold and you intend to start on the face within a few hours. Search around 9,200 ft first if the higher ground looks loaded — flat sites there are limited but out from under the wall.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents; flat ground is scarce and has to be dug

bivy.name: Liberty Cap saddle
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY bivy only, on the broad saddle between Liberty Cap and the summit, used by at least one party benighted after topping out. It is more sheltered than the true summit and less wind-hammered than climbers expect, but it is an unplanned option to know about, not a camp to aim for — going there means you are spending a night above 13,000 ft with whatever you carried up the face.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: improvised, no prepared ground

bivy.name: Glacier Basin camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the last established campground on the White River approach. Composting toilet a short walk away and bear boxes on site. Melts out early and is the last dependable running water before the route goes onto snow and ice for good — most parties fill here rather than carry from the car.
bivy.water: creek/White River at camp, filter
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required (reserve or self-register); designated site
bivy.capacity: five individual sites plus one group site

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED first-night option when the traverse from White River is split over two days; the park's own route notes list it as the standard intermediate camp before Ptarmigan high camp. Sits on the crest between the Winthrop and Carbon glaciers, which is the point — you hear serac collapse off Willis Wall all night but the crest keeps you out of the runout. Do not drop and camp on the open Carbon below the wall to save an hour.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: small parties; scattered flat ground on the ridge crest, no established platforms

bivy.name: Ptarmigan Ridge high camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one the route is built around. Comfortable bivy ground on the ridge crest, deliberately sited just outside the serac fall line off the Liberty Wall — that icefall is the single largest objective hazard on the climb, so the exact spot matters more than the comfort. Fully exposed to wind. Parties who want an acceptable risk margin wait for an overnight freezing level at or below about 12,000 ft.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: one to two tents on dug snow platforms

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: DESCENT camp, not an ascent camp — most parties come off Ptarmigan Ridge down the Emmons-Winthrop and use this. Has a ranger hut and a solar toilet, but both can be buried in snow well into the season, so plan to be self-sufficient and pack out waste. Reserve early; this is one of the first camps on the mountain to fill.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

bivy.name: Colonnade Ridge
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the first reasonable stopping point once you leave the Wonderland Trail and start up toward the Puyallup Cleaver. It is a snow camp, so it depends entirely on coverage — in a dry year the ground here is bare and the site is much less pleasant. Parties who stop here accept a very long summit day in exchange for an easier first day off the trail.
bivy.water: melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay, obtained in person; a separate paid climbing permit is required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft
bivy.capacity: snow platforms — build what you need

bivy.name: Puyallup Cleaver high camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the usual high camp for the route, on the cleaver at roughly this height before it is left at about 8,500 ft for the glacier traverse. Mixed snow and rock, wind-exposed on a west-facing rib with nothing upwind of it. Site on the cleaver crest rather than in a runnel, and keep clear of the loose rock edges.
bivy.water: melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit also required at this elevation and on the glaciers above
bivy.capacity: a few tents on cut platforms

bivy.name: Open bivouac near 9,600 ft
bivy.notes: PLANNED but committing — used specifically to cut the summit day down, and on record as an open bivouac rather than a sheltered site. There is nothing here but what you dig. In a dry season the transition from this height onto the face is the part that turns parties around, so the higher camp only pays off if the snow is in.
bivy.water: melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft
bivy.capacity: a bivy sack or two

bivy.name: Bergschrund camp in the Sunset Amphitheater
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp reached by leaving the cleaver near 8,500 ft, traversing the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers and climbing a steep snow gully to a small bergschrund with good ground beside it. The caution is the amphitheater itself: the headwall above sheds ice and rock, so this only makes sense sited where the schrund and the terrain put you out of the fall line, and it is worth reaching it early and cold rather than in afternoon sun.
bivy.water: melt snow
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit required for every overnight stay; paid climbing permit required on glaciers and above roughly 10,000 ft

bivy.name: Camp Muir
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for the Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar routes, reached by the roughly 4,500 ft slog up the Muir Snowfield from Paradise. The Public Shelter is first-come and cannot be reserved, so treat it as a bonus rather than a plan and carry a tent regardless; it has been closed for maintenance in past seasons and its status is worth re-checking each year. Weather is the main hazard to the camp itself, and the snowfield below is notorious for whiteout navigation, so record your descent bearings before you need them. The Paradise road is plowed year-round, so unlike the north-side camps this one is not gated by a seasonal road closure.
bivy.water: No running water and no reliable melt stream. Every party must carry a stove and fuel and melt snow; snow is normally available on the Cowlitz year-round, but late in a dry season the cleanest snow can be a walk from the tent platforms
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit required for any overnight, obtained through Recreation.gov with roughly two-thirds reservable in advance and about one-third held for walk-ups within a day of departure. Separately, anyone travelling on glaciers, going above high camp or attempting the summit owes the climbing cost recovery fee, paid on Pay.gov before arriving; the amount is revised periodically, so confirm it at booking. Walking to Camp Muir and back as a day trip needs neither. In-person registration at a ranger station is still required on or before the climb date.
bivy.capacity: Roughly 25-35 tent parties on the Cowlitz Glacier snow platforms in a normal season, plus the 1921 stone Public Shelter which sleeps on the order of 15-20 on its bunks; permits are issued against a party quota rather than numbered pads, so the practical ceiling moves with snow cover

bivy.name: Ingraham Flats
bivy.notes: About a thousand feet above Camp Muir past Cathedral Gap, this bench shortens summit day meaningfully and is the usual overflow when the Muir quota is full. The trade is real: less acclimatisation, a colder and more exposed camp, and objective exposure to icefall off the Ingraham headwall above, which is why parties argue about whether the higher start is worth it. Whether it is sound in a given week is conditions-dependent and worth asking the climbing rangers rather than deciding from a published description. Sites are dug into snow, so bring a shovel and expect to build your own platform and walls.
bivy.water: Snow only, melted on a stove. There is no liquid water source at this elevation
bivy.permit: Same Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit as Camp Muir, issued for a specific camp — a permit written for Camp Muir does not authorise a night here. The climbing cost recovery fee applies to everyone camping here, since reaching it means crossing the Cowlitz Glacier and going above Camp Muir.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties, typically under ten tents; the usable flat ground shifts year to year as the Ingraham Glacier changes and crevasses open across the bench

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: Between Longmire and Paradise on the southwest side, the practical roadhead camp for anything staging out of Paradise — Disappointment Cleaver, Ingraham Direct and Gibraltar. Because the Nisqually entrance road is kept open through the year, it is the least season-gated approach on the mountain, though the campground itself runs roughly late May to late September. It sits low and forested at just over 3,000 ft, which makes for comfortable sleeping but no acclimatisation value whatsoever. Book early, since it is one of only two campgrounds in the park taking reservations and fills on summer weekends.
bivy.water: Potable water available at the campground during the operating season

bivy.notes: PLANNED camp on the White River approach, which is now the practical way in — the Carbon River side lost public vehicle access when the Fairfax Bridge closed. Composting toilet and bear boxes. Last dependable running water; everything above is melt snow.
bivy.water: creek/White River at camp, filter
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; designated site
bivy.capacity: five individual sites plus one group site

bivy.name: St Elmo Pass bivy
bivy.notes: PLANNED staging bivy at the pass where parties change into glacier gear before stepping onto the Winthrop. A short rock wall gives some wind shelter and the site is out of any fall line. Useful when a late trailhead start makes the full traverse to Curtis Ridge too long.
bivy.water: none — melt snow, usually plentiful
bivy.capacity: one to two tents on a small flat bench

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge camp
bivy.notes: PLANNED high camp for the wall, on the northeast side of the ridge dividing the Carbon from the Winthrop. This is the camp the route is climbed from — parties leave here before midnight to reach the avalanche cones at the foot of the central rib while everything overhead is still frozen. **Do not camp out on the Carbon Glacier below the wall.** A party that pitched on the Carbon in the fall line watched a large collapse off Willis Wall run close to their tent; the ice cliff at the top of the wall is on the order of 300 ft high and it discharges straight down onto the head of the glacier. The ridge crest is the whole reason this camp exists.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: small parties; flat ground has to be built by moving rocks or stomping snow

bivy.name: Wing Lake
bivy.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Black Peak and the natural first night for Corteo as well. From the Rainy Pass west lot the loop trail is followed for a little over a mile, then a right fork leads to Heather Pass; from there a boot path crosses a boulder field and drops to Lewis Lake, and a further climb of about twelve hundred feet up the northwest slope reaches Wing Lake in the cirque under Black Peak. Reckon on four to six hours with a pack, and four to seven more from camp to summit and back. Camping here rather than at Lewis costs an hour on the way in and buys a much shorter summit day, which matters because everything above is talus and heather with route-finding rather than trail. The boundary detail is worth knowing: Black Peak's summit stands on the line between the forest and the national park, but this camp is on the forest side, so a party sleeping here needs no permit even though it is climbing a peak the park shares.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is dependable through the season. Snow patches under Black Peak feed it well into the autumn. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: None. This is Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, not the national park, so there is no backcountry permit, no quota and nothing to reserve. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass covers parking at Rainy Pass. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine from mid summer onward and at this elevation there is almost nothing to burn anyway, so plan on a stove and check the current order rather than assuming a fire is legal.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established pads in the boulders and heather around the outlet, most taking one or two tents. It is the best ground on this side of the peak and it fills on clear summer weekends and hard in larch season, so have Lewis Lake in mind as the fallback.

bivy.name: Lewis Lake
bivy.notes: Lewis sits in the bowl below Wing, reached by dropping off Heather Pass and picking a way through talus on goat paths around the left-hand shore. Most parties treat it as a waypoint rather than a destination, but it is a genuine camp and a sensible one for a late start, a heavy pack or a party that wants a shorter first day. It is also where the Corteo approach commits: from here the line follows the top of the moraine onto the Lewis Glacier and climbs southeast, bearing left at the top, to a notch on the ridge near seven thousand five hundred feet, then works west along the ridge and downclimbs several hundred feet of dirt or snow into the cirque under Corteo's west face, gaining the southwest ridge at a large notch by an easy gully. Nothing above Lewis is trail. Snow lingers on the traverse out of Heather Pass into early summer and an axe is worth carrying until it has gone.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet run all season. Reliable.
bivy.permit: None — national forest, no permit, no quota, no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Rainy Pass.
bivy.capacity: A few sites around the shore, fewer and rougher than Wing Lake's. Adequate for a party or two, and the obvious answer when Wing is full or when weather turns on the way up.

bivy.name: Rainy Pass trailhead lots, and the quarter-mile camping closures

It is also where the Pacific Crest Trail heads north, so the lots serve two entirely different sets of objectives and are busier than their size suggests. The closures above exist because the loop is one of the most walked trails in the state and its meadows were being trampled; they are enforced rather than advisory. Parties commonly sleep in the car here before an early start, and there is a toilet but no water. Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.
bivy.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
bivy.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.
