Everything depends on SR 20 being open — the highway shuts for the winter, usually in late November or early December, and reopens after avalanche control and snow clearing, most often between mid April and early May but occasionally very much later when a hard winter leaves washouts and rockslide damage behind it. Confirm the road is actually open before driving out from either side, and expect construction closures on this stretch in some seasons.
bivy.water: None at the pass. Fill in the valley or plan on filtering from the lakes once you are in.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. The rule that catches people out is a camping closure rather than a permit: no overnight camping within a quarter mile of Lake Ann, Rainy Lake, Heather Pass or Maple Pass, and none anywhere along the Heather-Maple Pass loop trail itself. Walk through to Lewis or Wing and you are legal with no paperwork; stop short of them and you are not.
bivy.capacity: Two large paved lots either side of the highway, with the Maple Pass loop starting from the west side. They fill early on summer and autumn weekends. This is staging and roadside parking, not a campground.

access.fees: None — no climbing permit fee (this is National Forest, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; day travel on the National Forest land near the trailhead needs no permit, but most of the route (Lewis Glacier basin, ridge, and summit) lies within North Cascades National Park/Stephen Mather Wilderness, where overnight camping requires a backcountry permit.
access.permit: Overnight backcountry camping in North Cascades National Park costs $10/person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee (charged mid-May-early Oct; free the rest of the year, per the NPS fee schedule updated in 2024). About 60% of permits are reservable in advance on recreation.gov; 40% are held for in-person walk-up at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. Day climbs with no overnight camping do not require an NCNP permit.
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter between the Ross Dam Trailhead (MP 134, west) and the Silver Star Gate (MP 171, east), typically mid-November through late April/early May; the exact reopening date varies year to year with snowpack and slide/storm damage, so check the WSDOT mountain pass report before driving.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Complex/Stephen Mather Wilderness (upper peak and glacier basin); Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (Rainy Pass trailhead and lower trail).
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass ($30/yr or $5/day) or an America the Beautiful Interagency Pass to park at the Rainy Pass/Lake Ann Trailhead.

bivy.name: Eldorado Creek basin
bivy.notes: Open basin above the boulder field; a lower camp for parties splitting the approach.

bivy.name: Inspiration Glacier high camp
bivy.notes: Rock outcrops at the edge of the Inspiration Glacier below Eldorado's East Ridge. The standard base for Eldorado and the start of the traverse.

bivy.name: Klawatti col
bivy.notes: Rock tent sites on the col below the south side of Klawatti Peak with running water and big views; well placed for Klawatti, Austera and Primus.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 fee in the summer season (mid-May to early October); youth 15 and under free
access.permit: Overnight backcountry permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, picked up in person in Marblemount
access.land_manager: North Cascades National Park

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

access.landManager: USFS Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District) at the Easy Pass Trailhead; the peak and climbing route are within North Cascades National Park, entered at Easy Pass (6,550 ft).

bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

bivy.name: Ragged Ridge crest bivy, south of Mesahchie Col
bivy.notes: This is the higher and more committing of the two Ragged Ridge camps, about a mile west-northwest of Easy Pass. Two ways reach it: sidehill west at roughly six thousand eight hundred feet on heather and scree, or climb the grassy slope just past the pass to gain the crest near seven thousand two hundred feet and follow the ridge until the ground steepens toward the 7,690-foot point, where it turns technical. The reward is a start already on the ridge for a long traverse day toward Katsuk and Kimtah; the cost is wind, cold and the water problem. Mount Arriva goes the other way from the pass, southwest, so a party after Arriva alone gains nothing by coming up here. Pitch on gravel rather than on the heather, which is thin and slow to recover, and expect a party of more than two to be split across separate patches of ground.
bivy.water: SEASONAL AND OFTEN GONE. Snow patches supply it early and it is commonly dry by late summer, which is the one reason to prefer the basin below. Coming up here late in the year means carrying water or dropping into the basin to fetch it.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required, reserved in advance and issued by park staff before the trip. Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Fisher Camp, Fisher Creek basin
bivy.notes: Fisher Camp sits in the forested basin west of and well below Easy Pass, reached by carrying on over the pass and descending into Fisher Creek. It is the comfortable option and it is also the alternative approach to Kimtah that some parties prefer: rather than the long sidehill traverse along the south flank of Ragged Ridge, they drop into the basin, losing something like eighteen hundred feet, and then climb a more direct line straight back up to the crest. Whether that trade is worth it depends on snow on the traverse and on how much the party dislikes scree. Further down the valley the trail passes additional designated camps toward the Thunder Creek junction, which is how a Ragged Ridge trip can be finished as a through-hike rather than an out-and-back. The descent to this camp is real elevation that has to be regained on the way out, and it is the reason a summit-focused party stays high instead.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek, right at the camp, and it runs all season. This is the most reliable water anywhere on the Ragged Ridge side.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required and reserved for this specific named site, not for a zone. Book in advance through the national online system and collect the permit from park staff shortly before the trip. Food must be stored properly; a canister is the simplest answer. No campfires, and no dogs anywhere beyond Easy Pass.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites — two taking a single tent each and one that will hold about four. A privy is provided. Being a named camp rather than a zone, it is reserved specifically and can simply be full.

access.fees: Trailhead parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency (America the Beautiful) Pass, or Recreation.gov Digital Day Pass ($5/vehicle/day or $30/year). Overnight backcountry permits — effectively required for this multi-day objective — cost $10/person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee.
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No dogs beyond the national park boundary, including at Easy Pass. No pack animals at the trailhead. Stay on durable surfaces — alpine vegetation in the meadows is fragile.
access.permit: A wilderness/backcountry permit is required for all overnight stays; reserve on recreation.gov and pick it up in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount by 11am on the trip's start date or the reservation is cancelled. access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.

access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at the Easy Pass trailhead on SR-20 between mileposts 151 and 152, which has a self-issue station — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / Interagency Pass for trailhead parking, plus an NPS wilderness/backcountry permit for the overnight approach.

bivy.name: Kool-Aid Lake
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, and the standard first night on the traverse — the first place with water and flat ground after Cache Col. Sites sit on the lip of a steep slope that drops thousands of feet toward the valley, so pitch back from the edge in wind. The col above holds snow well into July and there is no water at the col itself, so parties crossing late in the day carry water up or drop to this lake. Goats work the camp for salt; keep gear and urine spots away from tents. The national park boundary runs at Cache Col just above; camps from here south are commonly described as lying in the wilderness outside the park where no camping permit is required, but confirm the zone with the ranger station when you pick up your trailhead permit.
bivy.water: the lake, and snowmelt runnels feeding it
bivy.capacity: several tents

bivy.name: Yang Yang Lakes
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the usual second night, in heather meadow among granite boulders below the Le Conte Glacier. It is a low point on the traverse and melts out later than its elevation suggests — a party in late June found nothing bare and pitched on snow with running water alongside. Sheltered relative to the passes on either side, but the basin is a cold sink. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: the lakes; flowing water available even under snow cover
bivy.capacity: several tents

bivy.name: White Rock Lakes
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the last true alpine camp and the one most parties would not skip, looking straight across at the icefalls of Dome and Sinister. Dry dirt bivy platforms are usable by late June, earlier than the lower camps. It is an open basin with nothing to hide behind: one party sat out roughly twelve hours of rain and wind in tents here, so anchor well and pick a site with a boulder on the windward side. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: the lakes
bivy.capacity: at least three good sites; more on snow

bivy.name: Cub Lake meadows / Itswoot Ridge
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, the last night for parties exiting south to Downey Creek, in heather meadow below Itswoot Ridge. Melts out late — a late-June party found the lake still largely frozen, the basin barely opened up, and a marginal perch near 6,200 ft below the basin that they would not recommend sleeping on until more snow had gone. Popular enough that solitude is not the reason to stop here; proximity to the Bachelor Creek descent is. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: Cub Lake outlet and meadow streams
bivy.capacity: many parties; the meadows absorb a dozen or more groups on a holiday weekend

access.fees: N/A - no fee for day travel; overnight camping inside the North Cascades NP portion needs a wilderness permit costing $10 per person (youth 15 and under free), plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee for advance reservations. A walk-up permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center avoids the reservation fee, not the $10.
access.notes: The traverse crosses two jurisdictions: the southern Cascade Pass-to-Yang Yang Lakes stretch is Mount Baker-Snoqualmie/Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Glacier Peak Wilderness), and the northern Cascade Pass/Cache Col/Ptarmigan Traverse proper runs through North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness).
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones inside the park; 12 in on-trail National Forest corridors.
access.permit: Wilderness permit required for any overnight stay inside North Cascades National Park (obtain from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center); a free self-issue National Forest wilderness permit covers the southern, non-park portion.
access.closures: Cascade River Road (the standard entry trailhead) has a history of seasonal washouts/closures — check the current NPS road-conditions page before a trip.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness) / Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Glacier Peak Wilderness)
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park, and USDA Forest Service — Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest

bivy.name: Easy Pass trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the only practical trailhead for Mesahchie, Katsuk, Kimtah and Mount Arriva, and it is worth understanding what the walk in costs before committing to it. The trail climbs roughly three thousand feet in a little under four miles, gently through forest at first and then in steep switchbacks up a headwall of loose rock with real exposure to weather; the name is old optimism and nothing about it is easy under a climbing pack. Snow holds on the upper switchbacks and in the basin above into July in an ordinary year and later after a heavy winter, and that traverse is where parties turn around. There is a toilet at the lot and parties routinely sleep in the car here before a pre-dawn start. Dogs may come only as far as the pass, because the top of the pass is the national park boundary.
bivy.water: None at the lot. Granite Creek is crossed on a bridge a few minutes up the trail and is the last easy water low on the approach.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. No camping permit is needed on the forest side of the pass. THE MOMENT YOU CROSS THE PASS THE RULES CHANGE COMPLETELY — see the Ragged Ridge and Fisher Creek entries below.
bivy.capacity: A small lot with room for roughly ten cars, on a short spur off the highway between mileposts 151 and 152. It is genuinely small and can be full on a good weekend.

bivy.name: Mesahchie basin, below the col
bivy.notes: This is the base for Mesahchie and the usual first night of any Ragged Ridge traverse. From Easy Pass the line goes cross-country west-northwest, sidehilling on heather and tiresome scree at around six thousand eight hundred feet for roughly three hours to reach the basin below Mesahchie Col. It is not a trail and it is not fast — talus, sidehill and sustained scrambling are the whole character of this ridge and parties consistently underestimate the traverse. From camp Mesahchie goes by its south side, Katsuk lies about half a mile further west along the crest by its south spur and east ridge, and Kimtah is beyond that again and is rarely worth a trip on its own. Note that camping is prohibited at Easy Pass itself and in the meadows around it, so this basin or the crest bivy is where the first legal ground is. All of it is inside the park, so leave the dog at home.
bivy.water: Running water in the basin, fed by snow above, and this is what recommends it over the ridge bivy higher up. It is the dependable choice late in a hot summer when the crest has dried out.
bivy.permit: NORTH CASCADES NATIONAL PARK backcountry permit required, without exception. Permits are reserved in advance through the national online reservation system and issued by park staff shortly before the trip, by email or in person at the wilderness desk in Marblemount, with a per-person recreation fee and a small booking fee on top. Camping is in a cross-country zone rather than at a named site, and an approved bear-resistant canister is required wherever there is nothing to hang food from, which up here is everywhere. No campfires; carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: Unimproved ground for a couple of small tents on benches in the basin under Mesahchie and Katsuk. Nothing is built here — no pads, no privy, no fire ring, and there should not be.

Cross-country zone camping with an approved bear canister, and no campfires. There is no self-issue option anywhere on this side of the pass — the free trailhead-kiosk permits people are used to on the forest do not exist here.
bivy.capacity: A small high bivy on the south side of the crest, east of the 7,985-foot subpeak. Room for one or two parties on gravel and heather. Exposed, with no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: Wing Lake
bivy.notes: The standard base camp for Black Peak, roughly 6,900 ft in a basin of scree and boulders directly beneath the peak, with larches around the shore that turn gold in late September. It sits about 1,200 ft above Lewis Lake, reached by a rough boot path over a boulder field with one steep step. Nights are cold — near freezing even in good weather — and from here the South Ridge scramble is a half-day round trip. The better tent spots are in the larch groves just below the lake.
bivy.water: The lake itself, right at camp, all season
bivy.permit: No backcountry permit is described for camping here — the approach and the lake are on national forest land — but a Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is needed to park at Rainy Pass
bivy.capacity: A site at the lake outlet plus several more on benches above it; the basin is quiet compared with the Maple Pass loop below, and parties regularly have it to themselves midweek

bivy.name: Lewis Lake
bivy.notes: About 5,700 ft, the first lake past Heather Pass and the lower fallback if the light goes or the boulder field above looks unappealing. It is a legitimate base — parties do summit and return from here — but it adds 1,200 ft each way to summit day, and the bugs are worse than higher up.
bivy.water: The lake, though it runs silty
bivy.permit: Same as Wing Lake: no overnight permit described, parking pass required at the trailhead
bivy.capacity: At least one good site just above the lake beside the path, and room for a small party or two

bivy.name: Tumwater Camp, Stehekin valley road
bivy.notes: The first camp of consequence above the shuttle's turnaround at High Bridge, and its job on this trip is to absorb the arrival day. The boat gets in around the middle of the day and the last shuttle up the valley goes in the late afternoon, so nobody sensibly starts a twenty-mile approach on day one — you ride to High Bridge, walk a short way up the old road, and sleep in flat riverside forest with no view and no alpine character at all. It has a history of high-water damage and was closed after a bad flood, though it stands in the park's current camp table; confirm it is genuinely open when you arrange the permit rather than assuming, because there are not many camps up here and losing one reshapes the whole itinerary.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River is right there and runs all season. Treat it — it is a big glacial river carrying silt and everything else off the drainage.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park. THERE IS NO PERMIT DESK IN STEHEKIN — the visitor centre at the landing does not issue them and is closed. For a trip starting in the valley the permit is arranged by EMAIL with the park's wilderness office, sent early on the morning BEFORE your start date, with a short mandatory video to watch and a signed copy to print and carry. There is no cell service in Stehekin, so all of that has to happen before you get on the boat. Food lockers are provided at these valley camps and no bear canister is required.
bivy.capacity: Two sites, each taking up to six people, so six is the party ceiling. No stock. Assigned by night on the permit.

bivy.name: Shady Camp, Stehekin valley road
bivy.notes: Further up the old road than Tumwater and the only camp on this stretch that is held back from the booking system entirely, which is exactly why it is worth knowing about. A party whose permit request comes back with a hole in the middle of the itinerary can often fill it here. It is another flat forested river camp with nothing to look at, used purely for position. Note that the road above the washout is closed to BICYCLES as well as vehicles — the upper section is decommissioned or maintained as a non-motorized, non-mechanized trail, so the obvious idea of riding the old roadbed to save a day is not permitted. It is walking or stock, and that is what makes this approach as long as it is.
bivy.water: River water beside the camp, dependable through the season and needing treatment.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, arranged the same way as the rest of the valley — by email to the wilderness office the morning before you start, since nothing can be issued in Stehekin itself. Because the site is walk-up rather than reservable, it cannot be locked in months ahead; ask for it in that same email.
bivy.capacity: A single site taking up to eight people. No stock. WALK-UP ONLY — this one takes no reservations at all, which makes it the useful fallback when everything else on the road is booked out.

bivy.name: Park Creek Camp, at the valley road
bivy.notes: THIS IS THE CAMP THE PARK ITSELF POINTS OVERNIGHT PARTIES TO NOW THAT FLAT CREEK IS SHUT, and that closure is the single most important planning fact for this peak. The camp at the Flat Creek trailhead, which would otherwise be the obvious base, has its access trail closed for hazard trees and has dropped out of both the park's camp list and its booking system; no reopening date has been given anywhere. Park Creek sits lower down the same road, so using it lengthens an approach that is already long — you are walking further to the trailhead each morning rather than sleeping at it. Note this is the camp on the VALLEY ROAD where the Park Creek trail leaves it, not the stock camp several miles up that trail toward the pass. The four-person cap is worth checking against your party before you plan around it.
bivy.water: Park Creek at the camp, reliable all season.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit, arranged by email before you travel as above. A TOTAL CAMPFIRE BAN has been in force across the entire Stehekin valley since the end of June, covering anything that produces ash including propane fire pits, with no end date announced — so the ring here is out of use regardless of what the camp table says about fires. Gas and propane STOVES are still allowed, with clearance around them and a working shut-off valve. Confirm the ban's status when you get the permit.
bivy.capacity: Two sites, each capped at four people, so this is a small-party camp only. No stock. It has a fire ring, which is not the same as permission to use it right now.

bivy.name: Cottonwood Camp, end of the closed road
bivy.notes: At the very end of the closed road section, something under four miles past the Flat Creek junction, roughly twenty-three miles up from the landing. It is the upper valley's anchor camp and the obvious base for a larger party, at the cost of walking past your turning and back each day. It also marks where the OTHER approaches arrive: parties come down over Park Creek Pass from the Thunder Creek side, and over Cascade Pass from the Cascade River road, which reaches the Flat Creek junction in something over thirteen miles. Either is a genuine alternative to the boat and both are long. Worth knowing that the current fire closures in this park are all on the Ross Lake and Big Beaver side and do NOT reach the upper Stehekin valley — the camps up here are constrained by flood damage, hazard trees and the fire ban, not by an active fire.
bivy.water: River and tributary water at the camp, reliable and needing treatment like everything else in the drainage.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required. WHICH OFFICE DEPENDS ON WHICH WAY YOU COME IN, and getting this wrong costs a day: a party arriving by boat arranges it by email with the wilderness office before travelling, but anyone approaching over Cascade Pass from the Cascade River road must collect the permit IN PERSON at Marblemount, and that includes permits for this camp. The camp table allows campfires here, but the valley-wide ban currently overrides that.
bivy.capacity: Two sites, one taking six and one taking twelve, so up to twelve in a party — the largest allowance anywhere on this approach and the reason groups use it.

bivy.name: Bivouacs in the upper Flat Creek basin, beyond the end of the trail
bivy.notes: Rimrock Ridge is an obscure summit and should be described as one. It forms the southern rim of the upper Flat Creek valley — everything falling off its far side goes into the West Fork of Agnes Creek instead — and it looks across at the glaciated back of the crest that the classic traverse walks along. Accounts of that traverse do not mention it, because climbers up there are facing the other way, and no ascent account of it was found at all. The approach is the whole difficulty: boat, shuttle, most of a day walking the old road, a gentle valley trail of about four miles that gains only a few hundred feet through old growth and through forest still recovering from a fire early this century, and then trailless ground up the headwaters to whatever line goes. The trail ends well short of the head of the valley and the summit is beyond where it ends. Budget four days minimum for something that would be an afternoon if a road came near it, and build the itinerary around the boat timetable rather than the climbing, because a missed sailing costs a day at each end. Late summer into early autumn is the window; the valley walk is snow-free long before the head of it is.
bivy.water: Creek and snowmelt throughout the basin, which is at least the easy part — this is a wet valley fed off the glaciers on the crest above it, and running water is not the problem here that it is on a ridge camp.
bivy.permit: THE AGENCY CHANGES ON THIS TRAIL, and it is the thing most likely to be got wrong. The Flat Creek trail leaves the national park about two miles up and passes into the Glacier Peak Wilderness under the national forest, so the ground you actually camp and climb on is Forest Service. Checked against the boundary rather than assumed: the summit itself lies inside that wilderness. It takes a free self-issue permit filled in at the trailhead rather than a park permit, with no reservation and no fee, and a party limit of TWELVE counting people and pack animals together — larger than the park's limit down in the valley, and a rare case where walking further gets you a looser rule. Groups over twelve must split and stay a mile apart. Your park permit still covers the valley camps you slept in getting there, so a full trip needs both. There is NO park cross-country zone for Flat Creek; that is not a gap in the record, the zone system simply does not reach here because the ground is not the park's. Standard wilderness practice otherwise: durable surfaces, well back from the water, pack out what will not bury, and no fires.
bivy.capacity: No established camping and no site count. THERE IS NOTHING UP HERE. The trail stops, and a party going on picks whatever flat gravel, slab or old moraine it can find in the head of the valley. Anyone describing a camp here is describing a place they happened to sleep.

access.fees: 2026 NPS backcountry fees: $6 non-refundable permit reservation fee plus $10/person/night camping fee within the park boundary (ages 15 and under free); the Forest Service wilderness permit beyond the park boundary is free. Ferry fare to/from Stehekin and any High Bridge shuttle fee are separate.
access.rules: Leave No Trace travel required; camping is restricted to designated/permitted sites within the park/NRA portion of the approach. Food storage from bears is essential — aggressive bear activity has been reported in 2026 at PCT camps in this corridor (Fireweed and South Fork camps in particular).
access.permit: An NPS wilderness permit is required for any overnight camping within the park/NRA boundary near High Bridge (reserve on recreation.gov or get a walk-up permit at the Golden West Visitor Center in Stehekin). Once across into the Glacier Peak Wilderness (Forest Service land), only a free self-issue wilderness permit is required, available at trailhead registration boxes.
access.closures: As of mid-2026 the Stehekin area is still recovering from a historic December 2025 flood: Company Creek Road lost roughly 1,000 ft of roadbed and a levee (an elevated interim road was completed June 23, 2026); North Cascades Lodge at Stehekin is closed for the season (no lodging, dining, fuel, or showers, though ferry and postal service continue); the High Bridge shuttle bus is not running for 2026. On the trail itself, the Agnes Creek bridge at Hemlock Camp (south of the park boundary, in the Glacier Peak Wilderness) is out of service and camping at Hemlock Camp is considered unsafe due to hazard trees — use Cedar Camp or the South Fork Agnes Creek camp instead. Confirm current conditions with the Wilderness Information Center (360-854-7245) before going.

bivy.name: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col
bivy.notes: The standard first-night camp for Snowfield, Neve and Colonial, reached by a steep sustained climb from the Pyramid Lake trailhead with no easy water for much of it. Early in the season the ground is still under snow and flat bivy platforms are easier to find than proper tent pitches; by late summer the basin rim dries to sand and polished rock and the tent sites improve. accounts disagree on exactly where the best camp sits — some parties stop on the bench near 5,400 ft, others push over the col into the basin — and both are defensible depending on snow cover and how far you want to carry water. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin heather.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns; reliable in early summer, patchy to absent by late August in a dry year, so plan to carry up from lower on the trail
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a cross-country zone reached by the Pyramid Lake and Pyramid Peak trails, with permits from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or the park's online system.
bivy.capacity: Several small parties; a scatter of flat gravel and slab platforms rather than a defined number of sites

bivy.name: Neve-Colonial col high bivy
bivy.notes: Parties heading for Snowfield sometimes push past the basin and sleep at the pass above the Colonial Glacier to shorten summit day and get onto the Neve Glacier early. The trade is weather: this notch funnels wind badly and a night here can be miserable or unsafe in anything but settled conditions, so it suits a stable forecast and a party willing to retreat downhill. Snow cover varies enormously through the season, which changes both whether you can melt water and whether the ground under you is snow or bare rock. Sleeping on the glacier itself is a separate decision with crevasse-hazard implications — scout the site in daylight.
bivy.water: Melted snow only, and that assumes snow is still present at the col; there is no running water
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same cross-country zone as the basin camps below.
bivy.capacity: One to two small parties on flat snow or a cleared rock platform; genuinely exposed and not somewhere to spread out

access.fees: $10/person/night + a flat $6 nonrefundable reservation fee (charged mid-May–early Oct only; free the rest of the year). No separate climbing fee — North Cascades NP entrance itself is free.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Leave No Trace. No camping at Pyramid Lake itself (Research Natural Area) — camp at least 1/2 mile past the lake. Standard North Cascades NP backcountry rules apply (food storage, group size limits).
access.permit: A backcountry permit is required for any overnight stay in North Cascades National Park Complex: $10 per person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee (climbers 15 and under free). About 60% of sites can be reserved in advance on Recreation.gov; the rest are walk-up only, issued at the Wilderness Information Center, 7280 Ranger Station Road, Marblemount, WA 98267 (open mid-May to mid-October).
access.closures: SR 20 itself is normally open and plowed year-round past the Pyramid Lake trailhead (MP 126.8) — the highway's usual seasonal winter closure gate sits farther east at Ross Dam (MP 134). In heavy-snow or storm-damage years WSDOT sometimes moves the closure gate west to Newhalem (MP 120), which would also cut off this trailhead — check WSDOT's SR 20 pass report before a winter/spring trip.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Complex — North Unit of North Cascades National Park, reached via the Ross Lake National Recreation Area corridor along SR 20.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: None — the Pyramid Lake trailhead is an NPS trailhead within the park complex, not National Forest land, so no Northwest Forest Pass/Interagency Pass is needed for day parking.

bivy.name: Cosho Camp, Fisher Creek
bivy.notes: This forested camp on the north side of Fisher Creek is the usual base for Cosho Peak and the eastern end of Ragged Ridge, reached over Easy Pass from the SR 20 trailhead and then down roughly 1,400 ft of switchbacks to the valley. It is an easy first day from the car, which is why parties use it despite the elevation given back on the descent. Easy Pass sits well east of the winter gate, so this approach exists only while SR 20 is open across the pass — typically late spring through the first serious storms of autumn.
bivy.water: Fisher Creek runs right there and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a DESIGNATED camp assigned by night, not a first-come dispersed site, so a walk-up can be refused if it is already booked. Have a fallback.
bivy.capacity: Small designated backcountry camp, on the order of one to three parties

access.fees: $10 per person NPS backcountry recreation fee, plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee whether booked in advance on recreation.gov or issued first-come, first-served at the Wilderness Information Center.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: NPS requires packing out all solid human waste with blue bags above treeline. Stay on durable surfaces near Easy Pass — the alpine meadows there are fragile, and no camping is allowed at the pass or in the meadows themselves.
access.permit: North Cascades NP wilderness/backcountry camping permit (required for any overnight stay; day climbs need none)
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) gate closes seasonally, typically mid-November through mid/late April depending on snowpack, eliminating road access entirely during that window.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (Wilderness District) manages the backcountry beyond Easy Pass; the Easy Pass trailhead itself is on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest land.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/Interagency Pass required to park at the Easy Pass trailhead (day-use fee otherwise applies).

bivy.name: Devils Park Shelter, Jackita Ridge trail
bivy.notes: The obvious overnight stop for Crater Mountain and the eastern approaches, about eight miles in from Canyon Creek up a long hot climb through McMillan Park. The shelter is unmaintained and its condition is reported inconsistently year to year, so carry a tent and treat the roof as a bad-weather bonus rather than the plan. Access is seasonal at both ends: SR 20's winter closure puts the Canyon Creek trailhead behind a gate, and the Canyon Creek bridge on the Jackita Ridge trail has been reported out — check current Forest Service conditions, because the ford is dangerous in spring and early-summer runoff.
bivy.water: A stream just east of the shelter is normally flowing well; it can drop off late in a dry summer, and the ridge above Devils Park is dry, so fill here
bivy.permit: US Forest Service, Okanogan-Wenatchee — Pasayten Wilderness. NO reservation and NO fee: free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required to park at Canyon Creek. This is the sharpest contrast with the Park Service side of the same corridor.
bivy.capacity: An old log shelter with a few rough bunks, plus open meadow camping for several parties immediately around it

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes basin, Jack Mountain south side
bivy.notes: Reached by leaving the Crater Mountain trail and travelling several miles cross-country, this basin is the usual high camp for the south face of Jack Mountain. It is a long committing day from the Canyon Creek trailhead and route-finding on the approach is the crux for many parties, so budget for arriving late. An unplanned bivy on this mountain is common enough that carrying emergency shelter is a reasonable default rather than a precaution. The trailhead is behind the SR 20 winter gate, which closes this approach entirely for roughly half the year.
bivy.water: The lakes themselves plus inlet streams; reliable but standing water, so filter or treat
bivy.permit: CONTESTED BY LOCATION, and this is the one to get right. The administrative boundary runs through the Jack Mountain massif: ground east of the Little Jack ridge crest is Pasayten Wilderness under the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, needing only the free self-issue permit, while ground west of the crest falls in Ross Lake NRA and requires a National Park Service backcountry permit. Jerry Lakes sit on the Forest Service side of that divide — but if your route wanders west you have changed agencies. Carry both or confirm against the boundary before you go.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed; a few flat spots at the lakes and a hidden pocket among the trees, enough for one or two parties

access.fees: $5/vehicle/day or $30/year day-use fee at Canyon Creek Trailhead (Northwest Forest Pass / Interagency America the Beautiful Pass accepted, plus Digital Day Pass).
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the trailhead to enter the Pasayten Wilderness. access.closures: SR 20 access closes seasonally in winter; the highway (including the trailhead segment) was also closed January-June 2026 for emergency washout repairs, reopening June 14, 2026. Check current trail status with the Wilderness Information Center.

access.notes: Access via high-speed boat shuttle up Ross Lake to May Creek (Ross Lake Resort). Part of North Cascades National Park access area. Mountain rarely climbed due to alpine difficulty.

bivy.name: Crater Creek Meadows bench
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp and the standard staging point for the south face, on a heather bench above Crater Creek northwest of point 7001. Reached in roughly eight hours and eleven miles from the car, after the Jerry Glacier traverse and the drop into Crater Creek Basin. Parties choose it over Jerry Lakes specifically because it shortens the summit day onto the face. Terrain gives moderate wind shelter. Permit status is not confirmed for this basin — check the zone before you go.
bivy.water: Crater Creek, about 200 ft below camp
bivy.capacity: small — comfortable for a party of two

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes basin
bivy.notes: PLANNED camp, a grassy boulder-strewn bowl with several separate sites; the best of them sits by the small lake between the two large ones. Snow-free by mid-August. It is the more pleasant camp of the two and the obvious stop if you arrive late, but it leaves a longer traverse to the face on summit day. Open bowl, so afternoon wind. Fire-scarred forest on the approach into the basin. Check the zone for permits.
bivy.water: four alpine lakes
bivy.capacity: multiple parties across the basin

bivy.name: Jerry Lakes Peak south saddle
bivy.notes: EMERGENCY ledge, not a camp — on record only as an unplanned night out, sat through in a bivy sack and an emergency blanket with little wind protection and a cold, sleepless result. Worth knowing exists if a party is caught on the ridge between the lakes and the Crater Mountain saddle, and worth planning not to use.
bivy.water: none at the saddle

access.fees: $10 per person NPS backcountry camping fee (Ross Lake NRA/NOCA) plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee if booked in advance; no fee for the USFS Pasayten Wilderness permit.

access.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the Canyon Creek Trailhead for the USFS approach. bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. Fee campground, reservations through Recreation.gov for most of the season plus some first-come sites. No backcountry permit to sleep here — but one IS needed the moment you move uphill onto Colonial, Pyramid or Snowfield.
bivy.capacity: Large road campground, roughly 90-100 numbered sites including walk-in tent sites and a group site; a smaller north loop sits across the highway

bivy.name: Colonial Basin bench camps, below the Pyramid-Colonial col
bivy.notes: The standard first-night camp for Snowfield, Neve and Colonial, reached by a steep sustained climb from the Pyramid Lake trailhead with no easy water for much of it. Early in the season the ground is still under snow and flat bivy platforms are easier to find than proper tent pitches; by late summer the basin rim dries to sand and polished rock and the tent sites improve. accounts disagree on exactly where the best camp sits — some parties stop on the bench near 5,400 ft, others push over the col into the basin — and both are defensible depending on snow cover and how far you want to carry water. Camp on rock or snow rather than the thin heather.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns; reliable in early summer, patchy to absent by late August in a dry year, so plan to carry up from lower on the trail
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required — a cross-country zone reached by the Pyramid Lake and Pyramid Peak trails, with permits from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center or the park's online system.
bivy.capacity: Several small parties; a scatter of flat gravel and slab platforms rather than a defined number of sites

bivy.name: Neve-Colonial col high bivy
bivy.notes: Parties heading for Snowfield sometimes push past the basin and sleep at the pass above the Colonial Glacier to shorten summit day and get onto the Neve Glacier early. The trade is weather: this notch funnels wind badly and a night here can be miserable or unsafe in anything but settled conditions, so it suits a stable forecast and a party willing to retreat downhill. Snow cover varies enormously through the season, which changes both whether you can melt water and whether the ground under you is snow or bare rock. Sleeping on the glacier itself is a separate decision with crevasse-hazard implications — scout the site in daylight.
bivy.water: Melted snow only, and that assumes snow is still present at the col; there is no running water
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, same cross-country zone as the basin camps below.
bivy.capacity: One to two small parties on flat snow or a cleared rock platform; genuinely exposed and not somewhere to spread out

access.fees: No park entrance fee — North Cascades National Park is fee-free — and no parking pass (Northwest Forest Pass/Discover Pass) is required at the Pyramid Lake trailhead.
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Pyramid Lake and the trail corridor are closed to camping; overnight parties must camp at least 0.5 mi past the lake. Leashed dogs are allowed on the maintained trail. NPS wilderness group-size limits apply for overnight parties above the lake.
access.permit: No permit required for a day scramble. Overnight camping anywhere past Pyramid Lake requires an NPS wilderness/backcountry permit (Recreation.gov early-access lottery and general on-sale for peak season, or walk-up in person up to 24 hours ahead at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount, (360) 854-7245).
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) was closed between milepost 130 (Colonial Creek/Diablo Lake) and milepost 156.8 (Porcupine Creek) after a March 2026 storm and rockslide caused major roadway damage, and fully reopened June 14, 2026 — about ten days ahead of the announced target. The Pyramid Lake trailhead (MP ~126.8) sits just west of that closure zone and remained reachable from the Newhalem/Marblemount side throughout. The highway is also gated by winter avalanche hazard most years from late November/early December until April or early May — check WSDOT's SR-20 page before any shoulder-season trip.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Service Complex — Ross Lake National Recreation Area (trailhead and Pyramid Lake) transitioning into North Cascades National Park South Unit on the upper peak.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

bivy.name: Scatter Lake basin
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Abernathy Peak and it sits directly under both of its routes. From Twisp the Twisp River road runs about 22 miles, turning off on an unpaved spur immediately after the Scatter Creek crossing; pavement ends several miles before that. The trail is a hard 4.6 miles with roughly 3,800 ft of gain to a lake just under 7,000 ft, so most parties either take the whole day to reach it or accept a long day out and back. From camp the South Ridge is the straightforward line, a steep loose scree slog above the lake, and the North Ridge is reached by working around the basin. The whole face above the lake has a southern aspect and is normally snow free from early July; before that, expect firm snow in the gully and an ice axe is not optional. Late September and the first week of October is the classic window here for the larch, and it is also when the basin is busiest. Bring what you need for a cold dry camp: this is east-side country, the nights are colder than the drive up suggests, and there is no shelter of any kind.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and Scatter Creek is beside the trail for most of the climb. This is one of the more reliable water situations in the zone.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit is needed to hike or camp on the Forest Service side of this range. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Scatter Creek trailhead. Fill in the trailhead register where one is present. Firewood is scarce and the lakeshore vegetation is fragile, so treat this as a stove-only camp regardless of whether a formal fire ban is posted, and expect an actual east-side fire restriction from midsummer into September in most years.
bivy.capacity: Several established tent sites around the lake, plus a stock camp in the meadow about a mile below it. Small basin, and it fills on larch weekends in late September and early October.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass ($5/day or $30/annual) or an America the Beautiful/Interagency Pass at the trailhead
access.rules: Wilderness regulations; pack out all waste.
access.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required for Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness via this Forest Service trailhead (a permit is only needed for overnight stays inside the North Cascades National Park Complex, which this Twisp River Road approach does not enter)
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest / Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking

access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District; Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness

bivy.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
bivy.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. It is not a casual trip: about 20 miles round trip with close to 6,700 ft of gain, up an old moraine below Gray Peak, onto the Chelan Summit trail, over a pass east of Gray Peak, and down into the basin where the maintained trail ends at Middle Oval. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.
bivy.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
bivy.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
bivy.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.

bivy.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
bivy.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. Access is the Gold Creek side, not the Twisp River: turn off the highway onto the North Fork Gold Creek road, then a signed spur for several miles to the Eagle Lakes trailhead at about 4,760 ft. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
bivy.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
bivy.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

bivy.name: Boiling Lake basin
bivy.notes: The high camp for Star Peak and Courtney Peak, sitting on the west side of the crest under Sawtooth Ridge, and the natural meeting point of the two access systems. From the road it is reached over Horsehead Pass from Upper Eagle Lake in a short day. From the water it is the first high camp on the Chelan Summit trail after the long climb up from the Prince Creek boat landing, which is where most multi-day traverses of this range put their first night on the crest. Both Star and Courtney are scrambles from here and the pair is a reasonable single day. The position is the value: it is high, it is on the crest, and it is on water, which in this dry east-side range is an unusual combination. It is popular and it shows, so camp on existing ground rather than making new. Season is roughly mid-July to mid-October. There is no shelter and no trees worth the name at the lake, so plan for wind, and for a cold clear night at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The lake and its outlet, reliable through the season. The Chelan Summit trail on either side is long and dry in places, so fill here.
bivy.permit: Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness, Forest Service, so no overnight permit. If you arrive by boat and stay on the trail system you need no permit at all; if you drive, a Northwest Forest Pass covers the parking. Expect fire restrictions from midsummer, and treat the basin as stove only in any case.
bivy.capacity: Established sites at the lake and near the outlet, clearly heavily used. Room for several parties. No facilities.

bivy.name: Prince Creek Campground - boat-in
bivy.notes: The lake-side gateway to Star, Courtney and the southern crest. The boat drops you at roughly 1,100 ft, lake level, and the Chelan Summit trail climbs from there toward Boiling Lake and the Sawtooth crest - a serious first day in heat, on a south-facing slope, with almost no shade. Most parties land in the afternoon, camp here, and start the climb at first light. The other useful boat stop is Moore Point, about ten miles further up-lake and five and a half below Stehekin, a smaller camp with a dock, a picnic shelter, food storage and a toilet, from which the Fish Creek trail climbs to Round Lake and the Oval Lakes country - that is the water-side way to Oval Peak. The Lakeshore trail connecting the two took heavy damage in the storms of December 2025, with debris flows and washouts between Prince Creek and Moore Point, and Moore Point has also been closed at times for post-fire flood risk, so confirm both the camp and the trail are open before committing to an itinerary that depends on walking between them. The lake side is snow-free far earlier than the crest, often from April, which makes it the way in for an early-season trip.
bivy.water: Prince Creek and the lake. From here the Chelan Summit trail climbs thousands of feet with long dry stretches - this is the last easy water for a long time, so leave with full bottles.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, and no permit is needed to hike or camp along this stretch if you have been dropped by boat. The rules change further up the lake: the National Park Service boundary sits between here and Stehekin, and any camp inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area - Flick Creek, Weaver Point and everything nearer the head of the lake - needs a North Cascades backcountry permit, which is itinerary-based, allocated partly by an early-season lottery for the peak months and partly walk-up. Fires are permitted in the established grates here, but open fires are banned outright at several of the Park Service camps up-lake, and a valley-wide ban is common by late summer. The real constraint is the ferry: the up-lake passenger boat must be booked ahead in season, Prince Creek is a request stop rather than a scheduled one and can be skipped in poor conditions, and a missed pickup on the return means a long walk to Stehekin.
bivy.capacity: A developed lakeside camp with tables, fire grates and a toilet. Sizeable, and the standard first or last night for anyone traversing the range from the water.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass required at the trailhead
access.rules: Wilderness regulations: group size limited to 12 people; campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft elevation; store food and pet food bear-resistant (hard-sided container, vehicle, or hung 10 ft clear of the ground); pack out all waste; no bikes or motorized/mechanized equipment.
access.permit: No wilderness permit is required to hike or climb in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness itself (unlike neighboring North Cascades National Park, which does require permits); some trailheads keep a self-issue trail register for visitor-use statistics.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness)
access.passRequired: A Northwest Forest Pass (or an Interagency/America the Beautiful Annual, Day, Senior, Access, or Military Pass) is required to park at the West Fork Buttermilk Trailhead — it appears on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest's official list of day-use fee sites.

bivy.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
bivy.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
bivy.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
bivy.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

access.fees: No fee to climb; a round-trip passenger ferry (Lake Chelan Boat Co. 'Lady of the Lake' or Stehekin Ferry) or floatplane fare is required to reach Stehekin.
access.rules: Glacier Peak Wilderness group-size and camping regulations apply on USFS-managed sections; NPS backcountry regulations (bear canister requirements, designated-site rules) apply within the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area near Stehekin and Weaver Point.
access.permit: No permit is required for the Weaver Point boat-in campground itself (first-come, first-served). For off-trail/cross-country backcountry camping elsewhere on the route, NPS North Cascades now requires a paid backcountry permit — $10/person/night plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee (in effect since a March 2024 fee-structure change), booked via recreation.gov (60% of sites) or obtained walk-up (40% held); contact the park's wilderness office (noca_wilderness@nps.gov, 360-854-7200) or the Golden West Visitor Center in Stehekin (509-699-2080 ext. 14) if open for current conditions.
access.landManager: Chelan Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Glacier Peak Wilderness) for the upper mountain; Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, National Park Service (North Cascades NP Complex) for the Stehekin/Weaver Point trailhead corridor.
access.passRequired: None at the Stehekin-area trailheads (NPS land, no entrance fee or Northwest Forest Pass required); a Northwest Forest Pass may be needed only if accessing via a separate front-country Wenatchee NF trailhead.

bivy.name: Libby Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.
bivy.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass ($30/yr) or a $5 day-use pass is required at developed Methow Valley Ranger District recreation sites elsewhere in the forest, but not at this trailhead.
access.rules: Standard Wilderness regulations apply: groups limited to 12 people / 18 head of stock, no mechanized or motorized equipment, campfires prohibited above 5,000 ft elevation, Leave No Trace practices expected.
access.permit: No wilderness permit required to enter the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness.
access.closures: This drainage burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire; road and trail access can be affected by wildfire closures in dry summers — check current Methow Valley Ranger District alerts before driving in.

access.passRequired: No fee/pass required at the Libby Lake Trailhead itself (undeveloped, no fee station or facilities).

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency (America the Beautiful), or a Recreation.gov Digital Day Pass ($5/vehicle/day or $30 annually) is required to park at the Crater Creek Trailhead.
access.permit: No quota or reservation permit is required for this trailhead; standard Wilderness regulations apply once inside the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness boundary.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District / Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass / Interagency Recreation Pass / Digital Day Pass

bivy.name: Oval Lakes basin - West and Middle Oval
bivy.notes: This is the base for Oval Peak and the northern approach to Courtney and Star, all three of which are walk-and-scramble summits off the Chelan Summit trail once you are on the crest. It is not a casual trip: about 20 miles round trip with close to 6,700 ft of gain, up an old moraine below Gray Peak, onto the Chelan Summit trail, over a pass east of Gray Peak, and down into the basin where the maintained trail ends at Middle Oval. Much of that approach burned in the 2018 Crescent Mountain fire and is now open, dusty and hot with standing snags; do it early in the day, expect no shade, and be wary of dead trees in wind. From camp the Oval Peak scramble is short, and a fit party can link Courtney and Star along the crest, though it is a long day. Late July through early October is the practical season, with the larch turning in late September. The same basin can be reached from the lake side by ferry to Moore Point and up Fish Creek, which is the way in for a party that would rather ride a boat than drive the Twisp River road.
bivy.water: The lakes. Reliable all season. The long climb in from Eagle Creek has water low down and then very little, so carry enough for the ascent.
bivy.permit: No overnight permit on the Forest Service side. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Eagle Creek-Oval trailhead. Pack out your own toilet paper even where a pit toilet exists. Fires are a bad idea here even when legal, and are usually banned outright by August.
bivy.capacity: Good sites all around West Oval, with a marked pit toilet, and stock camping with grazing in the basin above Middle Oval. The largest camping capacity in the northern half of the range.

access.fees: $5 per vehicle per day at the Eagle Creek/Oval Trailhead — Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency Recreation Pass, or the Recreation.gov Digital Day Pass are accepted
access.rules: Standard wilderness rules apply: no campfires above 5,000 ft elevation, camp 100+ ft from trails/lakes/streams on already-impacted sites, no motorized or mechanized equipment (including bikes), pack out all waste.
access.permit: Free, self-issued wilderness permit at the trailhead register; no quota or advance reservation required
access.closures: Check Okanogan-Wenatchee NF alerts before a trip for Stage 1 fire restrictions (common in late summer/early fall) and storm-related washouts on FR 4420-080. Nearby drainages (e.g. War Creek Trail) still have blowdown from the 2018 Crescent Mountain Fire, so confirm current Eagle Creek/Oval Creek Trail conditions with the ranger district if it's been a while since the last trip report.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District — Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency Recreation Pass (or pay the $5 day-use fee)

bivy.name: Libby Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for both Raven Ridge routes and the usual base for Hoodoo Peak. Getting here is a different drive from the Twisp River trailheads: from Twisp go east on Highway 20 then south on Highway 153 about nine miles and turn up the Libby Creek road. The trail is a steep 5.3 miles to a lake at roughly 7,600 ft, gaining well over 3,000 ft, and it passes the remains of an old cabin at around four miles that makes a lower alternative camp if you run out of daylight or want water lower down. Raven Ridge rises about 800 ft directly above the lake, and the standard gully-and-ridge line starts from the shore, so this is as close as a camp gets to a route in this range. Hoodoo is a scramble from the same basin, and strong parties climb both in a day from here. The upper basin holds snow into July and the gullies can be firm and unpleasant early; late August through the first half of October is the good window, and the larch here is as good as anywhere in the Sawtooth. It is exposed and treeless at the lake, so a camp below the outlet is more comfortable in wind.
bivy.water: The lake, and Libby Creek along the trail below. The last several hundred feet of the climb are dry.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Libby Lake trailhead. This is a high, sparse, slow-growing basin; carry a stove and do not build a fire, and expect a formal restriction across the lower Methow through the summer.
bivy.capacity: A few small sites below the lake, and rougher ground around it. Room for two or three parties without crowding; the shoreline is fragile and there is little flat ground.

bivy.name: Upper Eagle Lake and Horsehead Pass
bivy.notes: The hub of the southern Sawtooth and the practical base for Switchback Mountain, with Hoodoo and Raven Ridge also within reach along the crest. It is roughly 12.5 miles round trip to Upper Eagle Lake at 7,110 ft with only about 2,350 ft of gain, so it is a gentle carry by the standards of this range. Lower Eagle Lake at about 6,490 ft is the quieter option. Horsehead Pass at roughly 7,540 ft sits just above camp and is the gateway both to Boiling Lake on the far side and to the ridge walking that reaches Switchback. Linking on to Martin Lakes and Cooney Lake makes a longer circuit that takes in more of the southern summits. Season is roughly July into October; the pass holds snow on its north side later than the approach suggests. Be aware that Upper Eagle can be crowded and noisy on a fine weekend - if you want quiet, camp at Lower Eagle or push over the pass.
bivy.water: Both Eagle Lakes, and Eagle Creek is bridged on the way up. Above the lakes, on the pass and along the crest, there is nothing; carry water for any traverse day.
bivy.permit: Forest Service, no overnight permit needed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Eagle Lakes / Crater Creek trailhead. This trail is open to motorcycles and stock as well as walkers, which surprises people. Fires are restricted most summers and firewood at 7,000 ft is not a renewable resource here.
bivy.capacity: Many sites - almost every level spot around Upper Eagle Lake gets used, plus a large horse camp just below it and further sites at Lower Eagle Lake about a mile off the main trail. This is the busiest backcountry camping in the range.

access.permit: Standard Wilderness regulations apply on the upper mountain; no permit required for day use
