From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. THERE IS NO LEGAL HIGHER CAMP. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.
bivy.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a NAMED QUOTA AREA, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. NO SITES ARE HELD AS SAME-DAY WALK-UPS — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
bivy.capacity: A modest number of designated individual sites scattered around the two lakes, plus one designated group site for parties of seven to twelve. The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.

bivy.name: Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
bivy.notes: Reached by branching left across Donahue Creek about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes and climbing further, which puts it around 4,500 ft and some 3,800 ft above the trailhead. It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the WRONG SIDE of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Budget an extra hour and a few hundred feet each way against a Flapjack start. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.
bivy.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.

bivy.name: Camp Pleasant — mid-valley staging on the North Fork Skokomish
bivy.notes: About 6.2 to 6.7 miles up the valley at low elevation, this is the standard first night for a First Divide trip and the obvious place to stop if you started driving late. It serves NONE of the Sawtooth peaks directly — the Flapjack junction is well behind you by here — but it breaks the long walk to Steel, Hopper and the Upper Duckabush into sensible pieces. From Camp Pleasant it is under three miles on to Nine Stream and about six and a half on to Home Sweet Home. Old-growth forest, deep shade, mosquitoes in early summer, and no views to speak of. Usable most of the year when the road is open, which makes it a genuine shoulder-season option in a zone where everything higher is under snow.
bivy.water: Reliable year round — the North Fork Skokomish runs beside the camp
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. This is not a quota camp, so it is generally available at short notice. Bear canisters are required. It sits below 3,500 ft, so campfires are allowed in the established rings using dead and down wood, subject to the seasonal bans that are usually in force from midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A roomy forested riverside camp with several sites, a privy and a bear wire; one of the more comfortable valley camps and it seldom fills

bivy.name: Nine Stream — last low camp before the First Divide climb
bivy.notes: At roughly 9.6 miles and just over 2,000 ft, this is where the valley trail stops being flat. Everything above it climbs hard to First Divide at about 4,690 ft. Its specific value is Mount Hopper: the Hopper way trail leaves the main trail around the 12.4 mile mark, and a party camped at Nine Stream can reach it and be on the summit and back in a long day without carrying over the divide. It is also the last sensible water-and-shelter stop for anyone pushing through to Home Sweet Home in one go from the trailhead, which is a 13-mile day most people do not want with a climbing pack. Buggy in early summer and gloomy, but sheltered, and the low elevation means it stays usable when the divide is still buried.
bivy.water: Reliable — the river and the side stream the camp is named for
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, booked through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp. Bear canisters are required. Below the 3,500 ft line, so fires are permitted in the established rings when no seasonal ban is in effect.
bivy.capacity: Several sites among the trees near the creek confluence, with a privy; usually quiet

bivy.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
bivy.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
bivy.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
bivy.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

bivy.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
bivy.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

bivy.name: Marmot Lake — the Duckabush-side high camp for Steel and Duckabush
bivy.notes: The eastern base for this group of peaks, about 20 miles up the Duckabush River trail from Brinnon and roughly 1.1 miles and 1,700 ft above the Upper Duckabush camp, in a saddle a little over a mile from O'Neil Pass. Mount Steel and Mount Duckabush both stand directly above it, and Steel's less-travelled route from this side leaves the trail a few miles above the Duckabush camp and follows a small creek into an amphitheatre on the west side of the summit, where easy slopes lead to the top. Mount Duckabush is a scramble from the same basin. THE APPROACH IS THE OBSTACLE, NOT THE CLIMBING. Twenty miles with the Big Hump early on, a river ford in the upper valley that is genuinely hazardous outside high summer, and a trail that goes long stretches between clearings — recent accounts describe dozens of downed trees between the trailhead and the upper ford and heavy brush. Most parties take two full days each way. The compensation is that this side stayed open when the Staircase side was closed by fire, so at present it is the only way in to Steel and Duckabush. Hart and LaCrosse Lakes a mile or two above make excellent extensions if you have the days. Season is mid-July through September.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake, and the outlet creek below it
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required and must be reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not one of the named quota camps, but it is remote enough that availability is rarely the problem. Bear canisters are required. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at this elevation.
bivy.capacity: A small subalpine camp with a few sites in and above the lake basin; a large slab above the lake is the traditional spot and the outlook from it is the reason people come

bivy.name: Belview and the Six Ridge camps — for Mount Olson only
bivy.notes: This camp serves Mount Olson and nothing else in the zone. Olson is a scree, boulder and brush scramble at about 5,290 ft on the crest of Six Ridge, reached by a way trail that runs along the ridge top. Six Ridge itself is a primitive, unmaintained route linking the North Fork and South Fork Skokomish over roughly ten miles of crest, with blowdown, overgrown meadow, cairn-to-cairn navigation and more than fifty switchbacks on the eastern climb out of the river. It is a route-finding trip, not a trail walk, and it is the one objective here where getting lost is a realistic outcome. From Staircase you walk the valley trail to the Six Ridge junction, climb the switchbacks to the ridge and camp at Belview, then work west along the crest to the Olson way trail — a long two days in. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead you come in over Sundown Pass and approach from the west, which is the more commonly described way and puts McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake in reach as camps. NOTHING ABOUT THIS SHARES GROUND WITH THE SAWTOOTH OR FIRST DIVIDE PEAKS — do not plan it as an add-on to a Flapjack Lakes trip. Best late July through September once the meadows dry out; earlier the tread is buried and the route is next to impossible to follow, and in winter it should not be attempted.
bivy.water: THE CRUX OF THIS RIDGE. Six Ridge is dry along the crest — there is essentially nothing reliable between the river and the tarns, and the ridge camps depend on small pools that shrink through the summer. Plan the day around the water, not the mileage, and carry a full load up the switchbacks.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site. Not a quota area and effectively never full. Bear canisters are required. The ridge camps sit near or above the 3,500 ft fire line, so assume no fires. THE EASTERN SIX RIDGE TRAIL IS CURRENTLY CLOSED from the east edge of Belview Camp down to its junction with the North Fork Skokomish trail because of the 2025 fire, which for now leaves the Upper South Fork Skokomish trailhead as the only legal way in.
bivy.capacity: A small old camp on the ridge, and further west the tarn camps at McGravey Lakes and Sundown Lake; all tiny, none developed, and you will very likely have them to yourself

access.fees: Olympic NP entrance: $30/vehicle (7-day) or $15/person on foot/bike; $55 park annual pass. Overnight wilderness permit: $8/adult/night plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee, or cover the nightly fee with a $45 annual NP Wilderness Pass.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: No campfires at Flapjack Lakes. Camp only in established sites or on durable/bare ground, at least 200 ft from water sources.
access.permit: Wilderness permit required for any overnight stay, reserved via Recreation.gov / the Olympic NP Wilderness Information Center (360-565-3100). Flapjack Lakes is a limited-entry, quota-managed camping zone — reserve well in advance for summer weekends.
access.closures: As of July 2026, the Staircase developed area and FS-24 access road have reopened following the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire closure. However, the North Fork Skokomish Trail beyond the Rapids Loop and the Flapjack Lakes Trail/campsite — the only practical approach to The Horn — remain closed while NPS crews complete hazard assessments and repair fire-damaged infrastructure (bridges, privies). Confirm current trail status with Olympic National Park before planning any trip.
access.landManager: Olympic National Park (Staircase/South District); the access road corridor runs through Olympic National Forest's Hoodsport Ranger District.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — Olympic National Park (Olympic Wilderness)
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: NPS entrance pass (America the Beautiful) at the Staircase entrance station

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

bivy.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
bivy.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
bivy.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

bivy.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
bivy.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
bivy.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
bivy.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.

bivy.name: West Fork Agnes Creek — the bivy under Agnes Mountain
bivy.notes: This is the working bivy zone for AGNES MOUNTAIN and it needs to be described honestly: THE TRAIL HAS ALL BUT VANISHED. What is marked on maps as the West Fork Agnes Creek trail is now a rough bushwhack up the drainage, last given any real maintenance a decade or more ago, and it leads nowhere except to the base of the mountain. Round trip from High Bridge is around seventeen miles of walking on top of the boat and the shuttle. The recommended line on the peak itself takes the northeast ridge of neighbouring Asa Peak first and then traverses to Agnes's south ridge, with short technical sections up to about 5.6 — so this is a climb rather than a scramble, on a peak that is seldom done precisely because the approach is so poor relative to its modest height. Navigation skill is not optional. Season is roughly July into September; earlier the creek is high and the brush is worse, later the days are too short for the mileage. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved ground and finding its own way up a drainage with no tread, this is the wrong objective.
bivy.water: The West Fork itself for as long as you are beside it, which is most of the way. Above it, snowmelt only and only early in the season. There is no reason to be short of water low down and every reason to carry it once you leave the creek.
bivy.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required for any overnight, and off-trail nights are handled as cross-country camping rather than as a named site — say what ground you intend to use when you arrange it rather than booking a camp that does not exist. Bear canisters are mandatory in cross-country ground where hanging is not possible, and free loaners come with the permit if you collect it in person. Camp on durable ground, gravel or rock rather than vegetation, and pack everything out.
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. Whatever gravel bar, forest bench or open ground you reach, and small parties by necessity.

bivy.name: Company Creek and Hilgard Pass — the lower-valley approach to Flora Mountain
bivy.notes: FLORA MOUNTAIN is the peak in this zone that does not start at High Bridge, and sending a party up the valley for it wastes a day. The Company Creek road leaves the Stehekin road about five and a half miles from the landing — the shuttle will drop you — and the trail from it climbs steeply, fords Company Creek at around five miles, and then follows Hilgard Creek to Hilgard Pass at 6,700 ft. THE FORD IS THE THING TO ASK ABOUT: it is a real crossing and in a high-water year it is the reason parties turn back, so check the level with a ranger before you commit to the day. Flora is one of the hundred highest summits in the state at a little over 8,300 ft and its southwest side is a talus and boulder hop rather than a climb, so once you are in position the summit is not the work. It can also be taken from a camp in the Bird Creek drainage on the Devore Creek side, which is the more commonly described base and is covered elsewhere; the Company Creek line is the one that starts from the lower valley road and it suits a party already camped at Harlequin. The views on the way up over Tupshin and Devore are the best part of the walk. July into early October, and the larch colour late in that window is worth planning around.
bivy.water: Company Creek and then Hilgard Creek for most of the climb, which is generous by the standards of these approaches. The pass itself and the ground above it are dry once the snow has gone, so fill in the basin before going up for the summit.
bivy.permit: The trail leaves the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area about two miles up and enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, so the rules change under your feet. A North Cascades backcountry permit covers the recreation area portion and any park camps; the wilderness above is national forest ground with a free self-issued permit and no quota. Work out which side of the line you intend to sleep on before booking anything. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass considerations apply on the forest side. Store food properly throughout; fires are inappropriate at the pass and restrictions are usual lower down by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed. There is workable ground in the upper Hilgard Creek basin and around the pass, room for a party or two, with nothing developed and no facilities. The lower valley has scattered spots along the trail.

access.fees: No NPS entrance fee; a free wilderness permit is required for overnight camping. The first ~2 miles from High Bridge (inside North Cascades NP) fall under the NPS backcountry-permit process; beyond that, in the Glacier Peak Wilderness (Okanogan-Wenatchee NF), a free self-issue trailhead permit applies.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) inside Glacier Peak Wilderness; larger groups must split with 1-mile separation. Campfires prohibited above 3,500 ft in wilderness.
access.permit: Free NPS backcountry permit (Wilderness Information Center/Golden West Visitor Center) only applies if camping within the first ~2 mi from High Bridge, inside North Cascades NP. For camps beyond that boundary — including the standard high camps used for this climb (Icy-Spruce Creek Pass, Upper Blue Basin, etc.) — a free, self-issue USFS wilderness permit obtained at the trailhead covers the Glacier Peak Wilderness portion; no NPS office visit is required for those.
access.closures: Stehekin-area roads/trails have been affected by Dec 2025 flood damage; North Cascades Lodge at Stehekin is not operating public services in 2026 — check the NPS Stehekin Flood Response Update page for current Agnes Creek Trail/High Bridge shuttle status before planning
access.landManager: Most of the route (beyond the first ~2 miles from High Bridge) and the summit itself lie within the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest's Glacier Peak Wilderness (USFS) — only the initial ~2 miles of the Agnes Creek Trail from High Bridge are within North Cascades National Park Service Complex (Stephen Mather Wilderness) / Lake Chelan National Recreation Area.
access.parking_pass: No trailhead parking — High Bridge has no road access. Park at Fields Point Landing to board the boat: overnight parking there is $9/night or $45/week.
access.passRequired: None — no day-use pass on either the NPS or USFS wilderness portions; only a free wilderness permit is needed.

bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. Bear canisters are mandatory in cross-country ground where hanging is not possible, and free loaners come with the permit if you collect it in person. Camp on durable ground, gravel or rock rather than vegetation, and pack everything out.
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. Whatever gravel bar, forest bench or open ground you reach, and small parties by necessity.

bivy.name: Company Creek and Hilgard Pass — the lower-valley approach to Flora Mountain
bivy.notes: FLORA MOUNTAIN is the peak in this zone that does not start at High Bridge, and sending a party up the valley for it wastes a day. The Company Creek road leaves the Stehekin road about five and a half miles from the landing — the shuttle will drop you — and the trail from it climbs steeply, fords Company Creek at around five miles, and then follows Hilgard Creek to Hilgard Pass at 6,700 ft. THE FORD IS THE THING TO ASK ABOUT: it is a real crossing and in a high-water year it is the reason parties turn back, so check the level with a ranger before you commit to the day. Flora is one of the hundred highest summits in the state at a little over 8,300 ft and its southwest side is a talus and boulder hop rather than a climb, so once you are in position the summit is not the work. It can also be taken from a camp in the Bird Creek drainage on the Devore Creek side, which is the more commonly described base and is covered elsewhere; the Company Creek line is the one that starts from the lower valley road and it suits a party already camped at Harlequin. The views on the way up over Tupshin and Devore are the best part of the walk. July into early October, and the larch colour late in that window is worth planning around.
bivy.water: Company Creek and then Hilgard Creek for most of the climb, which is generous by the standards of these approaches. The pass itself and the ground above it are dry once the snow has gone, so fill in the basin before going up for the summit.
bivy.permit: The trail leaves the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area about two miles up and enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, so the rules change under your feet. A North Cascades backcountry permit covers the recreation area portion and any park camps; the wilderness above is national forest ground with a free self-issued permit and no quota. Work out which side of the line you intend to sleep on before booking anything. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass considerations apply on the forest side. Store food properly throughout; fires are inappropriate at the pass and restrictions are usual lower down by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed. There is workable ground in the upper Hilgard Creek basin and around the pass, room for a party or two, with nothing developed and no facilities. The lower valley has scattered spots along the trail.

access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest

bivy.name: Purple Point and Harlequin — the landing camps, and the boat that decides the trip
bivy.notes: READ THIS BEFORE ANY OTHER SITE IN THE ZONE. Stehekin has no road to it. The only practical way in is the scheduled passenger boat up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, and the timetable, not your fitness, sets the shape of the trip. The slow boat takes roughly four hours each way and the express about two and a half; a typical summer sailing leaves Chelan mid-morning, reaches Stehekin around midday, and turns round after a layover of an hour or ninety minutes. That means a party arriving on the boat has half a day at most before the last sailing out, and a party finishing a climb has to be at the landing on the boat's schedule or spend another night. Book the boat and the permit together and treat the return sailing as a hard deadline. From the landing a valley shuttle runs eleven miles up to High Bridge, four times a day in each direction in season, and it is the second half of the same logistics problem — miss it and you are walking. Purple Point is where you sleep if the boat gets in too late to reach the upper valley, and Harlequin is where you sleep if you are heading for the Company Creek road in the morning. Neither serves a summit directly, and both are essential.
bivy.water: Purple Point has potable water and vault toilets. Harlequin has vault toilets, tables, fire rings and animal-resistant food lockers, with the Stehekin River alongside. Neither is a water problem.
bivy.permit: This is a two-jurisdiction valley and it matters. The landing and the lower road are in the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area; the upper valley and everything you climb from it are North Cascades National Park. A backcountry permit is required year round for every overnight in the park backcountry, and the valley campgrounds require a free permit as well. Permits are issued through the federal recreation booking site, with a lottery in early March, winners assigned booking dates through late March and April, and the general release at seven in the morning Pacific in late April. Roughly sixty percent of permits are reservable and forty percent held for walk-ups. THERE IS NO PERMIT OFFICE IN STEHEKIN — a walk-up permit has to be collected in person elsewhere in the park complex before you get on the boat, which is the trap that ends more trips here than weather. Bear canisters are not required at these particular camps but food must be stored in the lockers or hung; the valley has bears and they know the campgrounds. Purple Point was free for the 2026 season.
bivy.capacity: Purple Point has six walk-in tent sites about ten minutes on foot from the boat dock. Harlequin, four and a half miles up the valley road, has seven walk-in sites with shared parking. Both are first come, first served and both are small enough that a busy summer afternoon fills them.

bivy.name: High Bridge Camp — the shuttle terminus and the base for McGregor Mountain
bivy.notes: The bus stops here and the walking starts here, so almost every trip in this zone passes through it. Its own summit is MCGREGOR MOUNTAIN, whose trail leaves the valley road near the guard station a mile or so from the bridge and is one of the biggest sustained climbs in the state: about 7.7 miles and 6,400 ft of gain to within half a mile of the top, past Coon Lake in the first mile and then switchback after switchback with almost no relief. The last 1,100 ft to the summit is exposed scrambling rather than trail, and an ice axe is wanted while snow is still lying on it. Doing that in a day from High Bridge is a very long outing and most parties camp here the night before rather than trying to fit it around the boat. Water is the specific worry: the lake and Coon Creek are early on and the upper mountain has nothing. High Bridge is also the start of the Agnes Creek trail south and the Pacific Crest corridor, so it is where the Agnes, Needle, Lyall and Dark Peak trips begin as well. Bicycles are allowed on the valley road and some parties ride the fourteen miles up rather than wait for a shuttle.
bivy.water: The Stehekin River and Agnes Creek at the bridge, plus Coon Creek on the trail above. Reliable, and it is worth filling here because the McGregor trail is a long way between sources once it starts switchbacking.
bivy.permit: Free backcountry permit required through the federal recreation booking site, collected in person outside the valley. No fee for the camp itself. Food storage is required; bears work the road end hard. Fires only where rings exist and only when no restriction is in force — Stage restrictions are common on the east side by midsummer.
bivy.capacity: A small road-end camp with a handful of sites, plus Bullion and Dolly Varden further up the valley road at ten and thirteen miles with two sites each. All first come, first served, none reservable.

bivy.name: Fivemile Camp, Agnes Creek
bivy.notes: Five miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail through Agnes Gorge, this is the junction camp and the last comfortable night before things get serious. It is the departure point for AGNES MOUNTAIN — the West Fork Agnes Creek trail leaves here heading west, and it is the start of the standard approach to the 8,115 ft summit, first climbed in 1936 from this same drainage. It is also the first night for parties heading further up Agnes Creek toward DARK PEAK, which is usually described as a three-day trip built off this camp and the ground above it. The camp itself is unremarkable: deep valley forest at 2,200 ft, no views, mosquitoes early in the season, and the creek. What makes it matter is position. Anything you climb from here is thousands of feet above and mostly trackless, so the difference between sleeping at High Bridge and sleeping here is a full extra push tacked onto an already long day.
bivy.water: Reliable — Agnes Creek runs at the camp all season. Fill completely here if you are heading up the West Fork, because there is no camp, no trail and no certainty of anything above.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site or taken as a walk-up collected in person before you reach the valley. Bear canisters are not on the required list for this camp, but food must be hung or stored properly and this is a long-established camp in bear country. No fires above the valley floor rings; check what restriction is running.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp on the creek, a couple of parties at most. It sees Pacific Crest Trail traffic through the summer, so it is busier in late July and August than its remoteness suggests.

bivy.name: Swamp Creek Camp — the base for Needle Peak, Mount Lyall and Lyall Ridge
bivy.notes: About nine miles south of High Bridge on the Pacific Crest Trail and roughly three beyond Fivemile, this is the working base for NEEDLE PEAK, MOUNT LYALL at 7,892 ft and the ridge between them. The unmaintained Swamp Creek trail leaves the corridor here and climbs toward Needle Peak's north ridge; the ground above is class 3 and 4 scrambling with real exposure and a helmet is wanted, and the northeast ridge of DARK PEAK continues over to Lyall, so a party willing to spend the days can link several of these summits off one camp. Budget five days for the full set including the boat at both ends, and something close to forty miles of walking. THE APPROACH IS ALL OF THE DIFFICULTY. These are not hard climbs by North Cascades standards; they are remote, brushy and slow, and the price of admission is the boat, the shuttle, the mileage and a good deal of unpleasant bushwhacking once you leave the corridor. Nothing about this is a weekend. Cedar Camp further up the valley is the alternative if this one is taken; Hemlock Camp above it is unsafe from falling insect-killed timber and should be skipped.
bivy.water: Swamp Creek at the camp, reliable. THIS IS ALSO THE HAUL POINT. There is no water on the ridges above and parties putting a high camp on Lyall Ridge or the north ridge of Needle carry it up from here, which is the single biggest load consideration on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free North Cascades backcountry permit, booked through the federal recreation booking site or collected in person as a walk-up. Bear canisters not specifically required at this camp; store food properly regardless. Fires are not appropriate here and restrictions are usually in force anyway.
bivy.capacity: A small trail camp, one or two parties. Like everything on this corridor it is shared with through-hikers in high summer.

bivy.name: West Fork Agnes Creek — the bivy under Agnes Mountain
bivy.notes: This is the working bivy zone for AGNES MOUNTAIN and it needs to be described honestly: THE TRAIL HAS ALL BUT VANISHED. What is marked on maps as the West Fork Agnes Creek trail is now a rough bushwhack up the drainage, last given any real maintenance a decade or more ago, and it leads nowhere except to the base of the mountain. Round trip from High Bridge is around seventeen miles of walking on top of the boat and the shuttle. The recommended line on the peak itself takes the northeast ridge of neighbouring Asa Peak first and then traverses to Agnes's south ridge, with short technical sections up to about 5.6 — so this is a climb rather than a scramble, on a peak that is seldom done precisely because the approach is so poor relative to its modest height. Navigation skill is not optional. Season is roughly July into September; earlier the creek is high and the brush is worse, later the days are too short for the mileage. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved ground and finding its own way up a drainage with no tread, this is the wrong objective.
bivy.water: The West Fork itself for as long as you are beside it, which is most of the way. Above it, snowmelt only and only early in the season. There is no reason to be short of water low down and every reason to carry it once you leave the creek.
bivy.permit: A North Cascades backcountry permit is required for any overnight, and off-trail nights are handled as cross-country camping rather than as a named site — say what ground you intend to use when you arrange it rather than booking a camp that does not exist. Bear canisters are mandatory in cross-country ground where hanging is not possible, and free loaners come with the permit if you collect it in person. Camp on durable ground, gravel or rock rather than vegetation, and pack everything out.
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. Whatever gravel bar, forest bench or open ground you reach, and small parties by necessity.

access.fees: Lady of the Lake ferry from Chelan (fares vary by boat/season) or floatplane charter to reach Stehekin; Stehekin shuttle bus to High Bridge is about $10/adult, $5/child one-way. No separate climbing fee.
access.rules: Standard NPS wilderness regulations apply in the park/NRA portion (permit and, where applicable, designated-site camping, bear canister recommended); standard Leave No Trace and USFS wilderness group-size limits apply once past the wilderness boundary.
access.permit: An NPS wilderness/backcountry permit is required for any overnight camping within the North Cascades National Park Complex boundary (the lower Agnes Creek Trail corridor) — $10/person/night plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee if booked in advance via recreation.gov, or self-issued at the Stehekin Ranger Station when the Wilderness Information Center is unstaffed. Once across into the Glacier Peak Wilderness (USFS) near Swamp Creek, permits are free, self-issued trailhead registers.
access.closures: Stehekin Valley Road and the village have faced wildfire evacuation closures in recent fire seasons (e.g., the 2024 Pioneer Fire) — check NPS and Chelan County alerts before a trip.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park Complex / Lake Chelan National Recreation Area (NPS) covers the Stehekin–High Bridge–lower Agnes Creek corridor; the route transitions into the Glacier Peak Wilderness, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chelan Ranger District) for the Swamp Creek approach and the peak itself.
access.passRequired: None for day use of the National Forest portion; an NPS wilderness camping permit (see Permit) is required for overnight stays within the Park/NRA portion.

bivy.name: Lake Valhalla
bivy.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
bivy.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

bivy.name: Lichtenwasser Lake
bivy.notes: The direct camp for Lichtenberg Mountain, and quieter by an order of magnitude than Lake Valhalla on the other side of the peak. The fishing path leaves the first switchback on Smithbrook Road and is unsigned; it is a genuine bushwhack for the lower part, picking up a boot track around 4,400 feet on the northeast side of the lake. From the lake the scramble follows the inlet up into a steep boulder garden and gains the saddle on the southeast ridge in about half an hour, with the ridge itself giving the summit without difficulty. Reckon on seven miles and a little over two thousand feet for the round trip from the road. THIS IS A WINTER PEAK AS MUCH AS A SUMMER ONE: the boulder garden above the lake is far more pleasant under snow than bare, and the southeast ridge often melts out while the approach is still covered, but an ice axe is genuinely needed and the bowl below the ridge holds a cornice into early summer. In winter Smithbrook Road is not plowed past the highway, so parties park on US 2 at the road junction and add the road distance to the day.
bivy.water: The lake and its inlet stream. Treat it.
bivy.permit: National forest outside the wilderness boundary, so no wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass for parking on Smithbrook Road. Fires are legal here in most seasons but the district restricts them from midsummer, and the basin is small enough that a stove is the better answer regardless.
bivy.capacity: Rough informal spots for one or two tents in the trees at the outlet end. Nothing built, no toilet, and no reason to expect company.

bivy.name: Smithbrook trailhead and Union Gap
bivy.notes: This is the staging point for Union Peak, and worth having as its own entry because Union Peak is not climbed from any lake. The trail switchbacks about six hundred and fifty feet in a little over a mile from the road to the gap; the scramble leaves it after roughly a third of a mile, bushwhacks northeast to gain the southeast ridge, and follows that to a summit at about 5,700 feet. It is non-technical from summer through autumn and a popular winter objective when the snow simplifies the brush, which is the main reason to know where the road-end sits. Mount McCausland is reached from the same road by staying on the trail through the gap and taking the spur off the Pacific Crest Trail. From the top of Union Peak a party can drop north down meadows about seven hundred feet to the saddle below Jove Peak and add that summit, which is the usual outing. Smithbrook Road is a reasonable gravel road in summer and closed by snow through the winter, when the trailhead is a shoulder pullout on US 2 several miles and a thousand feet lower. This is a place to sleep before a start rather than a place to spend a night for its own sake.
bivy.water: Smith Brook crosses near the trailhead. Nothing at the gap itself — carry water up.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass at the trailhead. Union Gap is inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness, so the free self-issue permit applies from the register at the road. Camp well off the trail and out of the saddle proper if you stop there.
bivy.capacity: A gravel turnaround at the road end taking perhaps a dozen cars, with room to sleep in a vehicle. Union Gap itself is a forested saddle with a little flat ground and no established sites.

bivy.name: Skyline Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for Sky Mountain and Tye Peak, and the single most convenient high camp on this stretch of highway. The path leaves the north lot beside the buildings, and there are two ways up: the switchbacking service road, at roughly five hundred feet of gain per mile, or a steep climbers' track that cuts the switchbacks and saves twenty minutes at the cost of some route-finding the first time. It is about a mile and a half and eleven hundred feet to the lake. From camp, Sky Mountain is the high point of the horseshoe ridge north of the pass and is the peak most parties overlook in favour of the rockier sub-summit on the south arm of the same ridge; Tye Peak lies out along the ridge to the northwest and is best combined with Sky Mountain in one outing, since they share the whole approach. WINTER IS THE SEASON HERE, not summer: there is no trail on Tye Peak and in bare conditions it is a moderate to hard bushwhack with a very steep, mossy, branch-covered descent off the lower end of Skyline Ridge. Deep snowpack buries the brush and boulders and turns both peaks into straightforward outings, typically from December into April or May. The corollary is avalanche terrain on the slopes below the ridge and icy summit rocks that make the true scramble on the south arm dangerous in winter. The lot fills before nine on fine weekends when the ski area is running, and the resort operates a paid parking reservation on peak days for its own lots, so check before driving up.
bivy.water: The lake, which is small and shallow, or melted snow. Treat anything taken from the surface.
bivy.permit: National forest. No pass is required to park in the north lot at Stevens Pass, in summer or winter. No wilderness permit — this is outside the wilderness boundary. Fires are a bad idea in a basin this heavily used and this thinly timbered; the ground here is fragile.
bivy.capacity: A few established spots on the west side of the small lake, and plenty of room for snow camps around it in winter. No toilet, no water system.

bivy.name: The basin between Tye Peak and Spinnaker Peak
bivy.notes: A genuine winter camp rather than a summer one, and the natural base for Spinnaker Peak and its neighbour Martin Peak at the head of the Tye. The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
bivy.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
bivy.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Open snow basin in winter, holding as many parties as care to spread out. In summer it is brush and boulder with very little usable flat ground.

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
bivy.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
bivy.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
bivy.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

access.fees: $5 daily or $30 annual Northwest Forest Pass.
access.rules: Campfires (except self-contained stoves) are prohibited within 1/4 mile of Lake Valhalla per Forest Order 06-17-1995-289; camp at least 100 ft from trails and water; travel above the lake is off-trail cross-country within designated wilderness — practice Leave No Trace.
access.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required at the Smithbrook Trailhead; free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead for entry into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (Henry M. Jackson Wilderness)

A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED at the lake — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

bivy.name: Lichtenwasser Lake

access.fees: The Forest Service states that no fee is required for the Smithbrook Trailhead, but a Northwest Forest Pass is also reported to be expected there. Carrying a Northwest Forest Pass or an America the Beautiful pass costs nothing and removes the ambiguity.

access.closures: FR 6700 is unmaintained and effectively closed by snow through winter and early spring. Campfires are prohibited at Lake Valhalla; dispersed camping is allowed but must be set back from the lakeshore.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District, 600 Sherbourne St, Leavenworth WA 98826 — (509) 548-2550. The summit, Lake Valhalla and the whole approach above the trailhead lie inside the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. (The peak is sometimes mistakenly assigned to the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest; the mountain is east of the crest, in the Okanogan-Wenatchee.)
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful recommended (see fees — the Forest Service lists the site as no-fee, but a pass is also reported to be required).

The approach is from US 2 about two miles east of Stevens Pass, on the old road serving the Yodelin area, then up into the drainage on snowshoes or skis; the round trip to Spinnaker is around eight miles with a top out near 5,600 feet. From the basin the usual line traverses the northeast ridge past a subsidiary point around 5,300 feet, occasionally dropping onto the south side to avoid rock before regaining the crest. Parties combining Spinnaker with Tye Peak use this basin as the link between the two, which is the main argument for camping in it rather than doing either as a day trip. Everything here depends on snow cover — in summer the same ground is a slow thrash through slide alder and the peaks are seldom visited. Avalanche assessment is not optional; these are open, wind-loaded, lee slopes below a ridge crest, and the terrain traps in the drainage are real.
bivy.water: Melted snow in winter. In late summer the basin holds little or nothing reliable — carry what you need.
bivy.permit: National forest, no permit, no quota. Access from the highway east of the pass is across a mix of ownership near the old Yodelin development, so park on public ground and read the signs rather than assuming.
bivy.capacity: Open snow basin in winter, holding as many parties as care to spread out. In summer it is brush and boulder with very little usable flat ground.

bivy.name: Trap Lake
bivy.notes: The closest camp to Slippery Slab Tower and the best base for Thunder Mountain. Two trailheads reach it: Tunnel Creek, which climbs about a mile and a half to Hope Lake on the Pacific Crest Trail and then runs south a couple of miles over meadowy ground before the switchbacks up to Trap Pass; or Surprise Creek at Scenic, which climbs to Surprise Lake and joins the Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Trap Lake sits a little below Trap Pass on the east side. From the pass a faint but obvious climbers' track branches south along the ridge crest, follows it to a boulder field, and works up that to the base of the tower — the whole point of camping here rather than at the Scenic lakes is that it puts a party at the pass within half an hour of leaving the tent. Slippery Slab Tower is a single pitch of pleasant lower fifth class on an arete whose flakes are not to be trusted for protection, so it is a short climb with a long walk attached, and an overnight makes the arithmetic work. Thunder Mountain itself is a scramble from the same ground. The Thunder Mountain Lakes further south are a delicate basin where camping is discouraged; use this lake instead. Season is roughly July to October, with snow on the Trap Pass switchbacks well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake, and the inlet above it. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is required for day and overnight use, taken at the trailhead register from mid-May to the end of October. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Surprise Creek trailhead. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 feet west of the crest, and a stove is the right answer here in any case.
bivy.capacity: Several small informal sites in the trees at the lake, below the pass on the east side of the crest. Quiet, and rarely more than a party or two.

bivy.name: Surprise Lake and Glacier Lake
bivy.notes: The other half of the Thunder Mountain approach, and the one most parties use because the trailhead is simple to find and the walk is pleasant. From US 2 turn south into Scenic, ten miles east of Skykomish, cross the railway tracks and follow gravel a third of a mile to the trailhead at about 2,200 feet. It is four and a half miles to Surprise Lake and a further mile to Glacier Lake, climbing steadily through forest with the creek alongside. From either lake the Pacific Crest Trail runs north to Trap Pass, from where the climbers' track along the ridge reaches Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower. Camping here rather than at Trap Lake adds an hour or more to the summit morning but gives a better camp and a shorter, easier walk in with heavy loads, so it suits a party carrying a rope and rack. Both lakes are subalpine and hold snow into July in a normal year. The lower trail is steep enough in places to be slow with overnight packs, and the railway line at the trailhead is active and noisy at night, which is worth knowing before you pitch near the car.
bivy.water: Both lakes and the creek between them. Treat it.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness self-issue permit at the trailhead, free, required for day and overnight use from mid-May to the end of October. Northwest Forest Pass or the daily fee at the Surprise Creek trailhead. NO CAMPFIRES above 4,000 feet west of the crest, which includes both of these lakes. Camp only at the established sites on the west shores.
bivy.capacity: Established sites along the west shores of both lakes. Surprise is the larger and busier; Glacier, about a mile further and three hundred feet higher, is quieter and holds fewer parties.

access.fees: No trailhead fee - Smithbrook Trailhead is listed by the Forest Service as fee-free (no Northwest Forest Pass required)
access.rules: Standard National Forest/Wilderness etiquette applies near the PCT corridor (Leave No Trace, no mechanized travel within designated wilderness); the trailhead is not recommended for stock trucks or trailers due to limited parking
access.permit: None required for the day scramble; a free self-issue wilderness permit may apply where the route travels through Henry M. Jackson Wilderness along the PCT corridor
access.closures: Smithbrook Road (FR 6700) is not maintained in winter and is typically snowed in from roughly November into May/June; a winter approach adds about 2.8 extra miles of road travel each way from the US 2 pullout
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District (600 Sherbourne St, Leavenworth, WA 98826; (509) 548-2550)
access.passRequired: None

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
bivy.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
bivy.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley

bivy.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
bivy.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.
bivy.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
bivy.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers

bivy.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
bivy.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.
bivy.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
bivy.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites

bivy.name: Goat Pass bivies
bivy.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.
bivy.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
bivy.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
bivy.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Overnight groups inside the permit boundary capped at 8 people, must camp together at one previously-impacted site, max 14 consecutive days, no re-entry same trip, permits non-transferable. Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.
access.permit: Free Self-Issue Day Permit

bivy.name: Lake Stuart
bivy.notes: The north-side staging point, used by parties approaching the Complete North Ridge or the Sherpa Glacier from Mountaineer Creek rather than walking around the peak from Ingalls. Road access is seasonal in a way the Teanaway side is not: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road generally closes from November until sometime in May, which shortens the window from this side considerably. Where the Stuart Zone boundary falls relative to the upper Mountaineer Creek basin and the Stuart Glacier moraine is genuinely unclear — some maps place Stuart's north side outside the permit zones — so a party bivying high in that basin should confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District rather than assume, and carry a permit if in doubt.
bivy.water: The lake and Mountaineer Creek are reliable all season; treat lake water and camp well back from the shore
bivy.permit: Enchantment Permit Area, STUART ZONE, Wenatchee River Ranger District. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through Oct 31, allocated by group through the Recreation.gov advance lottery with a small remainder released otherwise. Outside that window no overnight permit is required, though self-registration at the trailhead is asked for. Day use needs only the free trailhead permit plus a Northwest Forest Pass.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites around the lake, but the real limit is the permit quota — the Stuart Zone releases only a small number of group permits per night

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

bivy.name: Mountaineer Creek basin (beneath the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers)
bivy.notes: The standard planned base camp for the north-side approach, and the last flat, sheltered ground with running water. Getting here means leaving the maintained trail before Stuart Lake, crossing the creek and following it cross-country for roughly two miles, then climbing a steep loose talus slope — the crossing runs high and fast in early season. From camp it is another four to five hours to the base of the ridge. Overnight camping on this side may fall inside the quota'd permit area for the range; check which zone your intended site is in before committing to sleeping here.
bivy.water: The south fork of Mountaineer Creek runs through the basin, plus snowmelt; reliable through the season
bivy.capacity: Several established gravel and heather sites in the hanging valley

bivy.name: The 8,200 ft notch on the North Ridge
bivy.notes: The classic place to split the complete ridge, reached by the snow-filled gully (usually climbed on 4th-class rock at its edge) above the Stuart Glacier. This is a planned bivy, not an emergency ledge, but only two spots are actually comfortable and a party of three or more will be spread out. Wind-scoured and fully exposed, with no water above it, so the summit day starts with everything you carried.
bivy.water: None reliable — seasonal snow patches only, and nothing at all once they melt out
bivy.capacity: Two genuinely good bivy spots, plus a number of mediocre ones nearby

bivy.name: Goat Pass
bivy.notes: The camp for the southern approach over Longs Pass and up Ingalls Creek — a longer, higher-gain walk in, but it sets up a much shorter car-to-car loop because the Cascadian Couloir descent drops back the same way. A planned camp with plenty of flat ground, though water becomes a carry once the snow patches are gone.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns early to mid season; Ingalls Creek is the reliable source, below the pass
bivy.capacity: Numerous good bivy sites on the pass

access.land_manager: U.S. Forest Service
